ready.q: A is (32, 10) and B is (10, 4). What is the shape of A @ B, and why?
ready.a: (32, 4). For A @ B the inner sizes must match (10 and 10), and they disappear: each of the 32 rows of A is dotted with each of the 4 columns of B, giving one number per (row, column) pair.

ready.q: What happens when you add a (3, 1) array to a (1, 4) array? Draw it.
ready.a: Broadcasting. Lined up from the right, 1 fits 4 and 3 fits 1, so the result is (3, 4): the column is stretched across 4 columns, the row is stretched down 3 rows, and they are added cell by cell, result[i, j] = a[i, 0] + b[0, j]. Draw a 3 × 4 grid with the column values down the left edge and the row values along the top; each cell is its row's value plus its column's value.

ready.q: Why is softmax usually computed as exp(x − max(x))?
ready.a: Because exp of a large number overflows: exp(1000) is inf, and inf / inf is nan. Subtracting the largest value makes the biggest exponent exp(0) = 1, so nothing can overflow, and the answer is unchanged, because the same factor exp(−max) appears on the top and the bottom and cancels.

topics.name: Meet machine learning: the big picture
topics.definition: Machine learning is getting a computer to learn a pattern from examples, instead of a person writing the rules by hand.
topics.problem: Some rules are too hard to write down. Try writing exact rules for "is this email spam?" or "what is this house worth?": there are too many cases and exceptions. But examples are easy to collect: thousands of emails already marked as spam or not, thousands of houses with their sale prices. Machine learning turns those examples into a working rule.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR D[("Examples
features + labels")] --> M["Model
(weights)"] M --> P["Prediction"] P --> L{"Loss:
how wrong?"} D -.->|"right answers"| L L --> O["Optimiser:
adjust weights a little"] O -->|"repeat many times"| M M ==>|"when the loss is low"| T["Test on new data"] ==> DEP["Deploy"]
diagram.caption: The loop in the middle is training: predict, measure the loss, adjust the weights, repeat. Only when it's good on new data does the model go live.

note.idea: Machine learning means learning a pattern from examples instead of writing the rules by hand. You give a model inputs (features) and the right answers (labels). The model makes a guess, a loss function measures how wrong it is, and an optimiser nudges the model's numbers (its weights) to make the loss smaller. Repeat that many times and the model learns. Then you test it on data it has never seen, and if it's good, you deploy it.
note.analogy: Learning to throw darts. You throw (a prediction), see how far you landed from the bullseye (the loss), adjust your arm a little (an optimiser update), and throw again. After hundreds of throws, you're accurate.
note.breaks: A person can feel why a throw missed. A model only gets one number, the loss; the gradient then tells it which way to adjust every weight at once — sometimes millions of them.
note.example: Predicting house prices. The feature is the size, the label is the price, the model is ŷ = w·size + b, the loss is the squared error, and gradient descent adjusts w and b. The code below learns that each square metre adds about £3,000.
note.code:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([50., 80., 120.])        # feature: size in m²
y = np.array([150., 240., 360.])      # label: price in £1,000s
w, b, lr = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0001

for step in range(1000):
    pred = w * X + b                   # 1. predict
    loss = np.mean((pred - y) ** 2)    # 2. measure how wrong
    grad_w = np.mean(2 * (pred - y) * X)
    grad_b = np.mean(2 * (pred - y))
    w, b = w - lr * grad_w, b - lr * grad_b   # 3. adjust, then repeat

print(round(w, 2))                     # about 3.0: £3,000 per m²

howItWorks: Collect examples. Each example has features (the inputs; here, the size in m²) and a label (the right answer; here, the price).
Choose a model: a formula with adjustable numbers called weights. Here it is ŷ = w·size + b, a straight line. w and b start at 0, so the model knows nothing yet.
Predict: run every example through the model. With w = 0, it predicts £0 for every house.
Measure the loss: one number that says how wrong the predictions are. Mean squared error squares each error and takes the average. At the start it is 69,900.

Adjust: the gradient of the loss says which way to move each weight to make the loss smaller. The optimiser moves each weight a small step that way, and the learning rate sets the size of the step. After one step, w = 4.66.
Repeat predict → loss → adjust. w swings 4.66, 2.08, 3.51, 2.72… and each swing is smaller. After 1,000 loops w ≈ 3.0 and the loss is almost 0: each m² adds about £3,000.
Test the model on data it never saw while training. Only if it does well there do you trust it and deploy it, so it can make predictions on new data in the real world.
keyPoints: Feature: an input the model uses (size). Label: the right answer it learns to predict (price). One example is one row of both.
Weights (also called parameters) are the numbers the model learns. Training means finding good weights.
The loss is a single number for "how wrong". Training is nothing more than making that number smaller.
Gradient descent: work out which way makes the loss smaller (the gradient), take a small step that way, and repeat.
The learning rate is the step size. Too small and training is very slow; too big and the loss explodes.
Always judge a model on data it was not trained on. Doing well on its own training data proves very little.
Regression predicts a number (a price). Classification predicts a category (spam or not spam).
This is supervised learning: every example has a label. Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels, such as grouping similar customers.
mistakes: Thinking the model "understands" houses. It only found the numbers that make the loss small on these examples.
Testing on the training data. A model can memorise its examples and still fail on new ones.
Believing that more training always helps. After a point the model starts fitting noise; Phase 2 calls this overfitting.
Mixing up the model and training. The model is the formula with weights; training is the loop that sets the weights.

followUps.q: What is the difference between a feature and a label?
followUps.a: A feature is an input the model sees, such as house size. The label is the right answer it should predict, such as the price. When the model is used for real, you only have the features.

followUps.q: What does the loss tell you, and what does training do with it?
followUps.a: The loss is one number for how wrong the model is on the examples. Training changes the weights again and again to make that number smaller.

followUps.q: Why test on data the model has never seen?
followUps.a: Because the goal is to work on new cases. A model can memorise its training examples and get a low loss on them, yet do badly on anything new.

followUps.q: With a learning rate 10 times bigger, the loss went from 69,900 to 14.8 million in one step. Why?
followUps.a: The step was so big that it jumped right past the best weight and landed further away on the other side. Every step overshoots by more, so the loss explodes instead of shrinking.

followUps.q: Is predicting tomorrow's temperature regression or classification?
followUps.a: Regression, because the answer is a number. "Will it rain tomorrow, yes or no?" would be classification.

practice.explain: Explain the learning loop — predict, measure the loss, adjust, repeat — with the dart-throwing picture.
practice.derive: For the model ŷ = w·x + b and the loss (ŷ − y)², write the gradients with respect to w and b on paper.
practice.build: Run the training loop above. Print the loss every 100 steps and plot it with Matplotlib.
practice.break: Make the learning rate 10 times bigger and run it again. What happens to the loss, and why?

derive.answer:
Call the error e = ŷ − y, so the loss is L = e². Use the chain rule: first how L changes with e, then how e changes with each weight.

dL/de = 2e.
Since ŷ = w·x + b, a small change in w changes e by x, and a small change in b changes e by 1.

So:
∂L/∂w = 2(ŷ − y) · x
∂L/∂b = 2(ŷ − y)

For many examples, the loss is the mean, so the gradients are means too: ∂L/∂w = mean(2(ŷ − y)·x) and ∂L/∂b = mean(2(ŷ − y)). These are exactly grad_w and grad_b in the lesson's code.

Read it in words: if the prediction is too high (ŷ − y > 0), both gradients are positive, so gradient descent makes w and b smaller. The x in ∂L/∂w means big houses push w harder than small ones.

build.answer:
Keep a list, append the loss every step, print every 100 steps, then plot the list. The loss falls very fast at first and then flattens: a healthy curve.

The numbers fall from 69,900 at step 0 to almost 0 by step 100, because this data fits a straight line exactly. The loss falls so far that a log y-axis is the only way to see the end of training.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

X = np.array([50., 80., 120.])
y = np.array([150., 240., 360.])
w, b, lr = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0001
losses = []

for step in range(1000):
    pred = w * X + b
    loss = np.mean((pred - y) ** 2)
    losses.append(loss)
    if step % 100 == 0:
        print(step, round(loss, 4))
    grad_w = np.mean(2 * (pred - y) * X)
    grad_b = np.mean(2 * (pred - y))
    w, b = w - lr * grad_w, b - lr * grad_b

plt.plot(losses)
plt.yscale("log")          # the loss falls by many powers of 10
plt.xlabel("step")
plt.ylabel("loss")
plt.title("Training loss")
plt.show()
# 0 69900.0
# 100 0.0001
# 200 0.0001  ... flat from here: w ≈ 3.0

break.answer:
With lr = 0.001 the loss explodes instead of shrinking: 69,900 at step 0, about 14.8 million after one step, and it keeps growing until it becomes inf, then nan.

Why: the step size is the learning rate times the gradient. Here the step is so big that w jumps right over the best value (3.0) and lands further away on the other side: 0 → 46.6 → −630.7 → 9,214 … Each jump overshoots by more than the last, so the error grows every step.

The fix is a smaller learning rate, or scaling the feature (sizes like 120 make the gradients big). The lesson: a loss that rises or turns into nan very often means the learning rate is too high.
break.code:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([50., 80., 120.])
y = np.array([150., 240., 360.])
w, b, lr = 0.0, 0.0, 0.001          # 10 times bigger

for step in range(4):
    pred = w * X + b
    print(step, round(np.mean((pred - y) ** 2)), round(w, 1))
    grad_w = np.mean(2 * (pred - y) * X)
    grad_b = np.mean(2 * (pred - y))
    w, b = w - lr * grad_w, b - lr * grad_b
# 0 69900 0.0
# 1 14767756 46.6
# 2 3119980329 -630.7
# 3 659157497506 9214.4

explain.answer:
Training a model is like learning to throw darts. You throw (the model makes a prediction), you look at how far the dart landed from the bullseye (the loss: one number for how wrong it was), and you adjust your arm a little in the direction that would have helped (the optimiser changes the weights, using the gradient). Then you throw again. Each throw gets a bit closer, and after hundreds of throws you hit the middle.

The size of each arm adjustment is the learning rate: too small and you need forever, too big and you over-correct and miss by more each time. And you only trust your aim once you can hit a board you've never practised on: that's testing on new data.

topics.name: NumPy arrays, shapes and indexing
topics.definition: A NumPy array is a grid of numbers, all of the same type, with a shape that says how long it is in each direction.
topics.problem: ML is arithmetic on huge piles of numbers: a dataset is a table, an image is a grid of pixels, and a batch of images is a stack of grids. Python lists are slow for this and have no idea of rows and columns. NumPy arrays keep the numbers packed together in memory, run maths on all of them at once in fast compiled code, and let you pick out any row, column or block with one short expression.

diagram.caption: A = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4): 3 rows and 4 columns. A[1, 2] means row 1, column 2 (counting from 0).

note.idea: An array is a grid of numbers of the same type. Its shape tells you how many numbers there are along each direction. Shape (3, 4) means 3 rows and 4 columns.
note.analogy: A spreadsheet. The shape is the number of rows and columns. Indexing means picking one cell, a whole row or a whole column.
note.breaks: A spreadsheet has only two directions. An array can have three or more, like a stack of spreadsheets. A batch of colour images has shape (batch, height, width, 3).
note.example: With A = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4): A[1, 2] is 6, A[:, 0] is the first column [0, 4, 8], A[1] is the row [4, 5, 6, 7], A[A > 6] is [7, 8, 9, 10, 11], and A.sum(axis=0) adds down each column to give [12, 15, 18, 21].
note.code:
A = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
A.shape      # (3, 4)
A[1, 2]      # 6   (row 1, column 2)
A[:, 0]      # array([0, 4, 8])   the first column

howItWorks: np.arange(12) makes the numbers 0 to 11 as a one-dimensional (1-D) array. Its shape is (12,): one direction, 12 long. The trailing comma just means "a tuple with one entry".
reshape(3, 4) shows the same 12 numbers as 3 rows of 4. The total has to stay the same: 3 × 4 = 12. A.ndim is 2 (the number of directions, called axes) and A.size is 12.
Index with one number per axis, counting from 0: A[1, 2] is row 1, column 2, which is 6. Negative numbers count from the end, so A[-1, -1] is 11.
Slice with start:stop, where the stop is not included: A[0, 1:3] is [1, 2]. A colon on its own means "all of this axis", so A[:, 0] is the whole first column, [0, 4, 8].
Leave out the later indexes and you get whole rows: A[1] is [4, 5, 6, 7].
Keep only the values that pass a test with a boolean mask. A > 6 is a grid of True and False the same shape as A, and A[A > 6] is [7, 8, 9, 10, 11].
Slices are views: B = A[0] shares memory with A, so changing B changes A as well. Call .copy() when you need a separate array. Masks always make a copy.
keyPoints: shape is a tuple: (12,) is 1-D, (3, 4) is 2-D. The number of entries in the shape is ndim, the number of axes.
Axis 0 runs down the rows; axis 1 runs across the columns. A.sum(axis=0) adds down each column and has shape (4,).
Indexing counts from 0, and a slice leaves out its stop value: 1:3 means positions 1 and 2.
Basic slices return views that share memory. Boolean masks and lists of indexes return copies.
Every value has the same dtype, such as float64 or int64. Put one decimal into a list of whole numbers and the whole array becomes float64.
Shapes to recognise in ML: a table of data is (n_samples, n_features); a batch of colour images is (batch, height, width, 3).
mistakes: Confusing (3,) with (3, 1) or (1, 3). They hold the same three numbers but behave differently in maths and broadcasting.
Off-by-one slices: A[0:2] gives two rows, not three.
Changing a slice and being surprised that the original changed too. Slices are views.
Looping over array elements in Python. One array operation is often 10 to 100 times faster.

followUps.q: A has shape (3, 4). What are A.ndim and A.size?
followUps.a: 2 and 12: two axes (rows and columns), and 3 × 4 = 12 numbers in total.

followUps.q: What does A[:, 1] return for A = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)?
followUps.a: Column 1 of every row: [1, 5, 9], with shape (3,).

followUps.q: What is the shape of A.sum(axis=0), and why?
followUps.a: (4,). Summing along axis 0 collapses the rows, leaving one total for each of the 4 columns.

followUps.q: B = A[0]; B[0] = 99. Does A change?
followUps.a: Yes. A basic slice is a view of the same memory, so A[0, 0] becomes 99 too. Use A[0].copy() to avoid this.

practice.explain: Explain the difference between shapes (3,), (3, 1) and (1, 3) to a friend, with a drawing.
practice.derive: Without running code: for A = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4), write down A.shape, A[1].shape, A[:, 0].shape and A[1, 2, 3]. Then check.
practice.build: Make a (5, 4) array of random numbers. Select the last row, the first two columns, every value above 0.5 (with a boolean mask), and the diagonal of its top-left 4 × 4 block.
practice.break: Try reshaping a 24-element array to (5, 5) and read the error. Then change a slice B = A[0] and check whether A changed too. Find out what a 'view' is.

derive.answer:
A = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4) is 2 blocks, each with 3 rows of 4 numbers.

A.shape → (2, 3, 4)
A[1].shape → (3, 4). One index picks block 1, and a whole 3 × 4 block is left.
A[:, 0].shape → (2, 4). Every block, row 0 of each: 2 rows of 4.
A[1, 2, 3] → 23. Block 1 starts at 12; row 2 adds 2 × 4 = 8; column 3 adds 3. So 12 + 8 + 3 = 23. It is the very last number, which makes sense: every index is the last one on its axis.

build.answer:
Use a fixed seed so the numbers are the same each run. Each selection is one short expression:

• last row: X[-1] (shape (4,))
• first two columns: X[:, :2] (shape (5, 2))
• every value above 0.5: X[X > 0.5] (a 1-D array; its length depends on the data)
• diagonal of the top-left 4 × 4: np.diag(X[:4, :4]), or X[np.arange(4), np.arange(4)]

Check the shapes, not just the numbers: shape mistakes are the most common bug.
build.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.random((5, 4))            # values between 0 and 1

last_row = X[-1]                  # (4,)
first_two = X[:, :2]              # (5, 2)
big = X[X > 0.5]                  # 1-D: only the values that pass
diag = np.diag(X[:4, :4])         # (4,)

print(last_row.shape, first_two.shape, big.shape, diag.shape)
# (4,) (5, 2) (12,) (4,)
assert np.allclose(diag, [X[i, i] for i in range(4)])

break.answer:
The reshape fails with: "cannot reshape array of size 24 into shape (5,5)". A reshape only rearranges the numbers you already have, and 5 × 5 = 25 is not 24.

The slice B = A[0] is a view: a new window onto the same memory, not a copy. So B[0] = 99 also changes A[0, 0]. np.shares_memory(A, B) is True, and B.base is A.

Why NumPy does this: copying is slow and uses memory, so basic slices share. When you need an independent array, write B = A[0].copy(). Boolean masks and lists of indexes always make copies.
break.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(24)
try:
    a.reshape(5, 5)
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)        # cannot reshape array of size 24 into shape (5,5)

A = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
B = A[0]
B[0] = 99
print(A[0, 0], np.shares_memory(A, B))   # 99 True

C = A[1].copy()
C[0] = -1
print(A[1, 0])                            # 4: the copy didn't touch A

explain.answer:
All three hold three numbers. The difference is how many directions (axes) they have.

(3,) is a plain list: one axis, no idea of rows or columns.
(3, 1) is a column: 3 rows, 1 column.
(1, 3) is a row: 1 row, 3 columns.

Why it matters: in maths they behave differently. A column plus a row broadcasts to a 3 × 3 grid, and (3,) acts like a row, so (3,) + (3, 1) silently gives a (3, 3) result instead of 3 numbers.
explain.code:
(3,)       [ a  b  c ]          one axis
(3, 1)     [ a ]                3 rows, 1 column
           [ b ]
           [ c ]
(1, 3)     [[ a  b  c ]]        1 row, 3 columns

topics.name: Broadcasting and vectorisation
topics.definition: Vectorisation means doing maths on whole arrays in one operation; broadcasting is NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes by stretching any direction of size 1.
topics.problem: Python loops are slow, because the interpreter handles one number at a time. ML needs the same operation on millions of numbers, such as adding a bias to every row of a batch. Vectorised NumPy runs the whole operation in compiled code instead, and broadcasting saves you from building big copies by hand just to make shapes match.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["scores, shape (3, 1)
70 / 80 / 90"] --> S1["stretched across
to (3, 3)"] B["bonus, shape (1, 3)
0 · 5 · 10"] --> S2["stretched down
to (3, 3)"] S1 --> R["add element by element
result shape (3, 3)"] S2 --> R
diagram.caption: Broadcasting stretches each direction of size 1 to match the other array, then adds number by number — with no Python loop.

note.idea: Vectorisation means one operation works on a whole array at once, instead of a Python loop. Broadcasting lets arrays with different shapes work together, by stretching dimensions of size 1.
note.analogy: A teacher says once: 'everyone add 5 to your score'. She does not walk to each student.
note.breaks: A teacher can talk to any group. Broadcasting only works when the shapes match from the right, or one of them is 1. Otherwise you get an error, or worse, a silent wrong result.
note.example: scores has shape (3, 1) and bonus has shape (1, 3). Compared from the right, 1 fits 3 and 3 fits 1, so both stretch to (3, 3) and every score gets every bonus. In a quick timing test, doubling a million numbers with x * 2 + 1 was about 77 times faster than a Python loop doing the same.

howItWorks: Write the two shapes one above the other, lined up on the right: (3, 1) and (1, 3).
Compare each pair of sizes, starting from the right. A pair fits if the sizes are equal or one of them is 1. Here 1 fits 3, and 3 fits 1.
If one array has fewer axes, its shape is padded with 1s on the left: (3,) is treated as (1, 3). That is why a 1-D array acts like a row.
Each size-1 direction is stretched to match the other array. scores is stretched across to 3 columns and bonus is stretched down to 3 rows. Nothing is really copied in memory.
The operation then runs cell by cell: result[i, j] = scores[i, 0] + bonus[0, j]. The result takes the larger size in each position, so it is (3, 3).
If any pair is unequal and neither is 1, such as (3,) and (4,), NumPy stops with "operands could not be broadcast together".
keyPoints: The rule: line the shapes up from the right; each pair must be equal or contain a 1.
Missing leading axes count as 1, so (3,) behaves like (1, 3).
Vectorised code is usually 10 to 100 times faster than a Python loop, and shorter.
x[:, None] (or x.reshape(-1, 1)) turns a shape (n,) array into a column (n, 1); x[None, :] turns it into a row (1, n).
Everyday ML uses: X - X.mean(axis=0) subtracts each feature's mean from every row; adding a bias to every row of a batch; all pairwise distances in one line.
keepdims=True keeps the summed axis with size 1, so the result broadcasts back: X / X.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) makes every row sum to 1.
mistakes: The silent bug: adding shapes (n,) and (n, 1) gives an (n, n) result and no error. Assert the shapes you expect.
Forgetting keepdims=True. X.sum(axis=1) has shape (n,), which lines up with the columns, not the rows: an error, or for a square X, a silently wrong answer.
Copying data with np.tile or np.repeat just to make shapes match. Broadcasting does this without using the memory.
Writing a Python loop over rows for something one array expression can do.

followUps.q: What shape is (4, 1) + (3,)? Use the rule.
followUps.a: (3,) is padded to (1, 3). From the right: 1 fits 3, and 4 fits 1. The result is (4, 3).

followUps.q: Does (4, 3) + (4,) work?
followUps.a: No. (4,) becomes (1, 4). From the right, 3 and 4 are unequal and neither is 1, so NumPy raises an error. Make it a column first: b[:, None] has shape (4, 1), which fits.

followUps.q: How do you subtract each column's mean from X with shape (100, 5)?
followUps.a: X - X.mean(axis=0). The mean has shape (5,), which acts as (1, 5) and is stretched across all 100 rows.

followUps.q: Why is a vectorised operation faster than a Python loop?
followUps.a: It runs one compiled loop over numbers packed together in memory, instead of the Python interpreter handling each number on its own.

resources.title: From Python to NumPy: the vectorisation chapters

practice.explain: Explain the broadcasting rule in two sentences, using the (3, 1) + (1, 3) example.
practice.derive: Predict the result shape, or 'error', for: (3, 1) + (4,); (2, 3) + (3,); (2, 3) + (2,); (5, 1, 4) + (3, 1). Then check in NumPy.
practice.build: Compute pairwise squared distances between the rows of X (n, d) and Y (m, d) with no loops. Compare with a double loop for small n, then time both for n = m = 1,000.
practice.break: Add a (3,) array to a (3, 1) array by mistake. You get a (3, 3) result and no error. Write a test that would catch this silent bug.

derive.answer:
Line the shapes up from the right, pad the shorter one with 1s on the left, and check each pair: equal, or one of them is 1.

(3, 1) + (4,) → (3, 4). (4,) becomes (1, 4). Right pair: 1 and 4 → 4. Left pair: 3 and 1 → 3.
(2, 3) + (3,) → (2, 3). (3,) becomes (1, 3), and it is added to every row.
(2, 3) + (2,) → error. (2,) becomes (1, 2). Right pair: 3 and 2 are unequal and neither is 1.
(5, 1, 4) + (3, 1) → (5, 3, 4). (3, 1) becomes (1, 3, 1). Pairs from the right: 4 and 1 → 4; 1 and 3 → 3; 5 and 1 → 5.

build.answer:
Expand the square: ‖x − y‖² = ‖x‖² + ‖y‖² − 2·x·y. Then all n × m distances come from one matrix product:

D = (X²).sum(axis=1)[:, None] + (Y²).sum(axis=1)[None, :] − 2·X @ Y.T

The first term is a column (n, 1), the second a row (1, m), and X @ Y.T is (n, m), so broadcasting gives the full (n, m) table.

Check it against a slow double loop on small inputs with np.allclose. Then time both at n = m = 1,000: the vectorised version takes a few milliseconds and the loop most of a second: over 100 times faster on a laptop. Rounding can make a distance that should be 0 come out as a tiny negative number, so clip it with np.maximum(D, 0).
build.code:
import time
import numpy as np

def pairwise_sq(X, Y):
    D = (X**2).sum(axis=1)[:, None] + (Y**2).sum(axis=1)[None, :] - 2 * X @ Y.T
    return np.maximum(D, 0)          # rounding can give tiny negatives

def pairwise_loop(X, Y):
    D = np.zeros((len(X), len(Y)))
    for i in range(len(X)):
        for j in range(len(Y)):
            D[i, j] = ((X[i] - Y[j]) ** 2).sum()
    return D

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xs, Ys = rng.normal(size=(5, 3)), rng.normal(size=(4, 3))
assert np.allclose(pairwise_sq(Xs, Ys), pairwise_loop(Xs, Ys))

X, Y = rng.normal(size=(1000, 3)), rng.normal(size=(1000, 3))
t = time.perf_counter(); pairwise_sq(X, Y); fast = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); pairwise_loop(X, Y); slow = time.perf_counter() - t
print(f"vectorised {fast*1000:.1f} ms, loop {slow:.1f} s, {slow/fast:.0f}x faster")

break.answer:
a has shape (3,) and b has shape (3, 1). (3,) acts like a row, b is a column, so a + b broadcasts to (3, 3): nine numbers instead of three, and no error.

The test that catches it checks the shape of the result, not just that it runs. Assert the shape you expect inside the function, and test it:

• assert out.shape == a.shape in the function itself, so the bug fails loudly the moment it happens;
• a pytest test that feeds a column by mistake and expects the error.

The fix in the caller is to make the shapes match on purpose: b.ravel() or b[:, 0] turns (3, 1) into (3,).
break.code:
import numpy as np
import pytest

def add_bias(x, bias):
    out = x + bias
    assert out.shape == x.shape, f"shape changed: {x.shape} -> {out.shape}"
    return out

def test_add_bias_keeps_shape():
    x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
    assert add_bias(x, np.ones(3)).shape == (3,)

def test_column_bias_is_caught():
    x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
    with pytest.raises(AssertionError):
        add_bias(x, np.ones((3, 1)))      # would silently be (3, 3)

print((np.ones(3) + np.ones((3, 1))).shape)   # (3, 3): the silent bug

explain.answer: Line the two shapes up from the right: each pair of sizes must be equal, or one of them must be 1, and a size of 1 is stretched to match the other. So (3, 1) + (1, 3) works: the column of 3 is stretched across 3 columns and the row of 3 is stretched down 3 rows, giving a (3, 3) grid where every value of the first meets every value of the second, with no copying and no loop.

topics.name: Plotting results with Matplotlib
topics.definition: Matplotlib is the standard Python library for drawing charts; in ML you use it mostly to see loss curves, data and predictions.
topics.problem: Training prints thousands of numbers, and you can't spot a trend by reading them. Is the loss still falling? Did it blow up at step 400? Is the model overfitting? A picture answers those questions in a second. Many training bugs are found by looking at a plot, not by reading the code.

diagram.code:
xychart-beta
  title "A healthy loss curve"
  x-axis "training step" [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
  y-axis "loss" 0 --> 3
  line [2.3, 1.6, 1.15, 0.9, 0.72, 0.6, 0.52, 0.47, 0.44]
diagram.caption: Loss falls fast at first, then flattens. Plotting it is the quickest way to see whether training is working.

note.idea: A plot turns numbers into a picture, so you can see patterns and bugs. In ML, the most important plot is the loss curve.
note.analogy: A car dashboard. You don't read engine data line by line. You glance at the gauges.
note.breaks: A dashboard shows only the present. A loss curve shows the whole history of training, and that history is where the clues are.
note.example: Four shapes to recognise: healthy (a fast fall, then a slow level), overfitting (training loss keeps falling while validation loss turns up), a learning rate that is too high (spiky, then NaN), and flat from the start (nothing is being learned).
note.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot(losses)
plt.xlabel("step"); plt.ylabel("loss")
plt.yscale("log")   # makes small changes visible
plt.show()

howItWorks: Keep a list during training: losses.append(loss) once per step, or once per epoch.
plt.plot(losses) draws a line: the position in the list goes on the x-axis and the value on the y-axis.
Label it: plt.xlabel("step"), plt.ylabel("loss") and a title. An unlabelled plot is easy to misread a week later.
For training and validation curves, call plt.plot twice with label="train" and label="validation", then plt.legend() to add the key.
If the loss spans several powers of 10, call plt.yscale("log") so the late progress is visible.
plt.show() opens the window; plt.savefig("loss.png", dpi=150) saves it for your README or report.
For several charts side by side, fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2) gives you two drawing areas: axes[0].plot(...) and axes[1].plot(...).
keyPoints: The loss curve is the main health check for any training run. Plot it every time.
Healthy: falls fast, then flattens. Spiky or rising: the learning rate is too high, or there is a bug. Flat from the start: nothing is being learned.
Training loss falling while validation loss rises means overfitting. Keep the model from the lowest validation point.
Use a log scale for anything that spans powers of 10: losses, learning rates, dataset sizes.
plt.scatter for data points, plt.hist for how values are spread, plt.imshow for images and matrices.
Always label the axes, and add a legend whenever there is more than one line.
mistakes: Plotting every step of a noisy loss and seeing only noise. Smooth it with a moving average, or plot once per epoch.
Comparing two runs drawn with different y-axis ranges. Fix the range with plt.ylim.
A normal y-axis that hides late improvement. Try a log scale.
Passing a PyTorch tensor straight to Matplotlib. Convert it first with loss.item() or tensor.detach().cpu().numpy().

followUps.q: Your loss curve is flat from the very first step. What might be wrong?
followUps.a: Nothing is being learned. The learning rate may be far too small, the gradients may be zero (for example, a missing loss.backward()), or the weights are never updated.

followUps.q: Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss started rising at epoch 20. What is happening, and what do you do?
followUps.a: Overfitting: the model is memorising the training data. Keep the model from epoch 20 (early stopping), or add regularisation or more data.

followUps.q: When should you use a log y-axis?
followUps.a: When the values span several powers of 10, such as a loss going from 1,000 to 0.01. On a normal axis the small late changes look flat.

followUps.q: How do you put training and validation loss on one chart, with a key?
followUps.a: Call plt.plot twice, each with a label= argument, then call plt.legend().

practice.explain: Explain in two sentences why loss curves are often drawn on a log scale.
practice.derive: Before plotting anything, sketch by hand: a healthy loss curve, an overfitting pair of train and validation curves, and a learning rate that is too high.
practice.build: Plot y = x², its derivative 2x, and 50 noisy samples of y on one figure, with a legend and axis titles. Save it as a PNG.
practice.break: Plot a loss that falls from 1,000 to 0.01, first on a normal y-axis, then on a log y-axis. Which one hides the late progress, and why?

derive.answer:
Loss goes up the side, steps along the bottom. Your three sketches should show these shapes:

1. Healthy: starts high, drops steeply in the first steps, then bends and flattens into a slow, almost level tail. It never climbs back up.

2. Overfitting: two curves. Both fall at first. Then the training curve keeps falling, but the validation curve reaches a lowest point and turns upward, so the gap between them grows. Mark that lowest validation point: that is where you would stop (early stopping).

3. Learning rate too high: jagged and jumpy, swinging up and down instead of falling smoothly. Often it creeps upward and finally shoots off the top (the loss becomes nan).

The code below draws all three, so you can hold your sketch next to it.
derive.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

t = np.arange(100)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
healthy = 0.4 + 2.0 * np.exp(-t / 12)
train = 0.1 + 2.0 * np.exp(-t / 15)
val = 0.6 + 1.6 * np.exp(-t / 12) + 0.0004 * np.maximum(t - 30, 0) ** 2
too_high = 1.5 + 0.03 * t + rng.normal(0, 0.6, 100)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
axes[0].plot(t, healthy); axes[0].set_title("healthy")
axes[1].plot(t, train, label="train"); axes[1].plot(t, val, label="validation")
axes[1].axvline(np.argmin(val), linestyle=":", color="grey")   # stop here
axes[1].legend(); axes[1].set_title("overfitting")
axes[2].plot(t, too_high); axes[2].set_title("learning rate too high")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("step"); ax.set_ylabel("loss")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

build.answer:
One figure, three things on it: the curve y = x², its derivative 2x as a dashed line, and 50 noisy dots scattered around the curve. Check that yours has:

• label= on every plot call, then plt.legend(). That is what makes the key.
• plt.xlabel, plt.ylabel and plt.title.
• plt.savefig(...) called BEFORE plt.show(). Once the figure has been shown and closed it is gone, so saving afterwards gives a blank PNG.
• a fixed random seed, so the noisy dots are the same on every run.

What to notice: the derivative line crosses 0 exactly where the parabola is lowest (x = 0). It is negative on the left, where the curve slopes down, and positive on the right, where it slopes up. That is the idea gradient descent uses: the sign of the derivative says which way is downhill.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 200)              # smooth x values for the two lines
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)           # fixed seed: same noise every run
xs = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 50)              # 50 random x positions
ys = xs**2 + rng.normal(0, 0.8, 50)      # y = x² plus noise

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(x, x**2, label="y = x²")
plt.plot(x, 2 * x, "--", label="derivative: 2x")
plt.scatter(xs, ys, s=15, alpha=0.7, label="50 noisy samples of y")
plt.axhline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.5)
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("value")
plt.title("y = x², its derivative, and noisy samples")
plt.legend()
plt.savefig("parabola.png", dpi=150)     # save BEFORE plt.show()
plt.show()

break.answer:
The normal y-axis hides the late progress.

Why: the axis has to reach 1,000 to fit the start, so every loss below about 10 is squashed into the bottom 1% of the chart. In the run below, the loss drops under 10 at step 80 of 200, and from then on the line looks as if it is lying flat on the floor. Yet it still falls another 1,000 times, from 10 to 0.01. You would wrongly think training had stopped.

The log y-axis gives every tenfold drop the same height: 1,000 → 100 takes as much space as 0.1 → 0.01. So late progress is as easy to see as early progress. This loss shrinks by the same percentage every step, and on a log axis that shows as a straight line.
break.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

steps = np.arange(200)
loss = np.geomspace(1000, 0.01, 200)     # 1,000 → 0.01, the same % each step

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
axes[0].plot(steps, loss)
axes[0].set_title("normal y-axis")
axes[1].plot(steps, loss)
axes[1].set_yscale("log")
axes[1].set_title("log y-axis")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("step")
    ax.set_ylabel("loss")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(np.argmax(loss < 10))              # 80: the first step below 10

explain.answer: A training loss often falls by several powers of ten, say from 1,000 to 0.01, and on a normal axis the big early values squash the small late ones flat, so it looks as if training stopped. A log scale gives each tenfold drop the same height, so late progress, plateaus and spikes stay visible, and steady exponential decay shows as a straight line.

topics.name: Git and GitHub for your projects
topics.definition: Git saves snapshots of your project, called commits, so you can go back, branch off and merge; GitHub stores those repositories online.
topics.problem: Without version control you end up with files like model_final_v3_REALLY_final.py, and no idea which version gave your best result. One bad edit can break working code with no way back. Git records every change with a message, lets you try ideas safely on a branch, and GitHub backs it all up and shows employers your work.

diagram.code:
gitGraph
  commit id: "start roadmap"
  commit id: "phase 0 notes"
  branch experiment
  checkout experiment
  commit id: "try a new idea"
  checkout main
  commit id: "fix typo"
  merge experiment
  commit id: "phase 0 done"
diagram.caption: Each dot is a commit (a saved snapshot). The experiment branch lets you try an idea safely, then merge it back into main.

note.idea: Git saves snapshots of your project, called commits, so you can go back in time. GitHub stores them online and shows your work to employers.
note.analogy: Save points in a video game. You can try something risky, and reload if it goes wrong.
note.breaks: Game saves are for one player. Branches let you, or a team, try several ideas side by side and then merge the good ones.
note.example: You edit linear_regression.py, stage it with git add, save a snapshot with git commit and a clear message, then git push it to GitHub. To try a new optimiser safely, make a branch, commit there, and merge it into main only if it works.
note.code:
git add linear_regression.py
git commit -m "Add gradient descent for linear regression"
git push

howItWorks: git init turns a folder into a repository (a repo). From now on, Git tracks changes in it.
You edit model.py. git status shows it as modified: the change exists only in your working folder.
git add model.py puts the change in the staging area: the list of changes for your next snapshot.
git commit -m "Add training loop" saves the snapshot, with its message, in your local repository. Each commit gets a unique id (a hash) and points back to the one before.
git switch -c experiment creates a branch: a separate line of commits for a risky idea. main stays untouched.
git switch main, then git merge experiment, brings the idea back. If both lines changed the same lines, Git stops and asks you to fix a merge conflict by hand.
git push sends your commits to GitHub; git pull brings down commits made somewhere else.
keyPoints: Four places: working folder → (git add) → staging area → (git commit) → local repo → (git push) → GitHub.
A commit is a snapshot of the whole project plus a message saying why. Small, focused commits are the easiest to understand and undo.
A branch is only a movable label on a commit, so making one is instant.
git log --oneline shows the history; git diff shows changes you have not staged yet.
A .gitignore file lists what Git must never track: datasets, model checkpoints, .venv, __pycache__ and secrets such as API keys.
GitHub is not Git. Git runs on your computer; GitHub is a website that keeps copies of repos and adds pull requests and issues.
mistakes: Committing large data files or model weights. They stay in the history forever and bloat the repo. Ignore them with .gitignore.
Committing secrets such as API keys or .env files. Deleting them later does not remove them from the history, so change the key.
Messages like "update" or "fix". Say what changed and why.
Doing every experiment directly on main, so one broken idea breaks everything.

followUps.q: What is the difference between git add and git commit?
followUps.a: git add stages a change: it chooses it for the next snapshot. git commit saves everything staged as a snapshot in your local repo.

followUps.q: You committed, but your friend can't see it on GitHub. Why?
followUps.a: Commits stay on your computer until you git push them to GitHub.

followUps.q: What is a merge conflict?
followUps.a: Both branches changed the same lines in different ways, so Git can't choose. You edit the file to keep the right version, then add and commit it.

followUps.q: Why put datasets and checkpoints in .gitignore?
followUps.a: They are large and change often. Git keeps every version forever, so the repo would become huge and slow. Store them somewhere else.

resources.title: Learn Git Branching
resources.recommended: You type real Git commands and watch the branch picture redraw itself. The fastest way to make branches and merges click.

practice.explain: Explain the difference between a commit, a branch and a push.
practice.derive: Write from memory the commands to: start a repo, save a change, create a branch, switch back, and push to GitHub.
practice.build: Create your roadmap repo. Commit each build separately with a clear message. Add a .gitignore for data files and notebook checkpoints.
practice.break: On a branch, change the same line in two different ways and merge. Resolve the merge conflict by hand.

derive.answer:
git init                      # start a repo in this folder
git add model.py              # stage the change (or git add . for everything)
git commit -m "Add model"     # save a snapshot with a message
git switch -c experiment      # create a branch and move to it (older: git checkout -b)
git switch main               # switch back
git remote add origin <url>   # once: connect the repo to GitHub
git push -u origin main       # upload; after the first time, just git push

Check yours has the two-step save: add, then commit. git status at any point shows what is staged and what is not.

build.answer:
1. Make the repo on GitHub (empty, no README), then on your machine: git init, add the remote, and push.
2. One commit per build, with a message that says what changed and why, such as "Add NumPy linear regression with gradient descent". Not "update" or "stuff".
3. Add a .gitignore before your first data file, so nothing big or private is ever committed.

A good starting .gitignore is below. Commit the .gitignore itself. If a data file was already committed, remove it from tracking with git rm --cached <file>; the .gitignore alone won't do it.
build.code:
# data and model files: too big for Git
data/
*.csv
*.npy
*.pt
# notebook and Python clutter
.ipynb_checkpoints/
__pycache__/
.venv/
# secrets: never commit these
.env

break.answer:
Make the conflict: on main, commit a line such as lr = 0.01. Create a branch, change it to lr = 0.1, and commit. Switch back to main, change the same line to lr = 0.001, and commit. Now git merge experiment stops with "CONFLICT (content)".

Git marks the file like the block below. Everything between <<<<<<< and ======= is your side (main); between ======= and >>>>>>> is the branch.

Resolve it by hand: edit the file to the version you really want, delete all three marker lines, then git add the file and git commit to finish the merge. git status tells you which files still have conflicts.

The lesson: Git merges automatically unless two people changed the same lines. Then a human has to decide.

explain.answer: A commit is a saved snapshot of your project with a message, on your own machine; it is a point you can always go back to. A branch is just a name that points at a line of commits, so you can try an idea without touching your main work, and a new commit moves the name forward. A push uploads your commits to the copy on GitHub. Until you push, nobody else can see them, and they are not backed up.

topics.name: Testing numerical code (np.allclose, pytest)
topics.definition: A test is a small program that runs your code on a case where you already know the answer, and fails loudly if the result is wrong; for decimals, it compares with a small tolerance.
topics.problem: ML code fails quietly. A wrong axis, a sign error or a broadcasting slip still runs and still prints a loss. It just learns worse, and you may never notice. Tests catch these bugs the moment you make them, when they are cheap to fix. And because computers round decimals, the tests have to allow tiny differences.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["Your function
softmax(x)"] --> T["Test with a case
you already know"] T --> Q{"np.allclose(result, expected)?"} Q -->|"yes"| P["Test passes ✓"] Q -->|"no"| F["Test fails ✗
bug found early"]
diagram.caption: A test runs your code on a known case and compares with a small tolerance, because decimals are never exact.

note.idea: A test runs your code on a case where you already know the answer. With decimals, compare with a small tolerance, because computers round numbers.
note.analogy: Checking a calculator with 2 + 2 before you trust it with your taxes.
note.breaks: Passing easy tests does not prove the code is right. Also test edge cases: zeros, one sample, very large numbers.
note.example: In Python, 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False, but np.allclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) is True. And softmax of [1000, 1001, 1002] gives NaN unless you subtract the largest value first; after that it gives [0.090, 0.245, 0.665].

howItWorks: Pick cases where you know the answer: softmax of [0, 0] must be [0.5, 0.5], and any softmax output must sum to 1.
Write a function whose name starts with test_, in a file whose name starts with test_, such as test_softmax.py.
Inside, run your code and check the result with assert. For decimals, use np.allclose(result, expected), or np.testing.assert_allclose, which also prints the values that differed.
Run pytest in the terminal. It finds every test, runs them all, and lists any that fail.
Add edge cases: very large inputs such as [1000, 1001, 1002], negative numbers, a batch with shape (batch, classes), a single element.
When you find a bug, first write a test that fails because of it, then fix the code. The test stays, so the bug can never come back unnoticed.
keyPoints: Never compare decimals with ==. Use np.allclose (returns True or False) or np.testing.assert_allclose (fails with a helpful message).
np.allclose checks |a − b| ≤ atol + rtol·|b| for every pair. By default atol = 1e-8 and rtol = 1e-5.
Good tests check properties as well as values: probabilities sum to 1, shapes are right, the order of values is kept.
Compare a fast vectorised version with a slow, obvious loop version on small random inputs.
A gradient check (Phase 1) is a test too: compare your gradient with an estimate from tiny nudges.
Fix the random seed in tests, for example rng = np.random.default_rng(0), so a failure can be repeated.
mistakes: Testing only the easy case. Bugs live in edge cases: zeros, huge values, one sample, empty input.
A tolerance so loose that wrong answers pass.
Writing tests after the code "works", and so only testing what you already know works.
Working out the expected value with the same code you are testing, so the test repeats the bug.

followUps.q: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 return False?
followUps.a: 0.1 and 0.2 can't be stored exactly in binary, so their sum comes out as 0.30000000000000004. == demands exact equality.

followUps.q: What does np.allclose check?
followUps.a: That every pair of values is within a small tolerance: |a − b| ≤ atol + rtol·|b|, with atol = 1e-8 and rtol = 1e-5 by default.

followUps.q: Name three edge cases for a function that returns the mean of an array.
followUps.a: Any three of: an empty array (division by zero), a single element, very large values that could overflow, NaN values in the input, a 2-D input.

followUps.q: You just fixed a bug. What should you do before moving on?
followUps.a: Add a test that fails without the fix, so the bug can't return unnoticed.

resources.title: Floating Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations

practice.explain: Explain why == is dangerous for decimal numbers, and what np.allclose does instead.
practice.derive: Before writing any test, list five edge cases for a softmax function.
practice.build: Write pytest tests for your softmax: it sums to 1, keeps the order of values, handles a (batch, classes) input, and matches a slow loop version.
practice.break: Call your softmax on [1000, 1001, 1002]. Do you get NaN? Fix it, and add a test so the bug can never come back.

derive.answer:
Good edge cases are the inputs most likely to break it. Five:

1. Very large values, such as [1000, 1001, 1002]: exp overflows to inf, and inf / inf gives nan.
2. Very negative values, such as [−1000, −1001]: exp underflows to 0, and 0 / 0 gives nan.
3. All values equal, such as [5, 5, 5]: the answer must be exactly uniform, [1/3, 1/3, 1/3].
4. A single value, [7.0]: the answer must be [1.0].
5. A 2-D batch of shape (batch, classes): each row must sum to 1 on its own, not the whole array.

Also worth adding: a shift test (adding the same number to every input must not change the output) and integer input.

build.answer:
Write a stable softmax that works along the last axis, then one test per property. Each test checks one thing, so a failure tells you exactly what broke. Compare decimals with np.allclose, never ==.

Run with pytest test_softmax.py. All four tests pass.

break.answer:
The naive version, np.exp(x) / np.exp(x).sum(), gives [nan, nan, nan] with an "overflow encountered in exp" warning. exp(1000) is far bigger than the largest float64 (about 1.8 × 10³⁰⁸), so it becomes inf, and inf / inf is nan.

The fix: subtract the largest value first. Softmax doesn't change when you shift every input by the same amount, because the extra factor exp(−c) appears on the top and the bottom and cancels. After the shift, the largest exponent is exp(0) = 1, so nothing can overflow. The answer is [0.090, 0.245, 0.665].

The regression test feeds the exact input that broke it, and checks there is no nan and the right answer comes back.
break.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0])
with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    print(np.exp(x) / np.exp(x).sum())          # [nan nan nan]

def softmax(x):
    e = np.exp(x - x.max())
    return e / e.sum()

print(softmax(x).round(3))                       # [0.09  0.245 0.665]

def test_large_inputs_do_not_overflow():
    p = softmax(np.array([1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0]))
    assert not np.isnan(p).any()
    assert np.allclose(p, softmax(np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0])))

explain.answer:
Computers store decimals in binary, and most decimals, such as 0.1, can't be stored exactly, so tiny rounding errors creep in: 0.1 + 0.2 is really 0.30000000000000004, and 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False. == demands every last digit to match, so a test using it fails on correct code, or passes only by luck.

np.allclose(a, b) instead asks "are these close enough?". For every element it checks |a − b| ≤ atol + rtol·|b|, where by default rtol = 1e-5 (a relative error of 0.001%) and atol = 1e-8 (for values near zero). It returns one True only if every element passes.

builds.text: A numerical gradient checker: compare your hand-derived gradients with finite differences. You will reuse it in Phase 3.
PCA from scratch with eigen-decomposition, then with SVD. Show both give the same answer on a real dataset.
Simulate the central limit theorem and plot it.
Fit a Gaussian with maximum likelihood. Show that the best mean is the sample mean.

ready.q: What does a matrix with rank lower than its size do to space?
ready.a: It squashes space into fewer dimensions. A 3 × 3 matrix of rank 2 flattens all of 3D space onto a plane through the origin; rank 1 flattens it onto a line. Whole directions are sent to zero, so many different inputs land on the same output: the matrix can't be undone (no inverse), and its determinant is 0.

ready.q: Compute the gradient of f(x, y) = x²y + sin(y) by hand.
ready.a: Treat the other variable as a constant each time. ∂f/∂x = 2xy. ∂f/∂y = x² + cos(y). So ∇f = [2xy, x² + cos(y)]. At (1, 0), for example, it is [0, 2].

ready.q: Why does the gradient point in the direction of steepest increase?
ready.a: The slope in any unit direction u is the directional derivative ∇f · u = |∇f| · cos(θ), where θ is the angle between u and the gradient. That is largest when θ = 0, when u points along the gradient, and the steepest slope is then |∇f|. Walking the opposite way, θ = 180°, is the steepest descent, which is what gradient descent uses.

ready.q: Show that minimising mean squared error is the same as maximum likelihood with Gaussian noise.
ready.a: Assume y = f(x) + ε with ε ~ N(0, σ²). One point's likelihood is (1/√(2πσ²)) · exp(−(y − f(x))² / (2σ²)). The log-likelihood of all n points is −(n/2) log(2πσ²) − Σ(y − f(x))² / (2σ²). With σ fixed, the first term is a constant and the second is minus the sum of squared errors over a positive constant, so maximising the likelihood is exactly minimising Σ(y − f(x))², and so the mean squared error.

ready.q: What is the difference between cross-entropy and KL divergence?
ready.a: Cross-entropy H(p, q) is the average cost of describing outcomes from p using a code built for q. KL(p ‖ q) is only the extra cost beyond the best possible, H(p): H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p ‖ q). When p is fixed, as with training labels, H(p) is a constant, so minimising cross-entropy and minimising KL give the same gradients. KL is 0 when q = p; cross-entropy is then H(p).

ready.q: Explain eigenvectors to someone who has never seen a matrix.
ready.a: Imagine a rule that moves every point in a picture, say by stretching it. Most arrows drawn on the picture end up pointing in a new direction. But a few special directions only get longer or shorter, never turned: those are the eigenvectors, and how much they are stretched is the eigenvalue. Like the axis of a spinning globe, which stays put while everything else moves.

topics.name: Vectors, span and basis
topics.definition: A vector is a list of numbers you can draw as an arrow; the span of some vectors is every point you can reach by scaling and adding them, and a basis is a smallest set whose span is the whole space.
topics.problem: Every piece of data in ML becomes a vector: a house is [size, rooms, age], a word is a list of 768 numbers, an image is a long list of pixel values. To reason about data you need to know what you can build from a few vectors, and whether a feature carries new information or just repeats what you already have.
howItWorks: A vector [3, 2] means "3 steps along x, then 2 steps along y". Drawn from the origin it is an arrow; written down it is just two numbers.
Scaling multiplies every entry: 3·[1, 0] = [3, 0]. A negative number flips the arrow round.
Adding goes tip to tail, entry by entry: [3, 0] + [0, 2] = [3, 2]. A sum of scaled vectors is called a linear combination.
The span of some vectors is every linear combination of them. [1, 0] and [0, 1] can reach any point in 2-D, so their span is the whole plane.
Vectors are linearly independent if none of them can be made from the others. [1, 2] and [2, 4] are not: [2, 4] = 2·[1, 2], so together they only span one line.
A basis is a set of independent vectors that spans the space. Every basis of 2-D has exactly 2 vectors; that number is the dimension of the space.
In code, stack the vectors as the columns of a matrix and ask for its rank with np.linalg.matrix_rank. If the rank equals the number of vectors, they are independent.
keyPoints: Two views of the same thing: an arrow (geometry) and a list of numbers (data).
Linear combination: scale each vector, then add. Almost everything in linear algebra is built from this.
The span is all the linear combinations. It is always a line, a plane or a higher-dimensional flat space through the origin.
Independent: no vector is a combination of the others. A dependent vector adds nothing new to the span.
Basis: independent and spans the space. In n dimensions every basis has exactly n vectors.
In ML, a duplicated or derived feature (a price in pounds and in dollars) is a dependent direction: no new information, and it can make some models numerically unstable.
mistakes: Thinking more vectors always means a bigger span. Extra dependent vectors add nothing.
Forgetting that every span passes through the origin: scale everything by 0 and you are there.
Testing independence with an exact "== 0" check on decimals. Use the rank with a tolerance, or look at the singular values.

followUps.q: Do [1, 0] and [3, 0] form a basis of 2-D space?
followUps.a: No. [3, 0] = 3·[1, 0], so both lie on the x-axis. Their span is a line, not the whole plane.

followUps.q: How many vectors are in a basis of 3-D space?
followUps.a: Exactly 3. Fewer can't reach every point; more can't all be independent.

followUps.q: Write [5, −1] as a combination of [1, 0] and [0, 1].
A dataset has height in centimetres and height in inches as two features. Why is that a problem?
followUps.a: One is a fixed multiple of the other, so they are dependent. The second adds no information and can make the maths of some models unstable.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["3 × [1, 0]"] --> S["add them"] B["2 × [0, 1]"] --> S S --> R["[3, 2]"] X["[1, 2] and [2, 4]"] --> N["the second is 2× the first
→ both lie on one line
→ not a basis"]
diagram.caption: Scaling and adding basis vectors reaches any point. Two vectors on the same line can only ever reach that line.

note.idea: A vector is an arrow, or a list of numbers. The span is every point you can reach by scaling and adding your vectors. A basis is the smallest set of vectors that can reach every point in the space.
note.analogy: Two ingredients, flour and water. Every mix you can make is the span. A third ingredient that is only 'flour plus water' adds nothing new.
note.breaks: Ingredient amounts cannot be negative. Vector weights can be negative.
note.example: In 2D, [1, 0] and [0, 1] form a basis: [3, 2] = 3·[1, 0] + 2·[0, 1]. But [1, 2] and [2, 4] are not a basis. The second is 2 times the first, so together they only reach points on one line. In ML, an embedding is a vector, and each feature is one coordinate.

practice.explain: Explain span and basis using a map and two directions of travel.
practice.derive: Are [1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 1] and [1, 3, 4] a basis of 3D space? Decide by hand, and show which vector (if any) is a combination of the others.
practice.build: Write is_independent(vectors) using the rank of the stacked matrix. Test it on the example above and on the standard basis.
practice.break: Test two almost-parallel vectors, like [1, 0] and [1, 1e-12]. Does your function call them independent? What does this teach you about floating point?

derive.answer:
No, they are not a basis.

Look for one vector made from the others: [1, 2, 3] + [0, 1, 1] = [1, 3, 4]. The third vector adds no new direction, so the three only span a flat plane through the origin, not all of 3D space.

Check with the determinant of the matrix whose rows are the three vectors:
1·(1·4 − 1·3) − 2·(0·4 − 1·1) + 3·(0·3 − 1·1) = 1 + 2 − 3 = 0.
A determinant of 0 means the vectors are dependent. A basis of 3D needs 3 independent vectors.

build.answer:
Stack the vectors as rows of a matrix. Its rank is the number of truly independent directions, so the vectors are independent exactly when the rank equals how many vectors there are.

The example from the derive step gives rank 2, so it is False; the standard basis gives rank 3, so True.
build.code:
import numpy as np

def is_independent(vectors):
    M = np.stack(vectors)                       # one vector per row
    return np.linalg.matrix_rank(M) == len(vectors)

print(is_independent([np.array([1, 2, 3]), np.array([0, 1, 1]), np.array([1, 3, 4])]))  # False
print(is_independent(list(np.eye(3))))                                                # True
print(is_independent([np.array([1, 2]), np.array([2, 4])]))                           # False

break.answer:
[1, 0] and [1, 1e-12] come out as independent: the rank is 2. Mathematically that is correct, since they are not exactly parallel. But in practice they point in almost the same direction, and any real data with a tiny bit of noise would look the same.

What this teaches about floating point: computers can't tell "exactly 0" from "very small", so rank is decided with a tolerance. np.linalg.matrix_rank counts singular values bigger than a tiny cutoff (about 1e-16 times the largest). 1e-12 is above that cutoff, so it counts. With [1, 1e-17], the rank drops to 1.

So "independent or not" is really a question of degree. The ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value, called the condition number, tells you how close to dependent a set of vectors is. Here it is about 10¹²: almost dependent, and any calculation that relies on them being independent will be unstable.
break.code:
import numpy as np

M = np.array([[1, 0], [1, 1e-12]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(M))                     # 2: counted as independent
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.array([[1, 0], [1, 1e-17]])))   # 1
print(f"{np.linalg.cond(M):.1e}")                   # 2.0e+12: almost dependent

explain.answer:
On a map you can walk east and you can walk north. By combining some amount of east with some amount of north, you can reach every point on the map: the span of those two directions is the whole map.

A basis is a set of directions that reaches everywhere with nothing wasted. East and north are a basis: you need both, and neither can be made from the other. Add "north-east" and you still reach the same places, because north-east is just some east plus some north, so it adds nothing new. And if both your directions were "north" and "a bit more north", you could only ever walk along one line: their span is a line, not the map.

topics.name: Matrices as transformations; matrix multiplication
topics.definition: A matrix is a recipe for moving every vector in space at once; multiplying two matrices means doing one movement after the other.
topics.problem: A neural network layer, a rotation of an image, a change of units, squeezing data down to fewer features: all of these are "do the same linear thing to every vector". A matrix stores that movement in a small grid of numbers, and matrix multiplication lets a computer apply it to millions of vectors, or chain several movements, very fast.
howItWorks: Watch where the two basis vectors land. A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] sends [1, 0] to [2, 0], its first column, and [0, 1] to [0, 3], its second column.
Every other vector follows, because it is a combination of the basis vectors: [1, 1] = [1, 0] + [0, 1] lands on [2, 0] + [0, 3] = [2, 3].
That is matrix-times-vector: Av = v₁·(first column) + v₂·(second column). Grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin stays put.
To do B first and then A, multiply AB, read right to left. Each column of AB is A applied to the matching column of B.
Order matters. With R a 90° rotation, A·R (rotate, then stretch) is [[0, −2], [3, 0]], but R·A (stretch, then rotate) is [[0, −3], [2, 0]].
Shapes must fit: an (m, n) matrix times an (n, p) matrix gives an (m, p) matrix. The two inner sizes must match.
keyPoints: The columns of a matrix are where the basis vectors land. Read a matrix column by column.
A linear transformation keeps grid lines straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and keeps the origin fixed.
The product AB means "do B, then A". In general AB ≠ BA.
Shapes: (m, n) @ (n, p) → (m, p). The inner sizes must match.
A neural network layer is y = Wx + b: a matrix movement, then a shift.
In NumPy, @ is matrix multiplication. * multiplies matching entries, which is something else.
mistakes: Using * instead of @ in NumPy. A * B multiplies entries in the same position; it is not the matrix product.
Reading AB left to right. B happens first.
Assuming AB = BA. It is rarely true.
Mixing up the shape: a (3, 2) matrix takes 2-D vectors to 3-D vectors, not the other way round.

followUps.q: Where does [[1, 2], [3, 4]] send the vector [1, 0]?
followUps.a: To [1, 3], its first column.

followUps.q: What shape is (32, 10) @ (10, 4)?
followUps.a: (32, 4). The inner 10s match and disappear.

followUps.q: Why does rotate-then-stretch differ from stretch-then-rotate?
followUps.a: The stretch acts along the fixed x and y directions. Rotating first changes which parts of the shape lie along x and y before the stretch, so the end shapes differ.

followUps.q: What is the difference between A * B and A @ B in NumPy?
followUps.a: A * B multiplies entries in the same position. A @ B is the matrix product: rows of A times columns of B.

flowchart LR V["vector [1, 1]"] --> A["A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]]
stretch x by 2, y by 3"] --> R["[2, 3]"] P1["rotate, then stretch"] --> D1["result 1"] P2["stretch, then rotate"] --> D2["result 2 ≠ result 1"]
diagram.caption: A matrix moves vectors. Doing two matrices in a different order usually gives a different result, so AB ≠ BA.

note.idea: A matrix is a machine that moves every vector in space. Its columns show where the basis vectors land. Multiplying two matrices means doing one movement after the other.
note.analogy: Instructions for a photo editor: rotate, then stretch.
note.breaks: In the analogy the order feels unimportant, but it matters. Rotate-then-stretch is usually different from stretch-then-rotate, so AB ≠ BA.
note.example: A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] stretches x by 2 and y by 3. R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]] rotates by 90°.

practice.explain: Explain what the columns of a matrix tell you, using [[2, 0], [0, 3]].
practice.derive: Find the matrix that rotates by 90° and then doubles x only. Then find the matrix for the opposite order. Draw where the unit square lands in each case.
practice.build: Write matmul(A, B) with three loops and no @. Test it against A @ B on random matrices. Then plot the unit square before and after a transformation.
practice.break: Try to multiply a (2, 3) matrix by another (2, 3) matrix. Read the error and explain which sizes must match, and why.

derive.answer:
Rotate 90° anticlockwise: R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]. Double x only: S = [[2, 0], [0, 1]].

Rotate first, then double x: the first step is on the right, so the matrix is S·R = [[0, −2], [1, 0]].
Double x first, then rotate: R·S = [[0, −1], [2, 0]].

Where the unit square lands (its corners (1, 0), (0, 1) and (1, 1)):
• S·R: (1, 0) → (0, 1), (0, 1) → (−2, 0), (1, 1) → (−2, 1). A rectangle 2 wide and 1 tall, to the left of the y-axis.
• R·S: (1, 0) → (0, 2), (0, 1) → (−1, 0), (1, 1) → (−1, 2). A rectangle 1 wide and 2 tall.

Both have area 2 (the determinant of each is 2), but they are different shapes in different places. Matrix multiplication depends on the order: S·R ≠ R·S.

build.answer:
Entry (i, j) of A·B is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. So: one loop over the rows of A, one over the columns of B, and one inner loop to add up the products. Check it against A @ B with np.allclose on random matrices of matching sizes.

For the picture, put the square's corners as columns of a matrix, multiply by the transformation, and plot both outlines.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def matmul(A, B):
    n, k = A.shape
    k2, m = B.shape
    assert k == k2, f"inner sizes differ: {k} and {k2}"
    C = np.zeros((n, m))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(m):
            for p in range(k):
                C[i, j] += A[i, p] * B[p, j]
    return C

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A, B = rng.normal(size=(4, 3)), rng.normal(size=(3, 5))
assert np.allclose(matmul(A, B), A @ B)

square = np.array([[0, 1, 1, 0, 0],      # x of each corner, back to the start
                   [0, 0, 1, 1, 0]])     # y of each corner
T = np.array([[0, -2], [1, 0]])           # rotate 90°, then double x
moved = T @ square
plt.plot(square[0], square[1], label="before")
plt.plot(moved[0], moved[1], label="after")
plt.axis("equal"); plt.legend(); plt.show()

break.answer:
NumPy refuses: "matmul: Input operand 1 has a mismatch in its core dimension 0 … (size 2 is different from 3)".

The rule: for A·B, the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B. (2, 3) times (3, 4) works and gives (2, 4); (2, 3) times (2, 3) doesn't.

Why: each entry of the result is a dot product of a row of A with a column of B. A row of a (2, 3) matrix has 3 numbers, but a column of the second (2, 3) matrix has only 2, so there is nothing to pair the third number with. A shortcut: write the shapes side by side, (2, 3)(3, 4). The inner numbers must match, and the outer ones give the result's shape.
break.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.ones((2, 3))
try:
    A @ np.ones((2, 3))
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
print((A @ np.ones((3, 4))).shape)    # (2, 4): inner 3s match

explain.answer:
The columns of a matrix tell you where the basic arrows land. The first column is where the arrow (1, 0) goes, the second is where (0, 1) goes.

For [[2, 0], [0, 3]]: the first column is [2, 0], so the arrow along x is stretched to twice its length. The second column is [0, 3], so the arrow along y is stretched three times. Every other point follows: (x, y) goes to x·[2, 0] + y·[0, 3] = (2x, 3y). So the unit square becomes a 2 × 3 rectangle.

That is why you can read a matrix as a transformation: look at the columns, and you see what it does to space.

topics.name: Determinants
topics.definition: The determinant of a square matrix is one number: how much the matrix scales area (or volume), with a minus sign if it flips space over.
topics.problem: You often need to know at a glance whether a matrix squashes space flat, because then it can't be undone and Ax = b has no unique answer. The determinant tells you: zero means squashed. It also appears whenever probabilities are moved through a transformation, as in the formula for a multivariate Gaussian and in normalising flows.
howItWorks: Start with the unit square: sides [1, 0] and [0, 1], area 1.
Apply the matrix. The square becomes a parallelogram whose sides are the matrix's two columns.
The determinant is that parallelogram's area, with a sign. For [[a, b], [c, d]] it is ad − bc.
[[2, 0], [0, 3]] gives 2·3 − 0·0 = 6, so every area grows 6 times.
A shear like [[1, 1], [0, 1]] gives 1·1 − 1·0 = 1. The square leans over but keeps its area.
[[0, 1], [1, 0]] swaps x and y: 0·0 − 1·1 = −1. Same area, but space is flipped like a mirror image.
[[2, 4], [1, 2]] gives 2·2 − 4·1 = 0. Both columns lie on one line, so the square is squashed flat, and the matrix has no inverse.
keyPoints: |det| is how much areas (in 2-D) or volumes (in 3-D) are scaled.
det < 0 means space is flipped; det = 0 means space is squashed into fewer dimensions.
det = 0 ⇔ no inverse ⇔ the columns are dependent ⇔ the rank is not full.
For 2 × 2: det [[a, b], [c, d]] = ad − bc.
det(AB) = det(A)·det(B): when you chain movements, their scale factors multiply.
For big matrices use np.linalg.slogdet, which returns the log, because determinants can be astronomically large or small.
mistakes: Using "the determinant is tiny" as a test for "nearly impossible to invert". 0.1 × the 100 × 100 identity has det 10⁻¹⁰⁰ but is trivial to invert. The condition number is the right measure.
Treating a negative determinant as an error. It just means a flip.
Asking for the determinant of a non-square matrix. It only exists for square ones.

followUps.a: 4·3 − 2·1 = 10. Areas grow 10 times, with no flip.

followUps.q: A matrix has determinant 0. What does that tell you?
followUps.a: It squashes space onto a line or a point, so its columns are dependent and it has no inverse.

followUps.q: det(A) = 2 and det(B) = −3. What is det(AB)?
followUps.a: −6. Scale factors multiply, and one flip makes the result flipped.

followUps.q: Why is "det(A) is close to 0" a poor test for "A is nearly singular"?
followUps.a: The determinant changes hugely just by rescaling: 0.1 × the identity in 100 dimensions has det 10⁻¹⁰⁰ yet is perfectly easy to invert.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR U["unit square
area 1"] --> M1["[[2, 0], [0, 3]]"] --> R1["rectangle
area 6 → det = 6"] U --> M2["[[0, 1], [1, 0]]"] --> R2["same area, flipped
→ det = −1"] U --> M3["a squashing matrix"] --> R3["flat line
area 0 → det = 0"]
diagram.caption: The size of the determinant says how much area grows; a minus sign means space was flipped; zero means it was squashed flat.

note.idea: The determinant has two parts. Its size tells you how much the matrix scales area (or volume in 3D). Its sign tells you whether space gets flipped over.
note.analogy: Stretching a rubber sheet with a square drawn on it. The determinant says how much bigger the square becomes.
note.breaks: A rubber sheet cannot pass through itself. A negative determinant does exactly that: it is like seeing the sheet in a mirror.
note.example: [[2, 0], [0, 3]] has det = 6: a 1×1 square becomes a 2×3 rectangle, area 6. [[0, 1], [1, 0]] has det = −1: the area stays the same, but x and y swap, so space is flipped. det = 0 means space is squashed flat, onto a line or a point.
note.code: np.linalg.det(np.array([[2, 0], [0, 3]]))   # ≈ 6.0
