practice.explain: Explain a confidence interval with the soup picture, and why a biased spoon ruins it.
practice.derive: A model gets 170 of 200 test examples right. Compute the 95% confidence interval by hand, using the standard error formula.
practice.build: Write a bootstrap: resample the 200 results with replacement 10,000 times and take the 95% interval. Compare it with your formula.
practice.break: Give two models the same accuracy gap on 50 examples, then on 5,000. When is the gap real? Try counting only the examples where the two models disagree.

derive.answer:
Accuracy: p̂ = 170 / 200 = 0.85.

Standard error: √(p̂(1 − p̂) / n) = √(0.85·0.15 / 200) = √(0.1275 / 200) = √0.0006375 ≈ 0.0252.

95% interval: p̂ ± 1.96·SE = 0.85 ± 1.96·0.0252 = 0.85 ± 0.049.

So roughly 80% to 90%. Read it as: on test sets like this one, the true accuracy is plausibly anywhere from 80% to 90%. Another model scoring 86% on these 200 examples would not be clearly better.

build.answer:
The bootstrap needs no formula: resample the 200 right-or-wrong results with replacement, recompute the accuracy, do it 10,000 times, and take the middle 95% of those accuracies. It gives about 80% to 90%, the same as the formula, which is reassuring.

Its strength is that the same recipe works for any metric, such as F1 or a median latency, where there is no simple standard-error formula.
build.code:
import numpy as np

results = np.array([1] * 170 + [0] * 30)          # 1 = right, 0 = wrong
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
boots = [rng.choice(results, size=200, replace=True).mean() for _ in range(10_000)]
low, high = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
se = np.sqrt(0.85 * 0.15 / 200)
print(round(low, 3), round(high, 3))                  # about 0.80 0.90
print(round(0.85 - 1.96 * se, 3), round(0.85 + 1.96 * se, 3))   # 0.801 0.899

break.answer:
The same 4-point gap means very different things at different sizes.

On 50 examples (40 right versus 42 right), each accuracy has a margin of about ±11 points, so a 4-point gap is well inside the noise. On 5,000 examples (4,000 versus 4,200), the margin is about ±1 point, so the same 4-point gap is almost certainly real.

Counting only the examples where the models disagree is sharper, because both models were tested on the same examples. If the gap is just luck, each disagreement is a coin flip for which model wins. With 50 examples, say they disagree on 8, B winning 5 and A winning 3: that is very possible by chance (p ≈ 0.73). With 5,000 examples, disagreeing on 800 with B winning 500: by chance that would almost never happen (p is about 1e-12). This is McNemar's test.
break.code:
from math import comb, sqrt

def sign_test(wins_b, wins_a):
    n, k = wins_b + wins_a, max(wins_b, wins_a)
    tail = sum(comb(n, i) for i in range(k, n + 1)) / 2**n
    return min(1.0, 2 * tail)                          # two-sided p-value

for n, a, b, b_only, a_only in [(50, 40, 42, 5, 3), (5000, 4000, 4200, 500, 300)]:
    margin = 1.96 * sqrt(0.8 * 0.2 / n)
    print(n, f"gap {(b - a) / n:.0%}, margin ±{margin:.1%}, p = {sign_test(b_only, a_only):.2g}")

explain.answer:
You taste one spoonful to judge a whole pot of soup. If you stirred first, one spoonful tells you a lot, but not everything, so you would say "it's about this salty, give or take a bit". That "give or take" range is a confidence interval. A bigger spoon, meaning more test data, gives a narrower range.

A biased spoon ruins it. If you never stir and only skim the top, where the oil floats, your spoonful is unlike the pot, and the interval is narrow and confidently wrong. A confidence interval only covers random luck in which spoonful you took, not a systematic bias in how you took it. In ML, a test set that doesn't look like real users is a biased spoon.

topics.name: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
topics.definition: Entropy measures how uncertain a distribution is; cross-entropy measures how surprised a model q is by data that really comes from p; KL divergence is the extra surprise caused by using q instead of p.
topics.problem: A classifier outputs probabilities, and you need a loss that rewards putting high probability on the right answer and punishes confident mistakes hard. Cross-entropy is that loss, and nearly every classifier and every language model is trained on it. KL divergence measures how far apart two distributions are, and it shows up in VAEs, knowledge distillation and RLHF.
howItWorks: The surprise of an event with probability q is −log q. Certain events (q = 1) cost 0; rare ones cost a lot.
Entropy is the average surprise under the true distribution: H(p) = −Σ p log p. A coin that lands heads 70% of the time has about 0.88 bits; a certain outcome has 0.
Cross-entropy uses the model's probabilities for the surprise but the true distribution for the averaging: H(p, q) = −Σ p log q.
With a one-hot true label, every term but one vanishes: the loss is −log of the probability the model gave the right class. For 0.7 that is 0.357.
If the model had said 0.99, the loss would be about 0.01; if it had said 0.05, about 3.0. Confident mistakes are punished hardest.
KL(p ‖ q) = H(p, q) − H(p). It is never negative, and it is 0 only when q = p. H(p) doesn't depend on the model, so minimising cross-entropy also minimises KL.
keyPoints: Surprise = −log(probability). The natural log gives nats; log base 2 gives bits.
Entropy H(p) = −Σ p log p: highest for a uniform distribution, zero for a certain one.
Cross-entropy H(p, q) = −Σ p log q, and it is always at least H(p).
KL(p ‖ q) = H(p, q) − H(p) ≥ 0, and it is not symmetric.
Classification loss = −log(probability of the true class), averaged over examples.
Language models are trained on exactly this: −log P(the next token).
mistakes: Taking the log of a probability that is exactly 0: −log 0 is infinite. Work with logits and log-softmax instead.
Treating KL as a distance. KL(p ‖ q) ≠ KL(q ‖ p).
Swapping the roles in cross-entropy: the true distribution does the averaging, and the model supplies the logs.

followUps.q: The model gives the right class probability 0.5. What is the cross-entropy loss?
Which has higher entropy: a fair coin, or a coin that lands heads 99% of the time?
followUps.a: The fair coin. It is the most uncertain coin possible: 1 bit.

followUps.q: Why is minimising cross-entropy the same as minimising KL divergence?
followUps.a: KL = cross-entropy − the entropy of the data, and the data's entropy doesn't depend on the model, so the two differ by a constant.

followUps.q: What happens to the loss if the model gives the true class probability 0?
followUps.a: It becomes infinite, because −log 0 = ∞. Implementations work in log space to avoid this.

diagram.code:
xychart-beta
  title "Cross-entropy loss: −log(probability given to the right answer)"
  x-axis "probability of the right answer" [0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.99]
  y-axis "loss" 0 --> 3.2
  bar [3.0, 2.3, 1.2, 0.69, 0.36, 0.11, 0.01]
diagram.caption: Being confidently wrong is punished hard; being confidently right costs almost nothing. That's the loss classifiers are trained on.

note.idea: Entropy measures uncertainty, or 'surprise', in a distribution. Cross-entropy measures your surprise when you use your model q to predict data that really comes from p. KL divergence is the extra surprise: KL(p‖q) = cross-entropy − entropy.
note.analogy: Packing for a trip. With the true weather forecast (p), you pack exactly right. With a wrong forecast (q), you pack badly. KL is the extra, wasted luggage.
note.breaks: In the analogy, swapping the two forecasts feels like the same mistake. KL is not symmetric: KL(p‖q) is usually different from KL(q‖p).
note.example: The true label is class 1 of 3, so p = [0, 1, 0]. The model says q = [0.2, 0.7, 0.1]. Cross-entropy = −log(0.7) ≈ 0.357. If the model said 0.99, the loss would be about 0.01. Here the entropy of p is 0, so KL equals the cross-entropy.

resources.title: Visual Information Theory
resources.recommended: Pictures that turn entropy, cross-entropy and KL into areas you can see. The best explanation of why the formulas look the way they do.

resources.title: A Short Introduction to Entropy, Cross-Entropy and KL-Divergence

practice.explain: Explain KL divergence with the packing-for-a-trip picture.
practice.derive: By hand, using log base 2: the entropy of a fair coin, of a coin with p = 0.9, and of a fair die. Which is most uncertain?
practice.build: Write entropy(p), cross_entropy(p, q) and kl(p, q). Check that kl = cross-entropy − entropy, and that kl(p, p) = 0.
practice.break: Compute kl(p, q) where q has a 0 where p does not. What happens? Then compare kl(p, q) with kl(q, p) for two distributions.

derive.answer:
Entropy H(p) = −Σ pᵢ·log₂ pᵢ, measured in bits.

Fair coin: −(0.5·log₂ 0.5 + 0.5·log₂ 0.5) = −(0.5·(−1) + 0.5·(−1)) = 1 bit.

Coin with p = 0.9: −(0.9·log₂ 0.9 + 0.1·log₂ 0.1) = −(0.9·(−0.152) + 0.1·(−3.322)) = 0.137 + 0.332 ≈ 0.47 bits. Less uncertain: you can usually guess heads.

Fair die: −6·(1/6)·log₂(1/6) = log₂ 6 ≈ 2.585 bits.

The fair die is the most uncertain: it has the most equally likely outcomes. For n equally likely outcomes, entropy is log₂ n, the most any distribution over n outcomes can have.

build.answer:
entropy(p) = −Σ p·log p, cross_entropy(p, q) = −Σ p·log q, and kl(p, q) = Σ p·log(p/q). Skip terms where p is 0, because 0·log 0 counts as 0.

Both checks pass: kl equals cross-entropy minus entropy, and kl(p, p) is 0. KL is the extra cost of using q when the truth is p, and there is none when they are the same.

break.answer:
KL becomes infinite. Where p says "this happens" but q says "probability 0", the term p·log(p/0) is infinite. The meaning is real: q claims something is impossible, and then it happens, which is infinitely surprising. It is the same reason a classifier that gives the right class probability 0 gets infinite cross-entropy loss, and why probabilities are clipped away from 0 in practice.

KL is not symmetric. For p = [0.9, 0.1] and q = [0.5, 0.5], kl(p, q) ≈ 0.53 bits but kl(q, p) ≈ 0.74 bits. They measure different things: kl(p, q) is the cost of using q when the truth is p. So KL is not a true distance, and which way round you use it changes what a model learns.
break.code:
import numpy as np

def kl(p, q):
    p, q = np.asarray(p, float), np.asarray(q, float)
    nz = p > 0
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
        return np.sum(p[nz] * np.log2(p[nz] / q[nz]))

print(kl([0.5, 0.5], [1.0, 0.0]))            # inf
p, q = [0.9, 0.1], [0.5, 0.5]
print(round(kl(p, q), 3), round(kl(q, p), 3))   # 0.531 0.737

explain.answer:
You are packing for a trip. With the true weather forecast, p, you pack exactly what you need. With a wrong forecast, q, you pack badly: an umbrella you never use, and no coat for the cold.

KL divergence, KL(p‖q), is the extra, wasted luggage: how much worse you do on average by planning with q when the weather really follows p. If the forecasts agree, there is no waste, so KL is 0. It can never be negative: a wrong forecast can't help you on average. And it isn't symmetric: packing for sunshine and getting snow costs differently from packing for snow and getting sunshine.

topics.name: Convex optimisation: constraints, Lagrange multipliers and duality
topics.definition: A convex function is bowl-shaped, so any local minimum is the global minimum; constrained problems are solved by adding the constraint with a Lagrange multiplier, and duality views the same problem from the constraint's side.
topics.problem: Gradient descent only promises a local minimum. For convex problems that is enough: the answer is the best possible and doesn't depend on where you start. Knowing which models are convex (linear and logistic regression, SVMs) tells you when to trust the optimiser. Constraints like "weights must add up to 1" or "every point on the right side of the margin" need Lagrange multipliers, and SVMs are usually trained through their dual problem.
howItWorks: Test convexity with the chord rule: the straight line between any two points on the curve lies on or above the curve. w² passes; w⁴ − 3w² + w fails.
For a smooth function, convex means the second derivative is never negative. In many dimensions: the Hessian matrix has no negative eigenvalues.
Convex ⇒ every local minimum is the global one. Gradient descent from any start reaches the same lowest value.
Now add a constraint: minimise x² + y² subject to x + y = 1.
At the best point, the contour of the objective just touches the constraint line, so their gradients are parallel: ∇f = λ∇g.
Write the Lagrangian L = x² + y² − λ(x + y − 1) and set all its derivatives to 0: 2x = λ, 2y = λ and x + y = 1. So x = y = 0.5 and λ = 1.
λ says how much the best value would change if you loosened the constraint a little: here about 1 per unit.
keyPoints: Convex: the chord lies above the curve; the second derivative is ≥ 0; there is one valley.
A sum of convex functions is convex, so loss + an L2 penalty stays convex.
Convex models: linear regression with squared error, logistic regression, SVMs. Neural networks are not convex.
Lagrange condition at a constrained optimum: ∇f = λ∇g.
The multiplier λ is the "price" of the constraint: how fast the best value changes as the constraint is relaxed.
Duality turns a constrained problem into a different one, often easier to solve. SVMs and their kernels come from the dual.
mistakes: Assuming deep-learning losses are convex. They are not, which is why initialisation and learning-rate schedules matter.
Forgetting that a convex function can have a flat bottom with many minimisers, all with the same value.
Dropping the constraint equation itself when solving the Lagrange conditions.

followUps.q: Is f(w) = |w| convex?
followUps.a: Yes. The chord between any two points lies on or above the V shape, even though it has a corner at 0.

followUps.q: Why can gradient descent end in different places on w⁴ − 3w² + w?
followUps.a: It isn't convex: it has two valleys, and each start rolls into the valley it begins above.

followUps.q: Minimise x² + y² subject to x + y = 2.
followUps.a: x = y = 1, minimum value 2, with λ = 2.

followUps.q: Name two convex ML problems.
followUps.a: Linear regression with squared error, and logistic regression. SVMs are convex too.

diagram.caption: The bowl (w²) has one bottom, so gradient descent always finds it. The wavy curve has two valleys, so where you end up depends on where you start.

note.idea: A convex function is shaped like a bowl, so any local minimum is the global minimum and gradient descent cannot get stuck in a wrong valley. Constrained problems ('minimise this, but keep that true') are solved with Lagrange multipliers, which add the constraint to the objective as an extra term. Duality looks at the same problem from the constraint's side, and it is how SVMs are usually solved.
note.analogy: A bowl versus a mountain range. Drop a marble into a bowl and it always ends at the same bottom. In a mountain range it can stop in any valley.
note.breaks: Real bowls are simple 3D shapes. Neural network losses are not convex at all, yet gradient descent still works well on them. Convexity is a guarantee we only get for simpler models, like linear regression, logistic regression and SVMs.
note.example: Minimise x² + y² subject to x + y = 1. The Lagrangian is x² + y² − λ(x + y − 1). Setting its gradient to zero gives 2x = λ and 2y = λ, so x = y = 0.5.
note.code:
# convex means the straight line between two points lies above the curve
f = lambda w: w**2
a, b, t = -1.0, 3.0, 0.3
f(t*a + (1-t)*b) <= t*f(a) + (1-t)*f(b)   # True for every a, b and t in [0, 1]

resources.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning, Ch 7 (Lagrange multipliers, convex optimisation)

practice.explain: Explain why convexity is a guarantee, with the bowl-and-mountains picture.
practice.derive: Minimise x² + 2y² subject to x + y = 3 with a Lagrange multiplier, by hand.
practice.build: Write a convexity checker that tests the line-above-the-curve rule at 10,000 random points. Run it on w², |w|, eʷ, sin(w) and w³.
practice.break: Run gradient descent on the non-convex f(w) = w⁴ − 3w² + w from 20 random starts. Where does it end each time? Compare with the convex f(w) = w².

derive.answer:
Minimise x² + 2y² subject to x + y = 3.

Lagrangian: L = x² + 2y² − λ(x + y − 3).
Set every partial derivative to 0:
∂L/∂x = 2x − λ = 0, so x = λ/2.
∂L/∂y = 4y − λ = 0, so y = λ/4.
∂L/∂λ = −(x + y − 3) = 0, so x + y = 3.

From the first two, x = 2y. Put that in the constraint: 3y = 3, so y = 1, x = 2 and λ = 4.
The minimum is 2² + 2·1² = 6.

What λ means: if the constraint were relaxed to x + y = 3 + ε, the best value would rise by about 4ε. λ is the price of the constraint. And it makes sense that x > y: y is twice as expensive in the objective, so the solution uses less of it.

build.answer:
A function is convex when the straight line between any two points on its graph lies on or above the curve: f(t·a + (1 − t)·b) ≤ t·f(a) + (1 − t)·f(b) for every a, b and t between 0 and 1.

Test that at 10,000 random choices of a, b and t, with a tiny tolerance for rounding. w², |w| and eʷ never break it. sin(w) and w³ break it quickly. Remember the test can only prove a function is not convex; passing it is strong evidence, not proof.

break.answer:
f(w) = w⁴ − 3w² + w has two valleys. Gradient descent ends in whichever valley it starts above: starts left of about w = 0.17 (the hump between them) end near w ≈ −1.30, the deeper valley with f ≈ −3.51; starts to the right end near w ≈ 1.13, a shallower valley with f ≈ −1.07. Same algorithm, same learning rate, different answers, and half the time it misses the best one.

On the convex f(w) = w², every start ends at w = 0. A convex function has only one valley, so there is nowhere else to get stuck.

Neural network losses are non-convex like the first one, which is why the starting weights, the random seed and the optimiser affect where training ends.
break.code:
import numpy as np

f = lambda w: w**4 - 3 * w**2 + w
grad = lambda w: 4 * w**3 - 6 * w + 1

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
ends = []
for start in rng.uniform(-2, 2, 20):
    w = start
    for _ in range(2000):
        w -= 0.01 * grad(w)
    ends.append(round(float(w), 2))
print(sorted(set(ends)))                         # [-1.3, 1.13]
print(round(f(-1.30), 2), round(f(1.13), 2))     # -3.51 -1.07

explain.answer:
Drop a marble into a bowl. Wherever you drop it, it rolls to the same bottom point: there is only one lowest point, and nothing to get stuck on. A convex function is a bowl. Any point that is lowest nearby is also the lowest overall, so gradient descent is guaranteed to find the true minimum.

Drop the same marble into a mountain range and it stops in whichever valley is below it, which may not be the deepest one. Non-convex functions, like neural network losses, are mountain ranges: there is no such guarantee, and where you end up depends on where you start.

ready.q: On a whiteboard: logistic regression model, loss, gradient and update rule.
ready.a: Model: p = σ(wᵀx + b), where σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ). Loss (binary cross-entropy): L = −(1/n) Σ [y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)]. Gradient: ∇w = (1/n) Xᵀ(p − y) and ∂L/∂b = mean(p − y). Update: w ← w − η ∇w and b ← b − η ∂L/∂b, repeated until the loss stops improving.

ready.q: Your fraud model has 99% accuracy. Why might it be useless?
ready.a: If only 1% of transactions are fraud, a model that always says "not fraud" is 99% accurate and catches no fraud at all. Accuracy is dominated by the easy majority. Look at recall and precision for the fraud class, the confusion matrix, and the precision–recall curve instead.

ready.q: Explain overfitting and three ways to reduce it.
ready.a: Overfitting is when a model learns the noise and quirks of its training data instead of the real pattern: it scores well on training data and badly on new data, and the gap between training and validation error is the sign. Three fixes: more (or augmented) data; regularisation, such as L2 weight decay or dropout; and a simpler model or early stopping at the lowest validation loss.

ready.q: Why does L1 regularisation give sparse weights, but L2 does not?
ready.a: L1's penalty pushes every weight towards zero with the same force, λ·sign(w), however small the weight is, so small weights are pushed all the way to exactly 0. L2's push, 2λw, shrinks as the weight shrinks, so weights get small but almost never reach exactly 0. Geometrically, the L1 constraint region has corners on the axes, and the best point often lands on a corner, where some weights are 0.

ready.q: How does a random forest reduce variance?
ready.a: It averages many deep trees, each trained on a different bootstrap sample and choosing from a random subset of features at each split. Each tree overfits in its own way, so averaging cancels much of the noise. The random features make the trees less alike, which matters because averaging only removes the part of the errors that differs between trees.

ready.q: What is data leakage? Give a real example.
ready.a: Leakage is when information that won't be available at prediction time gets into training or evaluation, so the model looks much better than it really is. Real examples: scaling features with the mean of the whole dataset, test rows included; a churn model using "date the account was closed"; the same patient's scans in both the training and the test set.

topics.name: The ML setup: features, labels, loss, train/validation/test
topics.definition: Supervised learning turns examples (features plus a label) into a model by minimising a loss on a training set, tuning choices on a validation set, and measuring the final result once on a test set.
topics.problem: A model that scores well on the data it learned from may still fail on anything new; it may simply have memorised. To know how it will really behave, you must measure it on data it never saw, and you must not let that data influence any of your choices. The three-way split is the simplest honest way to do that.
howItWorks: Decide what one example is (a house), its features (size, rooms, age) and its label (price). Every row of X is one example; y holds the labels.
Pick a loss that says how wrong a prediction is: squared error for numbers, cross-entropy for categories.
Shuffle the rows, then split them, for example 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. No row may appear in two sets.
Fit the model's weights on the training set only.
Use the validation set to compare models and settings (learning rate, tree depth, k) and keep the best one.
When every choice is final, score the chosen model once on the test set. That number is your honest estimate for new data.
If you go back and change things after looking at the test score, the test set has become a second validation set, and you need fresh test data.
keyPoints: Feature = input; label = the answer; example = one row of both.
Training set: learn weights. Validation set: make choices. Test set: report the final score, once.
Shuffle before splitting, unless the data has an order that matters (time series: train on the past, test on the future).
With little data, use cross-validation instead of a single validation set.
Keep the class balance similar in every split (a "stratified" split) when one class is rare.
Always compare against a simple baseline, such as predicting the average or the most common class.
mistakes: Tuning on the test set, even "just a little". The final score then over-promises.
Splitting rows that belong together (several photos of the same person) across train and test.
Shuffling time-series data, so the model trains on the future.
Reporting training accuracy as if it were real-world accuracy.

followUps.q: Why do you need a validation set as well as a test set?
followUps.a: You make many choices using the validation score, which slowly fits it. The test set stays untouched, so it still gives an honest final number.

followUps.q: You have 1,000 rows. How many go to each set in a 70/15/15 split?
followUps.a: 700 for training, 150 for validation and 150 for test.

followUps.q: Why not shuffle a stock-price dataset before splitting?
followUps.a: The model would train on later days and be tested on earlier ones: it would be using the future to predict the past, which never happens in real use.

followUps.q: What is a baseline, and why bother?
followUps.a: A trivial predictor, such as always guessing the average. If your model can't beat it, it hasn't learned anything useful.

derive.answer:
Features (inputs): floor area in m², number of bedrooms, age of the house (others: distance to the station, postcode).
Label (the answer to predict): the sale price.
Loss: mean squared error between predicted and real prices. (Many people predict log(price), so a £20,000 miss on a cheap house counts more than on a mansion.)

The split, for example 1,000 past sales:
• Train, 70%: the model learns its weights from these.
• Validation, 15%: used again and again to choose settings, such as which features or how much regularisation.
• Test, 15%: used once, at the very end, for an honest final number.

Two things to check: if a house was sold twice, keep both sales in the same set; and if the model will predict future sales, split by date (train on older sales, test on the newest) instead of at random.

build.answer:
Shuffle the row numbers once with a seeded random generator, then cut the shuffled list at the fraction boundaries. The same seed always gives the same split, which makes results reproducible.

Check two things: no row number is in two sets, and together the sets contain every row exactly once.
build.code:
import numpy as np

def train_val_test_split(X, y, fractions=(0.7, 0.15, 0.15), seed=0):
    assert np.isclose(sum(fractions), 1.0)
    order = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(len(X))
    cut1 = int(fractions[0] * len(X))
    cut2 = cut1 + int(fractions[1] * len(X))
    parts = np.split(order, [cut1, cut2])
    return [(X[idx], y[idx], idx) for idx in parts]

X, y = np.arange(1000).reshape(-1, 1), np.arange(1000)
(Xtr, ytr, a), (Xva, yva, b), (Xte, yte, c) = train_val_test_split(X, y)
assert not (set(a) & set(b) or set(a) & set(c) or set(b) & set(c))   # no overlap
assert sorted(np.concatenate([a, b, c])) == list(range(1000))        # every row once
again = train_val_test_split(X, y)[0][2]
assert (again == a).all()                                            # reproducible
print(len(a), len(b), len(c))                                        # 700 150 150

break.answer:
Try 20 "models" that are secretly guessing at random on a test set of 200 examples. Each one should score about 50%, but by luck some score higher, and if you keep the best you report something like 55%. Score that same model on fresh data and it drops back to about 50%.

That drop is the cost of choosing on the test set: you didn't find a better model, you found the luckiest one on these particular 200 examples. The more often you look at the test set, the more optimistic its score becomes. This is why choices are made on the validation set, and the test set is used once.
break.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y_test = rng.integers(0, 2, 200)
# 20 "models" that are really coin flips: each one's guesses on the test set
guesses = rng.integers(0, 2, (20, 200))
scores = (guesses == y_test).mean(axis=1)
print(f"best of 20 on the test set: {scores.max():.0%}")

y_fresh = rng.integers(0, 2, 2000)            # new data: the "best" model guesses again
fresh = (rng.integers(0, 2, 2000) == y_fresh).mean()
print(f"the same model on fresh data: {fresh:.0%}")

explain.answer:
Think of studying for an exam. The training set is the textbook exercises: you learn from them. The validation set is the practice papers: you take them again and again to decide how to study and when you are ready. The test set is the real exam: you sit it once.

If you peek at the real exam while you are still studying, your final grade no longer tells anyone what you actually know. That is why the test set stays locked away until the end.

topics.name: Linear regression: normal equation and gradient descent
topics.definition: Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of the features, ŷ = Xw + b, choosing the weights that make the mean squared error as small as possible.
topics.problem: Many questions ask for a number: a price, a temperature, a delivery time. Linear regression is the simplest model that learns how each feature pushes the answer up or down. It trains in a fraction of a second, its weights are easy to read, and it is the baseline every fancier model must beat. Its two training routes, a formula and gradient descent, are the same two routes used everywhere else in ML.
howItWorks: Put the examples in a matrix X (one row each) and add a column of 1s, so the bias b becomes just another weight.
The prediction for every row at once is ŷ = Xw.
The loss is the mean squared error: the average of (ŷ − y)². Squaring makes big misses count much more than small ones.
Route 1, the normal equation: set the gradient to zero and solve XᵀX w = Xᵀy in one step. For x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and y = [2, 4, 5, 4, 6] this gives ŷ = 1.8 + 0.8x.
Route 2, gradient descent: the gradient is (2/n)·Xᵀ(Xw − y). Step against it, again and again, and w walks to the same answer.
The normal equation is exact and fast for a few thousand features. Gradient descent scales to huge data and is how every neural network trains.
Read the weights: 0.8 means "one more unit of x adds 0.8 to the prediction, holding the other features fixed".
keyPoints: Model ŷ = Xw + b; loss = mean squared error.
Normal equation: w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. In code, solve the system (np.linalg.solve or lstsq); never form the inverse.
Gradient of MSE: (2/n)·Xᵀ(Xw − y).
Minimising squared error is maximum likelihood when the noise is Gaussian.
Curves need curved features: add x², x³ or interactions, and the model is still "linear" in its weights.
Check the residuals (y − ŷ): a pattern in them means the model is missing something.
mistakes: Using it when the relationship is strongly curved, without adding features.
Reading a weight as a cause. It only says how the prediction moves, with the other features held still.
Duplicated or near-duplicate features: XᵀX becomes nearly singular and the weights blow up.
Forgetting the bias column, which forces the line through the origin.

followUps.q: What does the weight 0.8 mean in ŷ = 1.8 + 0.8x?
followUps.a: Each extra unit of x raises the prediction by 0.8.

followUps.q: Why square the errors instead of just adding them up?
followUps.a: Positive and negative errors would cancel out, and squaring punishes big misses more. It is also smooth, so it is easy to differentiate.

followUps.q: When would you use gradient descent instead of the normal equation?
followUps.a: When there are very many features or rows, or when the data doesn't fit in memory. Solving XᵀX gets expensive as the number of features grows.

followUps.q: Can linear regression fit a curve?
followUps.a: Yes, if you add curved features like x². It stays linear in the weights, so the same maths works.

note.breaks: A ruler is straight. If the true pattern curves, linear regression cannot follow it, unless you add curved features such as x².

Xb = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]             # add a column of 1s for the bias
w = np.linalg.solve(Xb.T @ Xb, Xb.T @ y)    # normal equation

# gradient descent version, one step:

derive.answer:
The loss is the squared error L(w) = ‖Xw − y‖² = (Xw − y)ᵀ(Xw − y).

Expand it: L = wᵀXᵀXw − 2yᵀXw + yᵀy.

Take the gradient with respect to w (using ∇(wᵀAw) = 2Aw for a symmetric A, and ∇(bᵀw) = b):
∇L = 2XᵀXw − 2Xᵀy.

At the minimum the gradient is 0: XᵀXw = Xᵀy. These are the "normal equations".

If XᵀX is invertible: w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy.

Two notes: put a column of 1s in X so the model has a bias term; and in code use np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y), or better np.linalg.lstsq, rather than computing the inverse.

build.answer:
On the diabetes data (four features, standardised, plus a column of 1s for the bias), all three methods give the same weights to 4 decimal places: the normal equation, gradient descent after a few thousand steps, and np.linalg.lstsq.

They trade off differently. The normal equation is exact but needs XᵀX to be invertible and costs about d³ for d features. lstsq is exact and the most robust. Gradient descent is approximate, but it scales to huge datasets and is the same idea that trains neural networks.
build.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes      # only to load the data

d = load_diabetes(scaled=False)
X = d.data[:, [0, 2, 3, 8]]                      # age, bmi, blood pressure, s5
X = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])        # bias column
y = d.target

w_normal = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
w_lstsq = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
w_gd = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
for _ in range(5000):
    w_gd -= 0.05 * 2 * X.T @ (X @ w_gd - y) / len(y)

print(w_normal.round(4))
assert np.allclose(w_normal, w_lstsq) and np.allclose(w_normal, w_gd, atol=1e-4)

break.answer:
With an exact copy of a column, XᵀX is singular: two columns carry the same information, so infinitely many weight pairs fit equally well (for example w₁ = 10, w₂ = 0, or 5 and 5, or 105 and −95). The normal equation has no unique answer. Depending on rounding, np.linalg.solve either raises "Singular matrix" or returns huge, meaningless weights.

Gradient descent still works. Both copies get exactly the same gradient at every step, so starting from zero they stay equal, and each ends up with half of the original weight. The predictions are the same as without the copy. np.linalg.lstsq gives that same "split it evenly" answer, because it returns the smallest weights that fit.

The practical lesson: correlated or duplicated features make the weights unstable and hard to interpret, even when predictions are fine. Remove duplicates, or add L2 regularisation, which makes XᵀX + λI invertible.
break.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=100)
y = 3 * x + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=100)
X = np.column_stack([x, x])                       # an exact copy
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X.T @ X))             # 1, not 2: singular
try:
    print(np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y))      # huge numbers, or an error
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as e:
    print("solve:", e)

w = np.zeros(2)
for _ in range(2000):
    w -= 0.05 * 2 * X.T @ (X @ w - y) / len(y)
print(w.round(3), np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0].round(3))   # both ≈ [1.5 1.5]

explain.answer:
Picture dots scattered on a page, and you lay a ruler across them so it runs as close as possible to all of them. For each dot, measure the vertical gap between the dot and the ruler, square it, and add the squares up. Least squares is the position of the ruler that makes that total as small as possible.

Squaring does two things: gaps above and below can't cancel out, and big misses count far more than small ones. That second part is also its weakness: one far-away dot pulls the ruler strongly towards itself.

topics.name: Logistic regression and the sigmoid
topics.definition: Logistic regression answers yes/no questions: it computes a score z = Xw + b, turns it into a probability with the sigmoid σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ), and is trained with cross-entropy loss.
topics.problem: Many questions have a yes/no answer: spam or not, fraud or not, pass or fail. A straight line gives numbers below 0 and above 1, which can't be probabilities. Logistic regression keeps the simple weighted sum but squashes it into a probability, so it can say "83% likely". It is the standard first model for classification, and the single neuron at the heart of every neural network.
howItWorks: Compute a score for each example, exactly as in linear regression: z = Xw + b.
Squash it: p = σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ). A score of 0 gives 0.5, z = 2 gives 0.88, and z = −2 gives 0.12.
Measure the error with binary cross-entropy: −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)]. Confident mistakes cost the most.
The gradient comes out beautifully simple: Xᵀ(p − y)/n for the weights and the mean of (p − y) for the bias.
Train with gradient descent. There is no closed-form answer, but the loss is convex, so gradient descent finds the best weights.
To decide, pick a threshold (usually 0.5). p > 0.5 exactly when z > 0, so the decision boundary is the line (or plane) where Xw + b = 0.
keyPoints: σ(z) = 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ) maps any number to between 0 and 1; σ(0) = 0.5.
Train with binary cross-entropy, not squared error.
Gradient: Xᵀ(p − y)/n. Remember it — it appears again in neural networks.
The boundary is linear. Curved boundaries need extra features.
The weights are log-odds: one more unit of a feature adds w to log(p/(1 − p)).
More than two classes: replace the sigmoid with softmax (Phase 3).
mistakes: Training with squared error. The loss becomes non-convex and learning is slow.
Reading the output as certain truth. The probabilities are only as good as the model and the data.
Perfectly separable data with no regularisation: the weights grow forever. Add L2.
Always using 0.5 as the threshold, even when one kind of mistake costs much more.

followUps.q: What is σ(0), and what does it mean?
followUps.a: 0.5: a score of 0 means the model is undecided, exactly on the boundary.

followUps.q: Why not train logistic regression with squared error?
followUps.a: With the sigmoid inside, squared error is non-convex and its gradients become tiny when the model is confidently wrong. Cross-entropy is convex and punishes confident mistakes strongly.

followUps.q: Where is the decision boundary?
followUps.a: Where p = 0.5, which is where z = Xw + b = 0: a straight line in 2-D.

followUps.q: What is the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights?
followUps.a: Xᵀ(p − y)/n: the features weighted by how wrong each prediction was.

derive.answer:
For one example: z = wᵀx, p = σ(z), and the loss is L = −[y·log p + (1 − y)·log(1 − p)].

Chain rule in three pieces:
1. ∂L/∂p = −y/p + (1 − y)/(1 − p) = (p − y) / (p(1 − p)).
2. ∂p/∂z = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) = p(1 − p). (The sigmoid's famous derivative.)
3. ∂z/∂w = x.

Multiply: ∂L/∂w = (p − y)/(p(1 − p)) · p(1 − p) · x = (p − y)·x. The p(1 − p) cancels.

Averaging over n examples and writing it with matrices: ∇L = Xᵀ(p − y) / n.

In words: each example pushes the weights by its error (p − y) times its features. It is the same shape as linear regression's gradient, which is why the update rule looks identical.

build.answer:
On the breast-cancer data with two standardised features (mean radius and mean texture), gradient descent drives the loss down smoothly from 0.693 (that is ln 2, a model that says 50% for everything) to about 0.24, with about 84% validation accuracy using only those two features.

The decision boundary is the line where p = 0.5, which is where w₀ + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ = 0, so you can solve it for x₂ and draw it.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer     # only to load the data

data = load_breast_cancer()
X = data.data[:, [0, 1]]                             # mean radius, mean texture
X = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])
y = data.target.astype(float)
order = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(X))
tr, va = order[:450], order[450:]

sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
w, losses = np.zeros(3), []
for _ in range(2000):
    p = sigmoid(X[tr] @ w)
    losses.append(-np.mean(y[tr] * np.log(p) + (1 - y[tr]) * np.log(1 - p)))
    w -= 0.1 * X[tr].T @ (p - y[tr]) / len(tr)
acc = ((sigmoid(X[va] @ w) > 0.5) == y[va]).mean()
print(round(losses[0], 3), round(losses[-1], 3), f"validation accuracy {acc:.0%}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
axes[0].plot(losses); axes[0].set_xlabel("step"); axes[0].set_ylabel("loss")
axes[1].scatter(X[:, 1], X[:, 2], c=y, s=8)
xs = np.linspace(-2.5, 4, 50)
axes[1].plot(xs, -(w[0] + w[1] * xs) / w[2], "k")   # where p = 0.5
axes[1].set_xlabel("radius"); axes[1].set_ylabel("texture")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

break.answer:
When a straight line can separate the classes perfectly, the weights never stop growing. Any separating line can be made "more confident" by multiplying all its weights by 2: every correct p moves closer to 1 or 0, so the loss keeps shrinking towards 0, but never reaches it. Gradient descent keeps following that, and the size of w keeps rising (slowly, roughly like the log of the number of steps).

The result is a model that claims 99.99% certainty near the boundary, which is badly overconfident on new data.

What stops it: L2 regularisation (a penalty on ‖w‖² balances the push, so the weights level off), early stopping, or simply a fixed number of steps. In the run below, without regularisation ‖w‖ keeps climbing; with a small λ it settles.
break.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([-3., -2., -1., 1., 2., 3.])          # perfectly separable at 0
y = (x > 0).astype(float)
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
for lam in [0.0, 0.01]:
    w = 0.0
    for step in range(1, 100_001):
        p = sigmoid(w * x)
        w -= 0.5 * (np.mean((p - y) * x) + lam * w)
        if step in (100, 1_000, 10_000, 100_000):
            print(f"lambda {lam}: step {step}, w = {w:.2f}")

explain.answer:
A linear model gives a score, wᵀx, that can be any number: −50, 3, 1,000. But for a yes/no question we want a probability between 0 and 1.

The sigmoid is a dimmer switch. The score turns the dial, and the light always stays between fully off (0) and fully on (1). A score of 0 puts the light at half (0.5); big positive scores push it close to fully on, big negative scores close to off, and it never goes past either end. That makes the output usable as a probability, and it changes smoothly, so gradient descent can learn it.

topics.name: Regularisation: L1 and L2
topics.definition: Regularisation adds a penalty for large weights to the loss: L2 (λΣw²) shrinks every weight, while L1 (λΣ|w|) pushes the weak ones to exactly zero.
topics.problem: A flexible model with many features can fit the training data too well, using huge weights that balance each other out on noise. It then does badly on new data. Regularisation tells the model "simple explanations are better": it trades a little training error for much smaller weights, which usually generalise better. L1 also picks features for you.
howItWorks: Start from the normal loss, for example mean squared error.
Add a penalty: L2 adds λΣw², L1 adds λΣ|w|. λ (lambda) sets how strongly simplicity is preferred.
L2's gradient adds 2λw to each weight's gradient, so every step also shrinks each weight a little, in proportion to its size. This is "weight decay".
With uncorrelated, equally scaled features, L2 simply divides every weight by (1 + λ): smaller, but never exactly zero.
L1 pulls every weight towards zero by the same fixed amount, λ/2 in that simple case. Weights smaller than that land on exactly 0.
Choose λ with the validation set: try values like 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10, and keep the one with the best validation score.
Never penalise the bias, and scale the features first, so the penalty treats them fairly.
keyPoints: Loss = data error + λ × penalty. λ = 0 means no regularisation.
L2 (ridge, weight decay): small weights everywhere; smooth; has a closed form w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy.
L1 (lasso): many weights exactly 0, so it selects features.
Too big a λ underfits; too small overfits. Tune it on validation data.
Regularisation reduces variance at the cost of a little bias.
In deep learning, weight decay, dropout, data augmentation and early stopping all play this role (Phase 3).
mistakes: Regularising without scaling features: features measured in small units need big weights, so they get punished unfairly.
Penalising the bias term.
Picking λ by looking at the test set.
Expecting L2 to remove features. It only shrinks them.

followUps.q: Why does L1 give exact zeros, but L2 doesn't?
followUps.a: L1 pushes with the same force however small a weight is, so small weights reach 0. L2's push is proportional to the weight, so it fades as the weight shrinks and never quite reaches 0.

followUps.q: What happens with a huge λ?
followUps.a: All weights are squeezed towards 0 and the model underfits, predicting little more than the average.

followUps.q: What is another name for L2 regularisation in neural networks?
followUps.a: Weight decay.

followUps.q: How do you choose λ?
followUps.a: Try a range of values spaced by factors of 10 and keep the one with the best validation score.

shrinks every weight"] P --> L1["L1: λ Σ |w|
pushes some weights to exactly 0"]

note.idea: Add a penalty for large weights to the loss. L2 adds λΣw² and shrinks all weights a little. L1 adds λΣ|w| and pushes some weights to exactly zero.
note.analogy: A spending budget. L2 is a tax that grows fast for big spending, so you spend a little on everything. L1 is a flat fee per pound, so it is often best to spend nothing at all on weak items.
note.breaks: The 'cost' here is not money but model complexity. The right λ must be found with validation data, not guessed.
note.example: L2 adds 2λw to the gradient, so every step shrinks w a bit. This is called weight decay. L1 adds λ·sign(w): the same push however small w is, so small weights reach zero.
note.code:
loss = mse + lam * np.sum(w**2)      # L2
grad = grad_mse + 2 * lam * w

practice.explain: Explain why L1 gives exact zeros but L2 does not, with the budget picture.
practice.derive: Add λ‖w‖² to the squared-error loss and derive the new closed-form solution (ridge regression).
practice.build: Fit ridge and L1 regression for λ from 0.001 to 100. Plot each weight against λ.
practice.break: Use a huge λ and look at the predictions. Then forget to scale the features before using L2. Which features get punished unfairly?

derive.answer:
New loss: L(w) = ‖Xw − y‖² + λ‖w‖².

Gradient: ∇L = 2Xᵀ(Xw − y) + 2λw.

Set it to 0: XᵀXw − Xᵀy + λw = 0, so (XᵀX + λI)w = Xᵀy, and
w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy.

The only change from plain least squares is the +λI. It adds λ to every diagonal entry, which does two things: it shrinks the weights towards 0, and it makes the matrix always invertible for λ > 0, even with duplicate or highly correlated features. (Usually the bias is not penalised: centre y, or leave the bias column out of the λI.)

build.answer:
Ridge has the closed form above. L1 (the lasso) has no closed form because |w| has a corner at 0, so use proximal gradient descent: a normal gradient step on the squared error, then "soft-thresholding", which moves each weight towards 0 by λ times the step size and sets it to exactly 0 if it would cross.

On the standardised diabetes data the two plots look very different. Ridge weights shrink smoothly and all of them are still non-zero at λ = 100. Lasso weights drop to exactly 0 one by one as λ grows, and all ten are zero once λ passes about 45 (the largest |Xᵀy| / n: no feature is worth its fee beyond that). That is L1's feature selection.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes       # only to load the data

d = load_diabetes(scaled=False)
X = (d.data - d.data.mean(axis=0)) / d.data.std(axis=0)
y = d.target - d.target.mean()                    # centre y: no bias to penalise
n, p = X.shape
lams = np.logspace(-3, 2, 30)

def ridge(lam):                                   # minimises mean sq. error + lam·‖w‖²
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X / n + lam * np.eye(p), X.T @ y / n)

def lasso(lam, steps=3000):                       # minimises ½·mean sq. error + lam·‖w‖₁
    w, lr = np.zeros(p), 1 / np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X / n).max()
    for _ in range(steps):
        w = w - lr * X.T @ (X @ w - y) / n
        w = np.sign(w) * np.maximum(np.abs(w) - lr * lam, 0)   # soft-threshold
    return w

R = np.array([ridge(l) for l in lams])
L = np.array([lasso(l) for l in lams])
print("non-zero weights at lambda = 100:", (np.abs(R[-1]) > 1e-8).sum(), (np.abs(L[-1]) > 1e-8).sum())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, W, name in [(axes[0], R, "ridge (L2)"), (axes[1], L, "lasso (L1)")]:
    ax.plot(lams, W); ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_title(name); ax.set_xlabel("λ")
axes[0].set_ylabel("weight")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

break.answer:
With a huge λ, every weight is squashed to almost 0, so the model predicts nearly the same number, the average of y, for every input. It is a flat line: massive underfitting.

Forgetting to scale before L2 punishes features with small units unfairly. The penalty is on the size of the weights, not the size of the effect. Say a house's size is given in metres in one column and in millimetres in another. The millimetre column needs a weight 1,000 times smaller for the same effect, so the penalty barely touches it, while the metre column, needing a big weight, gets shrunk hard. The model ends up preferring features just because of their units.

In the demo, the same feature with the same true effect keeps almost all of its effect in millimetres but loses much of it in metres. Standardise first, so every feature competes fairly.
break.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
size_m = rng.normal(2.0, 0.5, 200)                  # one feature, two units
other = rng.normal(0, 1, 200)
y = 3 * size_m + 3 * other + rng.normal(0, 0.1, 200)

def ridge(X, y, lam):
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X / len(y) + lam * np.eye(X.shape[1]), X.T @ y / len(y))

for name, col in [("metres", size_m), ("millimetres", size_m * 1000)]:
    X = np.column_stack([col - col.mean(), other])
    w = ridge(X, y - y.mean(), lam=1.0)
    print(name, "effect of 1 metre:", round(w[0] * (1 if name == "metres" else 1000), 2))
# the true effect is 3 per metre in both cases

explain.answer:
Think of the weights as a spending budget, and the penalty as the cost of spending.

L2 is a tax that grows with the square of what you spend: spending a little costs almost nothing, spending a lot is very expensive. So it is best to spread the budget thinly across every item: each weight is shrunk, but small weights cost so little that there is no reason to cut them all the way to 0.

L1 is a flat fee per pound, however small the amount. Even a tiny bit of spending on a weak item costs the full rate, so it often makes sense to spend nothing on it at all. That is why L1 sets weak features exactly to 0, while L2 only makes them small.

topics.name: Bias–variance trade-off and overfitting
topics.definition: Bias is error from a model too simple to capture the pattern; variance is error from a model so flexible it chases the noise in its training data; good models balance the two.
topics.problem: Every model choice — degree, depth, number of features, k — moves you between underfitting and overfitting. Without this picture you can't tell whether to make a model bigger or smaller, or whether to collect more data. The bias–variance trade-off is the map for those decisions.
howItWorks: Take 12 noisy points from a smooth curve, and fit polynomials of growing degree.
Degree 1 (a line) can't bend: it misses the shape on training and validation data alike. That is high bias, or underfitting.
Degree 3 follows the real shape: training and validation errors are both low.
Degree 9 bends through almost every training point, but swings wildly in between: tiny training error, large validation error. That is high variance, or overfitting.
Plot both errors against degree. Training error keeps falling; validation error falls and then rises, a U shape. Choose the bottom of the U.
More data reduces variance, because a flexible model has less room to chase noise. A simpler model or regularisation reduces it too.
Formally: expected error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. You can trade the first two, but never beat the noise.
keyPoints: High bias: bad on training data too. Fix: a bigger model, better features, less regularisation.
High variance: good on training data, bad on validation. Fix: more data, regularisation, a simpler model, early stopping.
Training error alone can't tell you which problem you have. Compare it with validation error.
Learning curves (error against training-set size) also show it: a big, stable gap means variance.
Very large neural networks can break the simple U shape ("double descent", later in this phase).
mistakes: Picking the model with the lowest training error.
Adding complexity when the model is already overfitting.
Collecting more data to fix bias. It won't help a model that is too simple.

followUps.q: Training error 2%, validation error 25%. Bias or variance problem?
followUps.a: Variance: overfitting. Add data, regularise or simplify.

followUps.q: Training error 20%, validation error 21%. Bias or variance?
followUps.a: Bias: the model is too simple. Make it more flexible or add better features.

followUps.q: Why does more data reduce variance?
followUps.a: With more points, the noise averages out and a flexible model can't bend to every random wiggle.

followUps.q: What part of the error can never be removed?
followUps.a: The irreducible noise in the labels themselves.

derive.answer:
For a point x with true value y = f(x) + noise, averaged over many possible training sets:

E[(y − f̂(x))²] = (E[f̂(x)] − f(x))² + E[(f̂(x) − E[f̂(x)])²] + σ²
                       bias²                    variance                noise

Bias²: how far the average model is from the truth. If you could train on many different datasets and average the models, how wrong would that average still be? This is error from assumptions that are too simple, like a straight line for a curve.

Variance: how much the model jumps around between different training sets. This is error from being too sensitive to the particular sample you happened to get.

Noise (σ²): randomness in y itself that no model can predict. It is the floor: no model can do better than this.

build.answer:
Generate 30 training points from y = sin(2πx) plus noise, and 200 validation points the same way. Fit polynomials of degree 1 to 15 and record both errors.

Training error keeps falling as the degree rises, because a bigger polynomial can always bend closer to the training points. Validation error falls at first, reaches its lowest at a middle degree (3 to 5 on this data), then rises as the model starts chasing the noise. Choose the bottom of that U.

np.polynomial.Polynomial.fit rescales x internally, which keeps high degrees numerically stable.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
truth = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
x_tr, x_va = rng.random(30), rng.random(200)
y_tr = truth(x_tr) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 30)
y_va = truth(x_va) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 200)

degrees = range(1, 16)
train_err, val_err = [], []
for d in degrees:
    model = np.polynomial.Polynomial.fit(x_tr, y_tr, d)
    train_err.append(np.mean((model(x_tr) - y_tr) ** 2))
    val_err.append(np.mean((model(x_va) - y_va) ** 2))
best = degrees[int(np.argmin(val_err))]
print("best degree:", best)

plt.plot(degrees, train_err, label="train")
plt.plot(degrees, val_err, label="validation")
plt.axvline(best, linestyle=":", color="grey")
plt.yscale("log"); plt.xlabel("degree"); plt.ylabel("mean squared error")
plt.legend(); plt.show()

break.answer:
With 3,000 points, the validation curve barely rises at high degrees, and the best degree moves up (to around 6 to 10 on this data). The extra flexibility no longer hurts much.

Why more data reduces variance: a wiggly model overfits by bending to fit the noise in the few points it saw. With 30 points there is room between them to bend wildly. With 3,000, every bit of the curve is pinned down by many nearby points whose noise averages out, so the fitted curve hardly changes from one training set to the next. Variance shrinks roughly like 1/n, while bias doesn't change, so the best balance shifts towards more complex models.
break.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
truth = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
x_va = rng.random(2000)
y_va = truth(x_va) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 2000)
for n in [30, 3000]:
    x_tr = rng.random(n)
    y_tr = truth(x_tr) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n)
    errs = [np.mean((np.polynomial.Polynomial.fit(x_tr, y_tr, d)(x_va) - y_va) ** 2) for d in range(1, 16)]
    print(n, "points: best degree", int(np.argmin(errs)) + 1, "| error at degree 15:", round(errs[-1], 3))

explain.answer:
Two students prepare for an exam. The first memorises every answer in the practice book word for word. They score 100% on those exact questions, but a new question throws them completely: that is overfitting, or high variance. The second only learns "the answer is usually C". They do equally badly on old and new questions: that is underfitting, or high bias.

You want a third student, who learns the ideas behind the answers, so they do well on questions they have never seen. In ML, a model overfits when it learns the noise and quirks of its training data instead of the real pattern, and the sign is a big gap between training and validation scores.

topics.name: Metrics: precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, confusion matrix
topics.definition: Classification metrics count the four outcomes (true and false positives and negatives) and summarise them: precision, recall, F1, accuracy, and ROC-AUC across all thresholds.
topics.problem: Accuracy can lie. If 1% of transactions are fraud, a model that never flags anything is 99% accurate and completely useless. Different jobs care about different mistakes: a cancer screen must not miss cases (recall), a spam filter must not bin real email (precision). The right metric is what tells you whether a model does the job.
howItWorks: Pick a threshold and turn scores into yes/no predictions.
Count the four outcomes in a confusion matrix: TP (flagged, really positive), FP (flagged, really negative), FN (missed positive), TN (correctly left alone).
Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of everything flagged, how much was right?
Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of everything really positive, how much did we find?
F1 = 2·P·R / (P + R): one number that is only high when both are high.
Move the threshold: lower it and recall rises while precision usually falls; raise it and the reverse happens.

ROC curve: plot recall (true positive rate) against false positive rate for every threshold. The area under it (AUC) is the chance a random positive scores above a random negative: 0.5 is guessing, 1.0 is perfect.
keyPoints: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / everything. Misleading when classes are imbalanced.
Precision: "when it says yes, is it right?" Recall: "does it find them all?"
There is always a trade-off between them, controlled by the threshold.
ROC-AUC doesn't depend on the threshold. With very rare positives, the precision–recall curve is more telling.
Always report the threshold you used, and compare against a dumb baseline.
Choose the metric from the cost of each mistake, before you train.
mistakes: Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data.
Quoting precision without recall, or the other way round.
Choosing the threshold on the test set.
Mixing up FP and FN. Write out the 2 × 2 table every time.

followUps.q: TP = 60, FP = 20, FN = 40. Precision and recall?
For cancer screening, which matters more: precision or recall?
followUps.a: Recall. Missing a real case is far worse than a false alarm that a follow-up test can clear.

followUps.q: What does an AUC of 0.5 mean?
followUps.a: The model ranks positives above negatives no better than a coin flip.

followUps.q: You lower the threshold. What usually happens to precision and recall?
followUps.a: Recall goes up (more positives caught) and precision goes down (more false alarms).

100 are fraud"] --> F["model flags 80"] F --> TP["60 really fraud

false negatives"] TP --> PR["precision = 60 / 80 = 0.75"] TP --> RE["recall = 60 / 100 = 0.60"]

note.idea: A confusion matrix counts true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. Precision = TP/(TP + FP): of the items you flagged, how many were right? Recall = TP/(TP + FN): of the real ones, how many did you find? F1 balances the two. ROC-AUC measures how well scores rank positives above negatives.
note.analogy: Fishing with a net. Precision: how much of your catch is fish, not old boots? Recall: how many of the fish in the lake did you catch?
note.breaks: In fishing you can see your catch. In ML, the threshold you choose changes both numbers, so always say which threshold you used.
note.example: 10,000 transactions, 100 are fraud. The model flags 80, and 60 of those are fraud. Precision = 60/80 = 0.75. Recall = 60/100 = 0.60. F1 ≈ 0.67.

derive.answer:
TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 930, so 1,000 cases in total.

Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total = (40 + 930) / 1,000 = 0.97.
Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = 0.80. Of the 50 flagged, 40 were right.
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 60 ≈ 0.667. Of the 60 real positives, 40 were found.
F1 = 2·P·R / (P + R) = 2·0.8·0.667 / 1.467 ≈ 0.727. (Or directly: 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN) = 80 / 110.)

Notice that accuracy, 97%, looks far better than the model really is: it misses a third of the positives. Accuracy is flattered by the 930 easy negatives.

build.answer:
Precision, recall and F1 come straight from the counts. For ROC-AUC, sort by score from high to low and walk down the list, lowering the threshold one example at a time: each positive moves the curve up (true positive rate), each negative moves it right (false positive rate). The area under that curve, by the trapezoid rule, is the AUC.

Check it with its meaning: AUC is the chance that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative, which you can count directly by comparing every pair. Both give the same number. (Ties in scores need care; this version assumes distinct scores.)
build.code:
import numpy as np

def precision(y, pred):
    tp, fp = np.sum((pred == 1) & (y == 1)), np.sum((pred == 1) & (y == 0))
    return tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0

def recall(y, pred):
    tp, fn = np.sum((pred == 1) & (y == 1)), np.sum((pred == 0) & (y == 1))
    return tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0

def f1(y, pred):
    p, r = precision(y, pred), recall(y, pred)
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r) if p + r else 0.0

def roc_auc(y, scores):
    y = y[np.argsort(-scores)]                        # highest score first
    tpr = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(y) / y.sum()])
    fpr = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(1 - y) / (1 - y).sum()])
    return np.trapezoid(tpr, fpr)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y = rng.integers(0, 2, 500)
scores = y + rng.normal(0, 0.8, 500)                  # noisy but useful scores
pairs = np.mean(scores[y == 1][:, None] > scores[y == 0][None, :])
print(round(roc_auc(y, scores), 4), round(pairs, 4))   # the same
pred = (scores > 0.5).astype(int)
print(round(precision(y, pred), 3), round(recall(y, pred), 3), round(f1(y, pred), 3))

break.code:
import numpy as np

y = np.array([1] * 100 + [0] * 9900)          # 1% fraud
pred = np.zeros_like(y)                       # always "not fraud"
tp = np.sum((pred == 1) & (y == 1))
print("accuracy", (pred == y).mean())          # 0.99
print("recall", tp / y.sum())                  # 0.0
print("flagged", pred.sum())                   # 0: precision is 0 / 0

explain.answer:
Fishing with a net. Precision asks: of everything in your net, how much is actually fish, and not old boots? Recall asks: of all the fish in the lake, how many did you catch?

A huge net catches nearly every fish (high recall) but also lots of boots (low precision). A small, careful net catches only fish (high precision) but misses most of them (low recall). You choose the net by what a mistake costs: for a disease screening test, missing a sick person is worse, so you want high recall; for a spam filter, losing a real email is worse, so you want high precision.

topics.name: Cross-validation and data leakage
topics.definition: Cross-validation scores a model by rotating which slice of the data is held out, so every row is tested once; data leakage is any way information from the held-out data sneaks into training.
topics.problem: One train/validation split can be lucky or unlucky, especially with small datasets, so a single score can mislead you by several percent. Cross-validation gives a steadier score and tells you how much it wobbles. Leakage is the most common reason a model that looked brilliant in testing fails in real use, so you need to know where it hides.
howItWorks: Shuffle the rows and cut them into k equal folds, for example k = 5.
Round 1: train on folds 2–5, score on fold 1. Round 2: train on folds 1, 3, 4 and 5, score on fold 2. And so on.
After k rounds every row has been scored exactly once, by a model that never saw it.
Report the mean of the k scores and their spread (standard deviation). A big spread means one split could have misled you.
Every preprocessing step that learns from data (scaling, filling missing values, picking features) must be fitted inside each round, on that round's training folds only.
Group related rows: all scans of one patient must sit in the same fold. For time series, always train on earlier data and test on later data.
keyPoints: k-fold: k models, k scores; report mean ± spread.
k = 5 or 10 is typical; leave-one-out (k = n) is costly and noisy.
Stratified folds keep the class balance the same in every fold.
Group k-fold keeps related rows together; time-series splits only look forwards.
Leakage: anything at training time that would not be known at prediction time.
Suspiciously good results are a reason to hunt for leakage, not to celebrate.
mistakes: Scaling or selecting features on the full dataset before splitting.
The same person, house or document in both training and test folds.
A feature computed from the label, or from the future (a "days until churn" column).
Using cross-validation to choose settings and then reporting that same score as final.

followUps.q: Why use cross-validation instead of one validation split?
followUps.a: The score no longer depends on one lucky or unlucky split, every row is used for testing once, and you also learn how much the score varies.

followUps.q: Give an example of data leakage.
followUps.a: Standardising with the mean of all rows, test rows included; or the same patient's scans in both training and test data.

followUps.q: How should you split time-series data?
followUps.a: By time: train on earlier periods and test on later ones, never shuffled.

followUps.q: Your model scores 99.9% on a hard problem. What should you suspect?
followUps.a: Leakage: some feature or preprocessing step is giving away the answer.

build.answer:
k_fold shuffles the row numbers once and cuts them into k nearly equal folds; each fold takes a turn as the test set. Here it scores a simple nearest-centroid classifier (predict the class whose average is closest) on the breast-cancer data, with scaling fitted inside each fold on that fold's training rows only.

Report the mean and the spread across folds, such as 0.93 ± 0.03. The spread tells you how much the score depends on which rows ended up in the test set.
build.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer     # only to load the data

def k_fold(n, k, seed=0):
    folds = np.array_split(np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(n), k)
    for i in range(k):
        yield np.concatenate(folds[:i] + folds[i + 1:]), folds[i]

data = load_breast_cancer()
X, y = data.data, data.target
scores = []
for train, test in k_fold(len(X), 5):
    mean, std = X[train].mean(axis=0), X[train].std(axis=0)   # fit on training rows only
    Xtr, Xte = (X[train] - mean) / std, (X[test] - mean) / std
    centres = np.stack([Xtr[y[train] == c].mean(axis=0) for c in (0, 1)])
    pred = np.argmin(((Xte[:, None, :] - centres) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
    scores.append((pred == y[test]).mean())
print(f"{np.mean(scores):.3f} ± {np.std(scores):.3f}", np.round(scores, 3))

break.answer:
Two leaks, measured with 5-fold cross-validation on data that has no real pattern at all (random features, random labels), so the honest score should be about 50%:

1. A feature built from the label (a noisy copy of y): the score jumps to almost 100%. In real life this looks like "refund issued" when predicting fraud, or a date that is only filled in after the outcome.

2. Choosing features using all the data: pick the 20 features, out of 10,000, most correlated with the labels on the full dataset, then cross-validate. The score rises to roughly 80% or more, on pure noise. Doing the selection inside each fold, on training rows only, brings it back to about 50%.

Scaling with all the data is the same kind of mistake, but its effect is usually small; it is still wrong. The general rule: anything learned from data, whether scaling, feature selection or filling in missing values, must be fitted on the training rows only, inside each fold.
break.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 100
X, y = rng.normal(size=(n, 10_000)), rng.integers(0, 2, n)     # pure noise

def cv_accuracy(X, y, select=None, k=5):
    folds = np.array_split(rng.permutation(n), k)
    scores = []
    for i in range(k):
        test = folds[i]
        train = np.concatenate(folds[:i] + folds[i + 1:])
        cols = select(X[train], y[train]) if select else slice(None)
        Xtr, Xte = X[train][:, cols], X[test][:, cols]
        centres = np.stack([Xtr[y[train] == c].mean(axis=0) for c in (0, 1)])
        pred = np.argmin(((Xte[:, None, :] - centres) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
        scores.append((pred == y[test]).mean())
    return np.mean(scores)

top20 = lambda X, y: np.argsort(-np.abs(np.corrcoef(X.T, y)[-1, :-1]))[:20]

label_feature = np.column_stack([y + rng.normal(0, 0.1, n)])
print("feature built from the label:", cv_accuracy(label_feature, y))
print("features chosen on ALL data:", cv_accuracy(X[:, top20(X, y)], y))
print("features chosen inside each fold:", cv_accuracy(X, y, select=top20))

explain.answer:
Data leakage is like a student who saw the exam answers the night before. Their score is real, but it tells you nothing about what they know, and in the next exam, without the answers, they fail.

A model leaks when information it won't have at prediction time sneaks into training or evaluation: the test rows' statistics used for scaling, a feature that is really a consequence of the label, or future data used to predict the past. The model then looks brilliant in testing and disappoints in real use.

topics.name: Feature scaling and encoding
topics.definition: Feature scaling puts numeric features on similar ranges, and encoding turns categories into numbers, so that models treat every feature fairly and don't invent orders that aren't there.
topics.problem: Models only see numbers. A feature measured in thousands drowns out one measured in single digits in any distance or gradient, and coding "red, green, blue" as 1, 2, 3 tells the model green sits between the other two. Getting this wrong quietly ruins k-NN, SVMs, regularised models and neural networks, while trees barely notice.
howItWorks: Standardisation: for each numeric feature, subtract the training mean and divide by the training standard deviation. The result has mean 0 and spread 1.
Min–max scaling squeezes values into 0 to 1 instead. It is handy for pixel values, but sensitive to outliers.
Fit the scaler on the training rows only, then apply the same mean and standard deviation to validation and test rows.
After scaling, the loss surface is rounder, so gradient descent heads straight for the minimum instead of zig-zagging.
One-hot encoding: give each category its own 0/1 column. red = [1, 0, 0], green = [0, 1, 0], blue = [0, 0, 1].
Plan for categories you have never seen: map them to an "unknown" column, or all zeros.
For categories with a real order (small < medium < large), ordinal numbers 0, 1, 2 are fine.
keyPoints: Distance-based and gradient-based models need scaling. Trees and forests don't.
Standardise: (x − mean) / std, with statistics from the training rows only.
One-hot for categories with no order; ordinal numbers only for real orders.
Categories with thousands of values (postcodes, user ids) need other tricks: hashing, frequency or learned embeddings (Phase 3).
Log-transform heavily skewed values like prices or incomes before scaling.
Keep the fitted scaler and encoder with the model: they are part of it.
mistakes: Fitting the scaler on all the data: leakage.
Coding unordered categories as 1, 2, 3.
Forgetting to apply the same scaling at prediction time.
One-hot encoding a feature with 50,000 values into 50,000 columns.

followUps.q: A feature has training mean 50 and standard deviation 10. What does the value 70 become after standardising?
followUps.a: (70 − 50) / 10 = 2: two standard deviations above the mean.

followUps.q: Why don't decision trees need scaling?
followUps.a: They only compare a feature with a threshold. Stretching the feature moves the threshold, but the split stays the same.

followUps.q: Why is red = 1, green = 2, blue = 3 a bad encoding?
followUps.a: It invents an order and distances: the model would think green is "between" red and blue, and that blue is twice as far from red as green is.

followUps.q: What should the encoder do with a colour it never saw in training?
followUps.a: Map it to an "unknown" column (or all zeros) instead of crashing or guessing.

derive.answer:
Standardise [10, 20, 30]:
Mean = 20.
Standard deviation (dividing by n, as scalers do) = √(((10 − 20)² + 0² + (30 − 20)²) / 3) = √(200/3) ≈ 8.165.
Result: [(10 − 20)/8.165, 0, (30 − 20)/8.165] ≈ [−1.225, 0, 1.225].
(Dividing by n − 1 instead gives a standard deviation of 10 and the result [−1, 0, 1]. Either is fine if you are consistent.)

One-hot ['cat', 'dog', 'cat', 'bird'], with the categories in alphabetical order [bird, cat, dog]:
cat → [0, 1, 0]
dog → [0, 0, 1]
cat → [0, 1, 0]
bird → [1, 0, 0]
Each category gets its own column, so no false order like bird < cat < dog is invented.

build.answer:
Both have the same two-step shape: fit learns from the training data only (the means and standard deviations, or the list of categories), and transform applies what was learned to any data, including validation and test data. Fitting on all the data would leak information from the test set.

The tests check that the scaled training data has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, that test data is scaled with the training numbers, and that one-hot rows each contain a single 1.

break.answer:
k-NN without scaling: when one feature is in thousands (say, salary) and the other in decimals (say, a 0–1 score that really decides the label), the distance is almost entirely the salary difference. The useful feature is drowned out, and accuracy falls to about chance (around 50%). With both features standardised, accuracy jumps back up (above 90% here).

A category the encoder never saw: the code above raises a KeyError. In production that crashes on the first new value, such as a new country or product. Decide on purpose: either map unknown values to an all-zeros row (or an "other" column) and log them so you notice, or fail loudly if an unknown value means bad data. Either way, it should be a choice, not a surprise.
break.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 400
score = rng.random(n)                                  # decides the label
salary = rng.normal(40_000, 10_000, n)                 # big numbers, no signal
y = (score > 0.5).astype(int)
X = np.column_stack([salary, score])
tr, te = np.arange(300), np.arange(300, n)

def knn_accuracy(X, k=5):
    d = ((X[te][:, None, :] - X[tr][None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)
    nearest = np.argsort(d, axis=1)[:, :k]
    pred = (y[tr][nearest].mean(axis=1) > 0.5).astype(int)
    return (pred == y[te]).mean()

Xs = (X - X[tr].mean(axis=0)) / X[tr].std(axis=0)
print(f"unscaled {knn_accuracy(X):.0%}, scaled {knn_accuracy(Xs):.0%}")

index = {"bird": 0, "cat": 1, "dog": 2}
try:
    index["fish"]
except KeyError as e:
    print("unknown category:", e)

explain.answer:
Describe a house by its size in square metres (100) and its number of rooms (3). A distance-based model, like k-NN, compares houses by adding up the differences. A difference of 20 m² and a difference of 2 rooms are both big for a house, but the model just sees 20 and 2.

It is as if size is shouting and rooms are whispering: the model hears only the loudest feature, whatever its units happen to be. Scaling puts every feature at the same volume, so the model listens to all of them according to what they actually tell it.

topics.name: k-nearest neighbours
topics.definition: k-nearest neighbours predicts by finding the k training points closest to a new point and letting them vote (or averaging their values, for regression).
topics.problem: Sometimes the simplest idea is enough: things that are close together tend to be alike. k-NN needs no training, adapts to any shape of boundary, and makes a strong baseline. Learning it also teaches you why distances, scaling and the curse of dimensionality matter for every method that compares points, including vector search for LLMs.
howItWorks: Store all the training points. That is the whole "training".
For a new point, measure its distance to every training point, usually straight-line (Euclidean) distance.
Sort, and take the k nearest.
Classification: majority vote among those k labels. Regression: the average of their values.
Choose k with validation data. k = 1 follows every quirk of the data (high variance); a large k smooths everything out (high bias).
Scale the features first, or the feature with the largest units decides every distance.
keyPoints: No training step; all the work happens at prediction time, so prediction is slow on big data.
Small k: wiggly boundaries, overfits. Large k: smooth boundaries, underfits.
Use an odd k for two classes, to avoid ties.
Feature scaling is essential.
Curse of dimensionality: with hundreds of features, all points are nearly the same distance apart.
Fast approximate nearest-neighbour search (Phase 5) makes this idea work at the scale of millions of vectors.
mistakes: Forgetting to scale features.
Choosing k on the test set.
Using it with many irrelevant features: noise dimensions swamp the useful ones.
Expecting fast predictions on millions of rows without an index.

followUps.q: What does k-NN learn during training?
followUps.a: Nothing: it just stores the data. All the work happens when predicting.

followUps.q: What happens with k = 1?
followUps.a: Each prediction copies its single nearest neighbour, so the model follows every noisy point: low bias, high variance.

followUps.q: Why scale features for k-NN?
followUps.a: Distances add up feature differences, so a feature in large units would decide every distance on its own.

followUps.q: How would you use k-NN for regression?
followUps.a: Average the values of the k nearest neighbours instead of voting.

flowchart LR N["new point"] --> D["measure the distance
to every training point"] D --> K["take the k = 3 nearest"] K --> V["their labels: A, A, B"] V --> W["majority vote → A"]
