derive.answer:
A layer from a inputs to b outputs has an a × b weight matrix plus b biases.

Layer 1, 784 → 128: 784 × 128 = 100,352 weights + 128 biases = 100,480 parameters.
Layer 2, 128 → 10: 128 × 10 = 1,280 weights + 10 biases = 1,290 parameters.

Total: 100,480 + 1,290 = 101,770 parameters.

Notice that almost all of them are in the first layer: wide inputs are expensive. That is one reason CNNs, which share a small filter across the whole image, need far fewer parameters for images.
derive.code:
import torch.nn as nn
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 10))
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))     # 101770

build.answer: For a batch X of shape (batch, 784): h = relu(X @ W1 + b1) has shape (batch, 128), and the scores are h @ W2 + b2 with shape (batch, 10). The biases broadcast across the batch. Assert every shape: shape bugs are the most common bugs in deep learning code, and they are silent when broadcasting hides them.
build.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
W1, b1 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / 784), (784, 128)), np.zeros(128)
W2, b2 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / 128), (128, 10)), np.zeros(10)

def forward(X):
    assert X.ndim == 2 and X.shape[1] == 784, X.shape
    h = np.maximum(0, X @ W1 + b1)
    assert h.shape == (X.shape[0], 128), h.shape
    scores = h @ W2 + b2
    assert scores.shape == (X.shape[0], 10), scores.shape
    return scores

print(forward(rng.random((32, 784))).shape)        # (32, 10)

break.answer:
If every weight starts at the same number, every hidden neuron computes exactly the same thing. They get the same input, do the same sum, and give the same output. In the backward pass they receive the same gradient, so the update changes them all by the same amount, and they are still identical afterwards. Forever.

So a layer of 128 neurons behaves like one neuron copied 128 times: the network can't learn different features. This is "symmetry", and random initialisation is what breaks it. (Biases can start at 0; the weights must not all be equal.)
break.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 5), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(5, 1))
for p in model.parameters():
    nn.init.constant_(p, 0.3)                      # every weight the same
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
X, y = torch.randn(64, 4), torch.randn(64, 1)
for _ in range(50):
    opt.zero_grad()
    nn.functional.mse_loss(model(X), y).backward()
    opt.step()
W = model[0].weight
print(torch.allclose(W, W[0].expand_as(W)))         # True: all 5 neurons still identical

explain.answer:
Think of rows of judges. In the first row, each judge looks at all the evidence (the input numbers), weighs each piece in their own way, adds it up, and gives a score; if the score is below zero they say nothing (that is the ReLU). The next row of judges doesn't see the evidence at all, only the first row's scores, and combines those in their own way. The last row gives the final verdict, such as one score per digit.

Training adjusts how much every judge trusts every piece of what they hear. Because each row builds on the one before, later rows can recognise complicated patterns made out of simpler ones.

topics.name: Activation functions, and why non-linearity matters
topics.definition: An activation function is the non-linear step applied after each layer's weighted sum; without it, any number of layers collapses into a single linear layer.
topics.problem: The whole point of depth is to build curved, complicated functions. But a matrix times a matrix is just another matrix, so stacked linear layers can never do more than one linear layer. The activation is the small non-linear bend that makes depth useful. Your choice also decides whether gradients flow well through many layers.
howItWorks: Two linear layers: W2(W1x) = (W2W1)x, which is one matrix. No matter how many you stack, the result is a straight-line model.
Put a ReLU between them: W2·ReLU(W1x). Each hidden neuron now switches on only above its own threshold, adding one bend where it does.
Add more neurons, get more bends. With enough of them, a network can follow almost any smooth curve: the universal approximation idea.
ReLU(z) = max(0, z): cheap, with slope exactly 1 when active, so gradients pass straight through. The default for hidden layers.

Sigmoid squashes into 0 to 1, and tanh into −1 to 1. Both flatten at the ends, where their slope is nearly 0, so stacking many of them makes gradients vanish. They survive as gates (LSTMs) and as output squashers.
GELU and SiLU are smooth versions of ReLU that let small negative values through. Transformers use them.
keyPoints: No activation means no depth: the whole stack is one linear map.
ReLU is the default for hidden layers. GELU or SiLU in transformers.
Sigmoid for yes/no outputs and gates; softmax for picking one of several classes.
Saturating functions (sigmoid, tanh) give tiny gradients at their ends.
"Dead ReLUs": a neuron whose input is always negative outputs 0 and gets no gradient, so it never recovers. Big learning rates make this more likely.
Each ReLU neuron adds a hinge, so the network's output is a piecewise-linear function.
mistakes: Using sigmoid in every hidden layer of a deep network.
Forgetting the activation in a hand-written layer.
Putting ReLU on a regression output that should be able to go negative.

followUps.q: Why does W2(W1x) gain nothing over a single layer?
followUps.a: It equals (W2W1)x, which is just another single matrix applied to x.

followUps.q: What is ReLU(−3), and what is its slope there?
followUps.a: 0, and the slope is 0 too: no gradient flows through an inactive ReLU.

followUps.q: Why are sigmoids rarely used in deep hidden layers?
followUps.a: Their slope is small everywhere and almost zero at the ends, so gradients shrink layer after layer.

followUps.q: What is a "dead" ReLU?
followUps.a: A neuron whose input is negative for every example, so it always outputs 0, gets zero gradient and never changes.

diagram.caption: ReLU is 0 then a straight line; sigmoid squashes into 0 to 1; tanh squashes into −1 to 1. The bends are what let networks learn curves.

note.idea: Without a non-linear activation, stacking layers is useless: two linear layers equal one linear layer. ReLU(x) = max(0, x) is the default. Sigmoid and tanh squash values. GELU is a smooth ReLU used in transformers.
note.analogy: Straight Lego bricks can only build straight walls. Activations are the hinged pieces that let you build curves.
note.breaks: Lego hinges are few and fixed. A network learns where to bend, and with enough neurons it can approximate almost any shape.
note.example: W2(W1x) = (W2W1)x, which is just one matrix. A ReLU in between stops this collapse. A warning: the sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so ten sigmoid layers can shrink a gradient by 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 0.000001.

practice.explain: Explain why a network with no activations is just one linear layer.
practice.derive: Write the derivatives of ReLU, sigmoid and tanh. What is the largest possible value of each?
practice.build: Train the same small MLP on a curved 2D dataset (like two moons) with no activation, with ReLU, and with tanh. Plot the three decision boundaries.
practice.break: Stack 20 sigmoid layers and print the gradient size at each layer. Then count dead ReLU units after training with a huge learning rate.

derive.answer:
ReLU: relu(x) = max(0, x). Derivative: 1 if x > 0, 0 if x < 0 (undefined at exactly 0; frameworks use 0). Largest value: 1.

Sigmoid: σ(x) = 1/(1 + e⁻ˣ). Derivative: σ(x)(1 − σ(x)). It is largest at x = 0, where σ = 0.5, giving 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25.

Tanh: derivative 1 − tanh²(x). Largest at x = 0, where tanh = 0, giving 1.

Why it matters: in backprop the gradient is multiplied by these at every layer. With sigmoid, each layer multiplies by at most 0.25, so ten layers shrink it by at least 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 0.000001. ReLU passes 1 for active units, which is why deep networks use ReLU-like activations.

build.answer:
Same MLP (2 → 32 → 32 → 1), same training, three activations, on the two-moons data.

With no activation, the whole network is one linear function, so its boundary is a straight line, and it gets about 88% because a line can't follow the curve. With ReLU and with tanh, the boundary bends around the moons and accuracy reaches 100%. ReLU's boundary is made of straight pieces with corners; tanh's is smoother.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons           # only to make the toy data

X, y = make_moons(500, noise=0.1, random_state=0)
X, y = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32)
grid = torch.tensor(np.stack(np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1.5, 2.5, 200), np.linspace(-1, 1.5, 200)), -1).reshape(-1, 2), dtype=torch.float32)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4))
for ax, (name, act) in zip(axes, [("none", nn.Identity()), ("ReLU", nn.ReLU()), ("tanh", nn.Tanh())]):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), act, nn.Linear(32, 32), act, nn.Linear(32, 1))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
    for _ in range(1000):
        opt.zero_grad()
        nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(model(X).squeeze(1), y).backward()
        opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        acc = ((model(X).squeeze(1) > 0) == y.bool()).float().mean().item()
        ax.contourf(grid[:, 0].reshape(200, 200), grid[:, 1].reshape(200, 200),
                    (model(grid) > 0).reshape(200, 200), alpha=0.3)
    ax.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=y, s=6); ax.set_title(f"{name}: {acc:.0%}")
    print(name, f"{acc:.0%}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

break.answer:
20 sigmoid layers: the gradient that reaches the first layer is tiny, about 10¹⁷ times smaller than at the last layer in the run below, shrinking by a factor of about 8 per layer, because every layer multiplies it by σ′ ≤ 0.25 (and by weights smaller than 1). The early layers effectively stop learning: vanishing gradients.

Dead ReLUs: train with a huge learning rate and one big update can push a unit's bias so negative that its input is below 0 for every example. Then it always outputs 0, its gradient is always 0, and it never recovers. In the run below, about a quarter of the hidden units are dead after 50 steps with a learning rate of 10, against none with 0.1. Fixes: a sensible learning rate, good initialisation, or Leaky ReLU / GELU, which keep a small slope below 0.
break.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
layers = []
for _ in range(20):
    layers += [nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Sigmoid()]
deep = nn.Sequential(*layers, nn.Linear(64, 1))
deep(torch.randn(128, 64)).pow(2).mean().backward()
norms = [deep[i].weight.grad.norm().item() for i in range(0, 40, 2)]
print(f"gradient at layer 20: {norms[-1]:.1e}, at layer 1: {norms[0]:.1e}")

X = torch.randn(512, 10)
y = (X[:, 0] > 0).long()
for lr in [0.1, 10.0]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 100), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(100, 2))
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for _ in range(50):
        opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(X), y).backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        dead = (net[1](net[0](X)).max(dim=0).values == 0).float().mean().item()
    print(f"lr {lr}: {dead:.0%} of hidden units dead")

explain.answer:
A layer with no activation computes W·x + b, a linear function. Feed that into another linear layer and you get W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂ = (W₂W₁)x + (W₂b₁ + b₂). That is again just one matrix times x plus one bias: a single linear layer.

However many linear layers you stack, they collapse into one, so the network can only ever draw straight lines (or flat planes) between classes. A non-linear activation between the layers, like ReLU, stops the collapse: each layer can now bend the space, and stacking them builds complicated curved shapes.

topics.name: Backpropagation by hand
topics.definition: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule from the output backwards, reusing each intermediate result.
topics.problem: Gradient descent needs one gradient per weight, and a network can have billions of weights. Nudging each weight separately to measure its effect would need billions of forward passes. Backprop gets every gradient at the cost of about one extra pass, which is what makes training deep networks possible at all.
howItWorks: Forward pass: compute and remember every intermediate value. For L = (w·x − y)² with w = 1, x = 2 and y = 5: ŷ = 2, e = ŷ − y = −3, L = 9.
Start at the end: dL/dL = 1.
Each operation passes back (the gradient arriving from above) × (its own local derivative). L = e², whose local derivative is 2e = −6, so dL/de = −6.
e = ŷ − y has local derivative 1 with respect to ŷ, so dL/dŷ = −6.
ŷ = w·x has local derivative x = 2 with respect to w, so dL/dw = −6 × 2 = −12.
When one value feeds several later operations, the gradients coming back along each path are added together.
Gradient descent then uses it: w ← w − η·(−12), so w increases, which lowers the loss.
keyPoints: Every node only needs its local derivative; the chain rule glues them together.
Gradients flowing into the same value from different paths are summed.
A forward pass saves activations, and the backward pass reuses them: that is why training needs more memory than inference.
Matrix form for y = xW: dL/dW = xᵀ·(dL/dy) and dL/dx = (dL/dy)·Wᵀ.
Always verify hand-written gradients with a numerical gradient check.
The cost of a backward pass is roughly twice a forward pass.
mistakes: Overwriting a gradient instead of adding to it when a value is used twice.
Missing a transpose in the matrix version: the shapes usually tell you.
Forgetting that the local derivative uses the values saved from the forward pass.

followUps.q: In one sentence, what does each node do in the backward pass?
followUps.a: It multiplies the gradient arriving from above by its own local derivative and passes the result to its inputs.

followUps.q: A value feeds two later operations. How do you combine the gradients coming back?
followUps.a: Add them: the total effect is the sum of its effects along each path.

followUps.q: For y = xW, what is dL/dW?
followUps.a: xᵀ times dL/dy.

followUps.q: Why does backprop need to store the forward pass?
followUps.a: The local derivatives depend on the forward values, for example the x in d(wx)/dw.

diagram.caption: Solid arrows are the forward pass; dotted arrows carry gradients backwards. Multiplying them along the path is the chain rule.

note.idea: Backprop computes the gradient of the loss for every weight, using the chain rule from the output backwards. Each step passes back: (gradient from above) × (its own local derivative).
note.analogy: A factory makes a faulty product. You trace back station by station, asking how much each one contributed to the fault.
note.breaks: In a factory, blame often goes to one station. In backprop, blame is shared, and it is added up across every path.
note.example: L = (wx − y)², with x = 2, y = 5, w = 1. Forward: ŷ = 2, error e = ŷ − y = −3, L = 9. Backward: dL/de = 2e = −6, de/dŷ = 1, dŷ/dw = x = 2. So dL/dw = −6 × 2 = −12. The gradient is negative, so increasing w lowers the loss.

practice.derive: For y = w2 · relu(w1 · x), with x = 2, w1 = 0.5, w2 = −1, target 3 and loss (y − target)², compute every gradient by hand.
practice.build: Write the full backward pass for a 2-layer MLP with softmax and cross-entropy in NumPy. Check every gradient with your gradient checker.
practice.break: Plant a bug on purpose: forget one transpose in the backward pass. Does your gradient checker catch it? How big is the error?

derive.answer:
Forward pass, keeping every value:
a = w1·x = 0.5 × 2 = 1
h = relu(a) = 1 (a > 0, so ReLU passes it)
y = w2·h = −1 × 1 = −1
L = (y − target)² = (−1 − 3)² = 16

Backward pass, from the loss back:
∂L/∂y = 2(y − target) = 2 × (−4) = −8
∂L/∂w2 = ∂L/∂y × h = −8 × 1 = −8
∂L/∂h = ∂L/∂y × w2 = −8 × (−1) = 8
∂L/∂a = ∂L/∂h × relu′(a) = 8 × 1 = 8
∂L/∂w1 = ∂L/∂a × x = 8 × 2 = 16
(and ∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂a × w1 = 4, if you need it)

Sanity check: y = −1 is far below the target 3, so we want y bigger. ∂L/∂w2 < 0 says "increase w2", which raises y. ∂L/∂w1 > 0 says "decrease w1": since w2 is negative, a smaller h makes y less negative. Both make sense.
derive.code:
import torch
w1 = torch.tensor(0.5, requires_grad=True)
w2 = torch.tensor(-1.0, requires_grad=True)
L = (w2 * torch.relu(w1 * 2.0) - 3.0) ** 2
L.backward()
print(L.item(), w1.grad.item(), w2.grad.item())     # 16.0 16.0 -8.0

build.answer:
Forward: z1 = X·W1 + b1, h = relu(z1), z2 = h·W2 + b2, p = softmax(z2), loss = mean of −log p[correct class].

Backward, in reverse:
dz2 = (p − Y) / n (softmax and cross-entropy together, Y one-hot)
dW2 = hᵀ·dz2, db2 = sum of dz2 over the batch
dh = dz2·W2ᵀ
dz1 = dh × (z1 > 0)
dW1 = Xᵀ·dz1, db1 = sum of dz1

The gradient checker nudges every parameter by ±h and compares with these formulas. The relative error is around 1e-7 or smaller for all four parameter arrays, so the backward pass is right.
build.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d, hidden, k = 8, 5, 6, 3
X, labels = rng.normal(size=(n, d)), rng.integers(0, k, n)
Y = np.eye(k)[labels]
params = {"W1": rng.normal(0, 0.5, (d, hidden)), "b1": np.zeros(hidden),
          "W2": rng.normal(0, 0.5, (hidden, k)), "b2": np.zeros(k)}

def loss_and_grads(P):
    z1 = X @ P["W1"] + P["b1"]; h = np.maximum(0, z1)
    z2 = h @ P["W2"] + P["b2"]
    z2 = z2 - z2.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    p = np.exp(z2) / np.exp(z2).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    loss = -np.mean(np.log(p[np.arange(n), labels]))
    dz2 = (p - Y) / n
    dh = dz2 @ P["W2"].T
    dz1 = dh * (z1 > 0)
    return loss, {"W1": X.T @ dz1, "b1": dz1.sum(0), "W2": h.T @ dz2, "b2": dz2.sum(0)}

_, grads = loss_and_grads(params)
for name in params:
    numeric = np.zeros_like(params[name])
    for i in np.ndindex(params[name].shape):
        old = params[name][i]
        params[name][i] = old + 1e-5; up = loss_and_grads(params)[0]
        params[name][i] = old - 1e-5; down = loss_and_grads(params)[0]
        params[name][i] = old
        numeric[i] = (up - down) / 2e-5
    rel = np.abs(numeric - grads[name]).max() / (np.abs(numeric).max() + 1e-12)
    print(name, f"relative error {rel:.1e}")

break.answer:
Yes, the checker catches it, and loudly. With dW2 = dz2ᵀ·h instead of hᵀ·dz2, the shape is wrong, (3, 6) instead of (6, 3), so the comparison crashes at once. With square matrices a missing transpose doesn't crash, and that is the dangerous case: the gradient has the right shape but the wrong values. The relative error is then large, around 1 (100%), compared with about 1e-7 for correct code.

That gap is what makes gradient checking so useful: correct backprop agrees to about 7 digits; a bug disagrees in the first digit. A relative error above about 1e-4 almost always means a bug.
break.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X, W = rng.normal(size=(4, 4)), rng.normal(size=(4, 4))   # square: no shape error to save you
loss = lambda W: np.sum((X @ W) ** 2) / 2
right = X.T @ (X @ W)                                     # dL/dW
wrong = (X @ W).T @ X                                     # the forgotten transpose: same shape!
numeric = np.zeros_like(W)
for i in np.ndindex(W.shape):
    E = np.zeros_like(W); E[i] = 1e-5
    numeric[i] = (loss(W + E) - loss(W - E)) / 2e-5
rel = lambda g: np.abs(g - numeric).max() / np.abs(numeric).max()
print(f"correct: {rel(right):.1e}, missing transpose: {rel(wrong):.1e}")

explain.answer:
A factory turns out a faulty product. You don't blame everyone equally: you trace back station by station. The last station asks "how much of the fault came from my step?", keeps that share of the blame, and passes the rest back to the station that fed it, scaled by how strongly that station's work affects its own. Every station does the same, all the way to the start.

That is backprop: the loss is the fault, each layer is a station, and the "how much did this step affect the next?" is the local derivative. The blame gets shared at every point where one output fed several things, or several inputs fed one thing: a weight's gradient is its input times the blame arriving from above, and a neuron that feeds several later neurons adds up the blame from all of them.

topics.name: Autograd and computational graphs
topics.definition: Autograd records every operation into a computational graph as your code runs, then loss.backward() walks the graph in reverse to fill in every gradient automatically.
topics.problem: Writing backward passes by hand is slow and error-prone, and real models have thousands of operations. Autograd removes that work: you write only the forward computation and get exact gradients for free. Knowing how it works explains PyTorch's rules — why gradients add up, why you call zero_grad(), why no_grad() saves memory.
howItWorks: Mark the tensors that need gradients (requires_grad=True); model parameters already are.
As each operation runs, autograd creates a node that remembers its inputs and how to compute its local derivative.
For L = (a·b + c)·f with a = 2, b = −3, c = 10, f = −2: e = a·b = −6, d = e + c = 4, L = d·f = −8. Each line adds a node to the graph.
loss.backward() starts at L with gradient 1 and visits the nodes in reverse order.
Multiplication gives each input the other input's value times the incoming gradient: d gets f = −2 and f gets d = 4.
Addition passes the gradient through unchanged: e and c both get −2. Then a gets −2·b = 6 and b gets −2·a = −4.
Each result lands in the tensor's .grad, and is added to whatever is already there.
keyPoints: The graph is rebuilt on every forward pass, so ordinary Python if-statements and loops just work.
.grad accumulates, so call optimizer.zero_grad() once per step.
with torch.no_grad(): stops recording. Use it for evaluation and inference: less memory, faster.
tensor.detach() cuts a value out of the graph.
The memory cost of training comes largely from the activations saved for backward.
micrograd (Karpathy) is a complete autograd engine in about 100 lines of Python. Building one is the best way to understand it.
mistakes: Forgetting zero_grad(), so gradients from earlier batches pile up.
Evaluating without no_grad(), wasting memory on a graph you never use.
Calling .numpy() or .item() in the middle of a computation, which breaks the graph.
Changing a tensor in place that autograd still needs, which causes an error during backward.

followUps.q: What does loss.backward() do?
followUps.a: It walks the recorded graph from the loss backwards, applying the chain rule, and adds each gradient into the .grad of the tensors that need one.

followUps.q: Why does PyTorch need optimizer.zero_grad()?
followUps.a: Because .grad accumulates. Without clearing it, each step would use the sum of every earlier batch's gradients.

followUps.q: What does torch.no_grad() change?
followUps.a: Operations are no longer recorded, so no graph is kept: less memory and faster, but no gradients.

followUps.q: For d = e + c, what gradient does c receive?
followUps.a: Exactly the gradient arriving at d: addition passes it through unchanged.

diagram.caption: Autograd records every operation as a graph while computing, then walks it backwards to fill in each gradient.

note.idea: Autograd records every operation in a graph while you compute. Calling backward() walks the graph in reverse and applies the chain rule for you.
note.analogy: Breadcrumbs. On the way forward you drop a crumb at each step. On the way back you follow them home.
note.breaks: Breadcrumbs cost nothing. The graph costs memory: every intermediate value is stored until backward(). That is why training needs much more memory than inference.
note.example: L = (a·b + c)·f with a = 2, b = −3, c = 10, f = −2 gives L = −8. After L.backward(): f.grad = 4, c.grad = −2, a.grad = 6 and b.grad = −4, all without writing a single derivative by hand.
note.code:
import torch
w = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)
loss = (w * 2.0 - 5.0) ** 2
loss.backward()
w.grad    # tensor(-12.)  the same as the hand calculation

practice.derive: Draw the computational graph for L = (a · b + c)², and write the local derivative on every edge.
practice.build: Rebuild micrograd: a Value class with +, *, tanh, exp and backward(). Train a tiny MLP with it.

derive.answer:
Break L = (a·b + c)² into simple steps, each one a node:
m = a·b
s = m + c
L = s²

Local derivative on each edge:
L ← s: ∂L/∂s = 2s
s ← m: ∂s/∂m = 1
s ← c: ∂s/∂c = 1
m ← a: ∂m/∂a = b
m ← b: ∂m/∂b = a

Multiply along each path from L back to an input:
∂L/∂a = 2s · 1 · b, ∂L/∂b = 2s · 1 · a, ∂L/∂c = 2s · 1.

With a = 2, b = −3, c = 10: m = −6, s = 4, L = 16, so ∂L/∂a = 8 × (−3) = −24, ∂L/∂b = 8 × 2 = 16 and ∂L/∂c = 8.
derive.code:
a ──┐
    (×) ── m ──┐            each edge carries its local derivative:
b ──┘          (+) ── s ── (²) ── L      L←s: 2s,  s←m: 1,  s←c: 1
c ─────────────┘                         m←a: b,   m←b: a

build.answer:
A Value holds a number, its gradient, the Values it was made from, and a small function that knows how to pass gradient back to them. backward() sorts the graph so every node comes after the nodes that use it, sets the output's gradient to 1, and calls each node's function in reverse order.

The gradients use += so that a Value used in several places adds up all of its contributions (see the break exercise). A tiny MLP built from Values learns four points; its loss drops close to 0.

break.answer:
For y = x · x the gradient should be 2x: at x = 3, 6. If the backward function assigns (self.grad = ...) instead of adding (self.grad += ...), it gives 3.

Why: x appears twice, as both inputs of the multiplication. The backward step writes "other.data × out.grad" into x.grad for the first input (3), then writes it again for the second input (3) and overwrites the first. The true gradient is the sum of both paths: 3 + 3 = 6.

The rule: when a value is used in several places, its gradient is the sum of the gradients from every use. Always accumulate with +=, and reset gradients to 0 before each backward pass. That is exactly why PyTorch makes you call zero_grad().
break.code:
class Broken:
    def __init__(self, data): self.data, self.grad = data, 0.0
    def __mul__(self, other):
        out = Broken(self.data * other.data)
        def back():
            self.grad = other.data * out.grad       # BUG: = overwrites
            other.grad = self.data * out.grad
        out.back = back
        return out

x = Broken(3.0); y = x * x; y.grad = 1.0; y.back()
print(x.grad)       # 3.0, wrong

import torch
xt = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True); (xt * xt).backward()
print(xt.grad.item())   # 6.0, right: both uses add up

explain.answer:
On the way forward, autograd drops a breadcrumb at every step: "here I multiplied a by b, and these were the numbers". That trail is the computational graph. When you call backward(), it follows the breadcrumbs home in reverse order, and at each crumb applies the chain rule using the numbers it saved, so every input ends up knowing its gradient, without you writing a single derivative.

It costs memory because the breadcrumbs have to be kept until the backward pass: every intermediate result of the forward pass, for every example in the batch. That is why training uses far more memory than running the model, and why torch.no_grad() during evaluation saves memory: it tells autograd not to drop crumbs.

topics.name: Softmax and cross-entropy loss
topics.definition: Softmax turns a vector of raw scores (logits) into probabilities that sum to 1; cross-entropy loss is −log of the probability given to the correct class; together their gradient is simply p − y.
topics.problem: A classifier's last layer outputs arbitrary numbers, but you want probabilities, and a loss that strongly punishes confident wrong answers. Softmax plus cross-entropy is the standard pairing for every multi-class classifier and every language model, which predicts the next token from a softmax over tens of thousands of options.
howItWorks: Start with logits, one per class: z = [2, 1, 0.1].
Exponentiate: e^z = [7.39, 2.72, 1.11]. All positive, and the leader pulls further ahead.
Divide by the total (11.21): p = [0.66, 0.24, 0.10]. They add up to 1.
For stability, subtract the largest logit first. The answer is identical, but exp never overflows.
If the true class is the first one, the loss is −log 0.66 ≈ 0.42.
The gradient with respect to the logits is p − y = [0.66 − 1, 0.24, 0.10] = [−0.34, 0.24, 0.10]: raise the right score, lower the others in proportion.
keyPoints: softmax(z)ᵢ = exp(zᵢ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ).
Adding the same number to every logit doesn't change the softmax, so subtracting the max is free and safe.
Loss = −log p(correct class). Its gradient on the logits is p − one_hot(y).
In PyTorch, F.cross_entropy takes raw logits and applies log-softmax itself. Don't softmax first.
Scaling logits by 1/T (temperature) makes the distribution sharper (T < 1) or flatter (T > 1). Used in sampling (Phase 4).
At random initialisation with K classes, the loss starts near ln K.
mistakes: Applying softmax and then F.cross_entropy, which applies it again.
Computing exp of large logits without subtracting the max: overflow, inf, NaN.
Taking log(softmax) in two steps instead of using log-softmax, which loses precision.

followUps.q: Softmax of [1, 1, 1]?
followUps.a: [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]: equal scores give equal probabilities.

followUps.q: Does adding 100 to every logit change the softmax?
followUps.a: No. The factor e¹⁰⁰ appears in the top and the bottom and cancels.

followUps.q: What is the gradient of softmax + cross-entropy with respect to the logits?
followUps.a: p − y: the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot true label.

followUps.q: What loss would you expect at the start of training with 4 classes?
followUps.a: About ln 4 ≈ 1.39, because random weights give roughly equal probabilities.

derive.answer:
Softmax: pᵢ = e^(zᵢ) / Σₖ e^(zₖ). Cross-entropy with a one-hot y: L = −Σᵢ yᵢ log pᵢ.

Step 1, the softmax derivative: ∂pᵢ/∂zⱼ = pᵢ(δᵢⱼ − pⱼ), where δᵢⱼ is 1 if i = j and 0 otherwise. (Raising zⱼ raises pⱼ and lowers every other share.)

Step 2, the chain rule:
∂L/∂zⱼ = Σᵢ (∂L/∂pᵢ)(∂pᵢ/∂zⱼ) = Σᵢ (−yᵢ/pᵢ) · pᵢ(δᵢⱼ − pⱼ) = −Σᵢ yᵢ(δᵢⱼ − pⱼ) = −yⱼ + pⱼ·Σᵢ yᵢ.

Step 3: the labels add up to 1, so Σᵢ yᵢ = 1, and ∂L/∂zⱼ = pⱼ − yⱼ.

So the gradient is just "predicted probabilities minus the truth". For logits [2, 1, 0.1] and correct class 0: p ≈ [0.66, 0.24, 0.10], gradient ≈ [−0.34, 0.24, 0.10].

build.answer:
Stable softmax subtracts each row's maximum before exp. For the loss, compute log-probabilities directly with log-sum-exp: log pᵢ = zᵢ − log Σ e^(zₖ), which never takes log of 0.

Softmax regression is just one linear layer, 784 → 10, trained with gradient (p − Y) / n. On MNIST, five passes over the training set with mini-batches of 128 reach about 92% test accuracy, which is the classic number for a linear model. An MLP gets about 98%.
build.code:
import numpy as np
from torchvision import datasets              # only to download MNIST

train, test = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True), datasets.MNIST("data", train=False, download=True)
Xtr, ytr = train.data.numpy().reshape(-1, 784) / 255.0, train.targets.numpy()
Xte, yte = test.data.numpy().reshape(-1, 784) / 255.0, test.targets.numpy()

def log_softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return z - np.log(np.exp(z).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
W, b = np.zeros((784, 10)), np.zeros(10)
for epoch in range(5):
    for idx in np.array_split(rng.permutation(len(Xtr)), len(Xtr) // 128):
        logp = log_softmax(Xtr[idx] @ W + b)
        loss = -logp[np.arange(len(idx)), ytr[idx]].mean()
        g = np.exp(logp); g[np.arange(len(idx)), ytr[idx]] -= 1; g /= len(idx)   # p − y
        W -= 0.5 * Xtr[idx].T @ g
        b -= 0.5 * g.sum(axis=0)
    acc = (np.argmax(Xte @ W + b, axis=1) == yte).mean()
    print(f"epoch {epoch + 1}: last batch loss {loss:.3f}, test accuracy {acc:.1%}")

break.answer:
Softmax of [1000, 1000] without subtracting the max: exp(1000) overflows to inf, and inf / (inf + inf) = nan. The right answer is obviously [0.5, 0.5]. Subtracting the max turns it into softmax of [0, 0], which is exactly [0.5, 0.5].

log(softmax) computed directly breaks the other way. For logits [0, −1000], softmax gives [1, 0] (e⁻¹⁰⁰⁰ underflows to 0), and log(0) = −inf. If the correct class is the second one, the loss becomes inf and the gradients nan. Log-sum-exp computes log p = z − logsumexp(z) = [0, −1000] exactly, with no inf anywhere.

That is why frameworks fuse them: PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss takes raw logits and does the stable log-softmax inside. Never apply softmax yourself before it.
break.code:
import numpy as np

z = np.array([1000.0, 1000.0])
with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    print(np.exp(z) / np.exp(z).sum())                    # [nan nan]
print(np.exp(z - z.max()) / np.exp(z - z.max()).sum())     # [0.5 0.5]

z = np.array([0.0, -1000.0])
p = np.exp(z - z.max()) / np.exp(z - z.max()).sum()
with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
    print(np.log(p))                                       # [  0. -inf]
print(z - (z.max() + np.log(np.exp(z - z.max()).sum())))   # [    0. -1000.]

explain.answer:
Softmax turns raw scores into shares that add up to 100%, like turning vote counts into vote shares. But it first raises e to the power of each score, and exponentials grow fast. So a small lead in scores becomes a big lead in shares: scores [2, 1, 0.1] give shares of about [66%, 24%, 10%], and scores [4, 2, 0.2] give about [87%, 12%, 1%].

So softmax exaggerates the leader: a candidate ahead by a couple of points of score walks away with most of the vote. That makes the model's top choice clear and gives useful gradients, but it also means models can sound very confident even when the underlying scores are only slightly apart.

topics.name: Optimisers: SGD, momentum, Adam; learning-rate schedules
topics.definition: Optimisers decide how to turn gradients into weight updates: SGD steps straight down the gradient, momentum adds velocity, and Adam also adapts the step size for every weight; a learning-rate schedule changes the step size over training.
topics.problem: Real loss surfaces have long narrow valleys, flat plateaus and noisy gradients from small batches. Plain SGD zig-zags across steep valleys and crawls along flat ones. Better optimisers converge in far fewer steps and are much less fussy about the learning rate, which saves days of compute on large models.
howItWorks: SGD: w ← w − η·g, where g is the gradient on a mini-batch.
Momentum: keep a velocity v ← β·v + g (β ≈ 0.9) and step w ← w − η·v. Side-to-side gradients cancel out while consistent ones build up speed.
RMSProp: keep a running average of g² and divide each step by its square root, so directions with big gradients take smaller steps.
Adam combines both: m ← β₁m + (1 − β₁)g and v ← β₂v + (1 − β₂)g², then w ← w − η·m̂ / (√v̂ + ε), with β₁ = 0.9 and β₂ = 0.999.
Bias correction: m and v start at 0, so early on they are too small. Dividing by (1 − βᵗ) fixes this in the first steps.
AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights instead of through the gradient. It is the standard for transformers.
Schedules: warm up from a tiny learning rate over the first steps, then decay it (cosine or linear) so training settles into a good minimum.
keyPoints: SGD: simple, and with momentum and a good schedule still excellent for vision models.
Momentum smooths noisy gradients and speeds up travel along valleys.
Adam gives each parameter its own effective step size; it is robust to the learning rate.
Typical starting learning rates: SGD ≈ 0.1, Adam ≈ 0.001 (3e-4 is a famous default).
Warm-up prevents huge early steps while the weights and Adam's averages are still unreliable.
Adam stores two extra numbers per weight, which matters for memory in large models (Phase 6).
mistakes: Using Adam's learning rate with SGD, or the other way round.
Leaving out warm-up for transformers, which often makes early training diverge.
Adding L2 to the loss with Adam and calling it weight decay. Use AdamW.
Comparing optimisers without tuning each one's learning rate.

followUps.q: What problem does momentum solve?
followUps.a: Zig-zagging in narrow valleys and noise from small batches: the velocity cancels side-to-side swings and builds speed in consistent directions.

followUps.q: What extra does Adam keep for each weight?
followUps.a: A running average of its gradients (m) and of its squared gradients (v).

followUps.q: Why warm up the learning rate?
followUps.a: At the start the weights are random and Adam's statistics are unreliable, so big steps can wreck training. Warm-up starts small and ramps up.

followUps.q: How does AdamW differ from Adam with L2 regularisation?
followUps.a: AdamW shrinks the weights directly, separately from the adaptive gradient step, which works better in practice.

note.idea: SGD steps against the gradient. Momentum keeps a running average of gradients, so you keep moving in a consistent direction. Adam adds a separate step size for each weight, based on how large its gradients usually are. A schedule changes the learning rate over time, for example warm-up then decay.
note.analogy: SGD is a hiker who only looks at the ground under their feet. Momentum is a ball rolling downhill: it builds speed and rolls over small bumps. Adam is a ball that is careful in steep, bumpy directions and bolder in flat ones.
note.breaks: A ball has one mass. Adam gives every single weight its own effective step size, so it is really millions of different balls.
note.example: In a long, narrow valley, SGD with learning rate 0.09 bounces from wall to wall, because 0.09 is just under the value where it would blow up across the steep direction. Momentum averages those bounces away and speeds along the valley floor. Adam scales each direction by its typical gradient size, so its path is straighter from the start.

m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g
v = b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g**2
m_hat, v_hat = m / (1 - b1**t), v / (1 - b2**t)
w -= lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + eps)

derive.answer:
g is the gradient, η the learning rate.

SGD: w ← w − η·g

Momentum: v ← β·v + g, then w ← w − η·v (β ≈ 0.9). v is a running sum of recent gradients: speed that builds up.

RMSProp: s ← ρ·s + (1 − ρ)·g², then w ← w − η·g / (√s + ε). Each weight's step is divided by its typical gradient size.

Adam: both ideas together.
m ← β₁·m + (1 − β₁)·g (β₁ = 0.9)
v ← β₂·v + (1 − β₂)·g² (β₂ = 0.999)
m̂ = m / (1 − β₁ᵗ), v̂ = v / (1 − β₂ᵗ)
w ← w − η·m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)

Why bias correction: m and v start at 0, so early on they are averages of a few gradients and a lot of that starting 0. After step 1, m = 0.1·g and v = 0.001·g², far too small. Dividing by (1 − βᵗ) scales them back up to proper averages. Without it, m/√v would be 0.1/√0.001 ≈ 3.2 times too big at step 1, so the first few hundred steps would be wrongly sized. As t grows, βᵗ → 0 and the correction fades away.

build.answer:
Race all four on the Rosenbrock function, f(x, y) = (1 − x)² + 100(y − x²)², a long, curved, narrow valley with its minimum at (1, 1). Start at (−1.5, 2) and take 3,000 steps, each optimiser with a learning rate that suits it.

Plain SGD has to use a tiny learning rate (any larger and it bounces off the steep walls and blows up), so after 3,000 steps it has barely moved: loss about 5. Momentum, with the same learning rate, builds up speed along the valley floor and gets to a loss of about 0.05. RMSProp scales each direction by its typical gradient, so it copes with the steep walls, and gets to about 0.2. Adam combines both ideas and lands on the minimum (1, 1) almost exactly. Plot all four loss curves on one log-scale axis to compare.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

f = lambda p: (1 - p[0]) ** 2 + 100 * (p[1] - p[0] ** 2) ** 2
grad = lambda p: np.array([-2 * (1 - p[0]) - 400 * p[0] * (p[1] - p[0] ** 2), 200 * (p[1] - p[0] ** 2)])

def run(kind, lr, steps=3000):
    p, m, v, losses = np.array([-1.5, 2.0]), np.zeros(2), np.zeros(2), []
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        g = grad(p)
        if kind == "SGD":
            p = p - lr * g
        elif kind == "momentum":
            m = 0.9 * m + g; p = p - lr * m
        elif kind == "RMSProp":
            v = 0.99 * v + 0.01 * g**2; p = p - lr * g / (np.sqrt(v) + 1e-8)
        else:
            m = 0.9 * m + 0.1 * g; v = 0.999 * v + 0.001 * g**2
            p = p - lr * (m / (1 - 0.9**t)) / (np.sqrt(v / (1 - 0.999**t)) + 1e-8)
        losses.append(f(p))
    return p, losses

for kind, lr in [("SGD", 1e-4), ("momentum", 1e-4), ("RMSProp", 1e-3), ("Adam", 2e-2)]:
    p, losses = run(kind, lr)
    print(f"{kind:9s} ends at {p.round(3)}, loss {losses[-1]:.2e}")
    plt.plot(losses, label=kind)
plt.yscale("log"); plt.xlabel("step"); plt.ylabel("f"); plt.legend(); plt.show()

break.answer:
Adam with a learning rate 100 times too big (2.0 instead of 0.02 here): Adam's step size per weight is roughly the learning rate, whatever the gradient, so every step can jump by up to about 2 units. The minimum sits at the bottom of a very narrow valley, and steps that size can't settle into it: after 3,000 steps it is still at about (0.7, 0.49), a loss of about 0.09, while a learning rate of 0.02 lands on (1, 1) almost exactly.

SGD with a learning rate 100 times too small (1e-6): every step is tiny, so after 3,000 steps it has barely moved from the start. The loss curve is almost flat: no explosion, just no progress. Both are learning-rate failures, but they look completely different on a loss curve.

No bias correction: the first steps come out several times too large. On this problem the corrected first step moves each coordinate by exactly the learning rate (0.02), while the uncorrected one moves it by about 0.063, 3.2 times as far, and most of the next few steps are also 2 to 4 times too big. That can be enough to throw a sensitive model off at the start, which is one reason warm-up schedules exist.
break.code:
import numpy as np

f = lambda p: (1 - p[0]) ** 2 + 100 * (p[1] - p[0] ** 2) ** 2
grad = lambda p: np.array([-2 * (1 - p[0]) - 400 * p[0] * (p[1] - p[0] ** 2), 200 * (p[1] - p[0] ** 2)])

def adam(lr, correct=True, steps=3000):
    p, m, v, sizes = np.array([-1.5, 2.0]), np.zeros(2), np.zeros(2), []
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        g = grad(p)
        m, v = 0.9 * m + 0.1 * g, 0.999 * v + 0.001 * g**2
        mh, vh = (m / (1 - 0.9**t), v / (1 - 0.999**t)) if correct else (m, v)
        step = lr * mh / (np.sqrt(vh) + 1e-8)
        sizes.append(np.abs(step).max()); p = p - step
    return p, sizes

print("Adam lr 2.0 ends at", adam(2.0)[0].round(2))
p = np.array([-1.5, 2.0])
for _ in range(3000):
    p = p - 1e-6 * grad(p)
print("SGD lr 1e-6 ends at", p.round(3), "(started at [-1.5, 2.0])")
print("first steps, corrected:  ", np.round(adam(0.02)[1][:5], 3))
print("first steps, uncorrected:", np.round(adam(0.02, correct=False)[1][:5], 3))

explain.answer:
Plain SGD is a hiker who only looks at the ground under their feet: every step goes straight downhill from where they stand, so in a narrow valley they zig-zag from wall to wall.

Momentum is a ball rolling downhill. It keeps its speed from step to step, so the zig-zags cancel out and it rolls fast along the valley floor, even over small bumps.

Adam is a careful ball: it also keeps momentum, but it watches how rough each direction is. Where the ground is steep and bumpy, it takes small steps; where it is flat and smooth, it takes bigger ones. So one learning rate works well for every direction at once.

topics.name: Weight initialisation; vanishing and exploding gradients
topics.definition: Weight initialisation chooses the random starting weights so that signals and gradients keep roughly the same size from layer to layer, instead of vanishing towards zero or exploding towards infinity.
topics.problem: In a deep network the signal is multiplied by a weight matrix at every layer, and the gradient again on the way back. If each layer shrinks it a little, after 50 layers nothing is left; if each grows it a little, it overflows. Bad initialisation can make a network untrainable before it has seen a single example. Good initialisation, plus normalisation and residual connections, is what makes depth work.
howItWorks: Picture one layer: each output is a sum of fan_in terms, each an input times a random weight.
Adding fan_in independent terms multiplies the variance: Var(out) ≈ fan_in × Var(w) × Var(in).
To keep the size the same, choose Var(w) = 1 / fan_in. This is Xavier (Glorot) initialisation, for tanh-like activations.
ReLU zeroes about half its inputs, halving the variance, so double it: Var(w) = 2 / fan_in, std = √(2 / fan_in). This is He initialisation, for ReLU.
Too small (std 0.01 with 48 inputs): each layer shrinks the signal, so activations and gradients vanish.
Too big (std 1): each layer multiplies the signal by about √(fan_in/2), so it explodes to inf or NaN.
Check it: print the standard deviation of the activations at every layer of a freshly initialised network. It should stay roughly level.
keyPoints: Vanishing: early layers get almost no gradient and barely learn. Exploding: NaN.
He (ReLU): std = √(2 / fan_in). Xavier (tanh): std = √(1 / fan_in), or √(2 / (fan_in + fan_out)).
PyTorch's default layer initialisation is already sensible; custom layers need care.
Biases usually start at 0.
Normalisation layers and residual connections make networks much less sensitive to initialisation.
Gradient clipping limits the damage when gradients do explode, especially in RNNs.
mistakes: Starting every weight at 0, or at the same value: no symmetry breaking.
Using std = 1 for wide layers.
Blaming the optimiser when the real problem is initialisation.

followUps.q: What is He initialisation, and when do you use it?
followUps.a: Normal weights with std = √(2 / fan_in), for layers followed by ReLU.

followUps.q: Why does ReLU need the extra factor of 2?
followUps.a: It zeroes about half of its inputs, which halves the variance of the signal; doubling the weight variance makes up for it.

followUps.q: Multiply by 0.9 fifty times. Roughly what do you get, and why does it matter?
followUps.a: About 0.005. A small shrink per layer becomes a vanishing signal over many layers.

followUps.q: Give two fixes for exploding gradients.
followUps.a: Better initialisation and gradient clipping (also normalisation layers and a lower learning rate).

diagram.caption: Weights too small: the signal fades to nothing (vanishing). Too big: it explodes. Good initialisation keeps it steady (the flat line).

note.idea: If weights start too small, signals shrink layer by layer and gradients vanish. If they start too big, signals grow and explode. Good initialisation keeps the signal size steady: He initialisation for ReLU uses std = √(2 / fan_in).
note.analogy: Passing a message down a line of 50 people. Too quiet, and it fades to nothing. Too loud, and it turns into shouting and noise.
note.breaks: People can ask 'sorry, again?'. A network cannot. That is why we also add normalisation layers and residual connections.
note.example: Multiply by 0.9 fifty times and you get 0.005. Multiply by 1.1 fifty times and you get 117.
note.code: W = np.random.randn(fan_in, fan_out) * np.sqrt(2 / fan_in)   # He initialisation

derive.answer:
One output of a layer is y = Σᵢ wᵢxᵢ, summed over fan_in inputs. Assume the w's and x's are independent and the w's have mean 0.

Var(y) = Σᵢ Var(wᵢxᵢ) = fan_in × Var(w) × E[x²].
(For independent w and x with E[w] = 0, Var(wx) = Var(w)·E[x²]. If x also has mean 0, E[x²] = Var(x).)

So Var(y) ≈ fan_in × Var(w) × Var(x). To keep the variance the same from layer to layer, we need fan_in × Var(w) = 1.

The ReLU factor of 2: after ReLU, half of the values become 0. For a symmetric pre-activation z, E[relu(z)²] = Var(z)/2. So each ReLU layer halves the signal, and to make up for it we need fan_in × Var(w) / 2 = 1.

He initialisation: Var(w) = 2 / fan_in, so the standard deviation is √(2 / fan_in). For fan_in = 512, std ≈ 0.0625.

build.answer:
Push a batch of random inputs through 20 layers of width 512 with ReLU, and record the standard deviation of the activations after each layer.

With tiny weights (std 0.01) the signal shrinks by about 6 times per layer (0.01 × √(512/2) = 0.16) and is essentially 0 after a few layers. With huge weights (std 1.0) it grows by about 16 times per layer (1.0 × √256) until it is astronomically large, around 10²⁴ by layer 20. With He initialisation (√(2/512) ≈ 0.0625) it stays at the same level all the way through: a flat line.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
width = 512
for name, std in [("tiny 0.01", 0.01), ("He", np.sqrt(2 / width)), ("huge 1.0", 1.0)]:
    x, stds = rng.normal(size=(256, width)), []
    for _ in range(20):
        x = np.maximum(0, x @ rng.normal(0, std, (width, width)))
        stds.append(x.std())
    print(f"{name:10s} layer 1: {stds[0]:.2e}, layer 20: {stds[-1]:.2e}")
    plt.plot(range(1, 21), stds, marker="o", label=name)
plt.yscale("log"); plt.xlabel("layer"); plt.ylabel("std of activations"); plt.legend(); plt.show()

break.answer:
std = 1.0: activations grow by about 16 times per layer, so by layer 20 they are enormous, and so are the gradients on the way back. The first update multiplies weights by numbers in the billions, and the loss becomes inf or nan almost at once: exploding gradients.

std = 0.01: activations shrink to almost 0, and the gradient reaching the first layer is so tiny it rounds to exactly 0. The loss stays at ln 2 ≈ 0.69, guessing, because the network's output is basically 0 whatever the input: vanishing gradients.

With He initialisation, the same 20-layer network trains normally. The fix for both failures is the same: choose the weight scale so the signal keeps its size, and add normalisation layers or residual connections for very deep networks.
break.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

X, y = torch.randn(256, 64), torch.randint(0, 2, (256,))
for name, std in [("std 1.0", 1.0), ("std 0.01", 0.01), ("He", (2 / 64) ** 0.5)]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    layers = []
    for _ in range(20):
        lin = nn.Linear(64, 64); nn.init.normal_(lin.weight, 0, std); nn.init.zeros_(lin.bias)
        layers += [lin, nn.ReLU()]
    model = nn.Sequential(*layers, nn.Linear(64, 2))
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
    first = None
    for step in range(100):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X), y)
        loss.backward()
        if first is None:
            first = model[0].weight.grad.norm().item()
        opt.step()
    print(f"{name:8s}: first-layer gradient {first:.1e}, loss after 100 steps {loss.item():.3g}")

explain.answer:
Passing a message down a line of 50 people. If everyone whispers a bit more quietly than they heard it, the message fades to nothing by the end of the line. If everyone says it a bit louder, it turns into shouting and noise.

Gradients travel back through a deep network the same way, multiplied at every layer. If each layer multiplies by a bit less than 1 (0.9 fifty times is 0.005), the gradient vanishes and the early layers stop learning. If each multiplies by a bit more than 1 (1.1 fifty times is 117), it explodes. Good initialisation, normalisation and residual connections make every person pass the message on at the same volume.

topics.name: Batch norm and layer norm
topics.definition: Normalisation layers rescale activations to mean 0 and variance 1, then let the network re-scale and shift them with learned γ and β; batch norm normalises each feature across the batch, layer norm normalises each example across its features.
topics.problem: As earlier layers learn, the values reaching later layers keep changing scale, so each layer chases a moving target and training needs tiny learning rates. Normalisation keeps activations in a steady range, which allows bigger learning rates, makes deep networks far easier to train, and reduces sensitivity to initialisation. Every modern architecture uses one of these layers.
howItWorks: Take a batch of activations with shape (batch, features).
Batch norm: for each feature (column), compute its mean and variance over the batch.
Subtract the mean and divide by √(variance + ε): every column now has mean 0 and spread 1.
Multiply by a learned γ and add a learned β, so the network can undo the normalisation if that helps.
At test time, batch norm uses running averages of the mean and variance saved during training, so model.eval() matters.
Layer norm: for each example (row), use the mean and variance over its own features. No batch statistics, so training and test behave the same, and batch size doesn't matter.
Transformers use layer norm (or RMSNorm, which skips subtracting the mean). CNNs traditionally use batch norm.
keyPoints: Batch norm: statistics over the batch, per feature. Layer norm: statistics over the features, per example.
γ and β keep the layer flexible: it can learn any scale and shift.
Batch norm needs reasonable batch sizes and behaves differently in train and eval modes.
Layer norm is independent of the batch, ideal for variable-length sequences and transformers.
Normalisation allows higher learning rates and speeds up training.
Pre-norm transformers apply layer norm before each sub-layer, which trains more stably.
mistakes: Forgetting model.eval() with batch norm, so test predictions depend on the batch.
Using batch norm with a batch size of 1 or 2.
Normalising over the wrong axis: features versus batch.

followUps.q: For a batch of shape (32, 64), which axis does batch norm average over? Layer norm?
followUps.a: Batch norm averages over the 32 examples (per feature); layer norm averages over the 64 features (per example).

followUps.q: Why do transformers use layer norm instead of batch norm?
followUps.a: It doesn't depend on the batch, works for any sequence length and batch size, and behaves the same in training and inference.

followUps.q: What are γ and β for?
followUps.a: They let the network learn the best scale and shift after normalising, including undoing it.

followUps.q: What goes wrong if you leave batch norm in training mode at test time?
followUps.a: Each prediction depends on the other examples in the batch, and on tiny batches the statistics are noisy, so results change randomly.

note.idea: Normalisation rescales activations to mean 0 and variance 1, then lets the network rescale them with learned γ and β. Batch norm averages over the batch, for each feature. Layer norm averages over the features, for each example.
note.analogy: Grading on a curve. Batch norm curves each exam question across all students. Layer norm curves each student across all of their questions.
note.breaks: A curve is set once. Batch norm behaves differently at test time (it uses saved running averages), which is a common source of bugs. Layer norm does not depend on the batch, which is why transformers use it.
note.example: A batch of 4 examples with 5 features. Feature 2 has the values [1, 5, 3, 7]: mean 4, standard deviation √5 ≈ 2.24. Batch norm turns it into about [−1.34, 0.45, −0.45, 1.34]. Layer norm instead normalises each example's own 5 values, so example 1, [4, 1, 2, 3, 0], becomes about [1.41, −0.71, 0, 0.71, −1.41].

ln = (x - x.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / np.sqrt(x.var(axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-5)

derive.answer:
Batch values [1, 2, 3].

Mean: (1 + 2 + 3) / 3 = 2.
Variance (batch norm divides by n): ((1 − 2)² + 0² + (3 − 2)²) / 3 = 2/3. Standard deviation √(2/3) ≈ 0.816.

Normalise: (x − 2) / 0.816 gives [−1.225, 0, 1.225].

With γ = 1 and β = 0 that is also the output. The result has mean 0 and variance 1 across the batch. During training, γ and β are learned, so the layer can rescale and shift the output if that helps.

build.answer:
A 10-layer MLP on 10,000 MNIST images, trained with plain SGD for two epochs, with and without a BatchNorm1d after each linear layer.

Without batch norm, this 10-layer network barely learns at all in two epochs: the loss is still about 2.30, the value for pure guessing. With batch norm, at the same learning rate, it is down to about 0.14. Each layer's inputs keep a steady scale, so a bigger learning rate is safe and the deep stack trains like a shallow one.

Layer norm normalises each example across its own features: subtract that row's mean, divide by its standard deviation, then scale and shift. With the same γ, β and ε it matches torch.nn.LayerNorm to within about 1e-6.
build.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import datasets

mnist = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True)
X = mnist.data[:10_000].reshape(-1, 784).float() / 255.0
y = mnist.targets[:10_000]

def deep_mlp(batch_norm):
    layers, width = [], 784
    for _ in range(10):
        layers += [nn.Linear(width, 128)] + ([nn.BatchNorm1d(128)] if batch_norm else []) + [nn.ReLU()]
        width = 128
    return nn.Sequential(*layers, nn.Linear(128, 10))

for bn in [False, True]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = deep_mlp(bn)
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)
    for epoch in range(2):
        for idx in torch.randperm(10_000).split(64):
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X[idx]), y[idx])
            loss.backward(); opt.step()
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        print(f"batch norm {bn}: loss {nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X), y).item():.3f}")

def layer_norm(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5):
    mean = x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    var = x.var(dim=-1, unbiased=False, keepdim=True)
    return gamma * (x - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + eps) + beta

x = torch.randn(4, 16)
ln = nn.LayerNorm(16)
print(torch.allclose(layer_norm(x, ln.weight, ln.bias), ln(x), atol=1e-6))   # True

break.answer:
With batch size 1 in training mode, batch norm computes the mean and variance of a single value. The mean is that value and the variance is 0, so the output is (x − x) / √ε = 0 for every input. Every example looks the same to the rest of the network. PyTorch refuses outright for fully connected batch norm: "Expected more than 1 value per channel when training".

The fix for prediction is model.eval(). In eval mode, batch norm uses the running mean and variance it averaged during training instead of the batch's own statistics, so a single example is fine, and the output no longer depends on what else is in the batch.

If you must train with tiny batches, use layer norm or group norm instead, which don't depend on the batch at all.
break.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(4)
for _ in range(100):                          # learn running statistics from real batches
    bn(torch.randn(32, 4) * 3 + 5)
one = torch.randn(1, 4) * 3 + 5
try:
    bn.train(); bn(one)
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
bn.eval()
print(bn(one))                                 # fine: uses the running mean and variance
print(bn.running_mean.round(decimals=1))       # close to 5

explain.answer:
Grading on a curve: instead of using raw marks, you rescale them so the average becomes 0 and the spread becomes 1.

Batch norm curves each exam question across all the students who sat it today: for one feature, it uses the mean and spread of that feature across the batch. That works well with a big class, but it is odd with only one or two students, and it needs a remembered average for later exams (eval mode).

Layer norm curves each student across all of their own questions: for one example, it uses the mean and spread of that example's features. It doesn't care who else is in the room, which is why it suits transformers, small batches and text of any length.

topics.name: Regularisation: dropout, weight decay, augmentation, early stopping
topics.definition: Regularisation in deep learning is any trick that stops a network memorising its training data: dropout, weight decay, data augmentation and early stopping are the main ones.
topics.problem: Neural networks have so many parameters that they can memorise their training set exactly, even with random labels, and then fail on new data. Regularisation makes memorising harder or less attractive, so the network learns patterns that generalise. On small datasets it is often the difference between a useful model and a useless one.
howItWorks: Dropout: during training, zero each hidden activation with probability p (often 0.1 to 0.5) and scale the survivors by 1/(1 − p). Every step trains a different thinned network, so no neuron can rely on a particular partner.
At evaluation, dropout is switched off (model.eval()), and thanks to the scaling no change is needed.
Weight decay: shrink every weight a little each step (AdamW's weight_decay), pulling towards simpler functions.
Data augmentation: create new, label-preserving versions of each example — flips, crops, small rotations, colour changes for images; noise or masking for audio and text.
Early stopping: track validation loss during training and keep the checkpoint where it was lowest.
Other levers: a smaller model, more real data, label smoothing.
keyPoints: Dropout is only active in training mode; the 1/(1 − p) scaling keeps the expected activation the same.
Augmentations must keep the label correct: flipping a "6" makes a "9".
Weight decay = L2 regularisation for neural networks; use AdamW.
Early stopping needs a validation set and saved checkpoints.
More data is the most reliable regulariser of all.
Large pre-trained transformers often use little or no dropout; small models on small data need more.
mistakes: Leaving dropout on at evaluation time (forgetting model.eval()).
Augmenting the validation or test sets.
Augmentations that change the meaning: flipping text, rotating digits too far.
Stopping on training loss instead of validation loss.

followUps.q: With dropout p = 0.2, what is a kept activation multiplied by during training?
followUps.a: 1 / (1 − 0.2) = 1.25, so the expected value stays the same.

followUps.q: Why does dropout reduce overfitting?
followUps.a: No neuron can rely on any particular other neuron being present, so the network learns redundant, more general features. It is like averaging many thinned networks.

followUps.q: Give two augmentations for photos of cats and one that would be wrong for handwritten digits.
followUps.a: Flips and random crops (or colour jitter) for cats. A horizontal flip or a large rotation is wrong for digits: it can turn one digit into another.

followUps.q: How does early stopping work?
followUps.a: Watch validation loss during training and keep the model from the epoch where it was lowest, even if training continues.

diagram.caption: Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss turns up after about epoch 6 — that's overfitting. Early stopping saves the model at the lowest validation point.

note.idea: Tricks to stop a network memorising. Dropout turns off random neurons during training. Weight decay shrinks weights. Data augmentation makes 'new' data, such as flipped or cropped images. Early stopping stops when the validation loss starts to rise.
note.analogy: Dropout is a football team that trains with random players missing, so nobody relies on one star.
note.breaks: Missing players happens only in training. At test time all neurons are used, so the output size must match. 'Inverted dropout' fixes this by scaling during training.
note.example: With dropout p = 0.5 and four hidden activations [2, 4, 6, 8], one training step might keep [2, _, 6, _] and scale them by 2, giving [4, 0, 12, 0]. On average each activation keeps its value. At test time all four pass through unchanged.

h = h * mask                                      # training only

derive.answer:
Dropout with rate 0.5 keeps each activation with probability 0.5 and sets it to 0 otherwise.

Without rescaling, the expected value of a kept-or-dropped activation a is 0.5·a + 0.5·0 = 0.5a. So during training, the next layer sees inputs that are half as big on average as at test time, when nothing is dropped. The network would be trained for one scale and used at another.

Dividing the kept values by 0.5 (the keep probability) fixes this: E = 0.5·(a / 0.5) + 0.5·0 = a. The expected value during training now matches test time, so at test time you can simply switch dropout off with no other change. This is "inverted dropout", what PyTorch does.

build.answer:
Train a large MLP (784 → 512 → 512 → 10) on only 1,000 MNIST images, so it overfits: training accuracy hits 100% while validation accuracy stalls. Then add one regulariser at a time and keep the ones before it.

Typical results on this run: the plain model is a little under 90% on validation; dropout and weight decay each add under a point; augmentation (small random shifts of each image, so the model never sees the exact same image twice) helps most; early stopping keeps the best epoch instead of the last. Exact numbers vary from run to run by a point, so the trend matters more than any single value.
build.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import datasets

mnist = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True)
X = mnist.data.float().unsqueeze(1) / 255.0
y = mnist.targets
Xtr, ytr, Xva, yva = X[:1000], y[:1000], X[50_000:55_000], y[50_000:55_000]

def shift(images):                                  # augmentation: random shifts of up to 2 pixels
    dx, dy = torch.randint(-2, 3, (2,)).tolist()
    return torch.roll(images, shifts=(dy, dx), dims=(2, 3))

def run(dropout=0.0, weight_decay=0.0, augment=False, early_stop=False, epochs=60):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(784, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(dropout),
                          nn.Linear(512, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(dropout), nn.Linear(512, 10))
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=weight_decay)
    history = []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        for idx in torch.randperm(1000).split(64):
            xb = shift(Xtr[idx]) if augment else Xtr[idx]
            opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(xb), ytr[idx]).backward(); opt.step()
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            history.append((model(Xva).argmax(1) == yva).float().mean().item())
    return max(history) if early_stop else history[-1]

print(f"plain:          {run():.1%}")
print(f"+ dropout:      {run(dropout=0.5):.1%}")
print(f"+ weight decay: {run(dropout=0.5, weight_decay=0.1):.1%}")
print(f"+ augmentation: {run(dropout=0.5, weight_decay=0.1, augment=True):.1%}")
print(f"+ early stop:   {run(dropout=0.5, weight_decay=0.1, augment=True, early_stop=True):.1%}")

break.answer:
With dropout left on at test time, every prediction drops a random half of the units. Run the same image twice and you can get two different answers, and accuracy falls, because each prediction comes from a crippled, random sub-network instead of the full one. In the run below, the same trained model scores about 1.5 points lower with dropout on (about 90.6% against 92.3%), and the score changes every time you evaluate.

The fix: call model.eval() before evaluating or serving, and model.train() before training again. (Turning dropout on deliberately at test time and averaging many predictions, "Monte Carlo dropout", is a real technique for estimating uncertainty, but it is a choice, not an accident.)

explain.answer:
A football team that trains with random players missing in every session. Nobody can rely on one star striker to score every goal, because the striker might not be there. So every player learns to be useful, and the team learns several ways to win. On match day, the whole team plays, and it is stronger and more flexible for it.

Dropout does the same to a network: during training it switches off a random set of neurons at each step, so no single neuron can carry the answer on its own, and the network can't memorise the training set through a few fragile pathways. At test time every neuron is switched on.

topics.name: PyTorch: nn.Module, DataLoader and the training loop
topics.definition: In PyTorch, an nn.Module holds the layers and weights, a DataLoader serves shuffled mini-batches, and the training loop repeats the same few steps: forward, loss, zero_grad, backward, step.
topics.problem: Every deep-learning project, from MNIST to fine-tuning an LLM, uses this same skeleton. Getting its details wrong — no zero_grad, no eval mode, the wrong device — causes silent bugs that waste days. Knowing the loop cold lets you read any training script and write your own quickly.
howItWorks: Define the model as a class that inherits nn.Module: create the layers in __init__ and use them in forward. Its parameters are registered automatically.
Wrap your data in a Dataset (how to get item i) and a DataLoader (batch size, shuffling, worker processes).
Create an optimiser over model.parameters(), for example torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4).
For each batch: out = model(xb), then loss = loss_fn(out, yb).
opt.zero_grad() clears old gradients, loss.backward() computes new ones, and opt.step() updates the weights.
Validation: call model.eval() and use with torch.no_grad(): to measure without dropout or gradient tracking. Then call model.train() again.
Move the model and every batch to the same device: model.to(device), xb.to(device).
keyPoints: The five lines: forward, loss, zero_grad, backward, step.
model.train() and model.eval() switch dropout and batch norm behaviour.
torch.no_grad() for evaluation: no graph, less memory.
Shuffle the training loader, not the validation loader.
Log the training and validation loss every epoch, and save checkpoints (the model and optimiser state).
Set random seeds to make runs reproducible.
mistakes: Forgetting opt.zero_grad().
Forgetting model.eval() before validation.
Calling softmax before F.cross_entropy.
Model on the GPU, data on the CPU (or the other way round): a device-mismatch error.
Accumulating loss in a Python number without .item(), which keeps every graph alive and leaks memory.

followUps.q: List the five steps of a training iteration.
followUps.a: Forward pass, compute loss, zero_grad, backward, optimiser step.

followUps.q: What do model.eval() and torch.no_grad() each do?
followUps.a: model.eval() switches layers like dropout and batch norm to inference behaviour; no_grad() stops autograd recording the graph.

followUps.q: Why shuffle the training data each epoch?
followUps.a: So batches are random mixes: the gradient estimates are fair, and the model can't learn the order.

followUps.q: What happens if you forget zero_grad()?
followUps.a: Gradients from previous batches keep adding up, so the updates are wrong and usually far too large.

note.idea: nn.Module holds your layers and weights. DataLoader serves shuffled mini-batches. The training loop is almost always the same five steps.
note.analogy: A kitchen routine: get ingredients (a batch), cook (forward), taste (loss), adjust the recipe (backward and step), and clean the pan (zero_grad).
note.breaks: If you forget to clean the pan, flavours mix. If you forget zero_grad(), gradients from old batches add up.

derive.answer:
for xb, yb in loader:                 # 1. take the next batch
    opt.zero_grad()                   # 2. clear the old gradients
    loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)     # 3. forward pass and loss
    loss.backward()                   # 4. compute new gradients
    opt.step()                        # 5. update the weights

Why each line:
1. The DataLoader hands out shuffled mini-batches.
2. PyTorch adds gradients into .grad, so without clearing them each step's gradient would include every previous step's.
3. Run the model and measure how wrong it is.
4. Autograd fills .grad for every parameter.
5. The optimiser uses those gradients to change the weights.

Around it: model.train() before the loop, and for validation model.eval() with torch.no_grad().

build.answer:
nn.Module defines the model's layers in __init__ and the computation in forward. The DataLoader shuffles and batches the training set. After each epoch, the validation loop switches to model.eval() (so dropout and batch norm behave as at test time) and wraps everything in torch.no_grad() (no gradients needed, so it is faster and uses less memory), then switches back with model.train().

Three epochs reach about 97% validation accuracy.
build.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset
from torchvision import datasets

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.2), nn.Linear(256, 10))
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x.flatten(1))

mnist = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True)
X, y = mnist.data.float() / 255.0, mnist.targets
train = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X[:50_000], y[:50_000]), batch_size=128, shuffle=True)
val = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X[50_000:], y[50_000:]), batch_size=1000)

torch.manual_seed(0)
model, loss_fn = MLP(), nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for epoch in range(3):
    model.train()
    for xb, yb in train:
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    model.eval()
    correct = 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for xb, yb in val:
            correct += (model(xb).argmax(1) == yb).sum().item()
    print(f"epoch {epoch + 1}: validation accuracy {correct / 10_000:.1%}")

break.answer:
No opt.zero_grad(): gradients pile up. Step 500's gradient is really the sum of all 500 gradients so far, so the steps keep getting bigger and point in stale directions. At first it can even look fine, because the pile acts like a big push downhill. But soon the steps are far too big: in the run below the loss climbs back to about 2.3 (pure guessing) with spikes above 10, while the correct loop keeps falling to about 0.4. (Adam partly hides it because it divides by the gradient size, but the updates are still wrong.)

No model.eval() with dropout: validation runs with half the units randomly switched off (here dropout is 0.5), so the score is lower than the model really deserves and changes each time you evaluate. You might pick the wrong checkpoint, or think a good model is bad.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import datasets

mnist = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True)
X, y = mnist.data.reshape(-1, 784).float() / 255.0, mnist.targets
for zero_grad in [True, False]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 10))
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)
    losses = []
    for idx in torch.randperm(60_000).split(64)[:900]:
        if zero_grad:
            opt.zero_grad()
        loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X[idx]), y[idx])
        loss.backward(); opt.step(); losses.append(loss.item())
    print(f"zero_grad {zero_grad}: loss at steps 10, 200, 500, 900 = "
          f"{[round(losses[i], 2) for i in (9, 199, 499, 899)]}, worst after step 100: {max(losses[100:]):.1f}")

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.5), nn.Linear(256, 10))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for idx in torch.randperm(20_000).split(64):
    opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X[idx]), y[idx]).backward(); opt.step()
with torch.no_grad():
    model.eval(); right = (model(X[50_000:]).argmax(1) == y[50_000:]).float().mean().item()
    model.train(); wrong = (model(X[50_000:]).argmax(1) == y[50_000:]).float().mean().item()
print(f"validation with eval(): {right:.2%}, forgetting eval(): {wrong:.2%}")

explain.answer:
It is a kitchen routine, repeated for every batch. Get the ingredients: the DataLoader hands you the next batch. Clean the pan: zero_grad clears the last round's gradients so they don't mix in. Cook: the forward pass runs the model. Taste: the loss says how far off the dish is. Work out what to change: backward computes the gradients. Adjust the recipe: the optimiser's step changes the weights.

Then do it again with the next batch. Once you have been through every batch, that is one epoch. And when you serve the food (validation), you switch to "serving mode", model.eval(), and stop taking notes, torch.no_grad().

topics.name: Convolutional networks: convolution, pooling, receptive field
topics.definition: A convolutional layer slides small learned filters across an image, computing a dot product at every position, so the same pattern detector is reused everywhere; stacking layers builds up from edges to whole objects.
topics.problem: A fully connected layer on a 224 × 224 colour image would need about 150,000 weights per neuron, and would have to learn "cat" separately in every corner. Convolutions share a few weights across all positions, which saves enormous numbers of parameters and builds in the fact that a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears.
howItWorks: A filter (kernel) is a small grid of weights, for example 3 × 3.
Place it on the top-left patch of the image, multiply matching numbers and add them up: one output value.
Slide it across and down (by the stride) to fill a feature map. Big values mean "this pattern is here".
A layer has many filters, each producing its own feature map, so the output has many channels.
Output size = (W − K + 2P)/S + 1. With padding P = 1, a 3 × 3 filter at stride 1 keeps the size the same.
Pooling (for example 2 × 2 max pooling) shrinks the maps by keeping the strongest response in each patch.
Deeper layers combine earlier maps, and each output sees a bigger patch of the original image: its receptive field grows from 3 × 3 to 5 × 5 to 7 × 7 …
keyPoints: Weight sharing: the same filter at every position, so far fewer parameters.
Shift equivariance: move the input and the feature map moves too.
Parameters of a conv layer = K × K × C_in × C_out + C_out, whatever the image size.
Output size = (W − K + 2P)/S + 1.
Receptive field grows with depth, stride and pooling.
Vision transformers (Phase 4) now rival CNNs, but convolutions remain everywhere in vision, audio and on-device models.
mistakes: Getting the output size wrong, then hitting shape errors at the first linear layer.
Confusing channels-first (N, C, H, W, PyTorch) with channels-last (N, H, W, C).
Forgetting padding, so the feature maps shrink at every layer.

followUps.q: A 28 × 28 image, a 5 × 5 filter, no padding, stride 1. Output size?
Why does a CNN need far fewer weights than an MLP on images?
followUps.a: Each filter is a few weights reused at every position, instead of a separate weight for every pixel in every neuron.

followUps.q: What does 2 × 2 max pooling do to a 4 × 4 map?
followUps.a: It keeps the largest value in each 2 × 2 block, giving a 2 × 2 map.

followUps.q: How does stacking two 3 × 3 convolutions change the receptive field?
followUps.a: Each output then sees a 5 × 5 patch of the input.
