build.answer:
Single-head attention: project the inputs to Q, K and V, score every query against every key, scale by √d, apply the causal mask (set the scores for future positions to −infinity before softmax, so their weight becomes exactly 0), softmax each row, and mix the values.

The NumPy and PyTorch versions agree to about 1e-6 (and both match torch's built-in scaled_dot_product_attention). With the mask, the weight matrix is lower-triangular: token t only uses tokens 1 to t.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def attention_np(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, causal=True):
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[1])
    if causal:
        S = np.where(np.tril(np.ones_like(S)) == 1, S, -np.inf)
    W = np.exp(S - S.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    W /= W.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return W @ V, W

def attention_torch(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, causal=True):
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    S = Q @ K.T / K.shape[1] ** 0.5
    if causal:
        S = S.masked_fill(torch.tril(torch.ones_like(S)) == 0, float("-inf"))
    return F.softmax(S, dim=-1) @ V

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X, Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=s).astype(np.float32) for s in [(5, 8), (8, 4), (8, 4), (8, 4)])
out_np, W = attention_np(X, Wq, Wk, Wv)
out_t = attention_torch(*(torch.tensor(a) for a in (X, Wq, Wk, Wv)))
ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(*(torch.tensor(a)[None] for a in (X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv)), is_causal=True)[0]
print(np.abs(out_np - out_t.numpy()).max(), np.abs(out_np - ref.numpy()).max())
print(W.round(2))                                   # lower-triangular: no peeking ahead

break.answer:
Without the √d, the scores get far too big. If the entries of q and k have variance 1, their dot product is a sum of d = 512 terms, so its standard deviation is √512 ≈ 23. Softmax of numbers that far apart puts almost all the weight on the single largest score: in the run below, more than half of the rows become essentially one-hot (their largest weight is above 0.99), against none with scaling, and the average entropy of a row drops from about 3.7 (spread over many tokens) to about 0.16.

What that does to gradients: softmax passes gradient back as wᵢ(gᵢ − Σⱼ wⱼgⱼ). When one weight is about 1 and the rest about 0, every term is close to 0, so a saturated row sends almost nothing back to its scores. In the run below, the typical (median) row passes back about 37 times less gradient, and the most saturated rows pass back about 1e-17, nothing at all. The attention pattern for those tokens freezes: it can't learn to look anywhere else.

(One subtlety: the total gradient into q isn't smaller here, because without the division each score is also 23 times more sensitive to q, and the few unsaturated rows dominate. That is the other problem: training is driven by a handful of rows and becomes unstable.) Dividing by √d brings the scores back to a standard deviation of about 1, where softmax spreads its weight and every row keeps learning.
break.code:
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)
d, T = 512, 64
q, k, g = torch.randn(T, d), torch.randn(T, d), torch.randn(T, T)   # g: some downstream gradient
for scaled in [True, False]:
    scores = (q @ k.T / (d ** 0.5 if scaled else 1.0)).requires_grad_()
    weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    (weights * g).sum().backward()
    entropy = -(weights * torch.log(weights + 1e-12)).sum(-1).mean()
    rows = scores.grad.norm(dim=-1)
    print(f"scaled={scaled}: score std {scores.std().item():.1f}, "
          f"rows almost one-hot {(weights.max(-1).values > 0.99).float().mean().item():.0%}, "
          f"entropy {entropy.item():.2f}, median row gradient {rows.median().item():.1e}, smallest {rows.min().item():.0e}")

explain.answer:
A library. You arrive with a question: that is your query. Every book has a title on its spine: the keys. Each book's contents are its values. You compare your question with every title, and the better a title matches, the more of that book you read. You leave with a blend of the contents, mostly from the best matches.

In self-attention, every word does this at the same time: each word asks a question (query), advertises what it is about (key), and offers what it can tell (value). "it" asks "who am I referring to?", "animal" advertises "I am a noun, a creature", and "it" ends up reading mostly from "animal".

topics.name: Multi-head attention and the transformer block
topics.definition: Multi-head attention runs several smaller attentions in parallel and joins their results; a transformer block wraps attention and an MLP, each with layer norm and a residual connection, and a model stacks many identical blocks.
topics.problem: One attention pattern per layer is limiting: a word may need to look at its subject, its object and the previous word all at once. Several heads can each specialise. And attention alone only mixes information between tokens; the MLP then processes it inside each token. The block is the repeating unit of every transformer, so knowing it means you can read any model's architecture.
howItWorks: Split d_model into h heads: with d_model = 768 and 12 heads, each head works with 64-dimensional queries, keys and values.
Each head computes its own attention, with its own projection matrices, so each can learn a different relationship.
Join the heads' outputs back together (768 numbers per token) and mix them with one more matrix, W_O.
Pre-norm block: x = x + Attention(LayerNorm(x)). Attention lets tokens exchange information.
Then x = x + MLP(LayerNorm(x)). The MLP is usually 4 times wider inside (768 → 3,072 → 768) and works on each token on its own.
Stack N identical blocks (12 in GPT-2 small, dozens in large models). Every block reads from and writes to the residual stream.
After the last block: a final layer norm, then a linear layer to vocabulary-sized logits.
keyPoints: Heads run in parallel: reshape (batch, T, d) to (batch, heads, T, d/heads).
Total attention cost is about the same as one big head; the work is just split up.
Attention = communication between tokens; MLP = computation within each token.
Residual connections and layer norm make deep stacks trainable.
Most of a transformer's parameters are in the MLPs.
Grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key/value head, shrinking the KV cache.
mistakes: Reshaping heads in the wrong order and silently mixing tokens with heads.
Forgetting the output projection after joining the heads.
Leaving out the residual connections or the layer norms.

followUps.q: With d_model = 512 and 8 heads, how big is each head?
followUps.a: 512 / 8 = 64 dimensions.

followUps.q: What does the MLP in a block do that attention doesn't?
followUps.a: It processes each token's vector on its own (a per-token computation), while attention moves information between tokens.

followUps.q: Write the two lines of a pre-norm transformer block.
followUps.a: x = x + attention(layer_norm(x)), then x = x + mlp(layer_norm(x)).

followUps.q: Why use several heads instead of one?
followUps.a: Each head can learn its own attention pattern, so a token can gather different kinds of information at once.

flowchart LR
  X["x"] --> LN1["layer norm"] --> ATT["multi-head attention"] --> A1(("+"))
  X --> A1
  A1 --> LN2["layer norm"] --> MLP["MLP"] --> A2(("+"))
  A1 --> A2
  A2 --> O["to the next block"]
diagram.caption: One pre-norm transformer block: attention, then an MLP, each wrapped with layer norm and a residual shortcut.

note.idea: Multi-head attention runs several smaller attentions in parallel, so each head can track a different kind of relationship. A transformer block is attention plus an MLP, each wrapped with layer norm and a residual connection.
note.analogy: A team reading the same contract. One person checks dates, one checks names, one checks money. Then they merge their notes.
note.breaks: People choose their roles. Heads learn their roles on their own, and many heads do not have clean, readable roles.

derive.answer:
d_model = 768, so one d × d matrix has 768² = 589,824 weights.

Attention: four projections, Q, K, V and the output, each 768 × 768: 4 × 589,824 = 2,359,296. The number of heads doesn't change this: 12 heads of 64 dimensions just split the same matrices into 12 slices.

MLP with ratio 4: up from 768 to 3,072 and back down. 768 × 3,072 + 3,072 × 768 = 2 × 2,359,296 = 4,718,592.

One block: 2,359,296 + 4,718,592 = 7,077,888, about 7.1 million (the two layer norms and the biases add only about 10,000 more).

The MLP holds two-thirds of the block's weights. GPT-2 small stacks 12 of these blocks (about 85M) plus token and position embeddings (about 39M), for its 124M parameters.

build.answer:
Multi-head attention with one projection for all heads: compute Q, K and V as (batch, T, d), reshape each to (batch, T, heads, d/heads), and swap the axes to (batch, heads, T, d/heads). Now every head attends independently in one batched operation. Afterwards, swap back and reshape to (batch, T, d), then apply the output projection.

The pre-norm block is x = x + attention(layer_norm(x)), then x = x + MLP(layer_norm(x)). To check the attention, copy the same weights into PyTorch's nn.MultiheadAttention: the outputs agree to about 1e-6.
build.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.heads, self.qkv, self.out = heads, nn.Linear(d, 3 * d), nn.Linear(d, d)
    def forward(self, x, causal=False):
        B, T, d = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(d, dim=2)
        q, k, v = [t.view(B, T, self.heads, d // self.heads).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v)]
        scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / (d // self.heads) ** 0.5       # (B, heads, T, T)
        if causal:
            scores = scores.masked_fill(torch.ones(T, T).tril() == 0, float("-inf"))
        y = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) @ v                                 # (B, heads, T, d/heads)
        return self.out(y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d))

class Block(nn.Module):                                  # pre-norm transformer block
    def __init__(self, d, heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1, self.ln2, self.attn = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d), MultiHeadAttention(d, heads)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x), causal=True)
        return x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))

torch.manual_seed(0)
mine, ref = MultiHeadAttention(64, 8), nn.MultiheadAttention(64, 8, batch_first=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    ref.in_proj_weight.copy_(mine.qkv.weight); ref.in_proj_bias.copy_(mine.qkv.bias)
    ref.out_proj.weight.copy_(mine.out.weight); ref.out_proj.bias.copy_(mine.out.bias)
x = torch.randn(2, 10, 64)
print((mine(x) - ref(x, x, x, need_weights=False)[0]).abs().max().item())
print(Block(64, 8)(x).shape)                              # torch.Size([2, 10, 64])
print(sum(p.numel() for p in Block(768, 12).parameters()))   # 7,087,872 with biases and norms

break.answer:
Without residual connections, a 6-block model trains much worse: in the same number of steps its loss stays far higher than the normal model's (numbers below). Every block must now transform the whole signal, and the gradient has to pass through every block's layers in turn, with no shortcut, so the early blocks learn slowly.

Post-norm (LayerNorm after the addition, as in the original 2017 transformer) is fragile: at a learning rate of 5e-3, pre-norm trains fine (loss about 1.79), while post-norm fails to learn (about 3.37, barely better than guessing from letter frequencies). Without residuals the loss is equally stuck, about 3.37, against 1.86 for the normal model. With pre-norm, the residual path from input to output is an uninterrupted sum, so gradients reach every layer at a steady size. With post-norm, every addition is followed by a normalisation the gradient must pass through, which is why post-norm models needed careful learning-rate warm-up. Modern LLMs use pre-norm.

                      ("pre-norm, lr 5e-3", Config(n_layer=6), 5e-3),
                      ("post-norm, lr 5e-3", Config(n_layer=6, prenorm=False), 5e-3)]:

explain.answer:
A team reads the same contract. One person looks only at dates, one at names, one at amounts of money, one at who must do what. Each focuses on their own kind of detail, then they put their notes together into one summary.

Multi-head attention is that team: the model runs several attention "heads" side by side, each with its own queries, keys and values, so each can track a different kind of relationship, such as the previous word, the subject of the sentence, or a matching bracket. Their outputs are joined and mixed. The transformer block then adds a small MLP that thinks about each word on its own, with layer norm and residual connections around both, and that block is stacked many times.

topics.name: GPT-style models and next-token prediction
topics.definition: A GPT is a stack of transformer blocks with a causal mask, trained to predict the next token; it generates text by predicting a token, appending it and repeating.
topics.problem: Next-token prediction needs no labels: any text is its own training data, so models can learn from trillions of tokens. And one simple loop — predict, append, repeat — turns that single skill into writing, answering, summarising and coding. Every chat assistant is built on this.
howItWorks: Tokenise the text and look up embeddings plus positions.
Run the transformer blocks with a causal mask: position t can attend only to positions up to t.
At every position, a final linear layer gives logits over the whole vocabulary: the model's guess for the next token.
Training: the targets are the inputs shifted left by one. "The cat sat on the" trains the predictions cat, sat, on, the — every position at once.
The loss is cross-entropy between each position's predicted distribution and the true next token, averaged over all positions.
Generation: feed in the prompt, take the distribution at the last position, choose a token (greedy or sampled), append it, and repeat until a stop token or a length limit.
keyPoints: Self-supervised: the text supplies its own labels.
The causal mask makes training efficient (all positions in parallel) and honest (no peeking at the future).
Generation is sequential: one forward step per new token.
The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can look at.
The output at each step is a probability distribution; how you choose from it is decoding (next topics).
Chat assistants are GPTs plus instruction and preference tuning (later in this phase).
mistakes: Training without the causal mask: the loss looks great because the model copies the answer, but generation fails.
Off-by-one errors when shifting inputs and targets.
Expecting the model to know facts that weren't in its training text, or after its cut-off date.

followUps.q: What are the targets when training a GPT on a sequence?
followUps.a: The same tokens shifted left by one: each position must predict the token that follows it.

followUps.q: Why can a GPT train on all positions of a sequence at once?
followUps.a: The causal mask stops each position from seeing later tokens, so every position is a separate, fair prediction problem in the same forward pass.

followUps.q: Why is generation slower than training per token?
followUps.a: Each new token depends on the previous one, so tokens must be produced one at a time.

followUps.q: What does "self-supervised" mean here?
followUps.a: The labels come from the data itself — the next token — so no human labelling is needed.

derive.answer:
With word tokens, plus start and end markers: <s> I love deep learning </s>.

Input: <s>, I, love, deep, learning
Target: I, love, deep, learning, </s>

The target is the input shifted by one place. At each position the model must predict the next token, using only the tokens up to that position:
<s> → I
<s> I → love
<s> I love → deep
<s> I love deep → learning
<s> I love deep learning → </s>

One sequence gives five training examples at once, all computed in a single forward pass. The causal mask is what makes this honest: position 2 can't see "deep" while predicting it.

build.answer:
This is gpt.py, the small GPT the other answers import. It downloads Tiny Shakespeare (about 1 MB), uses each character as a token (65 of them), and stacks 4 pre-norm transformer blocks of width 128 with 4 heads and a context of 64 characters: about 0.8 million parameters. Training samples random 64-character windows; the targets are the same windows shifted by one.

generate() feeds the context in, takes the probabilities for the next character, samples one, appends it, and repeats, cropping the context to the last 64 characters.

After 2,000 steps (about a minute on a laptop CPU) the validation loss falls from 4.3 to about 1.7, and the samples look like Shakespeare from a distance: character names in capitals followed by a colon, line breaks, mostly real English words, and nonsense on closer reading.
build.code:
# gpt.py: a small character-level GPT, trained on Tiny Shakespeare (about 1 MB of text).
# Later answers import from this file, so keep it next to them.
import os
import urllib.request
from dataclasses import dataclass

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt"
PATH = "data/shakespeare.txt"
if not os.path.exists(PATH):
    os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(URL, PATH)
text = open(PATH, encoding="utf-8").read()
chars = sorted(set(text))
vocab_size = len(chars)                                   # 65 characters
stoi = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)}
encode = lambda s: [stoi[c] for c in s]
decode = lambda ids: "".join(chars[i] for i in ids)
data = torch.tensor(encode(text))
split = int(0.9 * len(data))
train_data, val_data = data[:split], data[split:]


@dataclass
class Config:
    block_size: int = 64          # how many characters the model sees at once
    n_embd: int = 128
    n_head: int = 4
    n_layer: int = 4
    dropout: float = 0.1
    vocab: int = vocab_size
    positions: bool = True        # add learned position embeddings
    causal: bool = True           # each position may only look at earlier ones
    residual: bool = True
    prenorm: bool = True          # LayerNorm before each sub-layer (False: after the addition)


def get_batch(split, block_size=64, batch_size=32, source=None):
    d = source if source is not None else (train_data if split == "train" else val_data)
    ix = torch.randint(len(d) - block_size - 1, (batch_size,))
    x = torch.stack([d[i:i + block_size] for i in ix])
    y = torch.stack([d[i + 1:i + block_size + 1] for i in ix])  # the same text, shifted by one
    return x, y


class Attention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.c = c
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(c.n_embd, 3 * c.n_embd)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(c.n_embd, c.n_embd)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(C, dim=2)
        q, k, v = [t.view(B, T, self.c.n_head, C // self.c.n_head).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v)]
        y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=self.c.causal,
                                           dropout_p=self.c.dropout if self.training else 0.0)
        return self.proj(y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C))


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.c = c
        self.ln1, self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(c.n_embd), nn.LayerNorm(c.n_embd)
        self.attn = Attention(c)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(c.n_embd, 4 * c.n_embd), nn.GELU(),
                                 nn.Linear(4 * c.n_embd, c.n_embd), nn.Dropout(c.dropout))

    def forward(self, x):
        for norm, layer in ((self.ln1, self.attn), (self.ln2, self.mlp)):
            if self.c.prenorm:
                x = x + layer(norm(x)) if self.c.residual else layer(norm(x))
            else:
                x = norm(x + layer(x)) if self.c.residual else norm(layer(x))
        return x


class GPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c=Config()):
        super().__init__()
        self.c = c
        self.tok = nn.Embedding(c.vocab, c.n_embd)
        self.pos = nn.Embedding(c.block_size, c.n_embd)
        self.blocks = nn.Sequential(*[Block(c) for _ in range(c.n_layer)])
        self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(c.n_embd)
        self.head = nn.Linear(c.n_embd, c.vocab)

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        x = self.tok(idx)
        if self.c.positions:
            x = x + self.pos(torch.arange(idx.shape[1]))
        logits = self.head(self.ln(self.blocks(x)))
        loss = None if targets is None else F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.reshape(-1))
        return logits, loss

    @torch.no_grad()
    def generate(self, idx, max_new_tokens, temperature=1.0):
        self.eval()
        for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
            logits, _ = self(idx[:, -self.c.block_size:])              # crop to the context window
            probs = F.softmax(logits[:, -1] / temperature, dim=-1)
            idx = torch.cat([idx, torch.multinomial(probs, 1)], dim=1)  # sample one token, append
        return idx


@torch.no_grad()
def estimate_loss(model, split="val", iters=20):
    model.eval()
    losses = [model(*get_batch(split, model.c.block_size))[1].item() for _ in range(iters)]
    model.train()
    return sum(losses) / len(losses)


def train(model, steps=2000, lr=1e-3, log_every=500):
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    model.train()
    for step in range(steps + 1):
        if log_every and step % log_every == 0:
            print(f"step {step}: train {estimate_loss(model, 'train'):.3f}, val {estimate_loss(model):.3f}")
        x, y = get_batch("train", model.c.block_size)
        _, loss = model(x, y)
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    return model


if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = train(GPT())
    print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()), "parameters")
    start = torch.tensor([encode("\n")])
    print(decode(model.generate(start, 400)[0].tolist()))

break.answer:
Without the causal mask, every position can see the whole window during training, including the very character it is supposed to predict, which sits right next to it. So the model learns to copy: the training loss plunges far below the honest model's (in the run below to about 0.04, against about 1.77), which looks like a fantastic result.

At generation time there is no future to copy. The model is asked about a position whose next character doesn't exist yet, a situation it never had to handle in training, so its predictions are meaningless. In the run below it produced nothing but blank lines: 150 newline characters in a row. (Other runs give random letters instead; either way, no text.) The lesson: a too-good training loss is a warning sign. The mask is what makes next-token prediction a real task, and training must match how the model is used.

import torch
from gpt import GPT, Config, train, estimate_loss, decode, encode

for causal in [True, False]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = train(GPT(Config(causal=causal)), steps=800, log_every=0)
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    sample = decode(model.generate(torch.tensor([encode("\n")]), 150)[0].tolist())
    print(f"causal={causal}: training loss {estimate_loss(model, 'train'):.3f}\n{sample}\n")

explain.answer:
Your phone keyboard suggests the next word as you type: after "see you", it offers "soon" or "tomorrow". A GPT is that idea, trained on a huge amount of text and far deeper. Given everything so far, it gives a probability to every possible next token, picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats. Long, sensible answers come out of doing that one small step thousands of times.

Where the picture breaks: your keyboard looks only at the last word or two and has learned your habits. A GPT reads the whole conversation so far, thousands of tokens, and the pressure of predicting text well over trillions of words forces it to learn grammar, facts and some reasoning along the way. Still, it has no separate fact-checking step: it predicts what text is likely, which is why it can sound sure and be wrong.

topics.name: Encoder models (BERT) vs decoder models (GPT)
topics.definition: Encoder models (like BERT) let every token attend in both directions and are trained to fill in masked words, which suits understanding tasks; decoder models (like GPT) attend only backwards and are trained to predict the next word, which suits generation.
topics.problem: Different jobs need different views of the text. Classifying a review or building a search embedding benefits from seeing the whole sentence at once. Writing text one word at a time needs a model that never peeks ahead. Knowing which family a model belongs to tells you what it is good for and how to use it.
howItWorks: Both families use the same transformer blocks. The difference is the attention mask and the training goal.
Encoder: no causal mask, so each token sees the whole input, left and right.
BERT's training: hide about 15% of tokens with [MASK] and predict them from the surrounding words (masked language modelling).
Decoder: a causal mask, so each token sees only earlier tokens. Training: predict the next token.
Encoder–decoder models (the original transformer, T5) use an encoder to read the input and a decoder that generates while attending to it through cross-attention. Common for translation.
Today most large models are decoder-only, and they are also used for classification and embeddings, but encoders remain cheap and strong for search and classification.
keyPoints: Encoder = bidirectional = understanding (classification, embeddings, named entities).
Decoder = causal = generation (chat, writing, code).
Encoder–decoder = read then write (translation, summarisation).
BERT-style models need fine-tuning or a task head; GPT-style models can often be prompted directly.
Sentence-embedding models used in search are often encoders.
mistakes: Trying to generate long text with a BERT-style model.
Assuming decoders can't do classification: they can, by prompting or with a small head.
Mixing up masked-language-model "masks" (hidden words) with attention masks (blocked connections).

followUps.q: What is BERT trained to do?
followUps.a: Predict randomly hidden (masked) tokens using the words on both sides.

followUps.q: Why is a decoder better at generating text?
followUps.a: It is trained exactly for left-to-right prediction with a causal mask, which matches how text is generated one token at a time.

followUps.q: Give one task that suits an encoder.
followUps.a: Sentiment classification or making embeddings for semantic search.

followUps.q: What does an encoder–decoder model add?
followUps.a: Cross-attention: the decoder generates the output while attending to the encoder's reading of the input.

derive.answer:
Rows are the token that is looking (the query); columns are the tokens it may look at. ✓ = allowed.

Encoder (BERT): every token sees every token, before and after it. All 16 cells allowed.

Decoder (GPT): token i may only see tokens 1 to i. Only the lower triangle, diagonal included: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 cells allowed; the 6 cells above the diagonal (the future) are blocked.

That single difference decides what each is good at: the encoder reads in both directions, so it understands a fixed text well; the decoder never sees the future, so it can write text one token at a time.

build.answer:
Three changes to the GPT turn it into a small BERT. Remove the causal mask (causal=False). Add one extra vocabulary entry for a [MASK] token. And change the task: in every training window, hide a random 15% of the characters by replacing them with [MASK], and compute the loss only at those hidden positions, where the model must recover the original character.

(Real BERT also sometimes swaps in a random token or leaves the token unchanged instead of masking, so it can't rely on seeing [MASK]; skipped here for simplicity.)

After 1,500 steps it recovers about a third of the hidden characters on validation text (35% in this run; guessing would get under 2%), using context from both sides. With 15% of characters hidden, several gaps often sit close together, which makes it harder than it sounds; longer training raises it further.
build.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from gpt import GPT, Config, get_batch, vocab_size

MASK = vocab_size                                          # one extra token id

def masked_batch(split):
    x, _ = get_batch(split)
    hidden = torch.rand(x.shape) < 0.15
    inputs = x.masked_fill(hidden, MASK)
    targets = x.masked_fill(~hidden, -100)                 # -100: ignored by the loss
    return inputs, targets

torch.manual_seed(0)
bert = GPT(Config(causal=False, vocab=vocab_size + 1))
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(bert.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for step in range(1500):
    inputs, targets = masked_batch("train")
    logits, _ = bert(inputs)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.reshape(-1), ignore_index=-100)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

bert.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    inputs, targets = masked_batch("val")
    pred = bert(inputs)[0].argmax(-1)
    hidden = targets != -100
    print(f"recovered {(pred[hidden] == targets[hidden]).float().mean().item():.0%} of hidden characters")
torch.save(bert.state_dict(), "bert.pt")

break.answer:
To generate with it, put a [MASK] at the end, predict what it is, keep that character, add a new [MASK], and repeat. The result is poor: short runs of plausible letters that soon fall into repetition or nonsense, much worse than the GPT of the same size.

Why: it was trained on a different task. It always had real text on both sides of a gap, and only 15% of positions were hidden. Here the gap is always at the very end, with nothing to its right, which it never practised, and every character it guesses becomes context for the next guess, so its mistakes pile up. It also never learned a proper probability for "what comes next given only the past", which is exactly what generation needs. Encoders are built to understand a whole text at once (classification, search, tagging); decoders are built to write.

explain.answer:
BERT, an encoder, does fill-in-the-blank exercises. It reads a whole sentence with some words blanked out, "Paris is the ___ of France", and uses the words on both sides to fill each gap. That makes it very good at understanding text that already exists: classifying it, searching it, finding the names in it.

GPT, a decoder, writes a story one word at a time. It can only look back at what it has written so far, never ahead, and predicts the next word, again and again. That makes it a writer. Because it never sees the future during training, it can keep going at generation time, which a fill-in-the-blank model can't do well.

topics.name: Vision transformers and CLIP
topics.definition: A vision transformer (ViT) cuts an image into patches and runs them through a standard transformer as if they were tokens; CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder together so matching pictures and captions get similar vectors.
topics.problem: CNNs needed hand-designed structure for images, and every vision task needed its own labelled data. ViT showed the same transformer recipe works for images given enough data, unifying vision and language architectures. CLIP links the two worlds, so you can search photos with words, classify images with no task-specific training, and give language models eyes.
howItWorks: Cut the image into a grid of patches, for example 16 × 16 pixels. A 224 × 224 image gives 14 × 14 = 196 patches.
Flatten each patch and map it to a d_model vector with one linear layer: the patch embedding.
Add position embeddings and (often) a special class token, then run ordinary transformer blocks. Read the class token (or the average) for the image's vector.
CLIP: an image encoder (a ViT) and a text encoder each map their input to a vector of the same size, normalised to length 1.
Train on huge numbers of image–caption pairs. In a batch of N pairs, compute the N × N matrix of similarities.
Contrastive loss: each image must pick its own caption out of the N (cross-entropy along each row), and each caption its own image (along each column).
Zero-shot classification: embed the image, embed texts like "a photo of a dog", and choose the most similar.
keyPoints: ViT = patches as tokens + a standard transformer.
ViTs have fewer built-in assumptions than CNNs, so they need more data (or pretraining) to shine.
CLIP puts images and text into one shared embedding space.
Contrastive learning: pull matching pairs together and push mismatches apart.
CLIP-style encoders power image search and give multimodal LLMs their vision input.
mistakes: Training a ViT from scratch on a small dataset and expecting it to beat a CNN.
Forgetting position embeddings, so patch order is lost.
Comparing unnormalised CLIP vectors with a raw dot product instead of cosine similarity.

followUps.q: How does a ViT turn an image into tokens?
followUps.a: It cuts the image into patches, flattens each one and maps it to a vector with a linear layer.

followUps.q: What is CLIP trained to do?
followUps.a: Give a picture and its caption similar vectors, and mismatched pairs dissimilar ones.

followUps.q: How does CLIP classify an image it was never trained to classify?
followUps.a: It compares the image's vector with the vectors of text prompts such as "a photo of a cat" and picks the closest.

followUps.q: Why do ViTs usually need more data than CNNs?
followUps.a: They lack a CNN's built-in assumptions about local, shift-invariant patterns, so they must learn them from data.

+ positions"] --> TR["transformer"] --> CL["class"] I2["image"] --> IE["image encoder"] --> SP["shared space"] T2["'a photo of a cat'"] --> TE["text encoder"] --> SP SP --> SIM["closest match wins"]

note.idea: A vision transformer (ViT) treats an image like a sentence: cut it into small patches, for example 16 × 16 pixels, turn each patch into a vector, add positions, and run a normal transformer. CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder together, so a picture and its caption land close together in the same embedding space. That lets you search images with text, and classify images with no task-specific training.
note.analogy: ViT reads a photo like a comic strip, panel by panel. CLIP is two translators, one for pictures and one for words, trained until they give the same 'meaning code' to a picture and its description.
note.breaks: Comic panels come in a set order. A ViT has no built-in sense of which patch sits next to which, so it must learn that from position embeddings. That is one reason ViTs need much more data than CNNs.
note.example: A 224 × 224 image cut into 16 × 16 patches gives 14 × 14 = 196 patches, so 196 'tokens'. For zero-shot classification, CLIP compares an image with texts like 'a photo of a cat' and 'a photo of a dog', and picks the closest.

img = F.normalize(image_encoder(images), dim=-1)    # (N, d)
txt = F.normalize(text_encoder(captions), dim=-1)   # (N, d)
logits = img @ txt.T / temperature                   # (N, N)
targets = torch.arange(N)                             # true pairs sit on the diagonal
loss = (F.cross_entropy(logits, targets) + F.cross_entropy(logits.T, targets)) / 2

practice.derive: For a 224 × 224 RGB image with 16 × 16 patches, how many patches are there, and how long is each flattened patch vector?
practice.build: Build a small ViT in PyTorch (patchify, linear embedding, positions, class token, transformer blocks) and train it on CIFAR-10. Compare it with your CNN. Then use a pretrained CLIP model for zero-shot classification on a few classes.
practice.break: Train your ViT on only 10% of CIFAR-10 and compare with the CNN again. Then shuffle the patch order at test time. What does each result tell you?

derive.answer:
224 ÷ 16 = 14 patches along each side, so 14 × 14 = 196 patches.

Each patch is 16 × 16 pixels with 3 colour channels: 16 × 16 × 3 = 768 numbers when flattened.

So the image becomes a sequence of 196 "tokens", each a 768-number vector, which a linear layer then projects to the model width. (ViT-Base's width is also 768, a coincidence of these sizes.) Add one class token and the transformer sees 197 positions. Halving the patch size to 8 × 8 would give 784 patches: four times as many tokens, and about 16 times the attention cost.

build.answer:
The small ViT: cut each 32 × 32 CIFAR image into 4 × 4 patches (64 patches of 48 numbers), project each to 128 dimensions, add a learned position embedding, put a learnable class token in front, run 4 pre-norm transformer blocks, and classify from the class token's output.

Trained for the same 2 epochs as the CNN in the convolution topic, it scores noticeably lower: about 48%, against the CNN's 60%. That is the expected result: a CNN has built-in assumptions that suit images (nearby pixels matter, the same pattern can appear anywhere), while a ViT has to learn them from data. ViTs win when trained on very large datasets.

Zero-shot CLIP: a pretrained CLIP turns the image and each label sentence, such as "a photo of a cat", into vectors in the same space; the label whose vector is closest wins. With no CIFAR training at all, it gets 92% of 200 test images right, far better than both models trained on CIFAR itself, because it learned from hundreds of millions of image–caption pairs. (The CLIP part downloads about 600 MB.)
build.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torchvision import datasets
from transformers import CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor

train, test = datasets.CIFAR10("data", train=True, download=True), datasets.CIFAR10("data", train=False, download=True)
Xtr = torch.tensor(train.data).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).float() / 255.0
Xte = torch.tensor(test.data).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).float() / 255.0
ytr, yte = torch.tensor(train.targets), torch.tensor(test.targets)

class ViT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, patch=4, d=128, depth=4, heads=4, classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.patch, n = patch, (32 // patch) ** 2
        self.embed = nn.Linear(3 * patch * patch, d)
        self.cls = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, d))
        self.pos = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, n + 1, d) * 0.02)
        layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, heads, 4 * d, dropout=0.0, batch_first=True, norm_first=True)
        self.blocks = nn.TransformerEncoder(layer, depth)
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.Linear(d, classes))
    def patchify(self, x):                                   # (B, 3, 32, 32) -> (B, 64, 48)
        p = self.patch
        x = x.unfold(2, p, p).unfold(3, p, p)                    # (B, 3, 8, 8, p, p)
        return x.permute(0, 2, 3, 1, 4, 5).reshape(x.shape[0], -1, 3 * p * p)
    def forward(self, x, shuffle=False):
        tokens = self.embed(self.patchify(x))
        if shuffle:                      # used by the Break answer: move the patches, keep the position numbers
            tokens = tokens[:, torch.randperm(tokens.shape[1])]
        tokens = torch.cat([self.cls.expand(len(x), -1, -1), tokens], dim=1) + self.pos
        return self.head(self.blocks(tokens)[:, 0])

def fit(model, X, y, epochs=2):
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for idx in torch.randperm(len(X)).split(128):
            opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(model(X[idx]), y[idx]).backward(); opt.step()
    return model

torch.manual_seed(0)
vit = fit(ViT(), Xtr, ytr)
with torch.no_grad():
    print(f"ViT test accuracy: {(vit(Xte).argmax(1) == yte).float().mean().item():.1%}")

clip, proc = CLIPModel.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32"), CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32")
prompts = [f"a photo of a {name}" for name in test.classes]
images = [test[i][0] for i in range(200)]
with torch.no_grad():
    inputs = proc(text=prompts, images=images, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
    guess = clip(**inputs).logits_per_image.argmax(dim=1)
print(f"CLIP zero-shot on 200 test images: {(guess == yte[:200]).float().mean().item():.0%}")

break.answer:
With only 10% of the training data (5,000 images, 10 epochs), the CNN still wins, about 50% against the ViT's 41%. In this small run the gap did not grow compared with the full data (60% against 48%): at this tiny scale both models are short of data and training. The famous result needs much larger scales: the original ViT lost to ResNets when trained on ImageNet's 1.3 million images, and only won when pretrained on hundreds of millions. The reason is the trade-off worth remembering: a CNN's built-in assumptions (look at small neighbourhoods, reuse the same filter everywhere) are worth a lot when data is limited; a ViT must learn even "neighbouring pixels belong together" from examples, and wins only once there are enough of them. Small experiments don't always reproduce large-scale effects, which is itself a useful lesson.

Shuffling the patch order at test time (moving the patches but keeping the position numbers in place, so each patch gets the wrong position): accuracy drops from about 41% to about 30%, but not to chance (10%). The drop shows the model does use the position embeddings: once patches are moved, shapes are scrambled. That it stays well above chance shows a lot of its decision comes from the contents of the patches alone, colours and textures, a bag-of-patches view. (A subtle trap: shuffling the tokens after the position embeddings have been added changes nothing at all, because attention without positions is order-blind, as the positional-encoding topic shows.) (A CNN can't be "shuffled" like this, because position is built into how it slides its filters.)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torchvision import datasets

train, test = datasets.CIFAR10("data", train=True, download=True), datasets.CIFAR10("data", train=False, download=True)
Xtr = torch.tensor(train.data[:5000]).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).float() / 255.0      # 10% of the data
ytr = torch.tensor(train.targets[:5000])
Xte, yte = torch.tensor(test.data).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).float() / 255.0, torch.tensor(test.targets)

class ViT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, patch=4, d=128, depth=4, heads=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.patch = patch
        self.embed = nn.Linear(3 * patch * patch, d)
        self.cls = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, d))
        self.pos = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, (32 // patch) ** 2 + 1, d) * 0.02)
        layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, heads, 4 * d, dropout=0.0, batch_first=True, norm_first=True)
        self.blocks, self.head = nn.TransformerEncoder(layer, depth), nn.Sequential(nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.Linear(d, 10))
    def forward(self, x, shuffle=False):
        p = self.patch
        x = x.unfold(2, p, p).unfold(3, p, p).permute(0, 2, 3, 1, 4, 5).reshape(len(x), -1, 3 * p * p)
        t = self.embed(x)
        if shuffle:                      # move the patches before positions are added
            t = t[:, torch.randperm(t.shape[1])]
        t = torch.cat([self.cls.expand(len(x), -1, -1), t], dim=1) + self.pos
        return self.head(self.blocks(t)[:, 0])

cnn = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                    nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                    nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 * 8 * 8, 10))
torch.manual_seed(0)
vit = ViT()
for model in (vit, cnn):
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(10):                                   # 10 epochs of the small set
        for idx in torch.randperm(5000).split(128):
            opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(model(Xtr[idx]), ytr[idx]).backward(); opt.step()
acc = lambda out: (out.argmax(1) == yte).float().mean().item()
with torch.no_grad():
    print(f"10% data: CNN {acc(cnn(Xte)):.1%}, ViT {acc(vit(Xte)):.1%}")
    print(f"ViT with patches shuffled: {acc(vit(Xte, shuffle=True)):.1%}")

explain.answer:
ViT reads a photo like a comic strip. It cuts the picture into a grid of small square panels, turns each panel into a vector, writes a panel number on each (the position), and then lets every panel look at every other panel with attention, just as a transformer does with words in a sentence. A special extra "summary" token gathers the whole story and makes the final decision.

CLIP is two translators trained side by side, one for pictures and one for sentences. Shown millions of photos with their captions, they are trained until the picture-translator and the sentence-translator give the same "meaning code" to a photo and its own caption, and different codes to mismatched pairs. After that, you can classify any image without training: write sentences like "a photo of a dog", translate them, and pick the one whose code is closest to the photo's.

topics.name: Sampling: greedy, temperature, top-k, top-p
topics.definition: Decoding turns the model's next-token probabilities into an actual choice: greedy takes the top token, temperature reshapes the distribution, and top-k and top-p cut off unlikely tokens before sampling.
topics.problem: The same model can sound dull and repetitive or creative and unhinged depending only on how you pick tokens. Greedy decoding tends to loop; pure sampling sometimes picks absurd words from the long tail. Decoding settings are the cheapest, most-used control you have over an LLM's output.
howItWorks: The model gives logits for every token in the vocabulary. Softmax turns them into probabilities.
Greedy: always take the most likely token. Deterministic, but prone to repetition.
Temperature T: divide the logits by T before the softmax. T < 1 sharpens the distribution (safer); T > 1 flattens it (more varied); T → 0 becomes greedy.
Top-k: keep only the k most likely tokens, set the rest to zero, renormalise, then sample.
Top-p (nucleus): sort tokens by probability and keep the smallest set whose probabilities add up to at least p (such as 0.9). The set is small when the model is sure and larger when it isn't.
Sample from what is left. A fixed random seed makes sampling repeatable.
Typical settings: T around 0.7 with top-p 0.9 for chat; T = 0 for extraction, classification and code that must be exact.
keyPoints: Temperature changes the shape of the distribution; top-k and top-p change which tokens are allowed.
Low temperature = focused and repetitive; high = diverse and error-prone.
Top-p adapts to the model's confidence; top-k uses a fixed count.
Beam search keeps several high-probability sequences; good for translation, often bland for chat.
One unlucky pick changes everything after it, so errors compound.
mistakes: Using high temperature for tasks that need exact, repeatable answers.
Using T = 0 for creative writing and getting loops.
Setting both a tiny top-k and a high temperature, then wondering why the settings seem to fight.

followUps.q: What does a temperature of 0.5 do to logits [2, 0]?
followUps.a: It divides them by 0.5, giving [4, 0], so the top token's probability rises (from about 0.88 to about 0.98).

followUps.q: How does top-p differ from top-k?
followUps.a: Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens; top-p keeps however many it takes for their probabilities to reach p.

followUps.q: Why does greedy decoding often repeat itself?
followUps.a: Once a phrase becomes likely, picking the top token every time can lock the model into the same loop.

followUps.q: Which setting would you use to extract a date from an email?
followUps.a: Temperature 0 (greedy): you want the single most likely, repeatable answer.

Temperature divides the logits by T before softmax: T < 1 makes choices sharper, T > 1 makes them flatter. Top-k keeps only the k best tokens. Top-p keeps the smallest set whose probabilities add up to p.
note.analogy: Ordering at a restaurant. Greedy: always the most popular dish. High temperature: feeling adventurous. Top-k: only choose from the top 5 dishes.
note.breaks: One restaurant order does not change the next one. In text, each choice changes everything after it, so one odd pick can send the text off track.

derive.answer:
Probabilities, already sorted: [0.5, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.05].

Top-k = 2: keep the 2 most likely tokens, 0.5 and 0.2. Renormalise so they add up to 1: 0.5/0.7 ≈ 0.714 and 0.2/0.7 ≈ 0.286.

Top-p = 0.8: keep the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least 0.8. Running total: 0.5, then 0.7 (not enough), then 0.85 (enough). So keep the first three: 0.5, 0.2, 0.15. Renormalise by 0.85: about 0.588, 0.235 and 0.176.

The difference: top-k always keeps exactly k tokens; top-p keeps a number that adapts. When the model is confident, a few tokens pass 0.8; when it is unsure, many do.

build.answer:
generate() gets three knobs. Temperature divides the logits before softmax. Top-k sets every logit outside the k largest to −infinity. Top-p sorts the probabilities, keeps the smallest prefix whose total passes p (always at least the top token), and zeroes the rest. Then renormalise and sample as before.

Comparing five short samples per setting from the trained Shakespeare GPT: temperature 1.0 is varied, with some made-up words; temperature 0.5 gives safer, more repetitive text with more common words; top-k = 10 and top-p = 0.9 cut off the rarest characters, so there are fewer odd letter combinations while keeping variety. For this tiny character model the differences are modest; for large models, these settings change the feel of the output a lot.
build.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from gpt import GPT, train, decode, encode

@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, idx, n, temperature=1.0, top_k=None, top_p=None):
    model.eval()
    for _ in range(n):
        logits = model(idx[:, -model.c.block_size:])[0][:, -1] / temperature
        if top_k is not None:
            kth = torch.topk(logits, top_k).values[:, -1, None]
            logits = logits.masked_fill(logits < kth, float("-inf"))
        probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
        if top_p is not None:
            sorted_p, order = probs.sort(descending=True)
            drop = sorted_p.cumsum(-1) - sorted_p > top_p           # drop once the total before it passes p
            sorted_p[drop] = 0
            probs = torch.zeros_like(probs).scatter(-1, order, sorted_p)
            probs = probs / probs.sum(-1, keepdim=True)
        idx = torch.cat([idx, torch.multinomial(probs, 1)], dim=1)
    return idx

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = train(GPT(), steps=1500, log_every=0)
for name, kwargs in [("T=1.0", {}), ("T=0.5", {"temperature": 0.5}),
                     ("top-k 10", {"top_k": 10}), ("top-p 0.9", {"top_p": 0.9})]:
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    start = torch.tensor([encode("ROMEO:")] * 5)
    out = generate(model, start, 50, **kwargs)
    print(f"--- {name}")
    for row in out:
        print(repr(decode(row.tolist())))

break.answer:
Temperature 0.01 is effectively greedy: the most likely next character every time. The text quickly falls into a loop, the same few words or the same line repeated over and over ("the the the", or one speaker's line again and again), because once the most likely continuation leads back to a state it has seen, it will repeat forever. It is also bland: it never takes the slightly less likely word that makes text interesting.

Temperature 3.0 flattens the probabilities so much that rare characters are almost as likely as common ones. The text becomes random-looking characters: mixed capitals, punctuation in odd places, and no words.

The useful range is in between, often 0.7 to 1.0 for creative text and close to 0 for factual or structured answers, usually combined with top-p to cut off the junk tail.

explain.answer:
Ordering at a restaurant. Temperature 0 means you always order the most popular dish: reliable, and boring after a while. A low temperature means you usually pick from the favourites. A high temperature means you feel adventurous and might order anything on the menu, including the dish nobody ever orders. Turn it up too far and you are choosing at random.

The model's "menu" is every possible next token with a probability. Temperature reshapes those probabilities before choosing: low makes the favourite even more likely, high flattens them so long shots get picked more often. Top-k and top-p are like crossing the worst dishes off the menu first.

topics.name: KV cache and the cost of generation
topics.definition: The KV cache stores the keys and values of every token already processed, so generating each new token only computes its own keys and values instead of recomputing them for the whole sequence.
topics.problem: Each new token attends to all earlier tokens. Recomputing every earlier key and value at every step makes generation cost grow with the square of the length, which is far too slow for long replies. The cache makes each step cheap, but its memory grows with every token, layer and user, and it often limits how many users a GPU can serve and how long a context can be.
howItWorks: The prompt is processed in one pass (prefill), and the keys and values of every layer are saved.
For each new token, compute only its query, key and value.
Append its key and value to the cache.
Attend from the new query to all cached keys, and mix the cached values.
Without the cache, step n recomputes n tokens' keys and values; with it, just one.
Memory ≈ 2 (K and V) × layers × tokens × d_model × bytes per number, per sequence. With 32 layers, d_model 4,096, 4,096 tokens and bf16 (2 bytes): about 2.1 GB.
Grouped-query or multi-query attention shares keys and values across heads to shrink this; paged attention (vLLM) manages the cache like virtual memory.
keyPoints: Prefill (the prompt) is compute-heavy; decode (new tokens) is memory-heavy.
The cache grows linearly with sequence length and with the number of users in a batch.
It can use more memory than the model's weights at long contexts.
Grouped-query attention, cache quantisation and paged attention reduce its cost.
Time to first token depends on prefill; time per output token depends on decode.
mistakes: Forgetting the cache when estimating how many users a GPU can serve.
Estimating memory from the parameter count alone.
Running past the cache's maximum length without a strategy (truncation, sliding window).

followUps.q: What exactly is stored in the KV cache?
followUps.a: The key and value vectors of every past token, at every layer (and every key/value head).

followUps.q: Why don't we cache the queries?
followUps.a: Each query is used only once, for its own token. Later tokens only need the earlier keys and values.

followUps.q: What happens to KV-cache memory if you double the context length?
followUps.a: It doubles: it grows linearly with the number of tokens.

followUps.q: How does grouped-query attention help?
followUps.a: Several query heads share one key/value head, so far fewer keys and values need to be stored.

flowchart LR P["prompt tokens 1…n"] --> PF["prefill: compute K and V
for all of them"] --> C[("KV cache")] N["each new token"] --> K1["compute K and V
for this token only"] --> C C --> A["attention reads
the whole cache"] --> T["next token"]
diagram.caption: Without the cache, every step would recompute the keys and values for the whole text. With it, each step only adds one row.

note.idea: When generating, each new token needs the keys and values of all earlier tokens. Instead of recomputing them at every step, we store them. This is the KV cache. It is much faster, but it uses a lot of memory.
note.analogy: Taking notes during a long meeting, instead of replaying the whole recording each time someone speaks.
note.breaks: Meeting notes are small. The KV cache grows with every token, every layer and every user, and it can use more memory than the model itself.
note.example: Memory ≈ 2 (K and V) × layers × tokens × d_model × bytes. With 32 layers, d_model 4,096, 4,096 tokens in bf16 (2 bytes): about 2.1 GB for one sequence. (Models with grouped-query attention use less.)

practice.explain: Explain the KV cache with the meeting-notes picture.
practice.derive: Work out the KV cache size for a model with 24 layers, d_model 2,048 and 8,192 tokens, in bf16.
practice.build: Add a KV cache to your GPT's generate(). Time 500 generated tokens with and without it.
practice.break: Generate past the cache's maximum length. What breaks? Then measure memory as the number of users in a batch grows.

derive.answer:
For every layer and every token, the cache stores one key vector and one value vector, each of size d_model.

Size = 2 (K and V) × layers × tokens × d_model × bytes per number
= 2 × 24 × 8,192 × 2,048 × 2 (bf16)
= 1,610,612,736 bytes ≈ 1.6 GB (1.5 GiB),
for a single sequence.

It grows linearly with every factor: 100 users at this length would need about 160 GB of cache, more than the model's own weights. That is why long context and large batches are limited by memory, and why grouped-query attention (several query heads sharing one key/value head), cache quantisation and paged caches exist.

build.answer:
Without a cache, generating each new token re-runs the whole context through the model, recomputing the keys and values of every earlier token, over and over. With a cache, the first step processes the prompt and stores every layer's keys and values; each later step feeds in only the one new token, computes its query, key and value, appends the key and value to the cache, and attends over the cache.

The check that matters first: with greedy decoding, both versions produce exactly the same tokens, so the cache changes speed, not results. On a model with a 512-character context, generating 500 tokens is several times faster with the cache here, and the gap grows with the context length, because the uncached cost per step grows with the number of tokens so far while the cached cost stays nearly flat.
build.code:
import time
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from gpt import GPT, Config

@torch.no_grad()
def generate_uncached(model, idx, n):
    for _ in range(n):
        logits, _ = model(idx[:, -model.c.block_size:])
        idx = torch.cat([idx, logits[:, -1].argmax(-1, keepdim=True)], dim=1)
    return idx

@torch.no_grad()
def generate_cached(model, idx, n):
    c, H = model.c, model.c.n_head
    cache = [None] * c.n_layer
    new, start = idx, 0
    for _ in range(n):
        T = new.shape[1]
        x = model.tok(new) + model.pos(torch.arange(start, start + T))
        for i, block in enumerate(model.blocks):
            h = block.ln1(x)
            q, k, v = block.attn.qkv(h).split(c.n_embd, dim=2)
            q, k, v = [t.view(1, T, H, -1).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v)]
            if cache[i] is not None:                       # reuse every earlier key and value
                k, v = torch.cat([cache[i][0], k], dim=2), torch.cat([cache[i][1], v], dim=2)
            cache[i] = (k, v)
            y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=(T > 1))
            x = x + block.attn.proj(y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(1, T, c.n_embd))
            x = x + block.mlp(block.ln2(x))
        logits = model.head(model.ln(x))
        nxt = logits[:, -1].argmax(-1, keepdim=True)
        idx, start, new = torch.cat([idx, nxt], dim=1), start + T, nxt
    return idx

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = GPT(Config(block_size=512)).eval()        # speed doesn't depend on training
prompt = torch.zeros((1, 1), dtype=torch.long)
t = time.perf_counter(); a = generate_uncached(model, prompt, 500); slow = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); b = generate_cached(model, prompt, 500); fast = time.perf_counter() - t
assert torch.equal(a, b)                           # identical tokens
print(f"without cache {slow:.2f} s, with cache {fast:.2f} s: {slow / fast:.1f}x faster")

break.answer:
Past the maximum length, a model with learned position embeddings simply has no embedding for position 512: the lookup fails with "index out of range". Models with rotary or similar encodings can technically keep going, but quality usually collapses beyond the lengths they were trained on. Real systems either stop at the limit, slide a window (drop the oldest tokens, which with a cache means also dropping and, for learned positions, recomputing), or use long-context techniques.

Memory with many users: each user in a batch has their own cache, so memory grows exactly linearly with the batch size: twice the users, twice the cache. For this tiny model in float32 that is about 2 MB per 512-token sequence, so 64 users take about 134 MB. For a real 7B-class model (32 layers, width 4,096, bf16) it is about 2 GB per user at 4,096 tokens, or about 0.5 GB with grouped-query attention, which is why the number of users a GPU can serve at once is usually limited by cache memory, not by compute.
break.code:
import torch
from gpt import GPT, Config

c = Config(block_size=512)
model = GPT(c).eval()
try:
    model(torch.zeros((1, 513), dtype=torch.long))
except IndexError as e:
    print("too long:", e)

for users in [1, 8, 64]:
    k = torch.zeros(users, c.n_head, c.block_size, c.n_embd // c.n_head)      # one layer's keys
    total = 2 * c.n_layer * k.numel() * k.element_size()                      # keys and values, all layers
    print(f"{users:3d} users x 512 tokens: KV cache {total / 1e6:.0f} MB")

explain.answer:
Taking notes during a long meeting. Without notes, every time someone speaks you would replay the whole recording from the start to remember what was said, which gets slower as the meeting goes on. With notes, you just add one line for each new remark and glance back at your notes.

In a transformer, every new token needs the keys and values of all the earlier tokens. The KV cache is the notes: it stores them once, so each new token only computes its own and adds them to the cache, which makes generation much faster. The cost is that the notes take up memory, a lot of it for long conversations and many users at once.

topics.name: Pretraining data and scaling laws
topics.definition: Pretraining is next-token prediction on an enormous text collection, and scaling laws describe how the resulting loss falls smoothly and predictably as model size, data and compute grow.
topics.problem: Training a large model costs millions, so you need to predict, before spending, how big to make it and how much data to use. Scaling laws let labs fit small experiments and extrapolate. They also explain the shape of the field: why models kept growing, why data quality became the bottleneck, and why small models are now trained on far more data than "optimal".
howItWorks: Collect web pages, books, code and papers, then filter them hard: remove duplicates, spam and low-quality pages, and personal data.
Tokenise everything and train a GPT on next-token prediction, usually for one pass (or a few) over the data.
Measure the final loss for many runs of different sizes. Plotted against compute on log–log axes, the points fall on a smooth power-law curve.
Compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens (in floating-point operations). For a fixed compute budget, you choose how to split it between parameters and tokens.
Chinchilla's result: grow both together, about 20 training tokens per parameter. A 1B-parameter model "wants" about 20B tokens.
In practice, models meant to be served cheaply are trained far past that point (Llama-style models use trillions of tokens): a smaller, longer-trained model costs less to run.
keyPoints: Loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute.
Training compute ≈ 6·N·D (N = parameters, D = tokens).
Compute-optimal: roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
Data quality, deduplication and mixture matter as much as size.
Lower loss doesn't map neatly to every ability; some skills seem to appear suddenly with scale.
Running out of high-quality text is a real constraint; synthetic data is one response.
mistakes: Assuming more data always helps, even when it is duplicated or low quality.
Reading scaling laws as guarantees for specific skills rather than for the average loss.
Comparing models trained on different data as if size were the only difference.

followUps.q: What is the Chinchilla rule of thumb?
followUps.a: For compute-optimal training, use about 20 training tokens per parameter.

followUps.q: Roughly how much compute does training take?
followUps.a: About 6 × parameters × tokens floating-point operations.

followUps.q: Why train a small model far past the compute-optimal point?
followUps.a: It costs more to train, but it is much cheaper to run for millions of users, and keeps improving.

followUps.q: Why does deduplicating pretraining data matter?
followUps.a: Repeated documents waste compute, encourage memorisation, and can make the model regurgitate text.

derive.answer:
About 20 training tokens per parameter (the Chinchilla rule of thumb for compute-optimal training):

125M parameters → 125M × 20 = 2.5 billion tokens
1B parameters → 20 billion tokens
7B parameters → 140 billion tokens

Modern models often train on far more than this, for example several trillion tokens for a 7B model, because the rule is about the best model for a fixed training budget. If the model will be used by millions of people, it is cheaper overall to train a smaller model for longer, since running it costs less every day.

build.answer:
Train three GPTs of increasing width and depth on the same Shakespeare data, with the same number of steps, and record the final validation loss. On log-log axes, loss against parameter count falls in a roughly straight line: each multiplication of the size gives a similar reduction in loss. That straight line is a scaling law.

With this tiny dataset (1 MB) and short training, the line already bends at the big end: the largest model is held back by too little data and too few steps, which is the same lesson the Chinchilla paper drew: size and data have to grow together.
build.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
from gpt import GPT, Config, train, estimate_loss

sizes, losses = [], []
for n_embd, n_layer in [(32, 2), (64, 3), (128, 4)]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = train(GPT(Config(n_embd=n_embd, n_layer=n_layer, n_head=4)), steps=1500, log_every=0)
    sizes.append(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))
    losses.append(estimate_loss(model, iters=50))
    print(f"{sizes[-1]:>8,} parameters: val loss {losses[-1]:.3f}")
plt.loglog(sizes, losses, marker="o")
plt.xlabel("parameters"); plt.ylabel("validation loss"); plt.show()

break.answer:
Make two training sets of the same size: one is 900,000 different characters of Shakespeare; the other is only the first 100,000 characters, copied 9 times. Train the same model for the same number of steps on each, and measure on the same held-out text.

The duplicated set gives a clearly worse validation loss. The model sees the same passages again and again and starts memorising them, which lowers its training loss but doesn't help on new text; meanwhile the unique set teaches it nine times as much real variety. Same compute, less learned.

Real web data is full of near-duplicates (boilerplate, mirrored pages, copied articles), which is why deduplication is a standard step in building pretraining data: it improves the model for free, and reduces memorisation of specific documents, a privacy and copyright concern.

import torch
from gpt import GPT, Config, get_batch, train_data, estimate_loss

unique = train_data[:900_000]
duplicated = train_data[:100_000].repeat(9)           # same length, a ninth of the variety
for name, source in [("unique", unique), ("duplicated", duplicated)]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = GPT(Config())
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(1500):

        loss = model(x, y)[1]
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

explain.answer:
Learning a language by reading a library. A bigger brain can hold more of what it reads, and a bigger library gives it more to learn from. Scaling laws are the discovery that this works in a smooth, predictable way: make the model and the data bigger together, and the loss falls along a straight line on a log-log chart, so you can predict how good a much bigger model will be before you train it.

But the library has to be good. A library of the same book photocopied a thousand times, or full of spam and broken pages, teaches far less than its size suggests: the brain memorises the copies instead of learning the language. That is why deduplication, filtering and careful mixing of data sources matter as much as raw size.

topics.name: Mixture of experts
topics.definition: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer replaces one big MLP with many expert MLPs and a router that sends each token to only a few of them, so the model has many parameters but uses only a fraction per token.
topics.problem: Bigger models know more, but every parameter normally runs for every token, so cost grows with size. MoE breaks that link: total knowledge can grow while compute per token stays modest. Many frontier models use it, and it changes how you think about model size, memory and serving.
howItWorks: Inside each block, replace the single MLP with E experts (for example 8), each an MLP of its own.
A small router (a linear layer) scores every expert for each token.
Keep the top k experts (often 2), turn their scores into weights with softmax, and run only those experts.
The token's output is the weighted sum of its chosen experts' outputs.
Different tokens choose different experts, so experts can specialise.
A load-balancing loss pushes the router to spread tokens evenly; without it a few experts get everything and the rest never learn.
All experts must be in memory even though each token uses only some of them, so memory scales with the total size while compute scales with the active size.
keyPoints: Total parameters ≠ active parameters. Mixtral 8x7B: about 47B total, about 13B active per token.
Top-k routing (usually k = 1 or 2).
Load balancing is essential.
MoE saves compute, not memory.
Experts across GPUs need fast communication (expert parallelism).
mistakes: Quoting the total parameter count as if it were the compute cost per token.
Training without a balancing loss and getting "dead" experts.
Forgetting that serving still needs memory for every expert.

followUps.q: What does the router do?
followUps.a: For each token, it scores every expert and picks the top few to run, with weights for mixing their outputs.

followUps.q: Why is MoE cheaper per token than a dense model of the same total size?
followUps.a: Each token runs through only k experts, not all of them.

followUps.q: Why add a load-balancing loss?
followUps.a: Without it, the router tends to send most tokens to a few experts, overloading them while the others stop learning.

followUps.q: An MoE has 8 experts per layer and top-2 routing. What share of the expert parameters does each token use?
followUps.a: 2 of 8, so a quarter.

flowchart LR

  R -->|"weight 0.7"| E2["expert 2"]
  R -->|"weight 0.3"| E5["expert 5"]

note.idea: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer replaces one big MLP with many smaller 'expert' MLPs and a router. For each token, the router picks only a few experts, often 2, to run. So the model can have a huge number of parameters in total while each token uses only a small part of them: more knowledge for about the same compute per token.
note.analogy: A hospital with many specialists. Each patient sees only the one or two doctors they need, not every doctor in the building.
note.breaks: A hospital can spread patients fairly. In an MoE, if the router sends too many tokens to the same few experts, they are overloaded and the others learn nothing, so training adds a load-balancing loss. And every expert must still sit in memory, even the unused ones.
note.example: Mixtral 8x7B has 8 experts per layer with top-2 routing. It has about 47B parameters in total, but uses only about 13B for each token.

derive.answer:
Total expert parameters: 24 layers × 64 experts × 100M = 153,600M, about 153.6 billion.

Used for each token: with top-2 routing, each token goes through 2 experts per layer: 24 × 2 × 100M = 4.8 billion.

So each token uses only 2 of 64 experts, about 3% of the expert parameters. The compute per token is like a 4.8B model (plus the shared attention and embeddings), while the model's total knowledge capacity is like a 150B+ model. But all 153.6B parameters must still sit in memory, because different tokens need different experts.

build.answer:
The MoE layer has 4 small expert MLPs and a router: a linear layer that gives each token a score for each expert. For each token, take the top 2 scores, softmax them into two weights, run the token through those 2 experts only, and add their outputs with those weights. Each block's MLP is swapped for this layer.

Logging how many tokens each expert receives shows how the router spreads the work. This version also computes the standard load-balancing loss (used in the break exercise), which is small when the experts are used evenly.
build.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from gpt import GPT, Config, get_batch, estimate_loss

class MoE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, n_experts=4, k=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.k, self.n = k, n_experts
        self.router = nn.Linear(d, n_experts)
        self.experts = nn.ModuleList(nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 2 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(2 * d, d))
                                     for _ in range(n_experts))
    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, d = x.shape
        flat = x.reshape(-1, d)
        probs = F.softmax(self.router(flat), dim=-1)                  # (tokens, experts)
        weights, chosen = probs.topk(self.k, dim=-1)
        weights = weights / weights.sum(-1, keepdim=True)
        out = torch.zeros_like(flat)
        for e, expert in enumerate(self.experts):
            rows, slot = (chosen == e).nonzero(as_tuple=True)
            if len(rows):
                out[rows] += weights[rows, slot, None] * expert(flat[rows])
        share = F.one_hot(chosen, self.n).float().sum(1).mean(0) / self.k  # fraction of tokens per expert
        self.counts = share.detach()
        self.balance_loss = self.n * (share * probs.mean(0)).sum()       # 1.0 when perfectly even
        return out.reshape(B, T, d)

def train_moe(balance_coef, steps=800, seed=0, n_experts=4, k=2):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = GPT(Config())
    for block in model.blocks:
        block.mlp = MoE(model.c.n_embd, n_experts, k)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x, y = get_batch("train")
        loss = model(x, y)[1] + balance_coef * sum(b.mlp.balance_loss for b in model.blocks)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return model

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = train_moe(balance_coef=0.01)
    print(f"val loss {estimate_loss(model):.3f}")
    for i, block in enumerate(model.blocks):
        print(f"layer {i}: share of tokens per expert {block.mlp.counts.numpy().round(2)}")

break.answer:
Without a balancing loss, the router is free to send most tokens to whichever experts got slightly ahead early on. Those experts get more training, so they become better, so the router prefers them even more: a rich-get-richer loop. With 8 experts and top-1 routing (an even share would be 12.5% each), the run below shows it: without a balancing loss, the busiest expert in a layer takes about 23% of the tokens on average, and some experts get only about 3%. Those starved experts barely train, and in large models this goes all the way to "dead" experts that receive almost no tokens and waste their parameters. (With only 4 experts and top-2 routing, as in the Build answer, it stays fairly even in a short run; imbalance grows with more experts, sparser routing and longer training.)

With the balancing loss, which is smallest when the share of tokens and the router's average probability are equal across experts, every expert stays between about 10% and 15%. Real MoE models also cap how many tokens one expert may take per batch (a capacity factor), so no expert is overloaded on the hardware.
