for coef in [0.0, 0.01]:
    model = train_moe(balance_coef=coef, steps=1500, n_experts=8, k=1)    # 8 experts, top-1: an even share is 12.5%
    shares = torch.stack([b.mlp.counts for b in model.blocks])
    print(f"balance loss x {coef}: share of tokens per expert, one row per layer\n{shares.numpy().round(2)}")
    print(f"  busiest expert, averaged over layers: {shares.max(dim=1).values.mean():.2f}, quietest anywhere: {shares.min():.2f}\n")

explain.answer:
A big hospital has many specialists. A patient doesn't see every doctor in the building, only the one or two the front desk sends them to. So the hospital as a whole knows an enormous amount, but each visit only uses a little of it, and visits stay quick.

In a mixture-of-experts model, each layer has many expert networks and a router (the front desk) that sends each token to its top one or two experts. The model has a huge number of parameters, but each token uses only a small part, so it is fast to run for its size. Memory is still a cost: every specialist must be employed and in the building even when idle, so all the experts must sit in GPU memory, ready for whichever tokens need them.

topics.name: Fine-tuning and LoRA
topics.definition: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on your own data; LoRA does it cheaply by freezing the original weights W and training a small low-rank update, so the layer uses W + B·A.
topics.problem: Pretrained models are general; you often need a specific style, format or domain. Full fine-tuning updates billions of weights, needs optimiser memory for all of them, and produces a whole new model copy per task. LoRA trains well under 1% of the parameters, fits on a single GPU, and produces small adapters you can swap in and out of one base model.
howItWorks: Pick the weight matrices to adapt, usually the attention projections (and often the MLP).
Freeze W. Add two small matrices: B (d_out × r) and A (r × d_in), with rank r such as 8 or 16.
Start B at zero, so B·A = 0 and the model begins exactly as the pretrained one.
The layer computes y = x·Wᵀ + x·(B·A)ᵀ, usually scaled by α/r.
Train only A and B. For a 4,096 × 4,096 matrix with r = 8, that is 65,536 weights instead of 16.8 million: about 0.4%.
Afterwards, keep the adapter separate (tiny files, swappable), or merge it: W′ = W + B·A, with no extra cost when running.
QLoRA goes further: the frozen base model is stored in 4-bit, so even large models can be fine-tuned on one GPU.
keyPoints: Full fine-tuning: every weight, most flexible, most expensive.
LoRA: frozen W plus a trainable low-rank B·A.
Trainable LoRA parameters per matrix = r × (d_in + d_out).
B = 0 at the start means no change at step 0.
Adapters can be merged into W for free inference, or swapped per task.
Fine-tuning teaches style and format well; it is a poor way to add lots of new facts (use RAG, Phase 5).
mistakes: Starting both A and B random, so the model is damaged at step 0.
Choosing a rank far too small for a big change in behaviour, or far too big for a small dataset.
Fine-tuning to inject facts that change often.
Forgetting the original chat template, so the tuned model loses its formatting.

followUps.q: Why does LoRA start B at zero?
followUps.a: So B·A = 0 and the model initially behaves exactly like the pretrained one; training then moves it gradually.

followUps.q: How many trainable parameters does LoRA add to a d_out × d_in matrix at rank r?
followUps.a: r × (d_in + d_out): B has d_out × r and A has r × d_in.

followUps.q: What is the advantage of keeping LoRA adapters separate?
followUps.a: One base model can serve many tasks by swapping small adapter files.

followUps.q: What does QLoRA add?
followUps.a: It keeps the frozen base model in 4-bit precision, cutting memory so large models can be fine-tuned on modest hardware.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR X["x"] --> W["W (frozen)
4,096 × 4,096"] --> ADD(("+")) X --> A["A (trained)
8 × 4,096"] --> B["B (trained)
4,096 × 8"] --> ADD ADD --> Y["output"]
diagram.caption: LoRA leaves the big weight W untouched and trains two thin matrices beside it — about 0.4% as many numbers.

note.idea: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on your own data. Full fine-tuning updates every weight. LoRA freezes the original weights W and learns a small update BA of low rank r (for example 8): W′ = W + BA.
note.analogy: Instead of rewriting a whole textbook, you add a few sticky notes with corrections.
note.breaks: Sticky notes can be removed, and so can LoRA adapters, so one base model can serve many tasks. But a small rank cannot teach big new skills.
note.example: A 4,096 × 4,096 layer has 16.8 million weights. LoRA with r = 8 trains B (4,096 × 8) and A (8 × 4,096): 65,536 weights, about 0.4%.

derive.answer:
A 1,024 × 1,024 layer has 1,048,576 weights. Full fine-tuning trains all of them.

LoRA trains B (1,024 × r) and A (r × 1,024), so 2 × 1,024 × r weights:
r = 4: 8,192 weights, 0.78% of the layer
r = 8: 16,384 weights, 1.56%
r = 64: 131,072 weights, 12.5%

The update B·A can only change the layer in r independent directions. Small r is very cheap but limited; larger r can express bigger changes. Most fine-tunes work well with r between 8 and 64.

build.answer:
A LoRA layer wraps an existing nn.Linear: the original weight is frozen, and the output adds (alpha / r) · x·Aᵀ·Bᵀ, with A starting small and random and B starting at 0, so at step 0 the model is exactly the original. Wrap the attention projections (qkv and proj) of every block and train only A and B.

Experiment: pretrain the Shakespeare GPT, then fine-tune it to a very different style, a list of first names, one per line. LoRA with r = 8 trains about 3% of the parameters and learns the new style: its samples already look like names. Full fine-tuning gets a clearly lower loss in the same number of steps (about 1.61 against 2.07 here), because it can change everything, including the MLPs and embeddings, which matters for a change this big, from Shakespeare's verse to bare first names. For smaller shifts in style, the gap is usually much smaller. LoRA's adapter is a tiny file, and the original model stays untouched, so you could keep one adapter per style.
build.code:
import math
import urllib.request
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from gpt import GPT, Config, train, encode, decode

class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base, r=8, alpha=16, init_b_zero=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.base, self.scale = base, alpha / r
        for p in self.base.parameters():
            p.requires_grad = False
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(r, base.in_features) / math.sqrt(base.in_features))
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(base.out_features, r) if init_b_zero else torch.randn(base.out_features, r) * 0.1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.base(x) + self.scale * (x @ self.A.T @ self.B.T)

def add_lora(model, r=8, init_b_zero=True):
    for p in model.parameters():
        p.requires_grad = False
    for block in model.blocks:
        block.attn.qkv = LoRALinear(block.attn.qkv, r, init_b_zero=init_b_zero)
        block.attn.proj = LoRALinear(block.attn.proj, r, init_b_zero=init_b_zero)
    return model

names = urllib.request.urlopen("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/master/names.txt").read().decode()
names = torch.tensor(encode(names))                        # lowercase letters and newlines: all in the vocabulary
tr, va = names[:200_000], names[200_000:]

def batch(d):
    ix = torch.randint(len(d) - 65, (32,))
    return torch.stack([d[i:i + 64] for i in ix]), torch.stack([d[i + 1:i + 65] for i in ix])

def finetune(model, steps=500):
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW([p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad], lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        loss = model(*batch(tr))[1]
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return sum(model(*batch(va))[1].item() for _ in range(20)) / 20

if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    base = train(GPT(), steps=1500, log_every=0)
    torch.save(base.state_dict(), "base.pt")
    for name, make in [("LoRA r=8", lambda m: add_lora(m, 8)), ("full fine-tune", lambda m: m)]:
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        model = GPT(); model.load_state_dict(torch.load("base.pt")); model = make(model)
        trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
        loss = finetune(model)
        torch.manual_seed(1)
        sample = decode(model.generate(torch.tensor([encode("\n")]), 60)[0].tolist()).split()
        print(f"{name}: {trainable:,} trainable parameters, names val loss {loss:.3f}, sample {sample[:6]}")

break.answer:
If both A and B start random, B·A is not zero, so the moment you attach the adapters the model is no longer the pretrained model: random changes have been added to every attention layer. At step 0 the loss jumps up (in the run below, from about 1.76 on Shakespeare to about 2.05), and the first part of fine-tuning is spent undoing damage. Starting B at zero is what makes LoRA begin exactly at the pretrained model and move away only as far as the data asks.

r = 1 on a task that needs a big change (Shakespeare to a list of names): the update can only move each layer along a single direction, so it learns the new style more slowly and ends at a higher loss than r = 8. Low rank is a strong restriction: it works when the change is small, like adjusting tone, and struggles when the model must learn a lot that is new.

explain.answer:
Instead of rewriting a whole textbook for a new course, you add a few sticky notes with corrections and extra tips next to the pages that need them. The textbook stays exactly as it was, the notes are cheap to write and easy to carry around, and you can keep a different set of notes for each class.

LoRA does this for a model: the huge pretrained weight matrices stay frozen (the textbook), and you train two small matrices per layer whose product is added on top (the sticky notes). Training needs far less memory, the result is a small file, and the base model can be shared by many adapters.

topics.name: Instruction tuning and preference tuning (RLHF, DPO)
topics.definition: Instruction tuning trains a pretrained model on example conversations so it follows requests, and preference tuning (RLHF or DPO) then trains it on pairs of answers so it prefers the better one.
topics.problem: A pretrained model is a brilliant autocomplete, not an assistant: ask it a question and it may continue with more questions. Instruction tuning teaches the format and habit of helpful answering; preference tuning sharpens qualities that are easy to judge but hard to demonstrate, like helpfulness, honesty and harmlessness. This is the step that turned GPT-3 into ChatGPT.
howItWorks: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): train on thousands of (prompt, ideal answer) conversations, written in a chat template, with the loss computed only on the answer tokens.
Collect preferences: for one prompt, sample two answers and have people (or a strong model) mark the better one: (prompt, chosen, rejected).
RLHF, step 1: train a reward model to give the chosen answer a higher score than the rejected one.
RLHF, step 2: use reinforcement learning (often PPO) to make the model produce high-reward answers, with a KL penalty that keeps it close to the SFT model so it doesn't game the reward.
DPO skips both the reward model and RL: a classification-style loss directly makes the chosen answer more likely than the rejected one, relative to a frozen reference model.
Evaluate carefully: preference tuning can teach shortcuts, such as longer or more flattering answers winning.
keyPoints: Pretraining → knowledge; SFT → format and instruction following; preference tuning → quality and safety.
RLHF = reward model + RL (PPO) + KL penalty.
DPO = learn directly from preference pairs; simpler and more stable.
Reward hacking: the model learns what the reward likes, not what people want.
Chat templates (special tokens marking roles) must match between training and use.
mistakes: Computing the SFT loss on the prompt tokens as well as the answers.
Preference data with hidden biases, such as "longer is always better".
Dropping the KL penalty, so the model drifts into strange, reward-gaming text.

followUps.q: What does instruction tuning add to a pretrained model?
followUps.a: The habit and format of answering requests helpfully, learned from example conversations.

followUps.q: What is the reward model in RLHF?
followUps.a: A model trained on preference pairs to score answers the way the human raters would.

followUps.q: How does DPO differ from RLHF?
followUps.a: DPO learns directly from the preference pairs with a simple loss, with no separate reward model and no RL loop.

followUps.q: What is reward hacking?
followUps.a: The model finds ways to score highly on the reward that people don't actually want, such as padding answers to look thorough.

Preference tuning trains it on pairs of answers where people marked the better one. RLHF uses a reward model and reinforcement learning. DPO learns from the pairs directly.
note.analogy: Pretraining is reading everything. Instruction tuning is an internship with worked examples. Preference tuning is a manager saying 'this version is better than that one'.
note.breaks: A manager explains why. Preference data only says which answer won, so models can learn shortcuts, such as 'longer answers win'.

derive.answer:
Instruction-tuning examples (prompt, ideal answer), for a cooking assistant:

1. User: "How long should I boil an egg for a runny yolk?" Assistant: "About 6 minutes from when you lower it into boiling water. Then move it to cold water for a minute so it stops cooking and peels easily."
2. User: "I have chicken, rice and spinach. Suggest a quick dinner." Assistant: "Make a one-pan chicken and spinach rice: brown bite-sized chicken pieces, add rice, stock and garlic, simmer for 15 minutes, then stir in the spinach until it wilts. Season with lemon and pepper."
3. User: "Can I swap butter for oil in a cake?" Assistant: "Yes. Use about three-quarters as much oil as butter, for example 75 g of oil for 100 g of butter. The cake will be moister but a little less rich in flavour."

Preference pairs (prompt, chosen, rejected):

1. Prompt: "Is it safe to eat chicken that is a bit pink?" Chosen: "Not reliably. Colour isn't a safe test; check that the thickest part reaches 74°C with a thermometer." Rejected: "Yes, a little pink is fine, just eat it."
2. Prompt: "Give me a quick pasta sauce." Chosen: a short, clear recipe with amounts and steps. Rejected: a long story about the history of tomatoes before a vague recipe.

The instruction examples teach the format and the job; the pairs teach which of two plausible answers is better, here safer and more to the point.

build.answer:
A character model can't learn real conversation in a few minutes, so use simple tasks it can learn, in a chat template: "Q: reverse king
A: gnik

", plus "upper" (make it capitals) and "first" (the first letter). Make a few hundred examples from Shakespeare's words and fine-tune the pretrained Shakespeare GPT on them.

Before fine-tuning, given "Q: reverse king
A:", the model just continues with Shakespeare-like text: it has no idea that a question expects an answer. After a few hundred steps it answers in the template's format, stops at the blank line, and gets most of the held-out words right (reversing is the hardest). That is instruction tuning in miniature: same model, same knowledge, now trained to respond to a request in a fixed format.
build.code:
import random
import re
import torch
from gpt import GPT, train, encode, decode, text

words = sorted({w for w in re.findall(r"[a-z]{3,7}", text)})
random.seed(0); random.shuffle(words)
train_words, test_words = words[:600], words[600:650]
tasks = {"reverse": lambda w: w[::-1], "upper": lambda w: w.upper(), "first": lambda w: w[0]}
example = lambda task, w: f"Q: {task} {w}\nA: {tasks[task](w)}\n\n"
corpus = torch.tensor(encode("".join(example(t, w) for w in train_words for t in tasks) * 3))

@torch.no_grad()
def ask(model, task, word):
    out = decode(model.generate(torch.tensor([encode(f"Q: {task} {word}\nA:")]), 12, temperature=0.01)[0].tolist())
    return out.split("A:")[1].split("\n")[0].strip()

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = train(GPT(), steps=1500, log_every=0)
print("before:", [ask(model, t, "king") for t in tasks])
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
model.train()
for _ in range(600):
    ix = torch.randint(len(corpus) - 65, (32,))
    x, y = torch.stack([corpus[i:i + 64] for i in ix]), torch.stack([corpus[i + 1:i + 65] for i in ix])
    loss = model(x, y)[1]
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
print("after:", [ask(model, t, "king") for t in tasks])
for t in tasks:
    right = sum(ask(model, t, w) == tasks[t](w) for w in test_words)
    print(f"{t}: {right}/{len(test_words)} held-out words right")

break.answer:
The shortcut: "longer is better". If the chosen answer is always the longer one, the easiest way to win the preference is simply to write more, with more caveats, more bullet points and more repetition, whether or not the extra text helps. The model learns length, not quality. This really happens: preference-tuned models are known to drift towards verbosity, and judges (human or LLM) often favour longer answers.

How to check for it:
• Look at the data first: compare the lengths of chosen and rejected answers. If chosen is longer in, say, 95% of pairs, the signal is mostly length.
• Measure after training: plot answer length before and after tuning on the same prompts, and check how much of the "win rate" against the old model is explained by length (compare wins only among answers of similar length, a length-controlled win rate).
• Add pairs where the shorter answer is better, and test on prompts where the ideal answer is very short ("What is 2 + 2?").

The general lesson: a model trained to win a comparison will find the cheapest feature that predicts winning. Every bias in the preference data becomes behaviour.

explain.answer:
Think of training a new employee in three stages.

Pretraining is reading everything: years of books, websites and code. Afterwards they know a huge amount, but if you ask them a question they might just continue your sentence, because nobody taught them that a question needs an answer.

Instruction tuning is an internship with worked examples: "here is a request, here is a good response", thousands of times. Now they know the job: answer questions, follow instructions, use the right format.

Preference tuning is a manager reviewing their work: "this version is better than that one". Shown many such comparisons (RLHF learns a scoring model from them; DPO learns straight from the pairs), they learn the finer points: more helpful, more honest, safer, better judgement in grey areas. Each stage builds on the last; the knowledge comes almost entirely from the first.

topics.name: Reasoning models and test-time compute
topics.definition: Reasoning models are trained to write out intermediate steps before answering, and test-time compute means spending more computation at answer time — longer reasoning, or many samples plus a vote — to get better answers.
topics.problem: Some problems can't be solved in a single forward pass: multi-step maths, tricky code, planning. Letting the model work step by step, and spend more tokens on harder questions, greatly improves accuracy. It gives a new knob — accuracy versus cost per query — alongside model size, and it is behind the jump in maths and coding ability of recent models.
howItWorks: Chain of thought: the model writes its reasoning first ("12 pens is 4 groups of 3 …"), then the answer. Each step is a smaller, easier prediction that the next step can build on.

Prompting ("think step by step") helps a little; training helps a lot. Reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning on problems whose answers can be checked, such as maths with known answers and code with unit tests.
The reward is simply "was the final answer right?" Over many attempts, the model learns reasoning habits that lead to right answers: checking work, trying again, breaking problems down.
Self-consistency: sample several reasoning paths at a temperature above 0 and take a majority vote on the final answers.
Best-of-N with a verifier: generate N answers and let a checker (tests, a reward model) choose.
More thinking costs more tokens and time, so it is worth it for hard, checkable problems, not for simple lookups.
keyPoints: Test-time compute is a new scaling axis: spend more per query for better answers.
RL with verifiable rewards trains models to reason.
Majority voting and verifiers turn several noisy attempts into one more reliable answer.
Written reasoning isn't guaranteed to be the true cause of the answer.
Cost and latency grow with reasoning length; use it where accuracy matters.
mistakes: Paying for long reasoning on simple factual questions.
Trusting a chain of thought as a faithful explanation.
Using self-consistency at temperature 0, which gives the same answer every time.

followUps.q: What is test-time compute?
followUps.a: Extra computation spent when answering — longer reasoning, or several samples — to improve accuracy, instead of a bigger model.

followUps.q: How does self-consistency work?
followUps.a: Sample several reasoning paths with some randomness and take the most common final answer.

followUps.q: Why train reasoning on maths and code first?
followUps.a: Their answers can be checked automatically, which gives a clear reward signal for reinforcement learning.

followUps.q: When is extra reasoning not worth it?
followUps.a: For simple lookups or questions the model already answers reliably: it only adds cost and delay.

note.idea: A reasoning model is trained to 'think' before answering: it writes out intermediate steps (a chain of thought) and can spend more tokens on harder problems. Spending more computation at answer time, by reasoning for longer or by sampling several answers and picking the best, is called test-time compute. Much of this ability is trained with reinforcement learning on problems whose answers can be checked, like maths and code.
note.analogy: A student allowed to use scrap paper and check their work, instead of shouting the first answer that comes to mind.
note.breaks: A student's scrap paper shows their real reasoning. A model's written steps are not guaranteed to be the true cause of its answer. And more thinking costs more time and money; it helps most on problems with checkable steps.
note.example: Self-consistency: sample 10 reasoning paths for a maths question and take the most common final answer. It is often more accurate than one greedy answer, at 10 times the cost.

practice.derive: A model is right 60% of the time on a type of question, independently each time. With a majority vote over 5 samples, is it right more or less often? Calculate it.
practice.build: On 50 arithmetic word problems, compare: a direct answer, 'think step by step', and self-consistency with 5 and 10 samples. Plot accuracy against tokens used.
practice.break: Try the same methods on simple factual questions, like capital cities. Does extra thinking still help, or just cost more? Find one case where the reasoning is wrong but the answer is right.

derive.answer:
The majority of 5 is right when at least 3 of the 5 samples are right. With p = 0.6 per sample, independently:

P(5 right) = 0.6⁵ = 0.07776
P(4 right) = 5 × 0.6⁴ × 0.4 = 5 × 0.1296 × 0.4 = 0.2592
P(3 right) = 10 × 0.6³ × 0.4² = 10 × 0.216 × 0.16 = 0.3456

Total: 0.07776 + 0.2592 + 0.3456 ≈ 0.683.

So the vote is right about 68% of the time, more often than one sample (60%). In practice it can be even better, because wrong answers usually disagree with each other (many different wrong numbers), so the right answer can win with fewer than 3 votes. And it can be worse when the samples aren't independent, for example when the model makes the same mistake every time.

build.answer:
The experiment: generate 50 word problems whose answers you know, then compare four methods. A direct answer ("reply with just the number"); "think step by step, then give the answer"; and self-consistency, which samples the step-by-step answer 5 or 10 times and takes the most common final answer. For each method record accuracy and the total output tokens, which is where the time goes, and plot accuracy against tokens.

It uses llm.py, the free helper from the Prompting topic in Phase 5 (Groq, then Gemini, then NVIDIA on free tiers, then a local Ollama model). Self-consistency needs varied samples, so those calls use temperature 1.0; the others use 0.

What to expect depends on the model. The first models in the chain (gpt-oss) are reasoning models: they think before answering anyway, so "think step by step" adds less, and self-consistency adds a few points on the hardest problems at 5 to 10 times the tokens. A small model without built-in reasoning, such as llama3.2:3b on Ollama (pass providers=[("Ollama", "http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions", None, "llama3.2:3b")]), shows the classic big jump from step-by-step. A 3-problem trial on qwen2.5:7b (local, no built-in reasoning) gave: direct 0 of 3, step by step 3 of 3, self-consistency 2 of 3. Sampling at temperature 1.0 made the small model sloppier, so self-consistency did worse than one careful answer; try a temperature of 0.6 to 0.8. It makes about 850 calls (50 × (1 + 1 + 5 + 10)), which will hit free-tier rate limits and fall back down the chain, so try 10 problems first.
build.code:
import random
import re
from collections import Counter
from llm import ask, text_of          # llm.py from Phase 5's Prompting topic: free APIs, then a local model

random.seed(0)
problems = []
for _ in range(50):
    a, b, c = random.randint(12, 99), random.randint(3, 19), random.randint(2, 9)
    q = f"A shop has {a} boxes with {b} apples each. It sells {c} full boxes, then gets {b} more apples. How many apples does it have now?"
    problems.append((q, (a - c) * b + b))

def solve(prompt, temperature):
    reply = ask(prompt, temperature=temperature, max_tokens=1500)
    numbers = re.findall(r"ANSWER:\s*(-?\d+)", text_of(reply))
    return (int(numbers[-1]) if numbers else None), reply["output_tokens"]

DIRECT = "{q}\nReply with only the final number, written as ANSWER: <number>."
STEPS = "{q}\nThink step by step, then finish with ANSWER: <number>."

def run(template, samples=1):
    correct = tokens = 0
    for q, truth in problems:
        answers = []
        for _ in range(samples):
            answer, used = solve(template.format(q=q), temperature=1.0 if samples > 1 else 0.0)
            answers.append(answer); tokens += used
        votes = Counter(a for a in answers if a is not None)
        correct += bool(votes) and votes.most_common(1)[0][0] == truth
    return correct / len(problems), tokens

for name, template, samples in [("direct", DIRECT, 1), ("step by step", STEPS, 1),
                                ("self-consistency x5", STEPS, 5), ("self-consistency x10", STEPS, 10)]:
    accuracy, tokens = run(template, samples)
    print(f"{name:22s} accuracy {accuracy:.0%}, output tokens {tokens:,}")

break.answer:
On simple factual questions ("What is the capital of Canada?"), extra thinking doesn't help: the model either knows the fact or it doesn't, and reasoning can't create knowledge that isn't there. Step-by-step and voting cost several times the tokens and the accuracy stays the same, already near 100% for easy facts. Occasionally overthinking even hurts, talking itself out of the right first answer. Test-time compute pays off on problems that need several steps (arithmetic, logic, code, planning), not on recall.

Reasoning wrong, answer right: look through the step-by-step outputs for cases like "15% of 80: 10% is 8, and 5% is 3, so 15% is 12". The answer, 12, is right, but the step "5% is 3" is wrong (it is 4), and 8 + 3 isn't even 12. The model reached the answer some other way and wrote a plausible-looking explanation. The lesson: a written chain of thought is not a guaranteed record of how the model got its answer. Check the answer, and don't treat the reasoning as proof; when the steps matter, verify them, for example with code or a calculator tool.

explain.answer:
A student in an exam can shout out the first answer that comes to mind, or use scrap paper: write out the steps, check the work, even solve it two different ways and see if they agree. The scrap paper costs time, but on a hard maths problem it makes a right answer far more likely.

Test-time compute is giving the model scrap paper: letting it generate reasoning before the answer, or sampling several answers and voting. Reasoning models are trained to do this well. It is worth the cost when the problem needs several steps and a wrong answer is expensive: maths, code, tricky analysis. It is wasted on simple lookups and chit-chat, where the first answer is already right and the extra tokens only add time and cost.

phases.title: AI engineering
phases.goal: Turn foundation models into real products: retrieval, evaluation, agents and deployment. This is the core of most AI engineer jobs.
phases.bigPicture: Phases 1 to 4 teach you how the engine works. Phase 5 teaches you to build the car around it: steering (prompts), fuel (data and retrieval), a dashboard (evaluation) and brakes (safety).

main.title: AI Engineering (Chip Huyen)
main.why: You are already reading it. Keep going. It is the main text for this phase.

main.title: Your AI Product Needs Evals (Hamel Husain)
main.why: The clearest guide to evaluation, the most important AI engineering skill.

main.title: Made With ML (Goku Mohandas)
main.why: Takes a model to production: testing, serving, CI/CD.

deeper.title: Designing Machine Learning Systems (Chip Huyen)
deeper.why: The standard book for ML system design interviews.

deeper.title: Stanford CS329S: Machine Learning Systems Design
deeper.why: Free course notes on the same topics.

deeper.title: FastAPI documentation
deeper.why: The simplest way to put a model behind an API.

builds.text: Semantic search in NumPy: embeddings plus cosine similarity. No vector database yet.
A RAG app without LangChain or any similar framework. Then swap in a real vector store.
An eval harness: 50 test questions, clear metrics, error categories. Show a before-and-after improvement.
Deploy one project with FastAPI and Docker, with a live demo link for your CV.
A tool-calling assistant that returns schema-validated JSON, plus an MCP server that exposes one of your own tools.
Add tracing, caching and a cheap-model-first router to your RAG app. Report cost per question and latency, before and after.

ready.q: Design a RAG system for company documents. Where can it fail?
ready.a: Ingest: parse documents, chunk them along headings, store metadata (source, date, permissions). Index with embeddings plus keyword search. At question time: retrieve with hybrid search, re-rank, build a prompt with numbered sources and an instruction to say "I don't know", then answer with citations. Evaluate retrieval and answers separately, and monitor. It can fail at chunking, at retrieval (the right chunk isn't found), with stale or duplicate documents, by cutting context, by hallucinating, by leaking documents a user shouldn't see, and through prompt injection hidden in documents.

ready.q: How do you prove your LLM app got better after a change?
ready.a: Run a fixed, representative test set before and after, changing only one thing, with the same scoring: code checks plus an LLM judge you have validated against human labels. Compare question by question, read the regressions, and check the difference is bigger than the noise. Then confirm with an online A/B test before rolling it out.

ready.q: What is prompt injection? Give two defences.
ready.a: Prompt injection is when text the model reads, from a user, a web page, a document or a tool, contains instructions that override yours. Two defences: give the model the least privilege it needs and require a human to confirm risky actions; and treat all retrieved or tool text as untrusted data, clearly separated from instructions, with checks on the output before acting on it.

ready.q: When would you fine-tune instead of using RAG?
ready.a: When the problem is behaviour rather than knowledge: a consistent style, tone or output format, a narrow task done the same way every time, or a smaller, cheaper and faster model for one job. Not for adding facts that change, which retrieval does better, with citations.

ready.q: Your app is too slow and too expensive. What do you try first?
ready.a: Measure first: where do the tokens and the time go? Then the cheap levers: send fewer tokens (shorter prompts, fewer chunks, a cap on output), use prompt caching for the fixed part, cache repeated answers, route easy requests to a smaller model, and stream so the first words appear sooner. Recheck quality after each change.

ready.q: How would you make an LLM return valid JSON every time, and what do you do when it doesn't?
ready.a: Use structured outputs: give the API a JSON schema so the reply is constrained to it, or strict tool definitions. Still validate in code, because the shape can be right and the values wrong. When something fails, retry once with the error message, fall back gracefully if it fails again, and log it so you can fix the cause.

ready.q: Your RAG app's bill doubled this month. Where do you look first?
ready.a: The usage logs. Did requests per day double (real growth, a bot, or a retry loop)? Did tokens per request grow (more chunks, longer history, a bigger system prompt, cache misses)? Did the model mix change (a router sending more traffic to the big model)? Did answers get longer? Compare the cost per request before and after to see which.

ready.q: What is MCP, and what problem does it solve?
ready.a: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data through MCP servers. Without it, every app needs its own integration for every tool. With it, you write one server for your data or service and any app that supports MCP can use it, like USB for AI tools.

topics.name: Prompting: clear instructions, examples, structured output
topics.definition: Prompting is writing the instructions, context and examples an LLM receives on each call; a good prompt is a complete, specific briefing that leaves the model little to guess.
topics.problem: The model knows nothing about your task, your users or your data except what is in the prompt. Vague prompts get vague, inconsistent answers that code can't parse. Prompting is the cheapest and fastest lever you have: improve it before reaching for RAG or fine-tuning, and measure the improvement on many inputs.
howItWorks: Say who the model is acting as and for whom: "You are a support triage assistant for engineers."
Give the context it can't know: where the text comes from, what the product is, what matters.
State the task precisely, with limits: "Summarise in 2 sentences", "list at most 3 risks".
Show one or more examples of input and the exact output you want (few-shot prompting). Examples often beat paragraphs of rules.
Ask for a fixed format when code reads the output: JSON with named fields, or text between tags.
Put long documents first and the question last, and mark data clearly (for example inside <document> tags) so it isn't mistaken for instructions.
Test the prompt on a set of real inputs, look at the failures, change one thing, and test again.
keyPoints: Specific beats short: role, context, task, constraints, examples, format.
Examples are the strongest signal for style and format.
Ask for structure (JSON, tags) whenever code consumes the answer.
Tell the model what to do when it can't answer ("say you don't know").
System prompts hold standing instructions; user messages hold the request.
Prompts are code: keep them in version control and evaluate changes.
mistakes: Judging a prompt on one example instead of a test set.
Contradictory instructions, or rules buried in long text.
Asking for JSON without saying which fields, types and allowed values.
Mixing untrusted data and instructions with no clear boundary.

followUps.q: What are the main parts of a strong prompt?
followUps.a: A role, the context, a precise task with limits, examples of the desired output, and the output format.

followUps.q: Why do examples help so much?
followUps.a: They show the exact style, length and format you want, which is hard to describe fully in words.

followUps.q: How do you know a prompt change helped?
followUps.a: Run old and new prompts on the same set of real inputs and compare the scores, rather than eyeballing one answer.

followUps.q: Why mark documents with tags like <document>?
followUps.a: So the model can tell your instructions apart from the data, which also makes prompt injection a little harder.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  R["role and context"] --> P["prompt"]
  T["the task"] --> P
  E["an example output"] --> P
  F["the output format (JSON)"] --> P
  P --> M["model"] --> O["JSON your code can read"]
diagram.caption: A strong prompt briefs the model like a new colleague: who it is, what to do, an example, and exactly what shape the answer must take.

note.idea: The prompt is the model's only briefing. Be clear and specific, give context, show examples of the output you want, and ask for a fixed format, like JSON, when code will read the answer.
note.analogy: Briefing a smart new colleague on their first day. They are capable, but they know nothing about your project unless you tell them.
note.breaks: A colleague asks when they are unsure. A model usually guesses instead, so leave less to guess.
note.example: Weak: 'Summarise this.' Strong: 'Summarise this support ticket in 2 sentences for an engineer. Then return JSON with product and urgency (low, medium or high).'

resources.title: Prompt engineering overview
resources.recommended: The official guide, with concrete before-and-after prompts for clarity, examples, structure and long documents. Practical and short.

practice.explain: Explain good prompting with the new-colleague picture.
practice.derive: Rewrite this weak prompt into a strong one: 'Tell me about this CV.' Add a role, context, the task, an output format and an example.
practice.build: Send 20 support tickets to an LLM API with your prompt, and parse the JSON output. Count how many parse correctly.
practice.break: Make the prompt vague on purpose, or remove the example. Measure how the parse rate and quality change.

derive.answer:
"Tell me about this CV" leaves the model guessing: who is asking, why, what matters, how long, in what shape. A strong prompt answers all of that, like a brief for a smart colleague on their first day:

• Role: who the model should be.
• Context: what this is for and who will read it.
• Task: exactly what to do, step by step if it matters.
• Output format: the shape of the answer, so your code (or reader) can rely on it.
• An example: one short sample of a good answer, so "good" is shown, not just described.
• What to do when information is missing.

Check yours: could someone who has never met you do the task well from your prompt alone? If not, add what they would ask you.
derive.code:
You are an experienced technical recruiter for AI engineering roles in the UK.

Context: I am screening CVs for a junior AI Engineer role. The job needs Python,
PyTorch, building and evaluating LLM applications (RAG, agents), and clear
communication. Hiring managers read your summary in under a minute.

Task: read the CV between the <cv> tags. Then:
1. List the candidate's three strongest pieces of evidence for this role.
2. List up to three gaps or risks, each with a question to ask in interview.
3. Give an overall fit: strong, possible, or weak, with one sentence why.
Only use what the CV says. If something is not stated, say "not stated".

Output format (exactly these headings):
Strengths: - ... (3 bullets, each with the evidence from the CV)
Gaps: - ... (up to 3 bullets, each ending with "Ask: ...")
Fit: strong | possible | weak. <one sentence>

Example of one good Strengths bullet:
- Built a RAG assistant and measured it: "retrieval recall 0.82 on 150 questions".

<cv>
{paste the CV here}
</cv>

build.answer:
This is llm.py, the small helper the other Phase 5 answers import, plus the ticket experiment. Everything in it is free. It works like CogniGraph's client: it tries Groq first, then Gemini, then NVIDIA, using free-tier API keys from a .env file, and finally a model running on your own computer through Ollama, which needs no key and has no limits. All four accept the same OpenAI-style chat request, so one request shape covers them all; if one provider is rate-limited (HTTP 429), has no key, or fails, the next one answers. Each reply records which provider answered, so you can see it.

ask() returns the reply as a small dictionary: the text, any tool calls, the token counts and the provider. Temperature 0 keeps answers as repeatable as possible, which is what you want for extraction and grading.

The experiment: a prompt with a role, the allowed categories, the exact JSON shape and one worked example, sent for each ticket. Parse each reply with json.loads and check the fields against the allowed values: "parses" is not enough, it must also be valid. A clear prompt like this one typically gets every reply right; the next exercise shows what happens without it, and the structured-outputs topic shows how to guarantee it.

The list has 8 sample tickets; add your own to reach 20. Free keys: console.groq.com, aistudio.google.com (Gemini) and build.nvidia.com; or skip the keys and run only the local model: install Ollama, then ollama pull qwen2.5:7b.

break.answer:
Make the prompt vague ("Classify this support ticket and give me JSON") and remove the example, then run the same tickets through the same parse() check.

What typically happens with a capable model: it still tries to give JSON, but you lose control of the details. Replies come wrapped in a markdown code fence (```json … ```), which json.loads rejects; key names drift ("type" or "issue" instead of "category"); and the categories are invented per ticket ("shipping delay", "refund request"), so even replies that parse fail validation. So the measured success rate falls sharply, and the replies that do parse are harder to use, because two similar tickets get different labels.

The lesson: what the prompt doesn't specify, the model decides for you, differently each time. Name the allowed values, show the exact shape, and give an example. When the shape must be guaranteed, don't rely on the prompt at all: use structured outputs, the next topic.
break.code:
# Uses llm.py from the Build answer above.
from llm import ask, text_of, parse, TICKETS, PROMPT

VAGUE = "Classify this support ticket and give me JSON: {ticket}"
for name, template in [("clear prompt", PROMPT), ("vague prompt", VAGUE)]:
    replies = [text_of(ask(template.replace("{ticket}", t))) for t in TICKETS]
    valid = sum(parse(r) is not None for r in replies)
    fenced = sum(r.strip().startswith(chr(96) * 3) for r in replies)   # chr(96) is a backtick
    print(f"{name}: {valid}/{len(TICKETS)} valid, {fenced} wrapped in a code fence")
    print("   first reply:", replies[0][:120].replace("\n", " "))

explain.answer:
Brief the model like a smart new colleague on their first day. They are capable, but they know nothing about your project, your customers or what "good" means here, unless you tell them. "Tell me about this CV" would confuse a new colleague too: for which job? For whom? How long?

So you give them the same things you would give a person: their role, the background, the exact task, what the result should look like, one example of a good result, and what to do if something is missing. The model can't ask follow-up questions, so the prompt must answer them in advance.

topics.name: Structured outputs and function calling
topics.definition: Structured output makes the model reply in a fixed, machine-readable format (usually JSON matching a schema); function calling lets the model reply with a request to run one of your functions, with arguments, which your code executes.
topics.problem: Free-form text is hard for programs to use reliably: a missing field or an extra sentence breaks parsing. And models can't look things up or take actions by themselves. Structured outputs make answers reliable to parse, and tool calling connects the model to live data and real actions — the basis of every agent.
howItWorks: Define the shape you want with a JSON Schema: field names, types, which are required, allowed values.
Send the schema with the request (many APIs can enforce it during generation), then validate every reply in code anyway.
For tools, describe each function: its name, what it does, and a schema for its arguments.
When a tool would help, the model replies with a tool call, such as {tool: get_weather, city: Leeds}, instead of prose.
Your code checks the arguments, runs the function, and sends the result back as a tool-result message.
The model then writes the final answer, or calls another tool. This loop is how agents work.
If validation fails, send the error back and ask once for a corrected reply.
keyPoints: The model chooses the call; your code runs it. Never execute arbitrary model output.
Valid JSON can still contain wrong values: check content, not just shape.
Good tool descriptions matter as much as good prompts.
Make optional fields explicit, and allow null for missing data instead of invented values.
Keep tools small and specific, with clear names.
mistakes: Trusting a reply because it parsed.
Letting a tool take dangerous actions without checks or confirmation.
Vague tool descriptions, so the model picks the wrong tool or invents arguments.
Forcing a required field when the data may genuinely be missing, so the model makes something up.

followUps.q: Who actually runs a function the model "calls"?
followUps.a: Your code. The model only outputs the function name and arguments.

followUps.q: Why validate output that is already valid JSON?
followUps.a: The structure can be right while the values are wrong, impossible or invented.

followUps.q: What goes in a tool definition?
followUps.a: A name, a clear description of what it does and when to use it, and a JSON schema for its arguments.

followUps.q: A field is often missing from the source text. How should the schema handle it?
followUps.a: Make it optional or nullable, and tell the model to use null rather than guess.

diagram.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant A as Your app
  participant M as Model
  participant T as Weather tool
  U->>A: what's the weather in Leeds?
  A->>M: question and the list of tools
  M-->>A: call get_weather(city = Leeds)
  A->>T: get_weather(Leeds)
  T-->>A: 14°C, light rain
  A->>M: here is the tool result
  M-->>A: It's 14°C with light rain in Leeds.
  A-->>U: final answer
diagram.caption: The model never runs the tool itself: it asks your code to, and then writes the final answer from the result.

note.idea: Structured output means making the model reply in a fixed format, usually JSON that matches a schema, so your code can read it reliably. Function calling (tool use) goes one step further: you describe functions to the model, and instead of answering in prose it replies with a function name and the arguments to call it with. Your code runs the function and sends the result back.
note.analogy: A form with labelled boxes instead of a blank page. The model fills in the boxes, and your program reads them.
note.breaks: A person filling in a form knows the boxes are strict. A model can still put a wrong value in the right box, like a real date that is the wrong date, so you check the content as well as the shape.
note.example: Instead of a sentence, a tool-calling model returns something like {"tool": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Leeds"}}. Your code calls get_weather, then sends the result back so the model can write the final answer.

resources.title: AI Engineering, Ch 2 (sampling and structured outputs)

practice.explain: Explain structured output and function calling with the form-with-boxes picture.
practice.derive: Write a JSON schema for extracting a job advert: title, company, salary range (may be missing), location and a list of skills. Decide which fields are required.
practice.build: Send 30 real job adverts to an LLM with your schema. Validate every reply in code, retry once on failure, and report the success rate. Then add one tool, such as a currency converter, and handle the tool-call loop.
practice.break: Remove the schema from the prompt, or give an advert with no salary. What breaks? Then find a reply that is valid JSON but has a wrong value, and add a check that catches it.

derive.answer:
Required fields are the ones every advert has, or where a missing value must be stated explicitly rather than skipped: title, company, location and skills always; salary is required too, but allowed to be null, so the model must say "not given" instead of inventing a number.

Design choices worth copying:
• Salary as a nested object with min, max and currency, each nullable. "£40,000–£50,000" fits, "up to £60k" fits (min null), and no salary fits (salary null).
• Numbers as integers in a fixed unit (per year, whole pounds), so code can compare them.
• Location with an explicit remote option, since "Remote (UK)" is common.
• additionalProperties: false, so no surprise keys appear.

build.answer:
Structured outputs (response_format with a JSON schema; ask(..., schema=SCHEMA) in llm.py) make the model return JSON that matches the schema, so json.loads can't fail on shape. But the values can still be wrong, so validate them in code: salary min not above max, salary numbers that really appear in the advert, at least one skill. On any failure, retry once, giving the model the error; report the success rate over all adverts.

Then one tool: convert_currency. The loop is: send the request with the tool definition; if the reply contains tool_calls, run each one (its arguments arrive as a JSON string), send each result back as a message with role "tool" and the matching tool_call_id, and repeat until the model gives its final answer (with a step limit).

The list has 3 sample adverts; paste in 30 real ones. It runs on the free chain from llm.py.
build.code:
import json
import re
from llm import ask, text_of

SCHEMA = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "title": {"type": "string"}, "company": {"type": "string"},
        "location": {"type": "string"}, "remote": {"type": "boolean"},
        "salary": {"anyOf": [{"type": "null"}, {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"min": {"anyOf": [{"type": "integer"}, {"type": "null"}]},
                           "max": {"anyOf": [{"type": "integer"}, {"type": "null"}]},
                           "currency": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["min", "max", "currency"], "additionalProperties": False}]},
        "skills": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
    },
    "required": ["title", "company", "location", "remote", "salary", "skills"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}
ADVERTS = [
    "Junior AI Engineer at Brightwave, Manchester (hybrid). £38,000 - £45,000. Python, PyTorch, RAG, SQL.",
    "ML Engineer, Northcode. Fully remote within the UK. Up to £60k. You'll need Python, AWS and Docker.",
    "Graduate Data Scientist - Lumen Health, Birmingham. Competitive salary. Python, statistics, pandas.",
]

def check(data, advert):
    """Problems that valid JSON can still have."""
    problems = []
    salary = data["salary"]
    if salary:
        if salary["min"] and salary["max"] and salary["min"] > salary["max"]:
            problems.append("salary min is above max")
        digits = re.sub(r"[^0-9k]", "", advert.lower())
        for value in (salary["min"], salary["max"]):
            if value and str(value)[:2] not in digits:
                problems.append(f"salary {value} does not appear in the advert")
    if not data["skills"]:
        problems.append("no skills found")
    return problems

def extract(advert):
    prompt = f"Extract the job advert into the schema. Salaries are yearly, in whole units. Advert:\n{advert}"
    for attempt in range(2):                                   # first try, then one retry
        data = json.loads(text_of(ask(prompt, schema=SCHEMA)))
        problems = check(data, advert)
        if not problems:
            return data
        prompt += f"\nYour previous answer had these problems: {problems}. Fix them."
    return None

results = [extract(a) for a in ADVERTS]
print(f"success rate: {sum(r is not None for r in results)}/{len(ADVERTS)}")

RATES = {("GBP", "EUR"): 1.17, ("GBP", "USD"): 1.27, ("EUR", "GBP"): 0.85, ("USD", "GBP"): 0.79}
TOOLS = [{"type": "function", "function": {
    "name": "convert_currency",
    "description": "Convert an amount of money from one currency to another, using today's fixed rates.",
    "parameters": {"type": "object",
                   "properties": {"amount": {"type": "number"}, "from_currency": {"type": "string"},
                                  "to_currency": {"type": "string"}},
                   "required": ["amount", "from_currency", "to_currency"]},
}}]

def convert_currency(amount, from_currency, to_currency):
    rate = RATES.get((from_currency.upper(), to_currency.upper()))
    return f"{amount * rate:.0f} {to_currency.upper()}" if rate else f"No rate for {from_currency} to {to_currency}"

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": f"What is the top salary in this advert in euros? Use the tool. {ADVERTS[0]}"}]
for step in range(5):                                          # a step limit, always
    reply = ask(messages=messages, tools=TOOLS)
    messages.append(reply["message"])
    if not reply["tool_calls"]:
        break
    for call in reply["tool_calls"]:
        arguments = json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"])
        messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call["id"], "content": convert_currency(**arguments)})
print(text_of(reply), "| answered by", reply["provider"])

break.answer:
Without the schema (just "extract this as JSON"), the reply's shape is up to the model: keys get renamed, the salary comes back as a string like "£38k–£45k" instead of numbers, and sometimes the JSON arrives inside a code fence. Your parsing code breaks, or worse, it runs on the wrong shape.

An advert with no salary ("Competitive salary") is the classic trap. Without a nullable salary field and an instruction, models are tempted to fill the box with a plausible figure, which is a hallucination that looks exactly like data. The schema's null option plus "null if the advert gives none" lets the model say so.

Valid JSON with a wrong value: for example "Up to £60k" extracted as min 60,000 and max null, or a monthly salary stored as yearly, or min and max swapped. Every one passes the schema. Checks that catch them: min ≤ max; every salary number must appear in the advert's text (which also catches invented salaries); a plausible range for the role (say £15,000 to £500,000 a year); and for "up to" adverts, the number must be the max. Structured outputs guarantee the shape; only your own checks protect the meaning.

explain.answer:
A paper form with labelled boxes ("Job title: ___", "Salary from: ___ to: ___", tick if remote) instead of a blank page saying "tell us about the job". Whoever fills it in can't wander off topic, every answer lands in a known place, and a computer can read the form straight away. Structured output is that form: you give the model a schema, and its reply must fill exactly those boxes.

Function calling is a form the model fills in to ask your program to do something: "call convert_currency with amount 45,000, from GBP, to EUR". Your code does the work and hands back the result, and the model continues. The model never runs anything itself; it only fills in the request form.

topics.name: Embeddings and semantic search
topics.definition: Semantic search finds texts with similar meaning by turning texts into embedding vectors and returning the ones whose vectors are closest to the query's vector.
topics.problem: Keyword search fails when users and documents use different words for the same thing: "can't sign in" versus "forgot my login". Embedding-based search matches meaning, which makes help centres, document search and RAG far better. It is also the retrieval half of almost every LLM application.
howItWorks: Choose an embedding model (a text encoder). It maps any text to a fixed-length vector, for example 384 or 1,024 numbers.
Embed every document (or chunk) once, ahead of time, and store the vectors, usually normalised to length 1.
At query time, embed the query with the same model.
Score each document by cosine similarity with the query: with unit vectors, that is just a dot product.
Return the top k documents. A matrix multiply scores thousands of documents in one step.
For exact terms (codes, names), combine with keyword search such as BM25: hybrid search, merging the two rankings.
keyPoints: Same model for documents and queries, always.
Cosine similarity: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated.
Normalise vectors once, then dot products are cosine similarities.
Semantic search handles synonyms and paraphrases; keyword search handles exact strings. Hybrid gets both.
Quality depends heavily on the embedding model and on how documents are chunked.
mistakes: Mixing embeddings from different models.
Relying on semantic search alone for product codes, IDs and names.
Embedding whole long documents as one vector, so specific details are blurred.
Not evaluating retrieval separately from the final answer.

followUps.q: Why can "can't sign in" find "I forgot my login"?
followUps.a: The embedding model maps texts with similar meaning to nearby vectors, even when they share no words.

followUps.q: Your vectors are normalised. How do you compute cosine similarity?
followUps.a: With a plain dot product.

followUps.q: Why add keyword search?
followUps.a: Embeddings capture meaning but can miss exact strings like codes or rare names; keywords catch those.

followUps.q: What must stay the same between indexing and querying?
followUps.a: The embedding model (and any text preprocessing).

diagram.code:
flowchart LR Q["question"] --> EQ["embed"] --> QV["question vector"] DOCS["200 FAQ entries"] --> ED["embed once"] --> DV[("document vectors")] QV & DV --> COS["cosine similarity
with every document"] --> TOP["top 5 matches"]
diagram.caption: Documents are embedded once in advance; each question is embedded and compared by meaning, not by exact words.

note.idea: An embedding model turns text into a vector. Texts with similar meaning get similar vectors, even with different words. Search means: embed the question, then find the closest document vectors with cosine similarity.
note.analogy: A library shelved by topic, not by title. 'How do I reset my password' sits next to 'I forgot my login'.
note.breaks: Meaning-based search can miss exact things like product codes or names. That is why many systems combine it with keyword search (hybrid search).
note.example: A help centre embeds 200 FAQ entries. The query "can't sign in" is embedded the same way, and the closest vectors are "I forgot my login", "reset my password" and "locked out of account", though none shares a word with the query. A search for the code "SKU-4471" fails semantically, so a keyword index is added alongside.
note.code:
D = doc_vecs / np.linalg.norm(doc_vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
q = q_vec / np.linalg.norm(q_vec)
top5 = np.argsort(-(D @ q))[:5]

resources.title: Embeddings: What they are and why they matter

practice.explain: Explain semantic search with the library-shelved-by-topic picture.
practice.derive: One pair of unit vectors has cosine similarity 0.9, another has 0.1. What does each say about the texts? Compute the angle for each.
practice.build: Embed 200 FAQ entries with an embedding model. Build search in NumPy that returns the top 5 for a question.
practice.break: Search for a product code or a rare name. Does semantic search find it? Add keyword search and combine the two scores.

derive.answer:
For unit vectors, cosine similarity is the cosine of the angle between them.

Similarity 0.9: angle = arccos(0.9) ≈ 25.8°. The vectors point in nearly the same direction, so the texts are close in meaning, for example a question and a paraphrase of it.

Similarity 0.1: angle = arccos(0.1) ≈ 84.3°. Almost at right angles, so the texts are basically unrelated.

Two cautions. What counts as "high" depends on the embedding model: with some models even unrelated texts score 0.6 or more, so compare scores within one model rather than using a fixed number. And similarity measures closeness in meaning as the model learned it, not truth: "the drug is safe" and "the drug is not safe" can score very high.

build.answer:
Embed every FAQ question once with a sentence-embedding model, normalise the vectors to length 1, and keep them in a NumPy array. For a new question, embed it the same way; because everything has length 1, the dot product with every stored vector is the cosine similarity, and np.argsort gives the top 5.

The search finds answers by meaning: "I forgot my login" finds "How do I reset my password?", although they share no words. The list here has 16 entries; the same code works unchanged for 200 or 20,000. The model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) is free, small (about 90 MB) and runs on a laptop.
build.code:
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

FAQ = [
    "How do I reset my password?", "How can I change my email address?", "Where is my order?",
    "How long does delivery take?", "Can I return an item?", "How do refunds work?",
    "Do you ship abroad?", "How do I cancel my order?", "Can I pay with PayPal?",
    "Why was my card declined?", "How do I delete my account?", "Do you have gift cards?",
    "Error E-4071 when paying with Apple Pay", "How do I use a discount code?",
    "Is my personal data safe?", "Can I change my delivery address after ordering?",
]
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
index = model.encode(FAQ, normalize_embeddings=True)          # (16, 384), each of length 1

def search(question, k=5):
    q = model.encode([question], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    scores = index @ q                                         # cosine similarities
    best = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
    return [(FAQ[i], round(float(scores[i]), 3)) for i in best]

for question in ["I forgot my login", "my parcel hasn't come", "send it to my new flat instead"]:
    print(question, "->", search(question)[:3])

break.answer:
Search for an exact code. In a list this small, semantic search may still put the right entry first for "error E-2210 on checkout", but look at the scores: it is judging by look-alike tokens, not by knowing what E-2210 is. The real failure shows with a code that isn't in the FAQ: "E-4072" returns the E-4071 entry as its best match, which is a different error. The embedding model has no meaning for codes, product numbers or rare names, so it matches them loosely to anything that looks similar.

The fix is hybrid search: add a keyword score that rewards exact token matches (BM25 in real systems; a simple token-overlap score here), and combine the two rankings. Reciprocal rank fusion is the standard simple combiner: each result scores 1/(60 + its rank) in each list it appears in, and the scores are added, so exact matches rise to the top while meaning-based matches still work for normal questions. Keyword search also lets you notice when a code has no exact match at all, so the app can say "I couldn't find error E-4072" instead of confidently answering about E-4071.
break.code:
import re
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

FAQ = ["How do I reset my password?", "Where is my order?", "Why was my card declined?",
       "Error E-4071 when paying with Apple Pay", "Error E-2210 when saving your address",
       "How do I use a discount code?", "Can I pay with PayPal?"]
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
index = model.encode(FAQ, normalize_embeddings=True)
tokens = lambda s: set(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9-]+", s.lower()))

def semantic_ranking(q):
    return list(np.argsort(-(index @ model.encode([q], normalize_embeddings=True)[0])))

def keyword_ranking(q):
    overlap = np.array([len(tokens(q) & tokens(doc)) for doc in FAQ])
    return [i for i in np.argsort(-overlap, kind="stable") if overlap[i] > 0]   # only real matches

def hybrid(q, k=3):
    score = np.zeros(len(FAQ))
    for ranking in (semantic_ranking(q), keyword_ranking(q)):
        for rank, i in enumerate(ranking):
            score[i] += 1 / (60 + rank)                      # reciprocal rank fusion
    return [FAQ[i] for i in np.argsort(-score)[:k]]

def exact_codes_missing(q):
    codes = [t for t in tokens(q) if re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+-\d+", t)]
    return [c for c in codes if not any(c in tokens(doc) for doc in FAQ)]

for q in ["error E-2210 on checkout", "E-4072"]:
    q_vec = model.encode([q], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    top = semantic_ranking(q)[:2]
    print(q, "| semantic:", [(FAQ[i], round(float(index[i] @ q_vec), 2)) for i in top])
    print("   hybrid:", hybrid(q)[:2], "| codes with no exact match:", exact_codes_missing(q))

explain.answer:
Imagine a library shelved by topic instead of by title. "How do I reset my password?" sits right next to "I forgot my login", because they are about the same thing, even though they share no words. To search, you walk to the shelf where your question would belong and look at what is there.

An embedding model is the librarian who decides where everything goes: it turns each text into a position (a vector), placing similar meanings close together. Semantic search embeds your question and returns the nearest texts. A keyword index is the old card catalogue, and you still want it for exact things such as product codes, which the topic shelves don't understand.

topics.name: Vector databases and approximate nearest-neighbour search
topics.definition: A vector database stores embeddings with their metadata and an approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) index, such as HNSW or IVF, that finds almost-the-closest vectors without comparing the query with every vector.
topics.problem: Exact search compares the query with every stored vector. With millions of vectors and many users, that is too slow and too expensive. ANN indexes search only a small, well-chosen part of the data, giving answers in milliseconds while keeping recall high. Choosing and tuning them is a core part of building retrieval at scale.
howItWorks: HNSW: build a graph where each vector links to its nearest neighbours, in several layers; higher layers hold fewer vectors and longer links.
Search starts at an entry point on the top layer and greedily hops to whichever neighbour is closer to the query.
When no neighbour is closer, drop a layer and continue. On the bottom layer, the closest vectors found are returned.
IVF: cluster the vectors with k-means, and at query time search only the few clusters nearest the query.
Product quantisation compresses vectors (for example to a few bytes each) to save memory, at some cost in accuracy.
Tune the speed–recall trade-off (HNSW's ef_search, IVF's number of probed clusters) and measure recall@k against exact search.
Store metadata (source, date, owner) with each vector, so you can filter and enforce permissions.
keyPoints: Exact search: perfect recall, cost grows with the number of vectors.
ANN: a little recall traded for a lot of speed.
HNSW: graph-based, fast and accurate, memory-hungry.
IVF: cluster-based; easy to understand and to scale.
Measure recall@k against brute force on your own data.
Metadata filters can hurt recall if applied after the search; good databases filter during it.
mistakes: Assuming an ANN index returns the exact nearest neighbours.
Never measuring recall after tuning for speed.
Using a vector database for a few thousand vectors, where NumPy brute force is simpler and fast enough.
Forgetting permissions, so search returns documents a user must not see.

followUps.q: What does "approximate" give up?
followUps.a: A small chance of missing some of the true nearest vectors (lower recall), in exchange for much faster search.

followUps.q: How does HNSW search?
followUps.a: It hops greedily through a layered graph towards the query, starting on a sparse top layer and dropping to denser layers.

followUps.q: How does IVF decide where to search?
followUps.a: It clusters the vectors in advance and only searches the clusters closest to the query.

followUps.q: How do you measure an ANN index's quality?
followUps.a: Recall@k: the share of the true top-k results (from exact search) that the index also returns.

flowchart LR Q["query vector"] --> BF["brute force:
compare with all 1 million"] Q --> IVF["IVF index:
find the 3 nearest clusters"] --> SUB["compare only
the vectors inside them"] BF --> EX["exact, but slow"] SUB --> AP["almost exact, much faster"]
diagram.caption: Approximate search skips most of the data by first finding the right neighbourhood. You trade a little recall for a lot of speed.

note.idea: Comparing a question with every document vector is exact but slow once you have millions. Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes, such as HNSW or IVF, find almost-the-closest vectors much faster by searching only a small part of the data. A vector database stores the vectors, the index and metadata (like source and date) together, so you can filter and search at once.
note.analogy: Finding a book by walking to the right section and shelf, instead of checking every book in the library.
note.breaks: A library's sections are exact. An ANN index can occasionally miss the true best match, so you trade a little accuracy (recall) for a lot of speed, and you should measure that trade.
note.example: HNSW builds a graph where each vector links to its near neighbours, in several layers. A search starts on the top, sparse layer and walks towards the query, dropping to denser layers as it gets close, like zooming in on a map.
