import os
import time
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.multiprocessing as mp
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP

def worker(rank, world, slow_rank, queue):
    os.environ.update(MASTER_ADDR="127.0.0.1", MASTER_PORT="29512")
    dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=world)
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = DDP(torch.nn.Linear(100, 100))
    x = torch.randn(32, 100)
    times = []
    for _ in range(5):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        if rank == slow_rank:
            time.sleep(0.2)                                    # this worker is slow
        model(x).sum().backward()                              # all-reduce waits for everyone
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
    queue.put((rank, slow_rank, sum(times) / len(times)))
    dist.destroy_process_group()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ctx = mp.get_context("spawn")
    for slow in [None, 1]:
        queue = ctx.SimpleQueue()
        mp.spawn(worker, args=(2, slow, queue), nprocs=2)
        results = sorted(queue.get() for _ in range(2))
        print(f"slow worker = {slow}: " + ", ".join(f"worker {r} step {t * 1000:.0f} ms" for r, _, t in results))

explain.answer:
Cooking a huge dinner for a wedding.

Data parallel: several kitchens each cook the full menu, each for different tables, and at the end of every course the head chefs compare notes so every kitchen improves its recipe in the same way. It needs each kitchen to be big enough for the whole menu.

Tensor parallel: one cake is too big for any single chef, so several chefs work on the same cake at the same time, each on their own slice, constantly passing tools and checking with each other. They must stand close together (fast links in one machine).

Pipeline parallel: an assembly line, with one station per course. Starters go to station 1 and then move on, while station 1 starts the next table's starters, so all stations stay busy, except at the very start and end of the service.

topics.name: Inference speed: batching, quantisation, FlashAttention
topics.definition: Inference is sped up by serving many requests together (batching), storing weights in fewer bits (quantisation), and computing attention without writing the full score matrix to memory (FlashAttention).
topics.problem: Generating text is mostly memory-bound: every token requires reading all the weights and the KV cache. Serving cost and speed decide whether a model is affordable to deploy. These three techniques are the main reasons modern models can be served cheaply and quickly, and on smaller hardware.
howItWorks: Batching: one pass over the weights serves many users' next tokens at once, so the cost of reading the weights is shared. Continuous batching adds and removes requests on the fly.
Quantisation: store weights as 8-bit or 4-bit integers plus a scale factor, instead of 16-bit floats.
Each weight snaps to its nearest allowed level. Per-channel or per-group scales keep errors small; an outlier weight in a group stretches the scale and hurts everyone else in it.
Smaller weights mean less memory and fewer bytes per token: a 70B model needs about 140 GB in bf16, 70 GB in int8 and 35 GB in 4-bit.
FlashAttention splits attention into tiles that fit in fast on-chip memory, computes the softmax piece by piece with running totals, and never writes the T × T matrix to slow memory.
The result is identical attention with far less memory traffic, and memory that grows linearly with sequence length.
keyPoints: Generation is usually memory-bound, so moving fewer bytes is the main lever.
Batching raises throughput; it can add a little latency per request.
int8 is usually near-lossless; 4-bit needs care; always evaluate quality.
Outliers are the main enemy of quantisation; finer-grained scales help.
FlashAttention is exact, not an approximation.
These combine with KV caching and speculative decoding.
mistakes: Quantising without measuring quality on your own tasks.
Using one scale for a whole tensor that contains outliers.
Assuming FlashAttention changes the model's outputs.
Tuning latency without measuring throughput, or the other way round.

followUps.q: Why does batching help so much in generation?
followUps.a: Each step must read all the weights; batching shares that one read across many requests.

followUps.q: How much memory do a 70B model's weights take in 4-bit?
followUps.a: About 35 GB (half a byte per parameter).

followUps.q: Why does an outlier weight hurt per-tensor quantisation?
followUps.a: It stretches the scale, so the allowed levels are spread far apart and every normal-sized weight is rounded more coarsely.

followUps.q: Does FlashAttention approximate attention?
followUps.a: No. It computes exactly the same result, just in an order that avoids storing the full score matrix in slow memory.

derive.answer:
13 billion parameters:
bf16 (2 bytes each): 13B × 2 = 26 GB.
int8 (1 byte): 13 GB.
4-bit (half a byte): 6.5 GB.

Plus a little extra for the scales that quantisation stores (one per row or per small group of weights), and, at run time, the KV cache and activations. So a 13B model that needs a large data-centre GPU in bf16 fits on a 16 GB consumer GPU in 4-bit, which is why quantisation is so popular for running models locally.

build.answer:
Int8 quantisation stores each weight as an integer from −127 to 127 plus a scale: w ≈ scale × q, with scale = max|w| / 127. Per-tensor uses one scale for a whole weight matrix; per-channel uses one scale per output row.

On the trained Shakespeare GPT, both are very accurate, because a typical weight matrix has no extreme values: the average relative error per weight is small, and the validation loss changes by less than a thousandth (1.7488 to 1.7487 per-tensor, 1.7486 per-channel). Per-channel is consistently more accurate than per-tensor, because each row gets a scale that fits its own range. The generated text looks just as good after quantisation. (This simulates quantisation by rounding the weights; real int8 kernels also do the maths in integers, which is where the speed comes from.)
build.code:
import copy
import torch
from gpt import GPT, train, estimate_loss, encode, decode

def quantise_(weight, per_channel):
    w = weight.data
    peak = w.abs().amax(dim=1, keepdim=True) if per_channel else w.abs().max()
    scale = peak.clamp(min=1e-12) / 127
    q = torch.round(w / scale).clamp(-127, 127)
    error = ((q * scale - w).abs() / w.abs().mean()).mean().item()
    weight.data = q * scale                            # simulate int8 storage
    return error

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = train(GPT(), steps=1500, log_every=0)
torch.manual_seed(1); base_loss = estimate_loss(model, iters=50)
print(f"original: val loss {base_loss:.4f}")
for per_channel in [False, True]:
    q = copy.deepcopy(model)
    errors = [quantise_(m.weight, per_channel) for m in q.modules() if isinstance(m, torch.nn.Linear)]
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    loss = estimate_loss(q, iters=50)
    torch.manual_seed(2)
    text = decode(q.generate(torch.tensor([encode("ROMEO:")]), 80)[0].tolist())
    print(f"{'per-channel' if per_channel else 'per-tensor '}: mean relative error {sum(errors) / len(errors):.4f}, "
          f"val loss {loss:.4f}\n{text}\n")

break.answer:
Put one huge weight (say 100 times the largest normal weight) into a layer and quantise per-tensor. The single scale is now set by the outlier: scale = 100 × normal max / 127. Every normal weight is now tiny compared with the step size, so almost all of them round to 0 or ±1: in the run below, most of the layer's weights become exactly 0, and the relative error for the other weights jumps from about 1% to around 100%. One number has destroyed the whole layer's precision.

Per-channel quantisation limits the damage to the outlier's own row: the other rows keep their own scales and stay accurate.

This is a real problem in LLMs: a few activation and weight channels have values far larger than the rest. That is why practical methods quantise per channel or in small groups (for example 128 weights per scale), keep the outlier channels in higher precision (as LLM.int8() does), or move the outliers into the weights before quantising (as SmoothQuant does).

import torch

def quantise(w, per_channel):
    peak = w.abs().amax(dim=1, keepdim=True) if per_channel else w.abs().max()
    scale = peak.clamp(min=1e-12) / 127
    return torch.round(w / scale).clamp(-127, 127) * scale

torch.manual_seed(0)
w = torch.randn(256, 256) * 0.02
w_out = w.clone(); w_out[0, 0] = 100 * w.abs().max()             # one huge outlier
others = torch.ones_like(w, dtype=torch.bool); others[0, 0] = False
for name, weights in [("normal", w), ("with outlier", w_out)]:
    for per_channel in [False, True]:
        dq = quantise(weights, per_channel)
        rel = ((dq - weights).abs()[others] / weights.abs()[others]).median().item()
        zeros = (dq[others] == 0).float().mean().item()
        print(f"{name:12s} {'per-channel' if per_channel else 'per-tensor '}: "
              f"median relative error of the other weights {rel:.1%}, rounded to zero {zeros:.0%}")

explain.answer:
Batching is a bus instead of many taxis. Each taxi takes one passenger and needs its own driver and fuel; a bus takes 50 passengers for barely more than the cost of one trip. A GPU serving one request at a time wastes most of its power reading the whole model from memory for a single token; serving a batch of requests together reads the weights once and uses them for every request, so each user's share of the cost drops sharply. The price is that each passenger may wait a moment for the bus to fill.

Quantisation is a compressed photo. A JPEG takes a fraction of the space of the original and usually looks the same, because it throws away detail you wouldn't notice. Storing weights in 8 or 4 bits instead of 16 makes the model half or a quarter the size, so it fits on smaller hardware and loads from memory faster, with a small loss in quality. Compress too hard, and the artefacts start to show.

topics.name: Profiling PyTorch code
topics.definition: Profiling measures where time is actually spent in your code — CPU, GPU, data loading, copies — so you optimise the real bottleneck instead of guessing.
topics.problem: Intuition about performance is often wrong: the slow part of training may be data loading, a tiny operation called thousands of times, or a hidden copy between CPU and GPU. Optimising the wrong thing wastes days. A profiler shows the timeline and tells you exactly where to look.
howItWorks: Wrap a few training steps in torch.profiler.profile(activities=[CPU, CUDA]), after a couple of warm-up steps.
Look at the table of operations sorted by total time on the CPU and on the GPU.
Open the timeline trace (in a browser trace viewer or TensorBoard) to see, over time, what the CPU and GPU are each doing.
Gaps on the GPU row mean it is waiting — usually for data loading or Python overhead.
Many tiny kernels mean launch overhead: fuse operations or use torch.compile.
Large CPU-to-GPU copies inside the loop mean data is being moved too often; keep tensors on the GPU and use pinned memory.
Fix one thing, profile again, and compare steps per second.
keyPoints: Measure first, optimise second.
GPU work is asynchronous: call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading a timer.
Warm up before measuring; the first steps include one-off setup costs.
Common bottlenecks: data loading, tiny operations, CPU–GPU copies, synchronisation points like .item().
More DataLoader workers and pin_memory=True often remove data-loading stalls.
mistakes: Timing GPU code with time.time() without synchronising.
Profiling the very first steps, which include compilation and caching.
Calling .item() or printing every step, which forces the CPU to wait for the GPU.
Optimising an operation that takes 2% of the time.

followUps.q: Why can a Python timer give the wrong answer for GPU code?
followUps.a: GPU work runs asynchronously; without torch.cuda.synchronize() the timer may stop before the GPU has finished.

followUps.q: The GPU row of the trace has big gaps. What is the likely cause?
followUps.a: The GPU is waiting for input: slow data loading, CPU preprocessing or Python overhead.

followUps.q: Why can calling loss.item() every step slow training?
followUps.a: It forces the CPU to wait for the GPU to finish before continuing, removing overlap.

followUps.q: Why warm up before profiling?
followUps.a: The first iterations include one-off costs like memory allocation and compilation that don't reflect steady-state speed.

flowchart LR
  P["profile 20 steps"] --> T["find the 3 slowest operations"] --> F["fix one"] --> M["measure again"]
  M -->|"repeat"| P
diagram.caption: Measure, fix the biggest cost, measure again. Never optimise by guessing.

note.idea: Measure where the time actually goes before you optimise. The profiler shows the time for each operation on the CPU and GPU. Common findings: the GPU waiting for data loading, many tiny operations, or slow copies between CPU and GPU.
note.analogy: Timing each station in a kitchen before hiring more chefs. Maybe the slow part is the dishwasher.
note.breaks: Kitchen timing is simple. GPU work runs asynchronously, so normal Python timers can lie. Call torch.cuda.synchronize() before you read the time.

Setting num_workers=8 and pin_memory=True keeps batches ready in advance, and steps per second roughly triple without touching the model.

derive.answer:
1. The data loader is too slow. The GPU sits idle between steps waiting for the next batch. In the profiler trace: gaps between GPU kernels, with time on the CPU in DataLoader or image decoding. Fix: more num_workers, pin_memory=True, pre-process the data.

2. Synchronising every step. Calling loss.item(), print(tensor) or moving a tensor to the CPU in every step forces the CPU to wait for the GPU. In the trace: cudaStreamSynchronize or "aten::item" with long waits, and the GPU queue running dry. Fix: log less often, and keep values on the GPU.

3. Many small operations. Lots of short kernels, each with launch overhead; the GPU is "busy" but mostly launching. In the trace: thousands of tiny kernels and a high share of CPU time in operator dispatch. Fix: batch the work, fuse operations (torch.compile), avoid Python loops over tensors.

4. Slow, memory-bound operations or the wrong precision. Element-wise and normalisation operations dominate, or matrix multiplies run in fp32. In the trace: top operations are not matmuls, or matmuls are slower than they should be. Fix: mixed precision (bf16), fused kernels such as FlashAttention.

(Also common: copying data between CPU and GPU in every step, which shows up as memcpy in the trace.)

build.answer:
Wrap 20 training steps in torch.profiler.profile, then print the operations sorted by total time. On this GPT, on a CPU, the top three are:
1. Attention (aten::scaled_dot_product_attention), about a quarter of the time, and it runs PyTorch's slowest "math" implementation.
2. The batched matrix multiplies (aten::bmm) inside that math attention.
3. Dropout, and specifically generating its random masks (aten::bernoulli_), about 16% of the time on its own.

The third one is a real finding: dropout isn't free, and the dropout inside attention is also what forces the slow math path, because the fast fused attention kernels on CPU don't support it. This small model trains on plenty of data and barely overfits in a few thousand steps, so dropout is a cost with little benefit here. Setting dropout to 0 raises throughput by about 40% in the run below (about 52,000 to 74,000 tokens per second); a bigger batch (64) then adds more, to about 106,000, by making each matrix multiply larger. Always profile again after a change: the bottleneck moves.
build.code:
import time
import torch
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity
from gpt import GPT, Config, get_batch

def steps(model, opt, n, batch_size):
    for _ in range(n):
        x, y = get_batch("train", batch_size=batch_size)
        _, loss = model(x, y)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

def throughput(dropout, batch_size):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = GPT(Config(dropout=dropout))
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    steps(model, opt, 3, batch_size)                              # warm up
    start = time.perf_counter()
    steps(model, opt, 20, batch_size)
    return 20 * batch_size * 64 / (time.perf_counter() - start), model, opt

_, model, opt = throughput(0.1, 16)
with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU] + ([ProfilerActivity.CUDA] if torch.cuda.is_available() else [])) as prof:
    steps(model, opt, 20, 16)
print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="cpu_time_total", row_limit=6))

for dropout, batch_size in [(0.1, 16), (0.0, 16), (0.0, 64)]:
    tokens_per_second, _, _ = throughput(dropout, batch_size)
    print(f"dropout {dropout}, batch {batch_size}: {tokens_per_second:,.0f} tokens per second")

break.answer:
On a GPU, operations are asynchronous: PyTorch queues the kernel and returns immediately, long before the GPU has finished. So time.time() around a GPU operation without torch.cuda.synchronize() measures only how long it took to queue the work, a few microseconds, however big the operation is. With synchronize() before stopping the clock, you wait for the GPU to finish, and get the real time, which for a large matrix multiply can be thousands of times longer.

The same trap appears elsewhere: the first call includes start-up costs (warm up first), and an innocent loss.item() somewhere synchronises and makes a later step look slow. For benchmarks, use torch.utils.benchmark or CUDA events, which handle this for you.

On a CPU, as in a run without a GPU, both numbers are the same, because CPU operations finish before they return. The code prints both on whatever device you have.

explain.answer:
Before hiring more chefs to speed up a slow kitchen, you time each station. Maybe the cooking is fast and the real hold-up is the dishwasher, or the one person fetching ingredients. Hiring more chefs wouldn't help at all.

Profiling is timing the stations of your program: which operations take the time, whether the GPU is busy or waiting, and on what. Without it, you optimise what you guess is slow, which is usually wrong. With it, you fix the actual bottleneck first, then time again, because fixing one station often reveals the next slowest one.

topics.name: GPU kernels with Triton
topics.definition: A GPU kernel is a function that runs as many parallel instances on the GPU; Triton lets you write kernels in Python-like code, and the biggest win is usually fusion — doing several steps in one kernel so data leaves slow memory only once.
topics.problem: Many deep-learning operations are memory-bound chains of small steps (normalise, activate, scale). Run as separate PyTorch operations, each one reads and writes the full tensor in slow memory. A fused kernel can be several times faster. Triton makes writing such kernels possible without learning CUDA C++, and it is what torch.compile uses under the hood.
howItWorks: Split the work into blocks: each kernel instance (a "program") handles one block, for example one row of a matrix.
Each program computes which addresses it owns from its program id, and loads that block with tl.load, using a mask for the ragged edge.
It does all the steps on the block in fast on-chip memory: for softmax, the max, the exponentials, the sum and the division.
It writes only the final result with tl.store.
A naive softmax as separate operations reads the data three times and writes twice; the fused kernel reads once and writes once.
Tune the block size: too small wastes parallel hardware, too large spills out of fast memory.
Always check correctness against PyTorch and benchmark across sizes.
keyPoints: Kernel = one program, run as many parallel instances over blocks of data.
Fusion cuts memory traffic for memory-bound chains.
Masks handle sizes that aren't a multiple of the block size.
Block size is a key tuning knob.
torch.compile can often fuse operations for you automatically.
Compute-bound operations (big matmuls) gain little from fusion.
mistakes: Forgetting the mask, so the last block reads or writes past the end of the tensor.
Benchmarking without warm-up and synchronisation.
Hand-writing a kernel for something torch.compile already fuses well.
Not checking numerical stability (for softmax, subtract the max inside the kernel too).

followUps.q: What is kernel fusion?
followUps.a: Combining several operations into one kernel, so intermediate results stay in fast on-chip memory instead of making round trips to slow GPU memory.

followUps.q: Why does fusion speed up a softmax but barely help a large matmul?
followUps.a: Softmax is memory-bound, so fewer memory trips help a lot; a large matmul is compute-bound already.

followUps.q: What does the mask in a Triton load do?
followUps.a: It disables reads and writes for positions beyond the end of the data, for the last, partly filled block.

followUps.q: What is a "program" in Triton?
followUps.a: One instance of the kernel, responsible for one block of the data, identified by its program id.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR subgraph Naive M1[("memory")] --> K1["kernel: max"] --> M2[("memory")] --> K2["kernel: exp and sum"] --> M3[("memory")] --> K3["kernel: divide"] --> M4[("memory")] end subgraph Fused N1[("memory")] --> KF["one kernel:
max, exp, sum, divide"] --> N2[("memory")] end
diagram.caption: The naive softmax travels to memory and back three times; the fused kernel does it once.

note.idea: A kernel is a small program that runs on the GPU as many parallel copies. Triton lets you write kernels in Python-like code. The biggest win is fusion: doing several steps, like the parts of a softmax, in one kernel, so data is read from slow GPU memory once instead of several times.
note.analogy: Cooking a dish in one trip to the fridge instead of fetching each ingredient separately.
note.breaks: In a kitchen, the fridge trip is the obvious cost. On a GPU you must measure: some operations are limited by the maths, not by memory, and fusion does not help them.
note.example: A naive softmax passes over the data several times (find the max, exponentiate and sum, divide). A fused Triton softmax reads each row once and writes it once, which can make it several times faster on large rows.
note.code:
@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offs = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offs < n                         # don't read past the end
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offs, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offs, mask=mask)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offs, x + y, mask=mask)

derive.answer:
A 4,096 × 4,096 fp32 matrix is 4,096² × 4 bytes ≈ 67 MB (64 MiB). Call that M.

Naive softmax in PyTorch runs several separate kernels, each going to memory and back:
1. row max: read M (the output, one number per row, is tiny)
2. subtract the max: read M, write M
3. exp: read M, write M
4. row sum: read M
5. divide: read M, write M
Total: about 5M read + 3M written = 8M ≈ 537 MB.

Fused softmax: one kernel loads each row into fast on-chip memory, does all five steps there, and writes the result once: M read + M written = 2M ≈ 134 MB.

Softmax is memory-bound (a few operations per number), so time is roughly proportional to bytes moved. Expected speed-up ≈ 8M / 2M = 4 times. The official Triton tutorial measures close to this on large rows.

build.answer:
These need an NVIDIA GPU with Triton installed (a free Colab GPU works). The vector-add kernel shows the basic pattern: each program instance handles one block of BLOCK_SIZE elements, computes its offsets from tl.program_id, masks off the elements past the end, loads, adds and stores. The fused softmax gives each row to one program, loads it once, computes max, exp, sum and divide in registers, and writes it once.

Benchmarks with triton.testing.do_bench: vector add matches PyTorch (both are limited by memory bandwidth; you can't beat the hardware); fused softmax is several times faster than the naive PyTorch version and roughly matches torch.softmax, which is itself a fused kernel. Matrix multiply, the third tutorial, adds tiling and is the place to learn how high-performance kernels reuse data; Triton's version gets close to cuBLAS.
build.code:
# Needs an NVIDIA GPU and: pip install triton
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n                                   # don't read past the end
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask)

def add(x, y, block=1024):
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(x.numel(), meta["BLOCK_SIZE"]),)
    add_kernel[grid](x, y, out, x.numel(), BLOCK_SIZE=block)
    return out

@triton.jit
def softmax_kernel(out_ptr, in_ptr, row_stride, n_cols, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    row = tl.program_id(0)
    cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    x = tl.load(in_ptr + row * row_stride + cols, mask=cols < n_cols, other=-float("inf"))
    x = x - tl.max(x, axis=0)                            # everything happens in registers
    e = tl.exp(x)
    tl.store(out_ptr + row * row_stride + cols, e / tl.sum(e, axis=0), mask=cols < n_cols)

def softmax(x):
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    softmax_kernel[(x.shape[0],)](out, x, x.stride(0), x.shape[1], BLOCK_SIZE=triton.next_power_of_2(x.shape[1]))
    return out

def naive_softmax(x):                                    # 5 separate passes over memory
    m = x.max(dim=1, keepdim=True).values
    e = torch.exp(x - m)
    return e / e.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)

x, y = torch.randn(10_000_000, device="cuda"), torch.randn(10_000_000, device="cuda")
assert torch.allclose(add(x, y), x + y)
print("add: triton", triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: add(x, y)), "ms | torch", triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: x + y), "ms")
m = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda")
assert torch.allclose(softmax(m), torch.softmax(m, dim=1), atol=1e-6)
for name, fn in [("triton fused", softmax), ("naive torch", naive_softmax), ("torch.softmax", lambda t: torch.softmax(t, 1))]:
    print(f"softmax {name}: {triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: fn(m)):.3f} ms")

break.answer:
Without the mask, with a size that isn't a multiple of BLOCK (say 1,000,001 with BLOCK 1,024), the last program reads and writes past the end of the arrays. The result: garbage in memory just past your tensor, a crash with "an illegal memory access was encountered" (which then poisons the whole CUDA context, so later calls fail too), or, worst of all, nothing visible at all because the memory happened to be accessible, and something else is silently corrupted. That is why every load and store at the edge of the data must be masked.

BLOCK size: very small (say 16 or 32) means a huge number of programs, each doing almost nothing: the scheduling overhead and the poor use of wide memory transactions make it much slower. Very large (say 65,536) means few programs, each needing a lot of registers, so fewer run at once and some of the GPU sits idle; very large blocks can also fail to compile. The sweet spot for a simple element-wise kernel is usually around 1,024 to 4,096; Triton's autotuner can try several and pick the best.

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def add_no_mask(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    offsets = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, tl.load(x_ptr + offsets) + tl.load(y_ptr + offsets))   # no mask!

@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    offsets = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask) + tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask), mask=mask)

n = 50_000_001                                          # not a multiple of the block size
x, y = torch.randn(n, device="cuda"), torch.randn(n, device="cuda")
for block in [32, 256, 1024, 4096, 16384]:
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: add_kernel[(triton.cdiv(n, block),)](x, y, out, n, BLOCK_SIZE=block))
    print(f"BLOCK {block:5d}: {ms:.3f} ms")
out = torch.empty_like(x)
add_no_mask[(triton.cdiv(n, 1024),)](x, y, out, n, BLOCK_SIZE=1024)    # reads and writes past the end
torch.cuda.synchronize()                                # may raise "illegal memory access", or silently corrupt

explain.answer:
Cooking a dish in one trip to the fridge instead of walking back and forth for each ingredient. Unfused code is like fetching the eggs, cracking them, putting the bowl back in the fridge, fetching it again to add milk, putting it back, fetching it again to whisk: most of the time is spent walking, not cooking.

A GPU kernel that reads data from memory, does one small thing and writes it back is one trip to the fridge. Kernel fusion does several steps, such as subtract, exp, sum and divide, in one kernel while the data sits in the GPU's fast on-chip memory, then writes the result once. For memory-bound work, fewer trips means proportionally less time, which is the whole idea behind FlashAttention and fused softmax.

topics.name: Pruning and distillation
topics.definition: Pruning removes weights, neurons or heads that matter little; distillation trains a small student model to imitate a large teacher's full output probabilities; both make models smaller and cheaper to run.
topics.problem: The best models are often too large, slow or expensive for phones, high-traffic services or tight latency budgets. Many of their parameters contribute little, and much of a big model's knowledge can be transferred into a smaller one. Pruning and distillation, alongside quantisation, are the standard ways to shrink models for deployment.
howItWorks: Magnitude pruning: set the smallest-magnitude weights to zero, for example 50%, then fine-tune briefly to recover accuracy. Repeat in stages for higher sparsity.
Unstructured pruning leaves the matrix the same shape with scattered zeros, which rarely runs faster on standard hardware.
Structured pruning removes whole neurons, channels, attention heads or layers, so the model really shrinks and really speeds up.
Distillation: run the teacher on training inputs and keep its full probability distribution (soft labels), not just the top answer.
Soften both teacher and student with a temperature T > 1 (divide the logits by T), so small probabilities carry more signal.
Train the student to match the teacher's softened probabilities (a KL loss, scaled by T²), usually mixed with the normal loss on true labels.
For LLMs, distillation also means fine-tuning a small model on text generated by a large one.
keyPoints: Soft labels carry "dark knowledge": which wrong answers are nearly right.
Temperature softens distributions; T = 1 is the normal softmax.
Structured pruning gives real speed-ups; unstructured mostly saves storage (unless hardware supports sparsity).
Prune gradually and retrain.
Distillation, pruning and quantisation combine well.
mistakes: Pruning heavily in one shot with no retraining.
Expecting scattered zeros to make inference faster on a normal GPU.
Distilling with T = 1 only, losing most of the soft-label information.
Evaluating the student only on the teacher's strengths.

followUps.q: Why train on soft labels instead of hard ones?
followUps.a: They tell the student how similar each wrong class is to the right one, which is extra information the one-hot label lacks.

followUps.q: What does a temperature above 1 do to the teacher's probabilities?
followUps.a: It softens them: the top class gets less, and the small probabilities become larger and more informative.

followUps.q: Why doesn't 80% unstructured pruning usually make a model 5 times faster?
followUps.a: The matrices keep their shape; standard hardware still multiplies the zeros unless special sparse support is used.

followUps.q: What does structured pruning remove?
followUps.a: Whole units — neurons, channels, attention heads or layers — so the computation genuinely shrinks.

derive.answer:
Distillation compares the student's softened probabilities q = softmax(z/T) with the teacher's p = softmax(v/T), where z and v are the logits and T is the temperature.

The gradient of the soft cross-entropy with respect to a student logit is:
∂L/∂zᵢ = (1/T) · (qᵢ − pᵢ).

Two factors of T shrink this gradient:
1. The 1/T from the chain rule, because the logits are divided by T.
2. The difference qᵢ − pᵢ itself: at high T both distributions are close to uniform, and expanding softmax for large T gives qᵢ − pᵢ ≈ (zᵢ − vᵢ) / (N·T), with N classes (when the logits have zero mean).

Together: ∂L/∂zᵢ ≈ (zᵢ − vᵢ) / (N·T²). The gradient shrinks with T².

Multiplying the soft loss by T² cancels that, so the soft-label term keeps roughly the same influence relative to the hard-label loss whatever temperature you choose. Without it, raising T from 1 to 4 would silently make the distillation signal 16 times weaker. (This is the argument in Hinton, Vinyals and Dean, 2015.)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torchvision import datasets

train, test = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True), datasets.MNIST("data", train=False, download=True)
X_all, y_all = train.data.reshape(-1, 784).float() / 255, train.targets
Xte, yte = test.data.reshape(-1, 784).float() / 255, test.targets
X_lab, y_lab = X_all[:5000], y_all[:5000]                  # the student's labelled data

def fit(model, X, y, loss_fn, epochs):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for idx in torch.randperm(len(X)).split(128):
            opt.zero_grad(); loss_fn(model, X[idx], y[idx], idx).backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (model(Xte).argmax(1) == yte).float().mean().item()

hard = lambda m, xb, yb, idx: F.cross_entropy(m(xb), yb)
torch.manual_seed(0)
teacher = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.3), nn.Linear(512, 512), nn.ReLU(),
                        nn.Dropout(0.3), nn.Linear(512, 10))
print(f"teacher: {fit(teacher, X_all[5000:], y_all[5000:], hard, 4):.2%}")
teacher.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    soft_lab, soft_all = teacher(X_lab), teacher(X_all)

T, alpha = 4.0, 0.7
def distill(m, xb, yb, idx):
    soft = F.kl_div(F.log_softmax(m(xb) / T, 1), F.softmax(soft_lab[idx] / T, 1), reduction="batchmean")
    return alpha * T * T * soft + (1 - alpha) * F.cross_entropy(m(xb), yb)
def soft_only(m, xb, yb, idx):                              # no true labels used at all
    return T * T * F.kl_div(F.log_softmax(m(xb) / T, 1), F.softmax(soft_all[idx] / T, 1), reduction="batchmean")

for name, X, y, loss_fn, epochs in [("hard labels, 5,000 images", X_lab, y_lab, hard, 10),
                                    ("distilled, same 5,000 images", X_lab, y_lab, distill, 10),
                                    ("teacher's labels only, 60,000 unlabelled", X_all, y_all, soft_only, 2)]:
    scores = []
    for seed in range(3):
        torch.manual_seed(seed)
        student = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 200), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(200, 10))
        scores.append(fit(student, X, y, loss_fn, epochs))
    print(f"student, {name}: {sum(scores) / 3:.2%} (mean of 3 seeds)")

break.answer:
Magnitude pruning sets the smallest weights to zero. Without retraining, accuracy holds at 50% sparsity, drops somewhat at 80%, and falls apart at 95%. With a short retraining after pruning (keeping the pruned weights at zero), the network recovers most of the accuracy even at 80%, and a good part of it at 95%: the remaining weights learn to compensate. Plotted, the "no retraining" curve falls off a cliff well before the "with retraining" curve does.

Is the pruned model faster? Not as it stands. The weights are zeros stored in an ordinary dense matrix, and the hardware multiplies zeros just as fast as any other number, so the time is the same. Real speed-ups need either structured pruning (remove whole neurons, heads or channels, so the matrices get smaller), hardware-supported patterns like 2:4 sparsity on recent NVIDIA GPUs, or sparse kernels that only win at very high sparsity. The run below shows the dense timing is unchanged.

import copy
import time
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torchvision import datasets

train, test = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True), datasets.MNIST("data", train=False, download=True)
X, y = train.data[:20_000].reshape(-1, 784).float() / 255, train.targets[:20_000]
Xte, yte = test.data.reshape(-1, 784).float() / 255, test.targets
accuracy = lambda m: (m(Xte).argmax(1) == yte).float().mean().item()

def train_(model, epochs, masks=None):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for idx in torch.randperm(len(X)).split(128):
            opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(model(X[idx]), y[idx]).backward(); opt.step()
            if masks:
                with torch.no_grad():
                    for layer, mask in masks.items():
                        layer.weight.mul_(mask)                  # keep pruned weights at zero
    return model

torch.manual_seed(0)
base = train_(nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 300), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(300, 100), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(100, 10)), 3)
print(f"dense: {accuracy(base):.2%}")
for sparsity in [0.5, 0.8, 0.95]:
    pruned, masks = copy.deepcopy(base), {}
    for layer in [m for m in pruned if isinstance(m, nn.Linear)]:
        cut = layer.weight.abs().flatten().kthvalue(int(sparsity * layer.weight.numel())).values
        masks[layer] = (layer.weight.abs() > cut).float()
        layer.weight.data.mul_(masks[layer])
    before = accuracy(pruned)
    after = accuracy(train_(pruned, 1, masks))
    print(f"{sparsity:.0%} pruned: no retraining {before:.2%}, after 1 epoch of retraining {after:.2%}")

with torch.no_grad():
    for name, model in [("dense", base), ("95% zeros", pruned)]:
        start = time.perf_counter()
        for _ in range(50):
            model(Xte)
        print(f"{name}: {(time.perf_counter() - start) / 50 * 1000:.2f} ms per pass over the test set")

explain.answer:
Pruning is trimming a tree's weakest branches. Many branches contribute almost nothing; cut them, and the tree keeps its shape and fruit, and if you give it a season to regrow (retraining), the remaining branches strengthen to make up for the loss. Cut too much at once, and the tree suffers.

Distillation is an expert teacher training a student. A normal answer key only says "the answer is 7". A good teacher also explains "it's a 7, but it looks a bit like a 1, and nothing like a 4": the soft probabilities. That extra information lets a much smaller student learn to behave like the teacher, faster and from less data, which is how small, fast models are made from big ones.

topics.name: Speculative decoding
topics.definition: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by letting a small draft model propose several tokens, which the large model then verifies in a single pass, keeping exactly the output the large model would have produced.
topics.problem: Large models generate one token per forward pass, and each pass is slow because it is memory-bound: the GPU spends its time reading weights, not computing. Checking several proposed tokens costs about the same as generating one. Speculative decoding turns that spare capacity into speed, with no change in output quality.
howItWorks: A small, fast draft model (or extra prediction heads) proposes the next k tokens, for example 4.
The large target model runs once over the context plus all k proposals, producing its own prediction at every position in parallel.
Walk through the proposals: accept each one the target model agrees with (with a probabilistic acceptance rule when sampling).
At the first disagreement, discard the rest and take the target model's own token there instead.
So each expensive pass yields between 1 and k + 1 tokens; with 3 of 4 accepted, you get 4 tokens from one pass.
The acceptance rule guarantees the output has exactly the target model's distribution: speed without any quality change.
keyPoints: The speed-up depends on the acceptance rate, so the draft must imitate the target well.
The draft must be much cheaper than the target.
Output quality is identical to the target model alone.
It helps most when generation is memory-bound (small batches, latency-sensitive serving).
Variants use extra heads or the model's own earlier layers as the drafter.
mistakes: Using a draft model that rarely agrees with the target, gaining nothing.
Assuming it changes or degrades the output (it doesn't, if done correctly).
Expecting big gains at very large batch sizes, where the GPU is already busy.

followUps.q: Why is checking 4 tokens about as cheap as generating 1?
followUps.a: Generation is memory-bound: the cost is reading the weights, which happens once whether you score one position or several.

followUps.q: What happens at the first rejected draft token?
followUps.a: It and all later draft tokens are discarded, and the target model's own token is used at that position.

followUps.q: Does speculative decoding change what the big model outputs?
followUps.a: No. The acceptance rule makes the output exactly match the big model's own distribution.

followUps.q: What decides how much faster it is?
followUps.a: How often the draft model's guesses are accepted, and how cheap the draft model is.

The big model then checks all the guesses in one pass, keeps the ones it agrees with, and replaces the first wrong one. The output is exactly what the big model alone would produce, only faster.
note.analogy: A junior writer drafts the next sentence, and a senior editor checks it in one read, instead of the senior writing every word slowly.
note.breaks: An editor can rewrite anything. Here, only the guesses up to the first rejected token are kept, so if the draft model guesses badly you gain almost nothing. The speed-up depends on the acceptance rate.
note.example: If the draft model proposes 4 tokens and on average 3 are accepted, each expensive pass of the big model gives about 4 tokens (the 3 accepted plus 1 of its own) instead of 1.

derive.answer:
The draft proposes k = 4 tokens; each is accepted with probability α = 0.8, and the first rejection stops the run. The big model's pass always adds one token of its own: a correction at the first rejection, or a bonus token if all 4 are accepted.

Tokens per pass = (number of accepted draft tokens) + 1.
P(at least i drafts accepted) = αⁱ, so the expected number accepted is α + α² + α³ + α⁴ = 0.8 + 0.64 + 0.512 + 0.4096 = 2.3616.
Add the big model's own token: 3.36 tokens per big-model pass.

The same in one formula: (1 − α^(k+1)) / (1 − α) = (1 − 0.8⁵) / 0.2 = (1 − 0.32768) / 0.2 ≈ 3.36.

So each expensive pass produces about 3.4 tokens instead of 1. The real speed-up is a bit lower, because the draft model's own passes cost something too.

alpha, k = 0.8, 4
print(sum(alpha**i for i in range(1, k + 1)) + 1, (1 - alpha**(k + 1)) / (1 - alpha))   # both ≈ 3.3616

build.answer:
Train two GPTs on Shakespeare: the big one (the shared gpt.py model) and a small draft (width 32, 1 layer). Greedy speculative decoding: the draft proposes k tokens one at a time; the big model then scores the context plus all k proposals in a single forward pass, giving its own greedy choice at every position; accept the proposals up to the first one where the big model disagrees, then append the big model's own token there. Repeat.

The key check: the output is exactly identical to the big model decoding greedily on its own, because every token that is kept is one the big model would have chosen. (The test stays inside the model's 64-character window: once the context has to be cropped, the two methods would show the big model slightly different windows, so a fair comparison needs a model with a long enough context, or a KV cache.) In the run below, about a quarter of the draft's proposals are accepted, giving about 2 tokens per big-model pass, but the total time is about the same as plain decoding (about 1.0 times). Two reasons: this draft model is weak (a 1-layer model agrees with the big one too rarely), and the big model is tiny, so it is barely more expensive than the draft, while Python overhead costs the same for both. Real systems, where the big model is billions of parameters and the draft is a well-matched smaller model, see 2 to 3 times speed-ups. The fair check is the one the code makes first: identical output.
build.code:
import time
import torch
from gpt import GPT, Config, train, encode, decode

@torch.no_grad()
def greedy(model, idx, n):
    for _ in range(n):
        logits, _ = model(idx[:, -model.c.block_size:])
        idx = torch.cat([idx, logits[:, -1].argmax(-1, keepdim=True)], dim=1)
    return idx

@torch.no_grad()
def speculative(big, draft, idx, n, k=4):
    target, passes, accepted, proposed = idx.shape[1] + n, 0, 0, 0
    while idx.shape[1] < target:
        k_now = min(k, target - idx.shape[1])                         # never draft past the end
        proposal = greedy(draft, idx, k_now)[:, idx.shape[1]:]
        logits, _ = big(torch.cat([idx, proposal], dim=1))             # one big pass checks them all
        passes += 1; proposed += k_now
        choices = logits[0, -k_now - 1:].argmax(-1)                    # big model's pick at each position
        n_ok = 0
        while n_ok < k_now and proposal[0, n_ok] == choices[n_ok]:
            n_ok += 1
        accepted += n_ok
        idx = torch.cat([idx, proposal[:, :n_ok], choices[n_ok].view(1, 1)], dim=1)
    return idx[:, :target], passes, accepted, proposed

torch.manual_seed(0)
big = train(GPT(), steps=1500, log_every=0).eval()
draft = train(GPT(Config(n_embd=32, n_layer=1, n_head=2)), steps=1500, log_every=0).eval()
plain_s = fast_s = 0.0
passes = accepted = proposed = tokens = 0
for prompt in ["ROMEO:\n", "JULIET:\n", "KING RICHARD III:\n", "First Citizen:\n", "MENENIUS:\n"]:
    ids = torch.tensor([encode(prompt)])
    n = 64 - ids.shape[1]                     # stay inside the 64-character window, so the big model's
    t = time.perf_counter(); plain = greedy(big, ids, n); plain_s += time.perf_counter() - t   # context is never cropped
    t = time.perf_counter(); fast, p, a, q = speculative(big, draft, ids, n); fast_s += time.perf_counter() - t
    assert torch.equal(plain, fast)                                    # identical output
    passes, accepted, proposed, tokens = passes + p, accepted + a, proposed + q, tokens + n
print(f"tokens per big-model pass: {tokens / passes:.2f}, draft acceptance {accepted / proposed:.0%}")
print(f"plain {plain_s:.2f} s, speculative {fast_s:.2f} s: {plain_s / fast_s:.2f}x")
print(decode(fast[0].tolist()))

break.answer:
A draft trained on very different text, here a list of first names instead of Shakespeare, rarely guesses what the big model would write next, so most proposals are rejected at the first token. In the run below, on real held-out text, a small draft trained on Shakespeare agrees with the big model's next character 37% of the time; the one trained on names agrees 3% of the time. Acceptance falls sharply and each big-model pass yields barely more than one token, while you still pay for the draft's k passes: the result is slower than plain decoding.

Where is the break-even? Each round costs one big pass plus k draft passes, c·k, where c is the draft's cost relative to the big model; it yields (1 − α^(k+1)) / (1 − α) tokens. Plain decoding gives 1 token per big pass. Speculative decoding only wins when tokens per round > 1 + c·k. With k = 4 and a draft costing 20% of the big model (c = 0.2), you need 1.8 tokens per round, which takes an acceptance rate of about 0.45 or more; with a draft costing 5% (c = 0.05), about 0.17 is enough. In practice: choose a draft trained on the same kind of data (often a smaller model of the same family), and lower k when acceptance is low.
break.code:
import urllib.request
import torch
from gpt import GPT, Config, train, encode, get_batch, val_data

def tokens_per_round(alpha, k):
    return (1 - alpha ** (k + 1)) / (1 - alpha) if alpha < 1 else k + 1
for c in [0.2, 0.05]:
    breakeven = next(a / 100 for a in range(1, 100) if tokens_per_round(a / 100, 4) > 1 + c * 4)
    print(f"draft cost {c:.0%} of the big model: speculative wins above acceptance {breakeven:.2f}")

@torch.no_grad()
def acceptance(big, draft, n=300):
    text = val_data[:n + 64].unsqueeze(0)                      # real held-out text
    hits = 0
    for i in range(64, 64 + n):
        ctx = text[:, i - 64:i]                                     # the 64 characters before position i
        hits += int(big(ctx)[0][0, -1].argmax() == draft(ctx)[0][0, -1].argmax())
    return hits / n

torch.manual_seed(0)
big = train(GPT(), steps=1500, log_every=0).eval()
names = torch.tensor(encode(urllib.request.urlopen("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/master/names.txt").read().decode()))
for name, source in [("Shakespeare draft", None), ("names draft", names)]:
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    draft = GPT(Config(n_embd=32, n_layer=1, n_head=2))
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(draft.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(1500):
        loss = draft(*get_batch("train", source=source))[1]
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    print(f"{name}: agrees with the big model's next token {acceptance(big, draft.eval()):.0%} of the time")

explain.answer:
A junior writer drafts the next few words, and a senior editor checks them in one read. Wherever the editor agrees, the words stay; at the first word the editor would have written differently, the editor writes their own word, and the junior starts drafting again from there. The final text is exactly what the senior would have written alone, but the senior only had to read in quick passes instead of writing every word slowly.

In speculative decoding, a small, fast model drafts several tokens, and the big model checks them all in a single forward pass (checking several tokens at once costs about the same as generating one, because a pass processes many positions in parallel). The better the junior knows the senior's style, the more words survive each check, and the bigger the speed-up.

ready.q: What does each term of the ELBO do? What happens if you drop one?
ready.a: The reconstruction term, E[log p(x | z)], makes the decoder rebuild the input from its code. The KL term, KL(q(z | x) ‖ p(z)), keeps the codes close to the prior, so random codes from the prior decode to sensible samples. Drop the KL and you get a plain autoencoder: good reconstructions, but random samples are nonsense. Drop the reconstruction and the codes carry no information: everything decodes to the same average output.

ready.q: Why do VAE samples tend to be blurry?
ready.a: Each image maps to a fuzzy region of codes, not a single point, and the decoder is trained with a per-pixel loss over that region. When it is unsure about a detail, the output that minimises the loss is the average of the plausible images, which looks blurred. A small latent space adds to it.

ready.q: What does a diffusion model learn to predict during training, and why is generation slow?
ready.a: Given a noisy image x_t and the step t, it learns to predict the noise that was added (equivalently, the clean image), by minimising the squared error to the true noise. Generation is slow because it runs the process in reverse, step by step, from pure noise: one full network pass per step, traditionally hundreds to a thousand steps.

ready.q: What is the credit-assignment problem in reinforcement learning?
ready.a: Rewards often arrive long after the actions that caused them, as in winning a chess game after 40 moves. The problem is working out which earlier actions deserve the credit or the blame. Returns with discounting, value functions learned by temporal-difference updates, and advantages are the tools that spread credit back to the right actions.

ready.q: Why does PPO clip the probability ratio?
ready.a: The advantages were estimated with the old policy, so they are only trustworthy while the new policy stays close to it. Clipping the ratio π_new / π_old to [1 − ε, 1 + ε] removes the incentive to move further than that in one update: a simple trust region. It stops one batch from wrecking a good policy, and makes it safe to reuse each batch for several epochs.

ready.q: How is reinforcement learning used in RLHF for language models?
ready.a: People compare pairs of model answers. A reward model is trained to predict those preferences. The language model is then the policy: it is optimised, usually with PPO, to produce answers the reward model scores highly, with a KL penalty keeping it close to the original model so it doesn't exploit the reward model. DPO reaches a similar result straight from the comparisons, without the separate RL step.

topics.name: Autoencoders and VAEs (the ELBO)
topics.definition: An autoencoder compresses data into a small code and rebuilds it; a variational autoencoder (VAE) makes the code a probability distribution pulled towards a simple bell curve, so you can sample new codes and decode them into new data.
topics.problem: A plain autoencoder learns good compression, but its codes are scattered with gaps, so a random code decodes into nonsense and it can't generate anything new. VAEs fix that by shaping the code space, giving a principled generative model with a smooth latent space. The same encoder–decoder idea is inside modern image generators, which run diffusion in a VAE's compact latent space.
howItWorks: Encoder: a network maps the input x to the mean μ and spread σ of a distribution over codes z.
Sample a code with the reparameterisation trick: z = μ + σ·ε with ε ~ N(0, I). The randomness is in ε, so gradients can flow through μ and σ.
Decoder: a network maps z back to a reconstruction of x.
The loss is the negative ELBO: a reconstruction term (rebuild x well) plus a KL term that pulls each q(z | x) towards the prior N(0, I).
The KL term packs codes into one smooth, gap-free cloud; the reconstruction term keeps them informative.
To generate: sample z from N(0, I) and decode it.
β-VAE weights the KL term by β: bigger β gives a tidier, more disentangled space but blurrier reconstructions.
keyPoints: Autoencoder: compress and rebuild; VAE: also a generative model.
ELBO = reconstruction − KL(q(z | x) ‖ p(z)); training maximises it.
The reparameterisation trick makes sampling differentiable.
KL too weak → gaps; too strong → codes ignore the input ("posterior collapse").
VAE samples tend to be blurry; diffusion and other models give sharper images.
Latent spaces support interpolation: walk between two codes and decode.
mistakes: Sampling z directly without the reparameterisation trick, so gradients can't flow.
Letting the KL term dominate early, so the decoder learns to ignore z.
Expecting crisp, photo-quality samples from a basic VAE.

followUps.q: Why can't a plain autoencoder generate new data well?
followUps.a: Its codes are scattered with gaps; random codes fall where it has never been trained and decode into nonsense.

followUps.q: What does the KL term in the ELBO do?
followUps.a: It pulls each input's code distribution towards a standard normal, packing the codes into a smooth, gap-free space you can sample from.

followUps.q: What is the reparameterisation trick?
followUps.a: Writing z = μ + σ·ε with ε random noise, so the sample depends smoothly on μ and σ and gradients can flow through them.

followUps.q: How do you generate a new sample from a trained VAE?
followUps.a: Draw z from N(0, I) and run it through the decoder.

note.idea: An autoencoder squeezes data into a small code and rebuilds it. A variational autoencoder (VAE) makes that code a probability distribution, so you can sample new codes and decode them into new data. It trains by maximising the ELBO: rebuild the input well, but keep the codes close to a simple bell curve.
note.analogy: Describing a face to a sketch artist in 10 numbers. The encoder writes the description and the decoder draws. A VAE also forces the descriptions to be tidy, so a random description still gives a sensible face.
note.breaks: A person's description is exact. A VAE's code is fuzzy on purpose (it adds noise), which is one reason VAE images are often blurry.
note.example: ELBO = reconstruction term − KL(q(z | x) ‖ N(0, I)). The reparameterisation trick writes z = μ + σ·ε with ε ~ N(0, 1), so gradients can flow through the sampling step.

mu, log_var = encoder(x)
eps = torch.randn_like(mu)
z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * log_var) * eps           # reparameterisation trick
x_hat = decoder(z)
recon = F.mse_loss(x_hat, x, reduction="sum")
kl = -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + log_var - mu**2 - log_var.exp())
loss = recon + kl                                 # minimising this maximises the ELBO

derive.answer:
The ELBO. A latent-variable model says p(x) = ∫ p(x | z) p(z) dz, which we can't compute. Bring in the encoder's distribution q(z | x) by multiplying and dividing by it:

log p(x) = log ∫ q(z | x) · [p(x | z) p(z) / q(z | x)] dz = log E_q[ p(x | z) p(z) / q(z | x) ].

Jensen's inequality: log is concave, so log E[Y] ≥ E[log Y]. Therefore

log p(x) ≥ E_q[ log p(x | z) + log p(z) − log q(z | x) ]
= E_q[ log p(x | z) ] − KL( q(z | x) ‖ p(z) ).

That lower bound is the ELBO. The first term rewards reconstructing x from z; the second keeps the encoder's distribution close to the prior. The gap between log p(x) and the ELBO is exactly KL(q(z | x) ‖ p(z | x)), so a better encoder makes the bound tighter.

The KL in closed form, for q = N(μ, σ²) and p = N(0, 1) in one dimension:
KL = E_q[log q − log p] = E_q[ −½ log(2πσ²) − (z − μ)²/(2σ²) + ½ log(2π) + z²/2 ].
Use E_q[(z − μ)²] = σ² and E_q[z²] = σ² + μ²:
KL = −½ log σ² − ½ + ½(σ² + μ²) = ½ (σ² + μ² − 1 − log σ²).
It is 0 exactly when μ = 0 and σ = 1, and for a d-dimensional diagonal Gaussian you add it up over the dimensions.

build.answer:
Encoder: 784 → 400 → two outputs of size 2, the mean μ and the log-variance log σ² (learning the log keeps σ positive). Sample z = μ + σ·ε with ε ~ N(0, 1), the reparameterisation trick, so gradients flow through the sampling. Decoder: 2 → 400 → 784 with a sigmoid. Loss: binary cross-entropy between input and reconstruction (summed over pixels) plus the closed-form KL.

After 5 epochs, the 2-D latent space coloured by digit shows the classes as overlapping regions arranged around the origin: similar-looking digits (4 and 9, 3 and 5) sit next to each other, with smooth transitions in between. Decoding a grid of points from −2 to 2 in each direction gives a map of digits morphing into one another, recognisable but blurry, which is the classic VAE picture.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from torchvision import datasets

mnist = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True)
X, labels = mnist.data.reshape(-1, 784).float() / 255, mnist.targets

class VAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, z=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc, self.mu, self.logvar = nn.Linear(784, 400), nn.Linear(400, z), nn.Linear(400, z)
        self.dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(z, 400), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(400, 784), nn.Sigmoid())
    def forward(self, x):
        h = F.relu(self.enc(x))
        mu, logvar = self.mu(h), self.logvar(h)
        z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)          # reparameterisation
        return self.dec(z), mu, logvar

def losses(model, x):
    recon, mu, logvar = model(x)
    rec = F.binary_cross_entropy(recon, x, reduction="sum") / len(x)
    kl = 0.5 * torch.sum(logvar.exp() + mu**2 - 1 - logvar) / len(x)
    return rec, kl

def train_vae(kl_weight=1.0, epochs=5, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = VAE()
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for idx in torch.randperm(len(X)).split(128):
            rec, kl = losses(model, X[idx])
            opt.zero_grad(); (rec + kl_weight * kl).backward(); opt.step()
    return model

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = train_vae()
    with torch.no_grad():
        rec, kl = losses(model, X[:10_000])
        mu = model(X[:10_000])[1]
        print(f"reconstruction {rec:.1f}, KL {kl:.2f} (per image)")
        grid = torch.tensor([[x, y] for y in np.linspace(2, -2, 15) for x in np.linspace(-2, 2, 15)], dtype=torch.float32)
        images = model.dec(grid).reshape(15, 15, 28, 28).permute(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(15 * 28, 15 * 28)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6))
    axes[0].scatter(mu[:, 0], mu[:, 1], c=labels[:10_000], cmap="tab10", s=2); axes[0].set_title("latent space by digit")
    axes[1].imshow(images, cmap="gray"); axes[1].axis("off"); axes[1].set_title("decoded grid")
    plt.show()

break.answer:
No KL term: the model becomes a plain autoencoder with noise. Reconstructions get a little sharper (the reconstruction loss is only slightly lower here, 150.0 against 150.6, because a 2-number code is the real bottleneck), but the encoder is free to put each digit wherever it likes, spread far from the origin with gaps in between, and it shrinks σ so the noise barely matters. Sampling z from N(0, 1) and decoding then lands in empty or meaningless regions, so random samples are mostly not digits: the model is good at copying, useless at generating. In the run below the latent codes spread out to a standard deviation of about 4, where the prior expects 1, and the KL rises from about 5.6 to 34.

KL multiplied by 10: now staying close to N(0, 1) matters ten times more than reconstructing well. The encoder squeezes all digits towards the origin and keeps the noise large, so less information about each image gets through. Reconstructions become very blurry, an "average digit" look, and distinct digits merge; in the extreme, the latent space is ignored completely (posterior collapse). In the run below the reconstruction loss is clearly worse (about 168 against 151) and the KL is pushed down to about 2.

The ELBO's two terms are a trade-off between faithful reconstructions and a tidy, sample-able latent space; β-VAEs tune that weight on purpose.

explain.answer:
You describe a face to a sketch artist using just a few numbers. The encoder writes the description (the latent code) and the decoder is the artist who draws from it. A plain autoencoder lets the descriptions be anything, so a random description gives nonsense. A VAE also forces the descriptions to be tidy: every face's code must look like it came from the same simple, rounded cloud of possible codes (the KL term), so any random code from that cloud still gives a sensible face. That is what makes it a generator.

Why the images are blurry: the description is fuzzy on purpose, because each image maps to a small cloud of codes, not one exact point. The decoder has to draw a picture that works for all codes in that cloud, and when it is unsure about a detail, say exactly where an edge is, the safest drawing under its loss is the average of the possibilities, which looks blurred. Sharp but wrong would cost more than blurry but close.

topics.name: Diffusion models
topics.definition: A diffusion model generates data by learning to remove noise: it is trained to predict the noise added to real data, then generates by starting from pure noise and denoising step by step.
topics.problem: Generating high-quality images, audio and video is hard: GANs are unstable to train and VAEs are blurry. Diffusion models train with a simple, stable loss and produce state-of-the-art images (Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, Imagen) and video. Their main cost is slow generation, which much current research tries to cut.
howItWorks: Forward process: take a real sample x₀ and add Gaussian noise. In one jump to step t: x_t = √ᾱ_t · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε, where ᾱ_t falls from 1 (clean) to almost 0 (pure noise).
Training: pick a random t, add noise ε, and train a network to predict ε from x_t and t. The loss is plain squared error.
The network is usually a U-Net or a transformer, told the noise level t through an embedding.
Generation: start from pure noise x_T and repeatedly use the predicted noise to take a small step towards cleaner data.
Classic DDPM uses hundreds to a thousand steps; samplers like DDIM, and distillation, cut that to a handful.
Conditioning: feed in a text embedding (for example from CLIP or a language model) so the denoiser follows a prompt; classifier-free guidance strengthens that effect.
Latent diffusion runs the whole process in a VAE's compressed latent space, which is much cheaper.
keyPoints: Training = predict the added noise; loss = mean squared error.
Forward noising has a closed form for any step t.
Generation = many small denoising steps from pure noise.
Slow sampling is the main drawback; better samplers reduce the steps.
Text-to-image = diffusion conditioned on a text embedding, usually in latent space.
mistakes: Thinking the model removes all the noise in one step.
Using far fewer sampling steps with a sampler not designed for it, and getting noisy images.
Forgetting to tell the network the noise level t.

followUps.q: What is a diffusion model trained to predict?
followUps.a: The noise ε that was added to a clean sample, given the noisy sample and the noise level.

followUps.q: Why is diffusion generation slow?
followUps.a: It applies the denoising network many times in sequence, once per step.

followUps.q: What does latent diffusion change?
followUps.a: It runs diffusion on a compressed latent code from a VAE instead of on full-size pixels, which is much cheaper.

followUps.q: How does a text prompt control a diffusion model?
followUps.a: The denoiser is conditioned on an embedding of the text at every step, often strengthened with classifier-free guidance.

note.idea: A diffusion model learns to remove noise. In training, you take a real image, add a random amount of noise, and teach a network to predict that noise. To generate, you start from pure noise and remove it a little at a time, over many steps.
note.analogy: A sculptor who starts with a rough block and removes a little stone at each step until a statue appears.
note.breaks: A sculptor sees the whole plan. The model only ever learns one small clean-up step, and the full picture comes from repeating it many times. That is also why generation is slow.
note.example: In DDPM, the noisy image is x_t = √ᾱ_t · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε. The training loss is just the squared error between the true noise ε and the predicted noise.

practice.explain: Explain diffusion with the sculptor picture, and why generation is slow.
practice.derive: Show that adding Gaussian noise step by step is the same as adding it in one jump: derive x_t = √ᾱ_t · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε.

derive.answer:
One step of the forward process adds a little noise: x_t = √(1 − β_t) · x_{t−1} + √β_t · ε_t, with ε_t ~ N(0, I) fresh each step. Write α_t = 1 − β_t and ᾱ_t = α₁ · α₂ · … · α_t.

Claim: x_t = √ᾱ_t · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε, with a single ε ~ N(0, I).

Proof by induction. For t = 1 it is the definition. Suppose it holds for t − 1: x_{t−1} = √ᾱ_{t−1} · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_{t−1}) · ε′. Then
x_t = √α_t · x_{t−1} + √(1 − α_t) · ε_t
= √(α_t ᾱ_{t−1}) · x₀ + √α_t · √(1 − ᾱ_{t−1}) · ε′ + √(1 − α_t) · ε_t.

The first term is √ᾱ_t · x₀, since α_t ᾱ_{t−1} = ᾱ_t. The two noise terms are independent Gaussians with mean 0, so their sum is a Gaussian whose variance is the sum of their variances:
α_t (1 − ᾱ_{t−1}) + (1 − α_t) = α_t − α_t ᾱ_{t−1} + 1 − α_t = 1 − ᾱ_t.
So they can be replaced by one Gaussian √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε. Done.

Why it matters: in training you can jump straight to any step t in one line, without simulating the t steps before it, so every training example picks a random t.

build.answer:
Data: 2-D points on a spiral. Forward process: 1,000 steps with β rising linearly from 0.0001 to 0.02. The model is a small MLP that takes a noisy point x_t and the step t (as a sinusoidal embedding) and predicts the noise ε that was added. Training: pick a random point, a random t and fresh noise, build x_t in one jump with the closed form, and minimise the squared error between the true and predicted noise.

Generation (DDPM sampling): start from pure noise and run the 1,000 steps backwards, each removing the predicted noise a little and adding back a small amount of fresh noise. Snapshots at t = 1,000, 750, 500, 250 and 0 show a shapeless cloud slowly gathering into the spiral; most of the shape appears in the last few hundred steps. The final samples sit on the spiral: in the run below their average distance to the nearest real point is about 0.025, against 0.32 for pure noise and 0.009 for fresh real spiral points. (A smaller network trained for fewer steps got only to about 0.22: diffusion models need enough capacity and training to learn the noise at every level.) Training takes about 10 seconds on a laptop.

break.answer:
Only 10 steps with the same DDPM sampler (using every 100th step): the samples come out as a shapeless cloud, about as far from the spiral as pure noise (0.32, against 0.025 with all 1,000 steps). The DDPM update is derived for one small step: it assumes that between step t and t − 1 only a tiny amount of noise changes. Jumping 100 steps at a time with that same formula removes far too little noise at each jump and adds the wrong amount back, so the process never reaches clean data. Fast samplers such as DDIM and DPM-Solver use update rules designed for big jumps, which is how modern models get good images in 20 to 50 steps.

A noise schedule that rises too fast (β up to 0.2 instead of 0.02): the signal is almost gone by about step 300 (√ᾱ ≈ 0.01, against 0.63 with the normal schedule), so the last 700 of the 1,000 steps are pure noise with no trace of the data. The model spends most of its training on steps where there is nothing to learn, and gets few examples of the in-between levels where the shape forms. The samples are clearly worse: in the run below, about 0.08 from the spiral against 0.025. Schedule design (like the cosine schedule) is about spreading the destruction evenly over the steps.

explain.answer:
A sculptor starts with a rough block of stone and removes a little at each step until a statue appears. A diffusion model starts from pure noise and removes a little noise at each step until an image appears. To learn this, it practises the reverse: take real images, add more and more noise until nothing is left, and train a network to guess, at any noise level, what noise was added, so it can take it away.

Generation is slow because the sculpting really is step by step: each step needs a full pass through a large network, and the classic method uses hundreds to a thousand steps, where a GPT-style model makes one pass per token and a GAN one pass per image. Faster samplers and distilled models cut this to a handful of steps.

topics.name: Reinforcement learning basics: states, actions, rewards, values
topics.definition: In reinforcement learning, an agent takes actions in an environment, receives rewards, and learns a policy — what to do in each state — that maximises the total (discounted) reward over time.
topics.problem: Many problems have no labelled "right answers", only outcomes: win or lose a game, finish a task, keep a robot upright. Reinforcement learning learns from those outcomes by trial and error. It powers game-playing systems, robotics, recommendation tuning, and the RLHF and reasoning training of modern language models.
howItWorks: The agent sees a state s, takes an action a, and the environment returns a reward r and a new state s′. This repeats over an episode.
The return is the sum of future rewards, discounted by γ (between 0 and 1) per step, so sooner rewards count more.
The value V(s) is the expected return from state s when following the policy; Q(s, a) is the expected return after taking action a in s.
Values satisfy the Bellman equation: the value of a state = the reward for the best next step + γ × the value of where it leads.
Value iteration applies that rule repeatedly; value spreads back from rewards. In a grid with γ = 0.8, the square next to the goal is worth 1, the one before that 0.8, then 0.64.
Q-learning learns Q from experience without knowing the rules: Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α·(r + γ·max Q(s′, ·) − Q(s, a)).
Balance exploration (try new actions) and exploitation (use the best known one), for example with ε-greedy: random action with probability ε.
keyPoints: Agent, environment, state, action, reward, policy.
Return = discounted sum of future rewards; γ sets how far ahead the agent cares.
V(s) values states; Q(s, a) values actions in states.
Bellman equation: a value equals immediate reward plus discounted next value.
Credit assignment: working out which earlier actions earned a delayed reward.
Exploration versus exploitation is a constant trade-off.
mistakes: No exploration, so the agent locks onto the first thing that worked.
γ = 0, so the agent ignores everything but the immediate reward.
Reward functions that can be "hacked": the agent maximises the number, not what you meant.

followUps.q: What does the discount factor γ do?
followUps.a: It makes future rewards count less than immediate ones; γ near 1 plans far ahead, γ = 0 only cares about the next reward.

followUps.q: What is the difference between V(s) and Q(s, a)?
followUps.a: V(s) is the expected return from a state; Q(s, a) is the expected return after taking a specific action in that state.

followUps.q: What is the credit-assignment problem?
followUps.a: When reward arrives late, the agent must work out which of its many earlier actions deserve the credit or blame.

followUps.q: Why does an agent need exploration?
followUps.a: Without trying unfamiliar actions it can never discover that they are better than what it already knows.

derive.answer:
The value of a state is the expected discounted sum of rewards from there: V(s) = r + γ · V(next state).

Goal is the end, so V(Goal) = 0 (no more rewards).

B: one step to Goal, and reaching Goal gives reward 1.
V(B) = 1 + 0.9 × V(Goal) = 1 + 0 = 1.

A: one step to B with reward 0.
V(A) = 0 + 0.9 × V(B) = 0.9 × 1 = 0.9.

Each extra step away from the reward multiplies its value by γ = 0.9: a state three steps away would be worth 0.81. That is how a discount makes the agent prefer shorter paths to the same reward.

build.answer:
FrozenLake (4 × 4, not slippery): start in the top-left, reach the goal in the bottom-right, fall into a hole and the episode ends with nothing. The only reward is 1 at the goal.

Tabular Q-learning keeps a 16 × 4 table, one value per (state, action). Each step: choose an action ε-greedily (random with probability ε, which decays from 1 to 0.05, otherwise the best known), take it, and update Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α · (r + γ · max Q(s′, ·) − Q(s, a)).

The reward per episode starts near 0 (random wandering rarely reaches the goal), climbs once the goal is found and its value spreads back through the table, and settles near 1, apart from the occasional exploratory step into a hole. The printed arrows show a shortest safe path from the start to the goal.

import numpy as np
import gymnasium as gym
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def q_learning(episodes=2000, gamma=0.95, alpha=0.8, eps_start=1.0, eps_end=0.05, seed=0):
    env = gym.make("FrozenLake-v1", is_slippery=False)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Q, rewards = np.zeros((16, 4)), []
    for ep in range(episodes):
        state, _ = env.reset(seed=seed + ep)
        eps = max(eps_end, eps_start * (1 - ep / (0.6 * episodes)))
        done, total = False, 0.0
        while not done:
            explore = rng.random() < eps
            action = rng.integers(4) if explore else int(np.argmax(Q[state]))
            nxt, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(action)
            target = r + (0 if terminated else gamma * Q[nxt].max())
            Q[state, action] += alpha * (target - Q[state, action])
            state, total, done = nxt, total + r, terminated or truncated
        rewards.append(total)
    return Q, rewards

if __name__ == "__main__":
    Q, rewards = q_learning()
    smooth = np.convolve(rewards, np.ones(50) / 50, mode="valid")
    print(f"success rate, first 200 episodes {np.mean(rewards[:200]):.0%}, last 200 {np.mean(rewards[-200:]):.0%}")
    lake = gym.make("FrozenLake-v1", is_slippery=False).unwrapped.desc.astype(str)
    arrows = np.array(["←", "↓", "→", "↑"])[Q.argmax(1)].reshape(4, 4)
    for row in range(4):
        print(" ".join(lake[row, c] if lake[row, c] in "HG" else arrows[row, c] for c in range(4)))
    plt.plot(smooth); plt.xlabel("episode"); plt.ylabel("reward (moving average of 50)"); plt.show()

break.answer:
No exploration from the start (ε = 0): with every Q value at 0, the "best" action is a tie, np.argmax always picks the first one (left), and moving left from the start corner just bumps into the edge. The agent repeats the same useless action until the episode times out, never reaches the goal, never sees a reward, so nothing in the table ever changes. Success rate: 0%, forever. Without exploration, an agent can only learn about things it already does; it needs to try new actions to discover where the rewards are. (Optimistic initial values, starting Q high, are another way to force exploration.)

γ = 0: the agent only cares about the reward of the very next step. Only the one state next to the goal learns that "right" or "down" is good, because only there does an action earn an immediate reward; every other state's values stay 0, since the future doesn't count at all. From the start, the agent has no reason to head anywhere, so its greedy policy fails. The discount is what lets a reward that is many steps away flow back to the states that lead to it.
