explain.answer:
Training a dog with treats. Nobody shows the dog the right move; it tries things, and some lead to treats. The hard part is credit assignment: the dog sits, rolls over, barks, and then gets a treat. Which of those earned it? If the treat comes several actions later, the dog has to work out which earlier choices led there.

Reinforcement learning has the same problem, often much worse: in chess, the reward (win or lose) comes after dozens of moves, and the agent must figure out which moves deserved the credit. Value functions solve it by passing value backwards: a state is worth the reward it leads to, discounted by how far away it is, so good early moves gradually learn that they were good.

topics.name: Policy gradients and PPO
topics.definition: Policy-gradient methods train a policy network directly by making actions that led to better-than-expected returns more likely; PPO adds a clipped objective that keeps each update small and safe.
topics.problem: Value-based methods like Q-learning struggle with huge or continuous action spaces — and a language model's "action" is a choice among tens of thousands of tokens. Policy gradients optimise the policy itself and handle such spaces naturally. PPO made them stable enough to use widely, including in classic RLHF for chat models.
howItWorks: The policy π(a | s) is a network that outputs a probability for each action (for an LLM, each next token).
Collect episodes by acting with the current policy and record the returns.
Advantage A = how much better the outcome was than expected (return minus a baseline, such as a learned value estimate).
REINFORCE update: increase log π(a | s) in proportion to A. Better-than-expected actions become more likely; worse ones less likely.
Subtracting a baseline doesn't change the expected direction but greatly reduces noise.
PPO measures the ratio r = π_new(a | s) / π_old(a | s) and maximises min(r·A, clip(r, 1 − ε, 1 + ε)·A), with ε around 0.2.
Clipping removes any reward for moving the policy beyond the trust range in one update, so the same batch can be reused for several small, stable steps.
keyPoints: Optimise the policy directly: ∇J ≈ E[∇log π(a | s) · A].
Advantages and baselines reduce variance.
PPO's clip keeps the new policy close to the old one.
On-policy: data must come from (nearly) the current policy.
In RLHF, the "environment" is a reward model, and a KL penalty keeps the model near its starting point.
mistakes: No baseline, so learning is extremely noisy.
Huge steps without clipping, so the policy collapses.
Reusing very old data with an on-policy method.

followUps.q: What does a policy-gradient update do to an action with positive advantage?
followUps.a: It raises that action's probability in that state, in proportion to how much better than expected it was.

followUps.q: Why subtract a baseline from the return?
followUps.a: It reduces the variance (noise) of the gradient estimate without changing its expected direction.

followUps.q: What does PPO's clipping prevent?
followUps.a: Updates that change an action's probability by more than about ±ε in one step, which could otherwise destabilise the policy.

followUps.q: How is PPO used in RLHF?
followUps.a: The language model is the policy, a reward model scores its answers, and PPO updates the model towards higher reward with a KL penalty to stay close to the original.

was each action? (advantage)"] ADV --> UPD["make good actions more likely,
bad ones less likely"] UPD --> CLIP["PPO: clip the change
so each update stays small"] --> POL

note.idea: Policy-gradient methods train the policy network directly: make actions that led to high reward more likely, and actions that led to low reward less likely. PPO adds a safety limit so each update cannot change the policy too much. PPO is the algorithm used in classic RLHF for language models.
note.analogy: A basketball player adjusting their shot: after a good shot, do a bit more of that; after a miss, a bit less. PPO is a coach who says 'small changes only'.
note.breaks: A player can feel which part of the shot went wrong. Policy gradients only see the total reward, so the signal is very noisy and needs many tries. Baselines and advantages reduce that noise.

derive.answer:
We want the gradient of the expected reward J(θ) = E_{a ~ π_θ}[R(a)] with respect to the policy's parameters θ. For a discrete policy (one step, for clarity):

J(θ) = Σ_a π_θ(a) · R(a)
∇J(θ) = Σ_a ∇π_θ(a) · R(a)      (R doesn't depend on θ)

The trick: ∇ log π = ∇π / π, so ∇π = π · ∇ log π. Substitute:

∇J(θ) = Σ_a π_θ(a) · ∇ log π_θ(a) · R(a) = E_{a ~ π_θ}[ R(a) · ∇ log π_θ(a) ].

Why it matters: the right-hand side is an expectation under the policy itself, so we can estimate it just by sampling actions, running them, and averaging R · ∇ log π. We never need to differentiate the reward or the environment. For whole episodes the same argument gives ∇J = E[ Σ_t ∇ log π(a_t | s_t) · G_t ], with G_t the return from step t.

Subtracting a baseline b(s) keeps it unbiased, because E[∇ log π] = Σ_a ∇π(a) = ∇ Σ_a π(a) = ∇1 = 0, but it can reduce the variance a lot.

build.answer:
CartPole: keep a pole balanced on a cart; +1 reward per step, up to 500.

REINFORCE with a baseline: run a whole episode with the policy network, compute each step's return G_t, subtract a learned value estimate V(s_t) (the baseline), and step along Σ ∇ log π(a_t | s_t) · (G_t − V(s_t)), while training V to predict G_t.

PPO: collect a batch of steps, estimate advantages with GAE, then do several epochs of minibatch updates on the clipped objective min(ratio · A, clip(ratio, 0.8, 1.2) · A), where ratio = π_new(a | s) / π_old(a | s), plus a value loss.

In the run below, PPO learns much better: over its last 20 episodes it averages about 480 of a possible 500, against about 220 for REINFORCE with a baseline after 500 episodes (both reach 500 at their best). REINFORCE updates once per episode from a single, noisy sample of what the policy does; PPO collects a batch of steps, uses a lower-variance advantage estimate (GAE), and reuses each batch for several careful updates. That efficiency and stability is why PPO became the standard, including for RLHF.
build.code:
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import gymnasium as gym

def mlp(out):
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, out))

def reinforce(episodes=500, baseline=True, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed); env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
    policy, value = mlp(2), mlp(1)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([*policy.parameters(), *value.parameters()], lr=3e-3)
    returns_per_episode = []
    for ep in range(episodes):
        obs, _ = env.reset(seed=seed + ep)
        log_probs, states, rewards, done = [], [], [], False
        while not done:
            s = torch.tensor(obs, dtype=torch.float32)
            dist = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=policy(s))
            a = dist.sample()
            obs, r, term, trunc, _ = env.step(a.item())
            log_probs.append(dist.log_prob(a)); states.append(s); rewards.append(r); done = term or trunc
        G, returns = 0.0, []
        for r in reversed(rewards):
            G = r + 0.99 * G; returns.insert(0, G)
        returns = torch.tensor(returns)
        v = value(torch.stack(states)).squeeze(1)
        advantage = returns - v.detach() if baseline else returns
        loss = -(torch.stack(log_probs) * advantage).mean() + ((v - returns) ** 2).mean() * baseline
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        returns_per_episode.append(sum(rewards))
    return returns_per_episode

def ppo(iterations=40, steps=2048, epochs=10, clip=0.2, lr=3e-4, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed); env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
    policy, value = mlp(2), mlp(1)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([*policy.parameters(), *value.parameters()], lr=lr)
    obs, _ = env.reset(seed=seed); episode_return, finished = 0.0, []
    for it in range(iterations):
        S, A, LP, R, D, V = [], [], [], [], [], []
        for _ in range(steps):
            s = torch.tensor(obs, dtype=torch.float32)
            with torch.no_grad():
                dist = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=policy(s)); a = dist.sample()
                S.append(s); A.append(a); LP.append(dist.log_prob(a)); V.append(value(s).squeeze())
            obs, r, term, trunc, _ = env.step(a.item())
            R.append(r); D.append(term); episode_return += r
            if term or trunc:
                finished.append(episode_return); episode_return = 0.0; obs, _ = env.reset()
        with torch.no_grad():
            next_v = value(torch.tensor(obs, dtype=torch.float32)).squeeze()
        adv, gae = torch.zeros(steps), 0.0
        for t in reversed(range(steps)):                              # GAE
            nv = next_v if t == steps - 1 else V[t + 1]
            delta = R[t] + 0.99 * nv * (1 - D[t]) - V[t]
            gae = delta + 0.99 * 0.95 * (1 - D[t]) * gae
            adv[t] = gae
        S, A, LP, V = torch.stack(S), torch.stack(A), torch.stack(LP), torch.stack(V)
        returns = adv + V
        adv = (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8)
        for _ in range(epochs):
            for idx in torch.randperm(steps).split(256):
                dist = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=policy(S[idx]))
                ratio = torch.exp(dist.log_prob(A[idx]) - LP[idx])
                if clip is None:
                    policy_loss = -(ratio * adv[idx]).mean()                 # no clipping
                else:
                    policy_loss = -torch.min(ratio * adv[idx], ratio.clamp(1 - clip, 1 + clip) * adv[idx]).mean()
                value_loss = ((value(S[idx]).squeeze(1) - returns[idx]) ** 2).mean()
                opt.zero_grad(); (policy_loss + 0.5 * value_loss).backward(); opt.step()
    return finished

if __name__ == "__main__":
    r = reinforce()
    p = ppo()
    for name, rets in [("REINFORCE + baseline", r), ("PPO", p)]:
        last = rets[-20:]
        print(f"{name}: {len(rets)} episodes, mean return of the last 20 {np.mean(last):.0f} (std {np.std(last):.0f}), "
              f"best {max(rets):.0f}")

break.answer:
Without the baseline, REINFORCE pushes up the probability of every action in proportion to the whole return that followed, and on CartPole every return is positive. So every action gets reinforced, the good ones only slightly more than the bad ones, and the signal is buried in noise. The learning curve becomes far noisier: in the run below, the return over the last 50 episodes swings with a standard deviation of about 160 without the baseline, against about 24 with it. (Its average happened to be higher in this one run, 246 against 195, which is what high variance looks like: run a few seeds and the no-baseline results scatter widely.) With a baseline, actions are judged against what was expected (the advantage), so below-average actions are pushed down and above-average ones up.

PPO without clipping, with large updates (a bigger learning rate and many epochs on each batch): the new policy can move far from the policy that collected the data. The advantages were measured for the old policy, so once the ratio π_new / π_old is far from 1 they no longer describe what the new policy does, and a few huge steps can wreck a policy that was working: the return collapses and may not recover. Clipping the ratio to [0.8, 1.2] removes the incentive to move further than that in one update, a cheap, safe trust region. In the run below, with the same aggressive settings (10 times the learning rate, 30 epochs per batch), the clipped version still reaches and holds the maximum return of 500, while the unclipped one ends lower, averaging about 400.

explain.answer:
A basketball player practising free throws. After a shot that goes in, they do a bit more of whatever they just did; after a miss, a bit less. That is a policy gradient: increase the probability of actions that led to good results, decrease it for bad ones, in proportion to how much better or worse than expected the result was (the baseline is "what I usually score").

PPO is a coach who says: small changes only. If one great shot made the player completely rebuild their technique, the next day could be a disaster: one shot is noisy evidence. So the coach limits how far the technique may change from one practice session to the next. That is the clipping: each update can move the policy only a little away from the one that collected the experience, which makes learning steady instead of erratic.

The non-linear function applied to each neuron's output (such as ReLU), and the values it produces.
A popular optimiser: momentum plus a separate step size for each weight. RMSProp is the part that adapts the step size.
How much better an action was than expected. A baseline is the 'expected' part you subtract.
Something that takes actions towards a goal: in AI apps, an LLM calling tools in a loop; in reinforcement learning, the learner acting in an environment.
A defined way for programs to ask another program or service to do something.
Finding almost-the-closest vectors very fast, instead of checking every one. HNSW and IVF are common methods; FAISS is a library for it.
How much maths is done for each byte moved from memory.
A grid of numbers of one type, like a spreadsheet that can have any number of directions.
Each token looks at every other token and takes a weighted mix of their information, focusing on the most relevant ones.
A network that squeezes data into a small code and then rebuilds it.
Automatic differentiation: the library records your calculations and works out all the gradients for you.
A direction. In a NumPy array, axis 0 runs down the rows and axis 1 across the columns; in a chart, the x-axis and y-axis are the two edges.
Working out the gradient of the loss for every weight, by applying the chain rule backwards from the output.
Training many models on random resamples of the data and averaging them, to reduce variance.
The smallest set of vectors whose combinations reach every point in the space.
A small group of examples processed together in one step.
Normalising each feature across the batch (batch norm) or each example across its features (layer norm), so training stays stable.
A formula for updating a belief with new evidence: P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B).
Bernoulli: one yes/no outcome with probability p. Uniform: every value in a range equally likely. Cauchy: a heavy-tailed distribution with no average.
An encoder model trained to fill in masked words; good for understanding text.
Two meanings: the extra number added in a model (ŷ = wx + b), and the error from a model that is too simple (as in bias–variance).
Error comes from models that are too simple (bias) or too sensitive to their training data (variance); reducing one often raises the other.
An array of True/False values used to pick out items, like A[A > 0.5].
Estimating uncertainty by resampling your own data, with replacement, many times.
Byte-pair encoding: building a token vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of symbols.
A separate line of work in Git, for trying ideas without breaking the main version.
NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes, by stretching any direction of size 1.
Checking every single possibility. Exact but slow at scale.
Fast storage that keeps answers or results you've already computed, so you don't pay for them again.
A rule stopping each token from looking at the tokens after it, so a GPT can only use the past.
An LSTM's long-term memory line, updated by adding rather than multiplying.
Averages of many samples follow a bell curve, whatever the original distribution looks like.
Subtracting the average from every value, so the data sits around zero.
A model writing out its reasoning steps before the final answer.
For a function inside a function, multiply their rates of change.
Splitting documents into small pieces before embedding them.
Predicting a category, such as spam or not spam.
A group of points that are close together.
Convolutional neural network: a network built from convolution layers, used for images.
One saved snapshot of your project in Git.
A map of every calculation, connecting inputs to the final result, used to compute gradients backwards.
Limited by how fast the chip can do maths (compute-bound), or by how fast data can reach it (memory-bound).
The probability of A when you already know B happened, written P(A | B).
A range that probably contains the true value, such as 85% ± 5%.
A table counting true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.
A rule a solution must obey, like 'x + y = 1'.
The maximum amount of text (in tokens) a model can read at once.
Bowl-shaped: any local minimum is also the global minimum.
Sliding a small filter over an image and computing a dot product at each position, to detect a pattern anywhere.
How alike two vectors' directions are: 1 means the same direction, 0 means unrelated (at 90°).
How two variables change together. A covariance matrix holds this for every pair of variables.
The computer's main processor: fast for one thing at a time, with only a few cores.
Working out which earlier actions deserve the credit for a reward that came much later.
The average surprise when you use your model's probabilities to predict data from the true distribution. The standard loss for classification.
Splitting data into k parts, training on k − 1 and testing on the last, and rotating so every part is tested once.
In very many dimensions, every point is almost equally far from every other, so 'nearest' stops meaning much.
Making extra training examples by changing existing ones, like flipping or cropping images.
Information from the test data sneaking into training, so the score looks better than it really is.
Every GPU holds the whole model and gets different data (data parallel); tensor parallel splits each layer across GPUs; pipeline parallel puts different layers on different GPUs.
A collection of examples used to train or test a model.
Ready-made tools for training on many GPUs: DDP (data parallel), and FSDP and ZeRO (which also split the weights and optimiser states).
Removing repeated examples from a dataset.
The line (or surface) where a classifier switches from one answer to the other.
A model that asks yes/no questions about features, one after another, to reach an answer.
Machine learning with neural networks that have many layers.
Putting a trained model into a live product so real users can use it.
The rate of change: how much a function's output moves when its input moves a tiny bit.
How much a matrix scales area (or volume), with a negative sign when it flips space.
A model that learns to remove noise, then generates by starting from pure noise and cleaning it step by step.
One direction a space or an array extends in. A 2D space has 2 dimensions.
γ, a number below 1 that makes future rewards count a little less than immediate ones.
Training a small 'student' model to copy a big 'teacher' model's full output probabilities.
Which values something can take, and how likely each one is.
A tool that packages an app with everything it needs into a container that runs the same anywhere.
Multiply matching entries of two vectors and add them up. It measures how much they point the same way.
Test error rising and then falling again as models grow past the point where they fit the training data perfectly.
The live data, or the world, changing over time, so a model trained on old data gets worse.
Turning off random neurons during training, so the network can't rely on any single one.
The type of number stored in an array, such as int32 or float64.
Looking at an optimisation problem from the side of its constraints; SVMs are usually solved this way.
Stopping training when the validation loss starts rising.
An unusual input at the limits — zero, one item, a huge number — where bugs often hide.
A direction a matrix only stretches, never turns. The eigenvalue is how much it stretches it.
Evidence lower bound: the quantity a VAE maximises — rebuild the input well, while keeping codes close to a simple bell curve.
Fitting a mixture model by alternating two steps: E-step (how much each point belongs to each part) and M-step (refit each part).
A learned vector for each item (word, user, product). Similar items get similar vectors.
Encoder models (like BERT) read text in both directions to understand it; decoder models (like GPT) read left to right to generate it.
Several models combined, usually by averaging or voting.
A measure of uncertainty — the average surprise — in a probability distribution.
The world the agent acts in, which responds to its actions with rewards and new states.
One complete run of an agent in its environment, from start to finish.
One full pass through all the training data.
Reading the failures one by one and grouping them into types, to see what to fix first.
model.eval() switches layers such as dropout and batch norm to their testing behaviour.
Measuring how good a model or AI app is, on a fixed set of test cases.
The long-run average of a random variable; also called the expected value or mean.
The share of the data's spread kept by each principal component.
Trying actions you're unsure about, to discover better ones, instead of always picking the best-known one.
One score balancing precision and recall (their harmonic mean).
The number of inputs coming into a layer.
A Python library for building web APIs quickly.
An input the model uses, such as house size or number of rooms.
Continuing to train a pretrained model on your own data, to adapt it.
A fast way to compute attention in small tiles kept in fast on-chip memory.
How computers store decimals. Tiny rounding errors are normal, so compare decimals with a tolerance.
Floating-point operations: a count of the additions and multiplications done. FLOPs per second measures speed.
Running inputs through the network to get the prediction and the loss.
Ways to store numbers: fp32 uses 32 bits; fp16 and bf16 use 16 bits (half the memory, faster). bf16 keeps fp32's range with less precision.
Not updated during training.
A model replying with the name of a tool to run and its arguments, instead of plain text.
Combining several steps into one GPU kernel, so data is read from memory only once.
In an LSTM, a number between 0 and 1 that controls how much information passes (forget, input and output gates).
The bell-shaped 'normal' distribution.
Solving equations step by step by subtracting rows, as you learn at school.
A model that says the data comes from several bell curves mixed together.
A measure of how mixed a group is: 0 means all the same class, higher means more mixed.
A tool that saves snapshots of your code, so you can go back in time. GitHub stores Git projects online.
A fixed list of test questions with known good answers, re-run after every change.
Generative pre-trained transformer: a decoder-only language model that predicts the next token.
Graphics processing unit: a chip with thousands of simple cores that do the same calculation on lots of data at once.
All the partial derivatives together in one vector. It points uphill: the direction in which a function increases fastest.
Adding up gradients over several small batches before one update, to act like a bigger batch in less memory.
Training models one after another, each fixing the mistakes left by the ones before.
Saving memory by not storing some activations and recomputing them during the backward pass.
Capping gradients at a maximum size so one huge update can't wreck training.
Repeatedly stepping against the gradient (downhill) to make a loss smaller.
Multiplying the loss before backpropagation in fp16, so tiny gradients don't round down to zero.
Checks around an AI system's inputs and outputs that block unsafe or wrong behaviour.
An RNN's memory: a vector updated at each step of the sequence.
The SVM loss: zero for points safely on the right side, growing as points get closer to or cross the boundary.
A check of whether a result could easily be just luck. A p-value is the chance of seeing a result at least this big by luck alone.
Not determined by the others. For vectors: none can be built from the rest. For random events: one doesn't change the chances of the other.
Picking parts of an array: A[1, 2] picks one value, and a slice like A[:, 0] picks a whole column.
How the weights are set before training starts. He and Xavier initialisation keep signals from shrinking or growing.
Fine-tuning on examples of good question-and-answer pairs, so a model follows instructions. Also called SFT.
The matrix that undoes another matrix.
The table of partial derivatives for a function with several outputs: one row per output, one column per input.
A maths rule: the log of an average is at least the average of the logs. Used to derive the ELBO.
A common text format for data, like {"name": "Ana", "age": 30}.
Grouping points into k clusters by repeatedly assigning each point to its nearest centre and moving each centre to the middle of its points.
Classifying a new point by a vote of the k closest training points.
A small program that runs on the GPU as many parallel copies.
The extra surprise from using the wrong distribution: cross-entropy minus entropy.
Stored keys and values of earlier tokens, so generation doesn't recompute them at every step.
L1 adds the sum of absolute weights to the loss and pushes some to exactly zero. L2 adds the sum of squared weights and shrinks them all.
The right answer for an example, which the model learns to predict.
A way to minimise something under a constraint, by adding the constraint to the objective as an extra term.
A model that assigns probabilities to text, usually by predicting the next token.
How long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests are handled per second.
The space of the small codes a model learns, where similar inputs end up near each other.
A group of neurons working side by side. Data flows through the layers one after another.
The size of each step in gradient descent.
Changing the learning rate during training, for example warming up then slowly decaying.
Choosing the weights that make the sum of squared errors as small as possible.
How probable the data you saw is, for one particular choice of model settings.
Adding vectors after multiplying each by a number, like 3·a + 2·b.
Predicting a number with a weighted sum of the features: ŷ = Xw + b.
Large language model: a very big language model, like the ones behind chat assistants.
Using an LLM to grade another model's answers against criteria you write.
Sending many requests at once to see how a system behaves under pressure.
A valley lower than everything around it, but not necessarily the lowest point overall (the global minimum).
An axis where each step multiplies the value (1, 10, 100, 1,000), so big and small values are both visible.
Classification with a weighted sum squashed into a probability by the sigmoid.
The raw scores a model outputs before softmax turns them into probabilities.
Low-rank adaptation: fine-tuning by training two small matrices added to frozen weights, instead of all the weights.
A number measuring how wrong the model's predictions are. Training tries to make it small.
A chart of the loss over training steps — the best tool for spotting training problems.
Long short-term memory: an RNN with a memory line and gates that decide what to forget, write and output. A GRU is a simpler version.
Learning a pattern from examples, instead of writing the rules by hand.
Maximum a posteriori: maximum likelihood plus a prior belief.
The gap between the decision boundary and the nearest points of each class.
Hiding some words so the model has to guess them, as BERT is trained to do.
A Python library for drawing charts.
A grid of numbers that transforms vectors: it can stretch, rotate or squash space.
Combining two matrices so the result does one transformation and then the other.
Choosing the model settings that make the observed data most probable.
Model Context Protocol: an open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data through 'MCP servers'.
The average of the squared differences between predictions and true values.
How fast data can move between memory and the processor.
Combining two Git branches. A merge conflict happens when both changed the same line.
Andrej Karpathy's tiny autograd engine, built step by step in a video lesson.
Doing most of the maths in 16-bit numbers while keeping sensitive parts in 32-bit.
A layer with many 'expert' sub-networks, where a router sends each token to only a few of them.
Short for machine learning.
Multi-layer perceptron: the simplest neural network — layers of neurons, each connected to all neurons in the next layer.
MNIST: 70,000 small images of handwritten digits. CIFAR-10: 60,000 small colour photos in 10 classes. Classic practice datasets.
The function that turns inputs into predictions. What it does is set by numbers (weights) learned from data.
Keeping a running average of recent gradients, so steps keep moving in a consistent direction.
Several smaller attentions running side by side, each free to track a different kind of relationship.
A classifier using Bayes' rule, with the 'naive' shortcut that features are independent given the class.
'Not a number': what you get from invalid maths, such as 0 / 0 or a number that overflowed.
A model made of layers of simple units (neurons) whose weights are learned together.
The basic unit of a neural network: a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation.
Training a language model to guess the next token, given everything before it.
PyTorch's building block for models: nn.Module holds layers and weights; DataLoader serves batches.
Random variation in data that isn't part of the real pattern.
How much noise is added at each step of a diffusion model.
Not a straight line. Non-linear activations let a network learn curves instead of only straight boundaries.
The length of a vector.
A formula that gives linear regression's best weights directly, without gradient descent.
Rescaling numbers to a standard range, or to mean 0 and spread 1 (standardisation).
Estimating a derivative by nudging the input a tiny bit and measuring the change, instead of using the formula.
A Python library for fast maths on arrays of numbers.
Being able to see exactly what your system did for any request: a trace of every step, with time and cost.
Turning a category into a vector with a 1 in its own position and 0 everywhere else.
The method that updates the weights from the gradients, such as SGD or Adam.
The extra numbers an optimiser keeps for every weight — Adam keeps two.
At 90 degrees to each other; their dot product is 0.
Learning the training data too closely, noise included, so the model does badly on new data.
A number becoming too big for the computer to store, turning into infinity.
Adding a border of zeros around an image so a filter can also be applied at the edges. Stride is how far the filter moves each step.
The rate of change when you move one input and keep all the others still.
A small square piece of an image (for example 16 × 16 pixels), treated like a token.
Principal component analysis: finding the directions in which data varies most, and keeping only those.
A series of steps that runs automatically, one after another, such as collect → clean → train → deploy.
A rule for what to do. In reinforcement learning, the policy is the agent's strategy: which action to take in each situation.
Training a policy directly: make actions that led to high reward more likely. REINFORCE is the basic method.
An expression with powers of x, like 3x² + 2x + 1. A higher degree means a wigglier curve.
Shrinking an image by keeping one value (like the maximum) from each small patch.
Information added to each token's vector saying where it sits in the sequence.
Finding the biggest eigenvector by multiplying a vector by the matrix again and again.
Proximal policy optimisation: a policy-gradient method that limits how much each update can change the policy.
Applying layer norm before each sub-layer (pre-norm) rather than after the addition (post-norm). Pre-norm trains more stably.
Precision: of the items you flagged, how many were right. Recall: of the real ones, how many you found.
The model's answer for one input.
Training on pairs of answers where people marked the better one.
The first, huge training stage: next-token prediction on a vast amount of text.
What you believed before seeing the data. The posterior is your updated belief afterwards.
A tool that measures how long each operation in your program takes.
The 'shadow' of one vector on another.
The text you send to an LLM: instructions, context and the question.
Hidden instructions inside text (a web page, an email, a document) that try to make an AI do something it shouldn't.
Removing weights, neurons or attention heads that matter little, to make a model smaller.
A Python tool that finds and runs your tests.
The most popular deep learning library: tensors, autograd and ready-made layers.
Learning how good each action is in each state, from the rewards you experience.
Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits (8 or 4 instead of 16), to save memory and time.
In attention, each token makes a query (what it's looking for), a key (what it contains) and a value (what it shares).
Retrieval-augmented generation: find relevant documents first, then give them to an LLM so it answers from them.
Many decision trees, each trained on random data and random features, averaged together.
A number decided by chance, like the result of rolling a die.
How many independent directions a matrix keeps. A low rank means it squashes space.
A second, more careful scoring step that reorders the top results.
How much of the original image one output can 'see'. It grows with depth.
Predicting a number, such as a price.
Adding a penalty to the loss that discourages over-complicated models.
Learning by trial and error: an agent takes actions and learns from the rewards it gets.
ReLU(x) = max(0, x): the most common activation. Tanh and sigmoid squash values; GELU is a smooth ReLU.
Writing a random sample as z = μ + σ·ε, so gradients can flow through the sampling step.
A project folder tracked by Git (short for repository).
What's left over: the true value minus the prediction.
A shortcut that adds a block's input to its output (x + F(x)), so gradients flow straight back.
In EM, how much a point belongs to each component, as a probability.
Finding the most relevant pieces of information for a question.
The score an agent gets after an action — how good that action was.
Ridge regression is linear regression with L2 regularisation; lasso uses L1.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: tuning a model with a reward model trained on people's preferences. DPO learns from preference pairs directly.
Recurrent neural network: reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory (hidden state) forward.
How well a model ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds: 1 is perfect, 0.5 is guessing.
Rotary position embeddings: encoding position by rotating each token's vectors.
Something that decides where each input goes: in mixture of experts, which experts process a token; in an AI app, which model answers a request.
A flat point that slopes up in some directions and down in others, like a horse's saddle.
A set of items picked from a bigger group. In language models, 'sampling' also means picking the next token at random according to its probability.
Loss falls smoothly and predictably as model size, data and compute grow.
Searching by meaning instead of exact words, by comparing embeddings.
Of the people who really have something, the share a test catches. A false positive is a wrong 'yes'.
Running a model behind an API so applications can use it.
Stochastic gradient descent: gradient descent using small random batches of data.
How many numbers an array has along each direction. (3, 4) means 3 rows and 4 columns.
A function that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1.
Adding a small count (like 1) to every word, so a word never seen in training doesn't get a probability of zero.
Turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1; bigger scores get much bigger shares.
Every point you can reach by scaling and adding a set of vectors.
Mostly zeros.
A small draft model guesses several tokens ahead and the big model checks them all in one pass, to speed up generation.
The typical distance of values from their mean: the square root of the variance.
How much an estimate (like an average or an accuracy) would wobble if you repeated the experiment.
A situation, or stored information. In reinforcement learning, the situation the agent is in; for an optimiser, the extra numbers it keeps for each weight.
Making a model reply in a fixed format, usually JSON matching a schema, so code can read it.
A classifier that finds the boundary with the widest gap (margin) to the nearest points of each class.
Singular value decomposition: splitting any matrix into three simple steps — rotate, stretch, rotate.
Training examples generated by a model rather than collected from real users.
A dial on randomness when generating: low temperature picks safe, likely tokens; high temperature takes more risks.
PyTorch's array: like a NumPy array, but it can run on a GPU and track gradients.
A small program that checks your code gives an answer you already know is right.
The cut-off score above which you call something positive.
A piece of text a language model reads or writes — often part of a word.
The tool that splits text into tokens, and joins tokens back into text.
Something used to do a job. In AI apps, a tool is a function the model can ask your code to run, like a calculator or a document search.
Top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens before sampling; top-p keeps the smallest set whose probabilities add up to p. Greedy always picks the top one.
A PyTorch feature that speeds up a model by compiling and fusing its operations.
Adjusting a model's weights using data, so its loss gets smaller.
The repeated cycle: get a batch, predict, compute the loss, backpropagate, update the weights.
Train on the training set, tune your choices on the validation set, and measure the final score once on the test set.
Features computed differently in training and in production, so the live model sees different inputs.
A rule that moves every point in space, such as a stretch or a rotation.
The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and MLP layers.
A Python-like language for writing fast GPU kernels.
A model too simple to capture the real pattern, so it does badly even on the training data.
Variational autoencoder: an autoencoder whose code is a probability distribution, so you can sample new data.
How good it is to be in a state (or take an action in it), counting all future rewards.
Gradients shrinking towards zero as they flow back through many layers (vanishing), or growing out of control (exploding).
How spread out values are around their average.
A measure of a model family's capacity: the most points it can separate in every possible way.
A list of numbers, often pictured as an arrow with a direction and a length.
A database for embeddings that can quickly find the most similar ones.
Doing an operation on a whole array at once instead of looping in Python — much faster.
Vision transformer: a transformer that reads an image as a sequence of small patches. CLIP links images and text in one shared space.
The full list of tokens a model knows.
A number inside a model that training adjusts. Together, the weights decide what the model does. Also called parameters.
Shrinking every weight a little at each step — the same idea as L2 regularisation.
A pattern that's 'yes' when exactly one of two things is true. No single straight line can separate it.
Doing a task with no task-specific training, just from a description or comparison.
